en: Commentary on the Mahāyānasaṃgraha, Volume One.
Explained by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Chen Dynasty.
The extreme blindness and darkness of the cognitive obscurations— consisting of the separate adherence to the ultimate and the conventional—
is destroyed by the light of non-conceptual wisdom, which accords with both reality and the full measure of things;
thereby, one achieves peerless enlightenment and extinguishes mental afflictions without remainder.
The eternally abiding one, perfected in virtue and wisdom, constantly follows with great compassion;
according to the capacities and natures of sentient beings, he proclaims the true path of ultimate liberation throughout the worlds of the ten directions,
able to do so with effortless, non-conceptual mind.
By means of non-conceptual wisdom, one does not abide in saṃsāra;
because of constantly giving rise to great compassion, one does not enter nirvāṇa.
By integrating wisdom and skillful means, one attains the ultimate benefit for both oneself and others.
With body, speech, and mind, I prostrate to the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
This is the unsurpassed True Dharma, spoken by the Tathāgata through his own self-awakening;
if one can practice it correctly, one will reach the wondrous path of ambrosia.
If one slanders this Dharma, one will fall into a bottomless pit of injustice;
therefore, through wisdom and faith, I prostrate to the True Dharma.
To the Saṅgha who abide in the Path and abide in the Fruits, who universally surpass all multitudes, [I prostrate].
The path of wisdom is a bath of purity, the unsurpassed field of merit in the world.
A single fragment of goodness cast into it becomes as vast as the earth and space;
it brings about worldly happiness as well as the coolness of nirvana.
With a single mind, I pay homage to the Buddha and the assembly of his noble disciples.
Those who are clever yet possessed by false pride have regressed from the study and realization of the Āgamas;
their practice and teaching follow their own attachments, and the true principle is not what they have realized.
Serving Maitreya Bodhisattva, Relying on the Sunlight Samādhi,
He illuminates the true characteristics of phenomena, Both the immovable and the supramundane.
For our sake, he proclaims The true principles of the True Dharma.
Like the light of the autumn moon and the sun, its literary expressions pervade the world.
Profound, vast, and manifold, with its phrases and meanings based upon the *Nītārtha* sūtras,
it is able to cause wise people to humble their minds and give rise to reverence.
The subtle and profound Dharma is difficult to penetrate; wisdom is unattached and unimpeded.
Regarding the eight worldly dharmas, such as gain and so forth, the mind is always free from defilement and attachment.
This meaning of "unimpeded renown" is constantly recited by those who are penetrating and agile.
Devas and humans all recognize him, and prostrate at the feet of the Great Teacher.
His eloquent discourse is ever inexhaustible, raining down the nectar of words and meanings;
according to their respective capacities, they listen to the Honored One, like birds seeking rain.

Having consulted the *Nirnayasamgraha*, I shall explain the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*; may these words benefit those who fear the vast ocean of textual detail. This chapter consists of three sections: first, the peerless sacred teaching;
second, the sequence of the ten meanings;
and third, the various names.
Chapter One: On the Peerless Sacred Teaching. The treatise states:
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* is itself the Abhidharma teaching and the Mahāyāna Sūtras.
The commentary asks:
On what basis is this statement made,
and by what cause does it arise?
Based on the profound and vast true nature of all phenomena, which is the basis of all that is to be known,
who else— apart from the power of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas— would possess the capacity to explain this meaning?
How is this treatise composed?

It is explained by means of these characteristics: if one were to omit the name "Abhidharma," one would not know that this treatise is the teaching of the Noble One; it is for this purpose [that the name is stated].
Furthermore, this serves to clarify the title of the sutra, such as, for example, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
What is the purpose of composing this treatise now?
It is because sentient beings are ignorant, doubtful, and deluded, and one wishes to enable them to attain understanding.

Furthermore, the reason this treatise mentions the name of the *Abhidharma-mahāyāna-sūtra* is to reveal the distinct category of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-gates and to clarify the specific title of this treatise itself.
The term "Mahāyāna" is used to distinguish it from the Abhidharma of the Hīnayāna.
Why, then, does it not merely state the name "Abhidharma," but also mention the name "Sūtra"?
There exists Abhidharma that is not part of the Noble Teaching (*ārya-śāsana*).
Furthermore, the reason for designating this treatise as "Abhidharma" is to reveal that it belongs to the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Moreover, for what purpose is the Piṭaka established?
In order to extinguish their own delusions, these are considered afflictions within the Mahāyāna for bodhisattvas. Why is this?
Because for all bodhisattvas, conceptual discrimination constitutes affliction.
The Abhidharma has the profound and vast nature of reality (dharmatā) as its characteristic.
How many kinds of this Bodhisattva-piṭaka are there?

There are also three kinds, namely: Sūtra, Abhidharma, and Vinaya. These three, through the distinction between the higher and lower vehicles, constitute two types: the Śrāvaka-piṭaka and the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Why are these three and two called "piṭakas"?
Because they are able to contain [the teachings].
What phenomena do they contain?
Regarding the meaning of "all that should be known," how is it established as threefold?
There are nine kinds of causes.
The separate establishment of the Sūtras is for the purpose of counteracting the doubts of others.
If a person gives rise to doubt regarding this meaning, the Sūtras are established so that they may attain definitive knowledge.
The Vinaya was established separately as an antidote to the two extremes of enjoyment:
the Vinaya was established by the Buddha prohibiting the enjoyment of what is faulty as an antidote to the extreme of indulgence in pleasure;
the Vinaya was established by the Buddha approving the enjoyment of what is faultless as an antidote to the extreme of asceticism.
The Abhidharma was established separately to counteract the biased attachment to one's own views, as it is able to reveal the unerring characteristics of real phenomena (*dharmas*).

Furthermore, the Sūtra was established separately to teach the three types of training (*śikṣā*); and the Vinaya was established separately to accomplish the training based on ethical discipline (*śīla*) and the training based on the mind (*citta*).

Why is this? If a person maintains the precepts, their mind will be free from remorse; through the absence of remorse and so forth, they are able to attain meditative concentration (samādhi) in successive stages.
To establish the training in wisdom (prajñā-śikṣā), the Abhidharma is set forth separately.
Why is this? Because it is capable of discerning the non-erroneous meaning.
Furthermore, the correct teaching of both the doctrine and its meaning is derived from the sūtras.
The realization of the meaning of the Dharma is through the Vinaya. Why is this?
Because if a person practices while afflicted by delusions, the Vinaya enables them to penetrate both these two phenomena and their meaning.
The definitive and superior knowledge of the meaning of the Dharma arises from the Abhidharma.
For these nine reasons, the Three Piṭakas are established.
What is their general function?
To be liberated from birth and death is its universal application.
How is liberation attained?
It is through the capacity for perfuming, awakening, tranquility, and penetration that liberation is attained.

Through hearing and reflecting upon the Tripiṭaka, one is able to cultivate; through cultivation, one awakens; through awakening, one becomes tranquil; through tranquility, one attains penetration; and through penetration, one achieves liberation.
If one were to briefly explain the three piṭakas, each possesses four meanings.
If a bodhisattva can discern these meanings, they will possess all-knowledge; if a śrāvaka can understand the meaning of a single phrase or a single verse, they will reach the exhaustion of outflows.
What are the four meanings for each of the individual piṭakas?
Regarding the four meanings of the Sūtra (Sūtrapiṭaka): first, the basis; second, the characteristics; third, the phenomena; and fourth, the meaning.
Because it can clearly manifest these four meanings, it is called the Sūtra.
"Reliance" refers to the place, the person, and the application; because the Buddha preached the sūtras based on these three, it is called "reliance.
"Characteristics" refers to the characteristics of the two truths, the ultimate and the conventional; therefore, it is called "characteristics."

"Dharma" refers to the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), sense bases (āyatanas), dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), truths (satyas), nutriments (āhāras), meditative concentrations (dhyānas), immeasurables (apramāṇas), formless attainments (ārūpyas), liberations (vimokṣas), spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatanas), spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatanas), factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣikadharma), the unhindered analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvids), the absence of contention (araṇā), and so forth; therefore, it is called "Dharma."
"Meaning" (*artha*) refers to that which is to be accomplished; thus it is called "meaning.
The accomplishment of the path and the cessation of delusions are these things.
Regarding the four meanings of *abhidharma*: first, opposition (*abhimukha*); second, enumeration (*abhikṣṇa*); third, subduing (*abhibhava*); and fourth, understanding (*abhijñā*).
"Facing toward" (pratimukha) means that this dharma faces toward the nirvana of non-abiding.
Why is this? Because it can manifest the gateway to the path of the truths, it is called "facing toward."

"Enumeration" (saṃkhyā) refers to any single phenomenon among all phenomena; it is called enumeration because one repeatedly manifests this single phenomenon by means of its name, its specific characteristic, or its general characteristic.

"Subduing" (*vibhāṣā*) means that this dharma can subdue all other doctrines; because it possesses the dual capacities of establishing and refuting through skillful means such as correct exposition and reliance [on scripture], it is called "subduing.
"Explanation" (*vyākhyā*) means that the meaning of the Abhidharma-sūtras is easily understood through it; therefore, it is called "explanation."
The Vinaya has four meanings: first, by way of offenses; second, by way of origins; third, by way of purification; and fourth, by way of renunciation.
"Offenses" refers to the five categories and seven groups of transgressions.
Regarding the conditions for origination, there are either four or eight.
The four are: first, ignorance; second, negligence; third, the intense proliferation of afflictions; and fourth, arrogance.

The eighth [category] consists of eight types: first, that which arises from the mind but not from body or speech; second, that which arises from the body but not from mind or speech; third, that which arises from the speech but not from mind or body; fourth, that which arises from the mind and body but not from speech; fifth, that which arises from the body and speech but not from the mind; sixth, that which arises from the mind and speech but not from the body; seventh, that which arises from the body, speech, and mind; and eighth, that which does not arise from the body, speech, or mind.

Regarding restoration to purity (*pratyāpatti*): it occurs through a virtuous mind and not by means of punitive measures; "virtuous mind" refers to the counteractive practice as originally undertaken.
Regarding deliverance (*niḥsaraṇa*), there are seven matters: first, each individual confesses their transgression to sever the continuity [of the offense];
second, they accept and undergo disciplinary training (*śikṣāpada*).
Third, that which was previously prohibited and subsequently permitted: having already established a precept, it is later permitted due to a specific intention;
fourth, further relinquishment: if the great assembly gathers and agrees to restore the rule as it was, the person who previously committed the offense is then restored to purity;
fifth, transformation of the basis: when a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī undergoes a change of gender from male to female or vice versa, provided it is not a non-common offense.

Sixth is observation according to reality (*yathābhūta-parīkṣā*): one observes all phenomena through four types of *udāna*, and furthermore, one constantly observes one's own faults as a remedy for the characteristics of those phenomena;

seventh is attainment through the nature of things (*dharmatā-pratilambha*): if one perceives the Four Truths, one does not intentionally commit minor or secondary offenses again, by virtue of what is attained through the nature of things.
Furthermore, one should know that the Vinaya has four meanings:
first, the person, upon whom the Buddha, the World-Honored One, established the precepts;
second, the establishment of the rules, wherein the Great Teacher, having already pointed out the faults, assembled the community to establish the training rules (śikṣāpada).
Third is the analysis, which provides a further detailed explanation after the rules have been briefly established.
Fourth is the determination, which clarifies within these established rules what constitutes an offense and what does not.
Now the main text shall be explained.
The treatise says:
"Before the Buddha, the World-Honored One."
The commentary states:
This is to manifest respect and the absence of divergent speech.
The treatise says:
Regarding the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Skillfully Entering the Words and Meanings of the Mahāyāna, the commentary states:

Having already attained meritorious qualities such as dhāraṇīs, he is able to skillfully uphold both the words and their meanings through these qualities, and can further explain them in accordance with reality; therefore, he is named "Skillfully Entering."
Why is it that only "bodhisattva-mahāsattva" is mentioned without stating their names?
It is because one wishes to show that the entire assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas universally possesses this capacity.
Why are two names [of specific individuals] mentioned?
To demonstrate that [the Mahāyāna] is fully endowed with both practices,
the treatise states:
"To demonstrate that the Mahāyāna possesses superior qualities, one relies upon the Mahāyāna teachings."
The commentary states:
Only within the Mahāyāna are there supreme qualities, which do not exist in other vehicles.
In order to clarify the unique qualities of the Mahāyāna, it is said that one wishes to manifest that the Mahāyāna possesses supreme qualities by relying on the Mahāyāna teachings.
The treatise says:
It is stated that the Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones, possess ten superior characteristics, and their teachings are peerless, surpassing all other doctrines.
The commentary asks:
What is intended to be clarified by these words?
It is to demonstrate that the Mahāyāna possesses superior qualities, exists as a reality, and is for the sake of benefiting others.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are as explained in the context of the Ten Epithets.
The treatise states:
"The ten superior characteristics."
The commentary states:
It is superior because of the differences among the ten aspects, such as the basis.
The ten meanings serve as the cause, and verbal expression serves as the result.
Because its meaning is preeminent, that which is taught is peerless.
The treatise says:
First, the preeminent characteristics of the basis of what is to be known.
The commentary states:
"That which should be known" refers to the dharmas of the pure and impure categories, which are the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
These three natures rely upon the causes of the three natures; this is the "supreme characteristic."
Because this basis possesses superior characteristics, the Tathāgata’s discourse is likewise superior.
That is to say, the ālayavijñāna is the basis, and it is that which possesses superior characteristics.
For example, from the seed-stone up to the superior characteristics of the fruit of wisdom, it is just so.
The Treatise says:
Second, the superior characteristics that should be known.
The Commentary explains:

Regarding "the superior characteristics of what is to be known" (*jñeyaviśeṣalakṣaṇa*): this means that one should know the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), or that what is to be known is itself the characteristic.
The Commentary says:
Third, the superior characteristics of entry into what is to be known.
The commentary states:
It should be understood that "that which is to be known" refers to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
"Entry" (*praveśa*) refers to both the entry that accomplishes and the entry that is accomplished; this is precisely consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
The Treatise says:
Fourth, the superior characteristics of entering into cause and effect.
The Commentary explains:

The causes for entering *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only) are the six mundane *pāramitās*, such as giving (*dāna*), which exist during the stage of aspiration and practice (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*).

Entering the result refers to the six *pāramitās* subsequent to the entry into *vijñaptimātra*, which, during the stage of penetration (*prativedha-bhūmi*), are transformed into results and are termed supramundane.
The Treatise says:
Fifth, the superior characteristics of the distinctions in the cultivation of entering into cause and effect.
The Commentary explains:
Entering into cause and effect refers to the six pāramitās, both mundane and supramundane.

"Cultivation" refers to the repeated practice of the four virtues; this cultivation differs from stage to stage, and is thus termed "differentiation," which consists of the ten stages beginning with the Joyous (pramuditā).
The Treatise says:
Sixth, regarding the distinction of cultivation, it concerns the superior characteristics of the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*).
The Commentary explains:

This refers to the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*) within the various stages of cultivation; based upon this ethical discipline, the bodhisattva practices contemplation, which consists of all the bodhisattva precepts throughout the ten stages, wherein he no longer forms the intention to commit any unwholesome dharmas.
The Treatise says:
Seventh, herein is the preeminent characteristic of training in the mind.
The Commentary explains:
The meaning of "learning" (*śikṣā*) is as explained previously.
"Mind" (*citta*) is itself concentration (*samādhi*); concentration takes the single mind as its essence and is cultivated based upon that single mind.
Thus, all concentrations of Bodhisattvas are termed the "learning based on the mind."
The Treatise says:
Eighth, herein lies the preeminent characteristic of training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*).
The Commentary explains:
It is called "relying on wisdom" because it is able to attain the fruit;
by taking wisdom as its support, one gives rise to the mind of practice. This reliance on wisdom is none other than non-conceptual gnosis (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
The treatise states:
9. The Superior Characteristics of the Quiescence of the Fruits of Training.
The commentary states:
There are three distinctions regarding cessation: first, the most excellent; second, the categories; and third, the individual counterparts.
The cessation of the obstacles to liberation, meditative concentration, and wisdom is precisely the nirvana without abiding.
The Commentary states:
Tenth, the superior characteristics of the distinctions of wisdom.
The commentary states:
This refers to the wisdom that has already abandoned all obscurations.
This wisdom is non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which is designated as the specific counteractive path (*pratipakṣa-mārga*).
That is to say, the wisdom of the Buddha-Tathāgata is already free from all latent obscurations (*anuśaya-āvaraṇa*); this wisdom is a differentiation of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
The treatise states:
"By virtue of these ten superior characteristics, that which is taught by the Tathāgata surpasses other teachings."
Explaining the words and phrases of the sūtra in this manner reveals that the Mahāyāna is truly the word of the Buddha.
The commentary asks:
How does it reveal this?
By means of this brief explanation of the textual passages, it is shown that ten meanings do not exist within the Hīnayāna, but are taught only in the Mahāyāna.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, how does this brief explanation herein manifest the superiority of the Mahāyāna over other teachings?
This brief explanation clarifies these ten meanings, which exist only in the Mahāyāna and not in the Hīnayāna.
What are the ten? They are as follows:
the *ālayavijñāna* is designated as the characteristic of the basis for what is to be known (*jñeyāśraya-lakṣaṇa*).
The three natures—the dependent nature, the imagined nature, and the perfected nature—are designated as the "characteristics of that which is to be known.
The teaching of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) is designated as the "characteristics of the entry into that which is to be known."
The six pāramitās are said to be the characteristics of entering into cause and effect.
The commentary asks: Why is this so?
By means of the path of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), one enters the three natures at the stage of "aspiration and joy" (*adhimukti-caryā*).

Although the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) are mundane phenomena, they can induce supramundane phenomena and give rise to the path of consciousness-only; therefore, they are said to be the causes for entering the three natures.
When a bodhisattva has already entered the supramundane purity of the six pāramitās of the stages (bhūmis), this is precisely the entry into the fruit of the three natures (trisvabhāva).
The Treatise says:
The ten stages of the bodhisattva are called the differentiated characteristics of the cultivation of entering cause and fruit.
The commentary states:
The ten supramundane bodhisattva stages are called the differentiation of the cultivation that enters into cause and fruit.
The treatise says:
The precepts that a bodhisattva receives, upholds, and guards are called the characteristics of the training in higher ethics (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*) in its various aspects.
The *Śūraṅgama*, the *Gaganagañja*, and other such meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) are called the characteristics of the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*).
Non-conceptual wisdom is designated as the characteristic of the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*).
Non-abiding nirvāṇa is designated as the characteristic of the quiescence that is the fruit of the training.

The three bodies of a Buddha—the essence body (*svābhāvika-kāya*), the enjoyment body (*sambhogika-kāya*), and the emanation body (*nairmāṇika-kāya*)—these three are designated as the characteristics of the fruit of non-conceptual wisdom.
The commentary states:
Within the stages (*bhūmi*), there are three kinds of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), which are designated as the three kinds of reliance upon training (*śikṣā*).
The fruit of this training is cessation (*nirodha*), namely, the cessation of the three obstructions (*āvaraṇa*).

Non-conceptual wisdom is called the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*). Regarding this wisdom, if it is considered from the perspective of the Śrāvaka, it is termed "non-conceptual" because it is free from the conceptualization of the four inversions;
if it is considered from the perspective of the Bodhisattva, it is termed "non-conceptual" because it is free from conceptualization regarding all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).
The two types of non-conceptuality differ in their characteristics in this way.

The three bodies of the Buddha are the fruit of non-conceptual wisdom; if one were separated from the self-nature body (*svābhāvika-kāya*), the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) would not be established, just as, for example, the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*).

If separated from the Dharma-body, the Response-body would not be established; it is like visual consciousness, which cannot be established apart from its sense organ. One should know that these two are in correspondence by virtue of being the supported and the support.
If one is separated from the response body (nirmāṇakāya), bodhisattvas who have already entered the great stages (mahābhūmi) would lack the enjoyment of the Dharma-pleasure (dharmasvabhoga).

If there were no enjoyment of the Dharma-pleasure, the provisions for enlightenment (bodhisambhāra) would not be fulfilled, just as, for example, one might see a form [without its accompanying flavor].
If the response body (saṃbhogakāya) were absent, the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) would not be established.

If there were no transformation body, then the bodhisattvas in the stage of aspiration and joy, as well as the śrāvakas who are emaciated and coarse yet have first resolved to practice, would all be unable to achieve their goals.
Therefore, it is certain that there must be three bodies.
The Treatise says:
These ten kinds of bases exist only within the Mahāyāna and differ from the Hīnayāna; therefore, they are called "foremost.
The Commentary explains:
These ten dharmas are the causes of unsurpassed bodhi; they lead one another in succession up to unsurpassed bodhi.
The Treatise says:
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, taught these ten meanings solely for the sake of bodhisattvas.
The commentary states:
The Mahāyāna is taught exclusively by the Buddha, whereas the Hīnayāna is taught in common [with others].
The Mahāyāna is taught solely for the sake of bodhisattvas, not for the sake of those of the two vehicles.
For these three reasons, it is superior to the Hīnayāna.
The treatise states:
Therefore, based on the Mahāyāna, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten superior characteristics; what they teach is peerless and surpasses other teachings.

Furthermore, how do these ten superior characteristics, as explained in the Peerless [Sūtra], manifest the Mahāyāna, and how does the Tathāgata’s correct teaching therein exclude the Hīnayāna as definitively not being the Mahāyāna?
These ten meanings have never been seen within the Hīnayāna; even when explaining a single meaning, it is only found explained within the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, these ten meanings can lead forth to unsurpassed bodhi, achieving accordance and non-contradiction.
The commentary states:
Three points prove that these ten points can lead to unsurpassed enlightenment, because they are the causes of unsurpassed enlightenment.

As for "establishment": if one investigates and contemplates them according to the sacred teachings and correct reasoning, these ten points are established and cannot be refuted, just as when one has already seen the characteristics of the path shown by a guide.

Regarding "conformity": when a person’s contemplative practice is in the stage of cultivation, these ten meanings abide in conformity with the cultivation of insight, just as one abides in conformity with the path shown by a guide.
Regarding non-contradiction: within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), there are no obstructing causes, just as there are no obstacles such as bandits, thieves, tigers, or wolves on the path shown by a guide.
Furthermore, within each stage, *saṃsāra* and *nirvāṇa* do not mutually hinder one another; therefore, these ten meanings can lead to unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*).
The Treatise says:
"For the sake of all sentient beings, so that they may attain the knowledge of all modes.
The Commentary explains:
By means of these ten meanings, the three virtues are fully perfected—namely, incomparable object, incomparable practice, and incomparable fruit.

If a person hears, contemplates, and cultivates this, they will certainly attain unsurpassed enlightenment; therefore, it is said that it is for the sake of all sentient beings attaining the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
The treatise says,
and states in verse:
One should know the basis and its characteristics, As well as the differences in entering, cause, fruit, and cultivation.
The three trainings and their fruit, cessation, And wisdom are subsumed within the Unsurpassed Vehicle.
These ten meanings do not exist elsewhere; Seeing them as the cause of enlightenment, The Mahāyāna is the word of the Buddha, For it is superior by virtue of teaching these ten meanings.
Chapter Two: The Sequential Order of the Ten Meanings. The Treatise says:
Why are these ten meanings explained in this particular sequence?

A bodhisattva who is a beginner should first contemplate the causes and conditions of all phenomena as they truly are. By virtue of this contemplation, one should develop wisdom regarding the twelvefold dependent origination. Subsequently, one should discern the essential nature and characteristics of dependently originated phenomena; through such wisdom, one can abandon the two extremes of the faults of superimposition and denial.

In this way, through correct cultivation, one should thoroughly penetrate the true characteristics of the object of focus as they really are; subsequently, one should be liberated from all hindrances; and thereafter, the mind will have already penetrated the true reality of what is to be known.
These six *pāramitās* previously practiced should be further perfected, rendered pure so that they are no longer subject to regression.

Because the internal mind has become pure, one should subsequently cultivate the various *pāramitās* subsumed under "internal purity" according to the distinctions of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), throughout each of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
Next, the Bodhisattva’s three trainings should be brought to fulfillment; once fulfilled, their fruits—nirvāṇa and unsurpassed enlightenment—should subsequently be attained.
Such is the sequence for cultivating these ten topics.
Within this sequential exposition, all Mahāyāna teachings are brought to fulfillment.
The commentary states:

These ten topics possess a sequence in their objective spheres (*viṣaya*), a sequence in their correct practice (*pratipatti*), and a sequence in their results (*phala*); it is by observing these sequences that the sequence of the ten topics is established.
Furthermore, if a person has thoroughly discerned the causes of all phenomena, they will attain wisdom regarding the twelvefold dependent origination. Why is this?

Because effects arise from causes; they do not arise from an unequal cause such as Īśvara, nor do they arise without a cause. For this reason, the two types of knowledge—of cause and effect—are established.
Next, this dharma arises from causes; the bodhisattva should recognize its characteristics.
What are these characteristics?
The nature of discrimination (parikalpita-svabhāva) actually has no essence, yet to insist that it exists is called "superimposition" (samāropa).
That which truly exists as reality, yet is clung to as being non-existent, is called "diminution" (apavāda).
To augment what is non-existent or diminish what exists is termed the "two extremes"; the wise are able to remain free from these two extremes.

Next, that which is grasped is merely consciousness; by means of this wisdom, it is appropriately realized. Through this realization, there is no further obstruction, and one subsequently enters into conformity with *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).
The six pāramitās of the world are attained by relying on conventional truth; one should also study the supramundane six pāramitās, which are subsumed within the pure intention of ultimate truth.

Subsequently, they should be cultivated according to their distinctions throughout the ten stages (bhūmis), each for three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, unlike the manner in which śrāvakas cultivate and attain them.
Why is this? Because a śrāvaka plants the seeds of the counteragent during three lifetimes and brings the path of the counteragent to maturity.
Since the path of the counteragent has matured, they attain liberation from the three realms and realize the fruit of arhatship within the third lifetime.
Next, within this differentiated cultivation, the three trainings—morality and the others—should be brought to perfection.

Subsequently, the results of these three trainings—the extinction of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), as well as unsurpassed enlightenment and the three bodies (*trikāya*)—are to be realized; it is for this reason that this sequence is taught.
If one establishes the Mahāyāna, it does not go beyond these teachings.
Why is this? If one wishes to explain the meaning of dependent origination, one enters into the ālayavijñāna.
If one wishes to explain the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), one enters the subsumption under the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
If one wishes to explain attainment (*prāpti*), one enters into Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*).
If one wishes to explain cause and effect (*hetuphala*), one enters the stage of the contemplation of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātropalambha*).
If one wishes to explain the stages (*bhūmi*), one enters the section on cause and effect.
If one wishes to explain the three trainings (*śikṣā*), one enters the section on the ten stages.
If one wishes to explain cessation (*nirodha*), one enters the section on the three trainings.
If one wishes to explain unsurpassed enlightenment and the three bodies, they are subsumed within non-abiding nirvāṇa.
Since the enumeration of the Buddha-body and its causes and effects is thus, the sequence is taught accordingly.
There is another interpretation:
these ten meanings are able to lead to unsurpassed enlightenment; because they give rise to non-erroneous, non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), they are called "accomplished" (*siddha*).

Because they do not contradict the four principles (*yukti*) and the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), they are called "conformable" (*anuloma*); it is not that they were conformable first and later became contradictory.
As the verse says:
"One who can maintain love and compassion, And who accords with what is wholesome, Is neither black nor white;
such a view of self Brings both benefit and harm."
Therefore, it is called "non-contradictory.

Regarding the phrase "capable of generating all-knowledge and omniscience": it is because the wisdom that conforms to reality (*yathābhūta*) and conforms to the extent of phenomena (*yāvadbhāva*) arises without interruption regarding all dharmas.
Furthermore, there is another interpretation:
The subsequent section explains what preceded it.
Chapter Three: On the Various Names. The Treatise says:

It has been stated at the outset that one should know this is established by name as the *āśraya* (basis); in what place did the Blessed One speak of this consciousness, and by what name did he designate it as the *ālayavijñāna*?
As the Blessed One stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-mūlakārikā*:
"This realm is without beginning; It is the support for all phenomena.
If there are various paths, they exist; And there is the attainment of nirvāṇa."
The commentary states:
Now, I wish to cite the *Āgama* to establish the essence and the name of the *ālayavijñāna*.
By "Āgama" here is meant the Mahāyāna Abhidharma, wherein the Blessed One, the Buddha, spoke these verses.
This is precisely this *ālayavijñāna*-element (*dhātu*), which has understanding as its intrinsic nature.
This element possesses five meanings:

first, the meaning of "essential category" (*svabhāva-jāti*); no sentient beings transcend this essential category, and by virtue of this essential category, sentient beings are not distinct from one another.
Second is the meaning of cause: all dharmas of the noble ones, such as the four foundations of mindfulness, arise by taking this realm as their object.
Third is the meaning of birth: the dharma-body attained by all noble ones is accomplished through faith and delight in the dharma-gate of this realm.
The four meanings of reality are not subverted in the world, nor are they exhausted in the supramundane.

Regarding the five meanings of the treasury: if they accord with this dharma, because their intrinsic nature is virtuous, they constitute the "inner"; if they are external to this dharma, even if they are associated with it, they constitute the "shell."
Therefore, summarizing this realm,
the Buddha, the World-Honored One, said:
"O Bhikṣus!"

The initial limit of sentient beings cannot be discerned; obscured by ignorance and bound by craving, they flow on or take rebirth, sometimes in the hells, sometimes among animals, sometimes in the realm of hungry ghosts, sometimes in the realm of asuras, sometimes in the human realm, and sometimes in the heavenly realms.
"Monks! You have suffered in this manner for such a long time, increasing your craving and constantly receiving drops of blood.
From this evidence, it is known that there is no beginning to time."
As the sutra says:
"World-Honored One!

This consciousness-element is the support, the sustainer, and the locus; it is eternally associated with, inseparable from, and never abandoning the unconditioned qualities of the Buddhas, which are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
"World-Honored One!
It is neither associated with nor dissociated from the wisdom of equanimity; conditioned phenomena are its support, its sustenance, and its locus.
Therefore, it is said that all phenomena rely upon it."
As the Sūtra says:
"World-Honored One!
If the Tathāgatagarbha exists, it can be said that birth and death exist because of a lack of understanding."
Therefore it is said that if there are various paths, they exist,
as the Sūtra states:
"World-Honored One!"
If the Tathāgatagarbha did not exist, one would have no aversion toward suffering, nor would there be any desire, pleasure, or aspiration for Nirvāṇa;
therefore, it is said that there is the attainment of Nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, the statement that "this realm is beginningless" serves to reveal the cause.
If a cause were not established, one could say that there is a beginning.
As for the statement that "all phenomena are dependent," it is because this consciousness serves as the cause for all phenomena that it is said that all phenomena are dependent upon it.

If there are various paths and those who attain nirvāṇa, all these phenomena depend upon them; if there is such a path, there is a karmic fruit, and there are also sentient beings who take birth by virtue of that fruit. It is easy to understand that the two explanations regarding the correct and the false differ from one another, and that through successive stages, one can attain superior practice and the excellent virtues that should be acquired.
Due to the basis of afflictions, there arise extremely heavy afflictions and afflictions that constantly manifest;
these four types of distinctions, such as karmic maturation, are termed "superiority of the basis."
To reverse these four points is called "relying on what is inferior.
Within saṃsāra, not only are the path and so forth non-existent, but even the meaning of nirvāṇa is non-existent. Why is this?
It should be understood that if there is affliction, there must also be liberation.
Furthermore, within the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, there is scriptural authority (*āgama*) that can serve as proof for the name "ālayavijñāna.
The treatise says:
In the Abhidharma, a verse is further spoken:
All phenomena abide supported by the store; The consciousness of all seeds is therefore called Ālaya;
I have taught this for the sake of the superior persons.
The commentary states:
Regarding the phrase "all dharmas abide supported by the storehouse," the second line explains the first.

This refers to the consciousness containing all seeds (*sarvabījaka-vijñāna*), which, through the power of afflictions and karma, transforms the continuity of the *ālaya-vijñāna* such that the preceding [moment] constitutes the fruit of retribution and the succeeding [moment] becomes the cause.
The phrase "therefore it is named *ālaya*" clarifies the meaning by establishing the name, using the term to designate the consciousness.

Regarding the statement "I speak for superior persons," "superior persons" refers to the bodhisattvas; because this is the basis for the sphere of the bodhisattvas and because it can obstruct the bodhisattva path, it is taught for the sake of the bodhisattvas.
The Commentary says:
These two verses from the Āgama establish the substance and the name of consciousness.
Why does the Buddha call this consciousness the *ālaya*?
The commentary states:
These words are intended to reveal the reason for establishing the name.
The treatise says:
"All impure dharmas that possess birth are hidden therein as effects.
The commentary explains:
"All" refers to the three periods of time; within these three periods, one takes up those that are currently arising and those capable of producing.
The category of impure dharmas refers to the inversion of the five types of pure categories; thus they are called the impure categories.
The treatise states:
This consciousness serves as the cause by being hidden within all dharmas.
The commentary states:
"All phenomena" refers to the fruits of the ālayavijñāna, namely the impure factors and so forth.
The ālayavijñāna dwells as a storehouse within these fruits, serving as their cause.
The Treatise says:
Furthermore, because all sentient beings store [their seeds] within this consciousness and grasp at it as a self-characteristic, it is therefore called the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
The Commentary says:

The *Abhidharmakośa* explains the term "sentient being" (*sattva*) by means of grasping at objects, referring specifically to the *ādāna-vijñāna* (appropriating consciousness) and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Why is this? Because no sentient being is ever without the grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha*).
If the grasping at a self arises, what object does it take as its condition, and from what does it arise?
It arises from the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), because that is subtle, of a single type, and continues in an uninterrupted succession.
The treatise says:
The Āgamas state, as in the verse spoken in the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā-sūtra*:
"The appropriating consciousness is profound and subtle; The seeds of phenomena flow forth constantly.
I do not speak of it as 'self' to the foolish; Let them not grasp it as a self."
The commentary states:
Previously, verses from the Abhidharma were cited as proof; here, verses from the Sūtras are further cited as proof.

The Abhidharma excels in its reliance on reasoning (*yukti*), while the Sūtra excels in its reliance on scriptural teaching (*āgama*). Since teaching must necessarily possess reasoning, and reasoning must necessarily accord with the teaching, these two are termed "proofs."
If one were to depart from these two proofs, the thesis could not be established.
These proofs are derived from the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Viśālamati:
Vipula-mati!

Within the cycle of birth and death across the six realms, these sentient beings, according to their respective congregations, undergo birth from eggs, birth from wombs, birth from moisture, or birth by transformation; therein they obtain a body and achieve its full development.

At the time of initial rebirth, the consciousness of all seeds first matures and coalesces into a large, elongated, and circular form, based upon two kinds of grasping: namely, the grasping of the material sense-faculties with their bases, and the grasping of the habitual tendencies of verbal expression regarding signs, names, and conceptual discrimination.
If there are two kinds of grasping in the form realm, there are no two kinds of grasping in the formless realm.
O Broad Wisdom!
This consciousness is sometimes called the *ādāna* (appropriating) consciousness.
Why is this? Because this fundamental consciousness is able to maintain and uphold the body;
it is therefore called the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
Why is this? Because this fundamental consciousness is constantly hidden within the body, as it shares in its formation and destruction.
It is also called *citta*.
Why is this? Because this consciousness is produced and grows from the various sense objects, such as forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
O Vipula-mati!
Depending on this fundamental consciousness as a condition, this collection of consciousnesses arises—namely, from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness.
Depending on the eye-faculty which possesses consciousness and conditioned by external visible objects, eye-consciousness arises.
Simultaneously with the visual consciousness and sharing the same object, a conceptualizing mental consciousness arises.
When a single visual consciousness arises, at that time a single conceptualizing mental consciousness arises, sharing the same object as the visual consciousness.

If this visual consciousness arises together with two, three, four, or five other consciousnesses, at that time a single conceptual mental consciousness arises together with the five [sensory] consciousnesses, taking the same object as its cognitive domain.

It is like a great flowing stream: if a single cause for ripples arises, then a single ripple arises; if two or many causes for ripples arise, then many ripples arise; yet this water flows constantly, without ceasing or interruption.

Furthermore, within the surface of a pure, circular mirror, if a single cause capable of producing a reflection arrives, then a single reflection arises; if two or many causes capable of producing reflections arrive, then many reflections arise. Yet this circular mirror-surface does not transform into those reflections, nor does it suffer any diminution.
This fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) is like a flowing stream or the surface of a mirror.

Depending upon this fundamental consciousness, if a single cause capable of producing visual consciousness arrives, then a single visual consciousness arises; likewise, if causes capable of producing up to five types of consciousness arrive, then five consciousnesses arise.
Viśālamati!
Thus, because these bodhisattvas possess wisdom that accords with the Dharma and the knowledge of suchness, they are able to penetrate the secret meaning of the manas, citta, and vijñāna.

For this reason, the Tathāgatas, in accordance with reality and in accordance with measure, do not declare that these bodhisattvas have already penetrated the secret meaning of the manas, citta, and vijñāna.
Vast Wisdom!

Because bodhisattvas do not perceive the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and the appropriating consciousness (*ādānavijñāna*) as they truly are, they do not perceive a storehouse or a dwelling within or without; they do not perceive birth, growth, and so forth; they do not perceive consciousness, the eye, forms, and visual consciousness; nor do they perceive the ear, sounds, and auditory consciousness, up to and including the body, tangibles, and tactile consciousness.
Vipula-mati!

Because all bodhisattvas possess wisdom based on the knowledge of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*), they are able to penetrate the secret meanings of the mental faculty (*manas*), the mind (*citta*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

For this reason, the Tathāgatas, in accordance with reality and in accordance with measure, declare that bodhisattvas are able to penetrate the secret meanings of the mental faculty, the mind, and consciousness.
Furthermore, a verse is cited to re-explain the meaning taught in the Sūtra.
Regarding the statement that the "appropriating consciousness (ādāna-vijñāna) is profound and subtle," why is this consciousness sometimes called the ādāna-vijñāna?
It is able to grasp and maintain all material sense faculties;

that is to say, because it can sustain the five sense faculties together with their bases, as well as their characteristics and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), this consciousness is also called *ādāna* (appropriation).
"Profound and subtle" means it is difficult to extinguish and difficult to understand.

"The seeds of phenomena flow constantly" means that they serve as the basis for the perfuming that gives rise to all impure phenomena, just as a stream of water flows on, arising and ceasing moment by moment in an uninterrupted succession.

Regarding those things I do not speak of to ordinary persons: because ordinary beings lack profound practice, do not seek omniscience, and possess dull faculties, I do not teach them to ordinary persons or those of the two vehicles.
Let them not grasp it as a self; for a single characteristic arises and its continuity persists for a long time.
If sentient beings, relying on the sūtras, give rise to false discrimination, they will then grasp this consciousness as a self.
Because I fear they might give rise to false attachments, I have not taught it to them.
The treatise asks:
Why is this consciousness sometimes called the *ādāna-vijñāna*?
The commentary states:

Previously, we have already cited correct reasoning and authoritative scripture to prove that this consciousness is named *ālaya*. Why, then, do you now further state that this consciousness is named *ādāna*?
The treatise says:
It is able to maintain all material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*), because it serves as the basis for the appropriation of all rebirths. Why is this so?
The material sense-faculties are grasped and maintained by this consciousness; they remain unimpaired and undestroyed until the end of their continuity.
Furthermore, at the time of actualizing rebirth, because it is capable of producing the appropriated aggregates (*upādāna-skandha*), the bodies of all six destinies are likewise thus appropriated.
Because it grasps the objects of activity and is sustained by consciousness, it is called *ādāna*.
The commentary states:
This establishes the logical principle to prove the designation *ādāna*.
As for the principle: it is capable of sustaining all the material sense faculties (*rūpīndriya*).
Because this consciousness sustains the five material faculties, they do not undergo the transformations seen in a dead person’s body during states such as blackening, swelling, or decay.
When one reaches the stage of death, the ālayavijñāna abandons the five sense-faculties; at that time, various signs such as blackening, swelling, and decay arise.
Therefore, it is certain that because they are sustained by this consciousness, the five sense-faculties do not undergo destruction throughout the course of a single lifetime.
Regarding the phrase "because it is the basis for the appropriation of all rebirths," this is a reiterated response to the previous question.

At the very moment a sentient being undergoes rebirth, this consciousness is able to produce the aggregates of appropriation (*upādāna-skandha*); the essential nature of these appropriations is that which is grasped and maintained by this consciousness.
Because this consciousness is the consciousness that undergoes rebirth, at the moment of rebirth, all categories of beings are subsumed within this consciousness.
Furthermore, the entire duration of receiving a body is also subsumed within this consciousness, because the seeds of the body are fully present within the ālayavijñāna.
For this reason, the ālayavijñāna is also called ādāna.
The treatise says:
It is sometimes called "mind" (citta), as the Blessed One said:
"Citta, manas, and vijñāna.
The commentary states:
Since the meanings of ālayavijñāna and manas differ from the meaning of citta, their respective meanings must also be distinct.
What are the distinct characteristics of these three?
The treatise states:

There are two kinds of *manas*: first, because it serves as the sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the arising of that [consciousness], the consciousness that has previously ceased is termed *manas*.
Furthermore, the basis for the arising of consciousness is designated as the "mind" (manas).
The commentary explains:
if a preceding state of mind ceases and a subsequent one arises, such that it can immediately give rise to the succeeding mind, this is called the "mind."
Furthermore, there is a mental faculty (*manas*) that can serve as the basis for the arising of consciousness, without obstructing the present consciousness.
Because these two act as the conditions for the arising of consciousness, they are called "mind" (*manas*);
that which is in the process of arising is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
This indicates that the manas is distinct from the consciousness (vijñāna).
The treatise states:
Second, there is the afflicted manas, which is constantly associated with the four afflictions.
The commentary states:
This is intended to explain the *ādānavijñāna*.
What are the four afflictions?
The Treatise says:
First, the view of a self-identity; second, the conceit "I am"; third, self-love; and fourth, ignorance.
The Commentary explains:
I perceive this grasping as "self," and following this mind, the conceit of "I" (asmimāna) arises.

As for this conceit of "I": from the grasping at a self, one gives rise to a haughty mind; though in reality there is no self, one gives rise to craving for a self, which is termed "self-love" (ātmasneha).
These three delusions all have ignorance (*avidyā*) as their cause.
That is to say, the mind’s confusion and lack of understanding regarding the reality of the truths, causes, and effects is termed ignorance.
The treatise states:
This consciousness is the basis for other afflicted consciousnesses.
These afflicted consciousnesses arise by means of the first basis and are defiled by means of the second.
The commentary states:
This afflicted consciousness arises by depending on the first consciousness and is defiled by the second consciousness.
Once it has sequentially ceased, it is designated as the *manas*; for when other consciousnesses are about to arise, it serves as their basis for arising.
The second consciousness is called the defiled consciousness (*kliṣṭa-vijñāna*), because it is the basis for the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Even when a person is giving rise to a wholesome mind, this consciousness is still present.
The Treatise says:
Because it takes objects as its conditions and is capable of successive discrimination, these two are called "mind" (*manas*).
The commentary states:
It is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) because it is able to grasp objects.
It is called "manas" because it provides a basis for the arising of others;
alternatively, the second consciousness is called "manas" because its characteristics are those of a self, or because it is the basis for conceptualization.
The treatise states:
How is it known that there exists a defiled mind?
The commentary asks:
By what reasoning can this point be established?
The Treatise says:
If this mind did not exist, it could not be said that there is独行无明 (solitary ignorance).
The Commentary explains:
What are the characteristics of independent ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*)?
If a person has not yet attained the path of antidote, the delusion that can obstruct true wisdom is called independent ignorance.
This ignorance does not exist within the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*).
Why is this? Because if a person is within the five consciousnesses, they cannot constitute an obstruction. Why is this?
If that which is the locus where the path of counteraction arises were itself a locus of obstruction, then this would not exist within the afflicted mental consciousness (*kliṣṭa-manovijñāna*). Why?
Because the mind would simply be defiled by virtue of these very afflictions (*kleśa*).
If it were associated with and co-arising alongside other afflictions, the designation "acting alone" would not be established.

If you claim that the sixth consciousness is defiled by ignorance acting alone, then the sixth consciousness would never be pure, as this ignorance would not cease even momentarily; how then could mental states such as generosity become virtuous?
Because the sixth consciousness is always associated with ignorance,
anyone who claims that the mind arises in association with wholesome states would be at fault.
If the sixth consciousness were constantly defiled, then it would be impossible to induce the arising of the path of counteraction (*pratipakṣa-mārga*).

If someone were to say that there exists a distinct wholesome mind associated with the defiled mind, and that this wholesome mind can induce the arising of the path of counteraction such that the defiled mind is thereby extinguished; [this would be untenable].
If this were asserted, there would be no fault.
The treatise says:
If it were similar to the five consciousnesses, this dharma should not exist.
Why is this? Because these five consciousnesses simultaneously possess their own bases, namely the various faculties such as the eye.
The commentary states:

Just as the five consciousnesses, such as visual consciousness, have the five sense organs, such as the eye, as their simultaneous supports, mental consciousness must likewise have a simultaneous support.
If another consciousness were not established, this support would also be absent; just as visual consciousness cannot arise without its support, so too should it be with mental consciousness.
The Treatise says:
Furthermore, the designation "mind" (manas) would then be devoid of meaning.
The Commentary says:
What is meant by "lacking a referent"?
If one posits the mind that has already ceased as the "mental faculty" (manas), this is merely a name without a referent. Why is this so?
The mental faculty (*manas*) has "discernment" as its defining characteristic; how, then, can it be established in the absence [of an object]?
This mental faculty perishes prior to the six consciousnesses; thus, this so-called "mental faculty" cannot be apprehended, nor can it discern, because it lacks substantial reality.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, the attainment of non-conception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) and the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) should not differ from one another. Why is this?
The attainment of non-conceptualization (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) is manifested by an afflicted mental state, whereas the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) is not so.
If this were not the case, these two attainments would not differ from one another.
The commentary states:

If a person maintains that there is a defiled mind [in these states], then for such a person, it is said that the attainment of non-perception possesses a defiled mind, whereas the attainment of cessation is said to be without a defiled mind; thus, for this person, there is a distinction between the two attainments.
If it were not so, then because mental consciousness does not function during the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), there would be no distinction between them.
The treatise says:

Furthermore, throughout one's lifespan in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), it would follow that [the state] is untainted (*anāsrava*) and without fault, since it would be free from defilement, provided that within it there is neither the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) nor the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*).
Furthermore, the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) arises at all times throughout good, evil, and neutral states of mind.
If this were not the case, then because the delusions of "I" and "mine" could only function when associated with an evil mind, they would be unable to function within good or neutral states of mind.
If one posits that two minds arise simultaneously, this fault does not occur.
However, if one posits [them] as concomitants associated with the sixth consciousness, this fault does occur.
The commentary states:

If one is born among the gods of the realm of non-conception (asaṃjñisattva) with an undefiled mind, then throughout that single lifetime there will be no grasping at a self (ātma-grāha) nor the conceit "I am" (asmimāna); thus, this birth would not involve any loss [of roots of goodness], and this meditative absorption (samādhi) ought not to be something loathed by the Noble Ones (ārya).
Since this state is loathed by the sages, we know that this meditative absorption possesses a defiled consciousness (*kliṣṭa-vijñāna*).
Because the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) constantly accompanies it, all wholesome states such as generosity are perpetually intermingled with self-grasping, and self-grasping is ever-present.
If one were free from ignorance, this [phenomenon] would not exist.
This ignorance cannot exist if it is separated from its support;
and this support of ignorance has no distinct entity apart from the ādāna-vijñāna.
The Treatise says:
There is no独行 (solitary) ignorance, nor is there [ignorance] similar to the five consciousnesses;
in the two meditative attainments there is no distinction, and the name "mind" (manas) has no referent.
In the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*), there is no grasping at a self;

throughout the duration of a single lifetime, within the states of the untainted (*anāsrava*), the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), grasping at a self ought not to arise.
Since it does not exist apart from a defiled mind, it contradicts both the second and the third [characteristics].
In the absence of all these [factors], the grasping at a self cannot arise.
When one realizes and perceives the true meaning, the afflictive hindrances are prevented from arising;
because it operates constantly in all circumstances, it is called "solitary ignorance" (*māna-moha*).
The treatise says:
Because this mind is defiled, it is subsumed under the category of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
The commentary explains:
This mind is the basis for ignorance; among the three natures, to which nature does this mind belong?
Because it is defiled, it belongs to the nature of obscured-neutral. Why is this so?
Because it is defiled. How is it defiled?
The treatise says:
It is always associated with the four afflictions.
The commentary states:

Because one fails to comprehend the object of non-self, the grasping at a self arises; from this grasping at a self, self-love and self-pride arise. These four afflictions arise constantly in all circumstances.
The Treatise says:
For example, the afflictions of the form and formless realms are obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), because the defilements of these two realms are concealed by *śamatha*.
The Commentary explains:
The realm (*dhātu*) has the sense of "birth-nature" as its meaning.
Because it is free from sensual desire and the desire for food, yet arises from the desire for form, it is called the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Because it is free from the desires of the two lower realms, yet arises from the desire for the formless, it is called the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Although the afflictions of these two realms are associated with the coarse sixth consciousness, they do not lose their neutral (avyākṛta) nature because they are concealed by the eight meditative attainments.
If these afflictions were present in the desire realm, the distracted mind would become unwholesome (akuśala), due to its reliance on a coarse basis.
If it is associated with the second consciousness, although one is not in meditative absorption, it is nonetheless not unwholesome because its basis is extremely subtle.

If it occurs in the realm of form or the formless realm, although its basis is coarse, it is still not unwholesome because the mind is supple and smooth due to being subsumed within the eight dhyānas; yet, because it can produce birth and death, it is also not wholesome. Therefore, it belongs to the nature of obscured-neutral (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*).

The second type of affliction arising from consciousness is likewise: because it relies upon the subtle [mind], it is not unwholesome; yet because it is the cause of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), it is also not wholesome.
The treatise says:
This mind arises constantly and never ceases.
The commentary states:

Among the three natures of this defiled mind, it constantly arises without interruption within the eight meditative attainments, the attainment of non-conception, and the station of the gods of non-conception.
The treatise says:
Upon examining the second substance, it cannot be found apart from the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
The commentary states:

The second consciousness arises in dependence upon the first consciousness by giving rise to the grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha*); if separated from the first consciousness, this [second] consciousness could not arise. Therefore, we know that the first consciousness exists.
Now, the second consciousness is established in order to clarify the first consciousness.
The treatise says:
Therefore, the ālayavijñāna is established as the manas; depending upon this as its seed, the other consciousnesses arise.
The commentary states:
Apart from the first consciousness, there is no separate conscious entity that serves as the cause for a second consciousness or as the cause for the arising of consciousness.
The Buddha spoke of the name "mind" (*citta*); this name refers to the second consciousness.
When the Buddha speaks of the name "consciousness" (vijñāna), this name refers to the six consciousnesses.
When the Buddha speaks of the name "mind" (manas), this name refers to the first consciousness. Why is this so?

The second consciousness and the evolving consciousness, if the former has already ceased and the subsequent consciousness is about to arise, must necessarily arise in dependence upon the first consciousness;
and because it can also produce its own kind, it is designated as the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*).
The treatise says:
Why is this *manas* further called "mind" (*citta*)?
Because it is a collection of various seeds of perfuming (*vāsanā*).
The commentary states:
The first consciousness is also called *citta*.
What is the meaning of the term *citta*?
This refers to the meaning of "various" and the meaning of "growth.
Regarding "various," there are ten meanings: first, the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*);

second, the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*); third, the characteristic of understanding (*vijñapti-lakṣaṇa*); fourth, co-arising (*sahakārin*); fifth, defilement (*saṃkleśa*); sixth, the perfuming of karma (*karma-vāsanā*); seventh, cause (*hetu*); eighth, fruit (*phala*); ninth, the path (*mārga*); and tenth, the stages (*bhūmi*).
Within this meaning, there are many distinct senses, hence it is called "various.
There are three senses of "growth":

first, by the gathering of these ten dharmas, the mental continuum is caused to endure for a long time; second, this mind is able to sustain the seeds of all dharmas; third, it is the growth of the seeds perfumed by various dharmas.
The "seed" refers to the cause consisting of specific functional capacities (*śakti-viśeṣa*).
That which is "nourished and increased" refers to the transformation [of consciousness] into the three realms.
For this reason, the Buddha stated that the primary consciousness is also called *vijñāna-mātra* (the mind-base).
The treatise says:
Why is this characteristic of mind not taught in the Śrāvaka vehicle, yet the names *ālaya* and *ādāna* are taught?
Because it is subsumed within a subtle sphere of experience.
The commentary states:
The question asks about the name and the nature of the name; the answer addresses both questions comprehensively.
This consciousness is the most subtle among all objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), because it is not an object of perception for those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

This consciousness is also an object-field; those seeking the fruit of Buddhahood must thoroughly penetrate this consciousness, for it is the foundational storehouse (*ālaya*) upon which the nine meanings—beginning with "that which is to be known"—depend. Therefore, it is termed "that which is subsumed."
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva possesses a subtle realm-treasury (*sūkṣmaviṣayagarbha*); because this consciousness is difficult to understand, it is subsumed under the subtle realm-treasury.
The treatise asks:
For what reason?
Śrāvakas lack the superior status required to attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
The commentary asks:
For what reason is the subtle sphere not taught within the Śrāvaka Vehicle?
Śrāvakas do not apply right effort to seek to know the realm of the Tathāgata, for their practice is solely for the sake of their own benefit.
The afflictive obstructions of śrāvakas can be eliminated through the coarse and shallow contemplative practices of the knowledge of suffering and so forth.
The Treatise says:
Therefore, for the sake of those who are śrāvakas, apart from this teaching, [the Buddha] does not preach it, because he fulfills their original vows through the accomplishment of wisdom.
The Commentary explains:
The Buddhas see that the śrāvakas have few desires and are content, seeking only to eliminate the obscurations of their own delusions.
If these obscurations could be eliminated by other forms of knowledge apart from this [great] wisdom, then their original vows would be fulfilled.

Because they do not act to remove the obstacles of others from liberation, nor do they generate the aspiration to seek the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body by practicing the subtle and profound path, [the Buddha] does not preach it for them.
The treatise says:
Bodhisattvas ought to possess a superior station; because they seek the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), the Buddha preaches it for them.
The commentary states:

Because all bodhisattvas seek to extinguish the obstacles of afflictions and the obstacles to knowledge for both themselves and others, and because they practice right effort, [the Buddha] teaches this for the sake of all bodhisattvas.
The treatise says:
Why is this? It is because it is impossible to attain unsurpassed enlightenment apart from this wisdom.
The commentary states:
If one is separated from the profound and subtle object, the ten stages of gradual cultivation cannot be accomplished.
If one were to depart from this cultivation of the mind, there would be no such principle as easily removing the afflictions and easily attaining the Dharma-body.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, this consciousness was previously revealed by the Tathāgata under a different name within the Śrāvaka vehicle.
The commentary states:
Furthermore, there is another reasoning by which one may believe that this consciousness exists. Why is this?
In the Śrāvaka vehicle, this meaning is manifested in various places under different names.
The treatise says:
As it is stated in the *Ekottarika Āgama*:

In this world, beings delight in the *ālaya*, love the *ālaya*, are habituated to the *ālaya*, and are attached to the *ālaya*; therefore, for the sake of extinguishing the *ālaya*, the Tathāgata teaches the True Dharma.
The commentary states:
The first phrase provides a brief explanation of the root; the subsequent three phrases further elaborate upon it by means of the present, past, and future.
"Attachment to the ālaya" refers to the present world.
"One who is habituated to the *ālaya* refers to the past life;
one who craves the *ālaya* refers to the future life.
Furthermore, there is another interpretation:
The delight in the noble (ārya) is the present time.
What is the present time?
It is because the delight in the noble arises from attachment to the noble in the past.
Because one has repeatedly cultivated the *ālaya* in the past and present, one will thus crave the *ālaya* in the future.
Furthermore, some maintain that the meaning of these four propositions is not different.
If they are not distinct, how can there be four propositions?
As clarified in the *Viniscayasamgrahani*, there are two kinds of craving: namely, craving for existence (*bhavarāga*) and craving for non-existence (*vibhavarāga*).
"Craving for existence" (*bhavataṇhā*) refers to craving for the three realms; "craving for non-existence" (*vibhavataṇhā*) refers to craving for the cessation of the three realms.
Regarding "joy and pleasure": if a person is born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they experience joy based on objects already obtained.

Regarding "attachment arising from not having attained the objects [of the higher realms]": if a person is born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) but has not yet abandoned desire for that realm, they are greedily attached to birth in the form realm and to the objects (*viṣaya*) of the form realm. Because they have already attained the meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) of the form realm, they become defiled by that absorption and do not delight in absorptions they have not yet attained; therein, they grasp it as liberation. Therefore, this is called "attachment" (*niveśa*).
Regarding "practice": if a person is born in the formless realm but has not yet abandoned desire for the formless realm, they first contemplate the faults of the desire realm.

Having abandoned desire for the desire realm, they subsequently contemplate the faults of the form realm, thereby abandoning desire for the form realm and giving rise to desire for the formless realm.
This desire is called "cultivation" because it is accomplished through the practice of various meditative concentrations;
these three are termed "craving for existence.

As for the craving that arises based on the view of permanence: if a person frequently commits evil deeds and fears receiving the retribution of suffering, or if they hold the view of annihilationism and seek non-rebirth, this is termed "craving."
This first [type] is the craving for non-existence (*vibhava-tṛṣṇā*), which arises based on the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).

Alternatively, the four phrases may be explained in terms of the four perversions (*viparyāsa*), or they may be explained in terms of the four types of craving: craving for food and drink, clothing, dwelling, and for existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*) and non-existence (*vibhava-tṛṣṇā*).
Alternatively, it may be intended to manifest one's own skill in the Dharma, so that disciples may obtain the cause for skill in the Dharma;
or to demonstrate that a single meaning has many names;
or to enable those of dull faculties to recall this meaning again by means of another name should they forget it.
Alternatively, it may be intended that those of dull faculties might attain understanding by means of repeated explanations of names.

Or, it may be intended that disciples from other regions who do not understand one name might nevertheless attain understanding through other names; for this reason, four sets of phrases are taught where the names differ but the meaning is the same.
The Treatise says:
"The world delights in hearing.
The Commentary explains:
It relies upon the two faculties of faith and wisdom.
The treatise says:
"Therefore, it belongs [to them]."
The commentary states:
To manifest the mind free from distraction is precisely the faculty of concentration (*samādhi-indriya*).
The treatise says:
"Intentionally desiring to know.
The commentary states:
This reveals the arousal of reverence and non-negligence, which is precisely the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*).
The Treatise says:
"One generates right effort.
The Commentary explains:
Therefore, to give rise to vigor and abandon evil while adopting good is precisely the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*).
What is clarified here is the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*).
The treatise states:
"Only then can one extinguish the *ālaya*.
The commentary states:
This clarifies the fruit of the Path, which is precisely the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
The Treatise says:
"Up to and including the practice of the Tathāgata’s true Dharma and its semblance.
The Commentary explains:
To practice according to the teaching is called "receiving and practicing" (pratipatti).

The names, phrases, and syllables spoken by the Tathāgata are called the True Dharma (saddharma); the meaning indicated by those names, phrases, and syllables is called the Counterfeit Dharma (pratirūpadharma).
Furthermore, the True Dharma (saddharma) refers to correct teaching; that which resembles the Dharma refers to correct practice and correct attainment.
Furthermore, the True Dharma has the scriptures (āgama) as its essence, while that which resembles the Dharma has what is attained through them as its essence.
The treatise states:
Because the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is the foremost rarity, inconceivable dharmas manifest in the world.

Just as with the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), these four kinds of merits of a Tathāgata’s appearance in the world have already been revealed through a different perspective within the Śrāvaka vehicle regarding this consciousness.
The commentary states:
There are three types of distinct meanings. First, the distinct intention: the Tathāgata wishes to explain his own supramundane merits, not wishing to manifest the *ālayavijñāna*.
This consciousness is associated with meritorious qualities; therefore, it is called "this consciousness.
Regarding its two distinct names, the Tathāgata has taught only the names and not their meanings.

Regarding its three distinct meanings, it is subsumed within a subtle realm that is unsuitable for exposition to those of the Two Vehicles; because it corresponds only to the meaning, he taught the name without explaining the meaning.
Commentary on the Mahāyānasaṃgraha, Scroll One;
Commentary on the Mahāyānasaṃgraha, Scroll Two;
Explained by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Chen Dynasty.
Commentary on the Chapter on the Various Names of the Basis for the Superior Characteristics, Part Two. Regarding the remaining discussion on the various names, it says:
Furthermore, in the Āgamas of the Mahāsāṃghika school, this consciousness manifests through the differentiation of its fundamental [seeds], just as a tree depends upon its roots.
The commentary states:
Because this consciousness is the cause of all consciousnesses, it is the root of all consciousnesses.
It is like the root of a tree; because it is that upon which the sprouts, nodes, branches, leaves, and so forth depend, it is called the "root of the tree."
If one is separated from these roots, sprouts and the like cannot be produced;
it is the same with this consciousness being the root of other consciousnesses.
The treatise says:
The Mahīśāsaka school also describes this consciousness by another name, namely, the "aggregate that exhausts birth and death" (*ātyantika-saṃsāra-skandha*). Why is this?
Because while sometimes matter and mind appear to have their continuity severed, within this mind those seeds are never interrupted.
The commentary says:
Why is this consciousness called the "aggregate that exhausts birth and death" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti-skandha*)?
