The six consciousnesses are called "mind" (*citta*); because the three subsequent minds arise from this initial mind, they are termed "mental factors" (*caitasika-dharma*).
The Treatise says:
These two consciousnesses serve as mutual causes for one another, as stated in a verse from the Mahāyāna Abhidharma:
"All phenomena are stored within consciousness, and consciousness is likewise [stored] within phenomena."
"These two are mutually causes, and they are also constantly mutually effects.
The commentary states:

These words are intended to reveal that the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and the appropriating consciousness (*upabhoktṛvijñāna*) are mutually cause and effect, as evidenced by the *Āgama*.
If it does not contradict the Āgamas, it can certainly be trusted.
Furthermore, had this statement not been made, one would not know from where this proof originated—whether it is the word of the Sage or not the word of the Sage.
Therefore, this statement was made:

"All dharmas [reside] in the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), and the storehouse consciousness likewise [resides] in all dharmas. This means that if the fundamental consciousness acts as the cause for the dharmas of cognition, and all dharmas are its effects, they must necessarily depend upon the storehouse consciousness.

If all phenomena act as the cause for the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and the fundamental consciousness acts as their effect, they must necessarily reside within the storehouse (*ālaya*) of those phenomena.
Regarding these two being mutually causes and also constantly mutually effects: if the fundamental consciousness is the cause for them, they are the effect of the fundamental consciousness;
if they are the cause for the fundamental consciousness, the fundamental consciousness is their effect.
Such is the principle of cause and effect; whether a Buddha appears or not, this Dharma remains eternally constant.
Chapter Seven: The Four Conditions. The commentary states: These three types of dependent origination are:
first, dependent origination that extends to the limits of saṃsāra; second, dependent origination of the paths of the desirable and the undesirable; and third, dependent origination of experience.
These three types of dependent origination consist of four kinds of conditions.
The treatise says:
Within the first type of dependent origination, all phenomena and consciousness act as mutual causes and conditions for one another.
The commentary states:
Since the causes and conditions have already been explained, there is no need to ask again. Why is this?
Because all phenomena (*dharmas*) are perfumed within the *ālayavijñāna*, they are able to function as mutual causes and effects.
The treatise says:
Within the second type of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), what are the conditions (*pratyaya*) for these phenomena?
This is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
The commentary states:
"Because of the dominance of ignorance (*avidyā*) and the other [links], formations (*saṃskāra*) and the rest arise."
There are two kinds of predominance (*adhipati*):
first, inseparable; second, merely present.
Regarding the inseparable, it is as the eye-faculty acts as the predominant condition for visual consciousness.
As for "only when it exists," it is like how white and other colors can manifest black and others.
If ignorance and so forth exist, they possess two kinds of predominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) with respect to formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and so forth.
If there were no ignorance underlying suffering, the various formative forces would not arise.
If the formations that have already arisen lack the cultivation of the path and ignorance, those formations will not ripen. Why is this?
Because a *srotāpanna* does not create karma that results in rebirth, and an *anāgāmin* does not undergo rebirth in the lower realms.
The Treatise says:
Furthermore, how many conditions can give rise to the six consciousnesses?
There are three conditions, namely: the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
The commentary states:

Because it arises from the sense-faculties (*indriya*), it is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*); because it takes an object (*viṣaya*) as its condition, it is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*); and because the preceding consciousness ceases and the subsequent consciousness arises, it is the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Because the preceding consciousness can give rise to the subsequent consciousness without any interval between them, it is called "succession.
The treatise states:

Thus, arising through these three conditions—first, the condition of arising that exhausts birth and death; second, the condition of arising on the path of love and hatred; and third, the condition of arising through enjoyment—possesses all four conditions.
The commentary states:

Regarding the presence or absence of the four conditions within the three types of dependent origination, if one follows the explicit meaning (*nītārtha*), none possess all four; however, if one follows the implicit meaning (*neyārtha*), all possess the four conditions.
Commentary on the Mahāyānasaṃgraha, Scroll Second;
Commentary on the Mahāyānasaṃgraha, Scroll Third;
Explained by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha from Central India.

Chapter Three: Exposition of Quotations (Vyākhyāna-saṃgraha-varga), Part One. Section One: The Impurity of Afflictions (Kleśa-aśuddhi-pariccheda). Commentary states: This chapter consists of six sections: first, the section on the impurity of afflictions;

second, the section on the impurity of karma; third, the section on the impurity of birth; fourth, the section on mundane purity; fifth, the section on supramundane purity; and sixth, the section on accordance with reason.
The Treatise says:
This ālayavijñāna has already been established by means of its various names and its essential characteristics.
The Commentary says:

Thus, the various names for this fundamental consciousness have been explained and its essential nature established; these two points are logically established only with respect to the fundamental consciousness, and not with respect to any other consciousness.
Now, in order to clarify these two meanings, this treatise engages in debate with various masters regarding what is logical and what is illogical.
The treatise says:

How is it known that the Ālayavijñāna is designated by such various names, and that the Tathāgata likewise taught its essence and characteristics in this way, rather than teaching the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*)?
The commentary states:
He says that such various names and essential characteristics as these also exist within my own doctrine, yet the *ālaya-vijñāna* is not [explicitly] mentioned therein.
How can it be said that these various names and essential characteristics necessarily belong to the *ālaya-vijñāna* and do not belong to other consciousnesses?
To answer this question, the treatise states:
"If one were to set aside this ālayavijñāna established by means of these names and characteristics, then neither the impure nor the pure categories would be established."
The commentary states:

If you were to establish this name and its essential characteristics upon another consciousness apart from the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), such an establishment would be untenable. Why is this so?
Because it is contradicted by three points,

these three points constitute the *siddhānta* of the Tathāgata’s True Dharma— namely, the impure category, the pure category, and correct reasoning— and these points are established by means of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
If you negate the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), then these three meanings would have no basis for their establishment, and thus this doctrine would not be proven.
What the Tathāgata has established is firm and accomplished; it contradicts what you maintain, and thus your position is destroyed.
Therefore, various names and their essential characteristics are not separate from the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
The Treatise states:

The category of afflictions (*kleśa*), the category of karma, the category of birth—all these impure categories, as well as the worldly pure category and the supramundane pure category—are all unestablished [without it].
The commentary states:
This name is repeated in order to open three chapters into six.
The treatise says:
How is it that the category of impurity consisting of afflictions is not established?
The seeds of perfuming produced by the root afflictions and the secondary afflictions cannot be established within the six consciousnesses.
Why is this? Because visual consciousness arises and ceases simultaneously with the two categories of afflictions, both great and small, such as desire (*rāga*).
The commentary states:
Since desire arises dependent upon the mind, it arises and perishes simultaneously with the mind; this is to demonstrate that desire and the like perfume the mind.
The treatise states:
"This visual consciousness is established as a seed perfumed by afflictions, whereas other consciousnesses are not so."
The commentary states:
This visual consciousness arises and ceases simultaneously with desire and other mental factors; because it is repeatedly perfumed by them, it becomes a seed.
Auditory consciousness and the others, however, are not perfumed, as they are obstructed by other consciousnesses.
The treatise says:
This visual consciousness has already ceased, or other consciousnesses have arisen in between; thus, neither the perfuming nor its basis can be apprehended.
The commentary explains:
If one is in a state devoid of consciousness, such as the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and so forth, it is said that consciousness has already ceased;
or if one is in a state possessing consciousness, the ear-consciousness and others arise intermittently, and thus the eye-consciousness ceases.
Within these two types of cessation, neither the seeds produced by perfuming nor the eye-consciousness that serves as their support can be found.
The treatise states:

Since the preceding moment of eye-consciousness has already passed away and currently lacks any substantial entity, or is interrupted by other consciousnesses, it is impossible for it to arise simultaneously with desire from a non-existent dharma that has already ceased.
The commentary states:

If, at a time prior to the visual consciousness, both [the eye and the object] have already ceased, and there is currently neither the visual consciousness nor the entity of desire, then these are non-existent dharmas that have already perished.

If, subsequent to a visual consciousness, a [subsequent] visual consciousness and desire arise simultaneously with that desire, it would mean that they take as their seeds the previously ceased visual consciousness and desire in order to produce the presently arising visual consciousness and desire; this principle cannot be established.
Why is this? Because the cause has already ceased and perished.
The treatise says:
For example, from karma that has already ceased in the past, a retribution cannot arise.
The commentary states:
Past karma is of two kinds, namely, that which possesses functional capacity and that which lacks functional capacity.
If the retribution has already matured, it no longer possesses functional efficacy.
This karma has two characteristics: first, it has already passed away; second, it has already been extinguished. Thus, there is no sense in which the fruit of retribution arises from this karma.
The same should apply to visual consciousness that possesses desire; it cannot be said to arise from seeds that have already ceased.
This would be the case if one maintains that a previously ceased consciousness exists because past phenomena exist, as the Vaibhāṣikas maintain.
This position is merely words without meaning. Why?
If a dharma exists, how can one speak of "past dharmas"?
For this reason, the arising of the fruit of retribution is not logical, because there is no perfuming (*vāsanā*).
The treatise says:
Furthermore, when visual consciousness arises simultaneously with desire and so forth, perfuming is not established.
The commentary states:
When visual consciousness has not yet entered the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and has not been interrupted by other forms of consciousness, it arises together with desire;
however, once it has subsequently entered the meditative absorption of cessation or been interrupted by other forms of consciousness, the perfuming (*vāsanā*) cannot be established.
The treatise says: Why is this?
This seed cannot abide within desire, because desire depends upon consciousness.
Furthermore, because it desires to continue in succession rather than remaining fixed.
The commentary states:
If a seed were to remain, it would necessarily depend upon a dharma that is sovereign and a dharma whose continuity is firm.
Since these two meanings are entirely absent within the desire-consciousness (*kāma-vijñāna*), desire is not the locus that serves as the support for seeds.
The treatise states:
This desire is also not perfumed by other consciousnesses, because their bases are distinct, and because the remaining consciousnesses do not arise and perish simultaneously with it.
The commentary states:
If the seed were unable to abide within the desire realm, it would have to abide within other consciousnesses;
however, this is not the case.
Why is this? Because their bases are distinct, and furthermore, because arising and ceasing do not occur simultaneously.

Regarding the distinction of bases: visual consciousness has the eye-faculty as its basis, auditory consciousness has the ear-faculty as its basis, and so on up to mental consciousness, which has the mind-faculty as its basis. Since these various consciousnesses have different bases, they cannot be associated; therefore, the perfuming of one consciousness cannot abide within another consciousness.

As for the fact that arising and ceasing do not coexist: because the sense organs (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and mental attention (*manasikāra*) are all distinct, there is no principle of simultaneous arising and ceasing.
Since arising and ceasing do not occur at the same time, how could this consciousness infuse (perfume) that consciousness?
Therefore, all meanings regarding the perfuming (vāsanā) cannot be established.
If you say that these seeds reside within a consciousness of the same kind,
this too is not the case.
Why is this? The treatise states:
"Like categories cannot mutually perfuse one another, because they do not arise and perish simultaneously."
The commentary states:
Visual consciousness cannot permeate visual consciousness. Why is this?
At any given moment, two visual consciousnesses cannot arise simultaneously.
If they do not arise simultaneously, there can be no simultaneous cessation; therefore, the principle of perfuming (*vāsanā*) is not established.
The treatise says:
Therefore, visual consciousness is not perfumed by various afflictions, whether great or small, such as desire, nor is it perfumed by consciousnesses of its own kind.
The commentary explains:
For the reasons stated above, visual consciousness is neither perfumed by consciousnesses of a different category, nor is it perfumed by consciousnesses of its own kind.
The treatise says:
Just as one should thus reflect upon visual consciousness, so too should one reflect upon all remaining forms of consciousness.

Furthermore, if sentient beings fall from the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva) and above, receiving birth in a lower realm with an initial consciousness defiled by great and small afflictions, this consciousness would have no seed at the time of its arising.
The commentary states:

When one falls from a higher realm to undergo birth in a lower realm, the consciousness that first takes up birth must necessarily be defiled by afflictions (*kleśa*). From what seeds do this consciousness and these afflictions arise?
If it is claimed that [the mind] arises from a higher realm,
this is not the case. Why?
Because the two realms, upper and lower, are mutually contradictory and do not arise simultaneously, they cannot mutually perfuse one another.
If it is argued that the initial mind born in the lower realm arises from a preceding mind that has not yet attained a state in the upper realm, this too is not the case.
The treatise says:
Why is this? Because these latencies of affliction and their basis have both already passed away and ceased without remainder.
The commentary states:
This initial consciousness would have to arise without a cause, for this perfuming and its support have long since ceased and perished; therefore, it cannot be taken as its cause.
The Commentary says:

Furthermore, when the consciousness that serves as the antidote to the afflictions has arisen and all other mundane consciousnesses have been extinguished, if the ālayavijñāna did not exist, it would be impossible for this antidotal consciousness to coexist with the seeds of both minor and major afflictions; thus, this principle would not be established.
The commentary states:
If you deny the existence of the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna), then two faults will inevitably arise that cannot be avoided.
First, it would follow that for those on the path of the noble ones (ārya-mārga), the noble path and other afflictions (kleśa) would coexist simultaneously; this proposition is untenable.

If these afflictions did not exist, then there would be no basis for cultivating other paths; consequently, there would be no individuals belonging to the four paths or three fruits, and only those who have attained the state beyond training (aśaikṣa) would exist.
This position incurs the fault of contradicting the authentic teachings, which cannot be avoided.

Once the two types of untainted consciousness (*anāsravavijñāna*) have ceased and a mundane mind (*laukikacitta*) seeks to arise again, there would be no cause capable of allowing this mind to be produced.

If a tainted mind were to arise spontaneously after an untainted mind without a cause, then there would be no one who has attained the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); this fault could not be avoided.

For example, when a person on the path toward the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*) generates the path that serves as the antidote for the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-pratipakṣa-mārga*), the six worldly consciousnesses are incompatible with that path and cannot arise simultaneously; thus, all worldly consciousnesses have already ceased. Because their basis has been extinguished, the remaining afflictions also lose their functional capacity. Consequently, while the antidotal consciousness exists, the seeds of both minor and major afflictions remain present alongside it.
This argument is not established; if that were so, what would be the use of cultivating the path?
The treatise asks: Why is this?
Because it is liberated by its very nature (*svabhāva-vimukta*), the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) cannot arise or cease simultaneously with the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The commentary explains:

"Being of the same category constitutes 'nature. For example, while the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) possesses afflictions and the untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*) is free from them, despite this difference between having and not having afflictions, they are both of the same category of consciousness; therefore, it is called 'nature'."

Liberation (*vimukti*) has the meaning of separation. If the afflicted consciousness were to arise simultaneously with the untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*), its intrinsic nature would not attain liberation; for when the untainted consciousness arises, other consciousnesses necessarily cannot arise. Since they are thus separated from one another, it is called liberation.
The Treatise says:
Furthermore, at a later time, upon emerging from meditative equipoise, one correctly gives rise to a mundane mind.
The Commentary says:

Once those in training, such as the stream-enterers and others, have attained the path and subsequently emerge from meditative observation, do they give rise to supramundane thoughts or do they give rise to mundane thoughts?
If one gives rise to a supramundane mind, there would be no sense of emerging from contemplation;
if one gives rise to a mundane mind, by what cause could it arise?
The treatise says:
"The latencies of the various afflictions have long since ceased and been extinguished.
The commentary explains:
Since the latencies of the various afflictions have already been extinguished at the time one first enters meditative observation, how can a mundane mind arise without a cause?
The Treatise says:
The arising of the contaminated mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) would be established even without seeds.
The Commentary explains:

If this consciousness were not produced from causes, then the possibility of attaining liberation would be non-existent; even the deluded mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) would likewise have to arise without a cause.
The treatise states:
"Therefore, apart from the ālayavijñāna, the defilement of afflictions cannot be established."
The commentary states:
If you deny the existence of this consciousness, how can the meaning of defilement by the afflictions (*kleśa*) be established?
Chapter Two: The Impurity of Karma. The commentary states:
If a person negates the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna), it is logically impossible for that person to establish the meaning of karmic defilement.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, why is it that karmic defilement cannot be established?
The proposition that consciousness arises conditioned by volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) cannot be established.
The commentary states:
Volitional formations are of three types—meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable—and they arise and perish moment by moment.
If one were to exclude the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna), upon what could the functional capacity (śakti) be established?
If you say it is established within the six consciousnesses, this is not the case;

for the six consciousnesses cannot maintain the functional capacities of various karmas, as has already been fully demonstrated in the previous discussion on the defilement of afflictions (kleśasaṃkleśa).
The Treatise says:

If this principle did not exist, then the arising of *bhava* (existence) conditioned by *upādāna* (clinging) would also lack established meaning; therefore, the defilement of karma would not be established.
The Commentary explains:

If there were no consciousness possessing karmic efficacy—namely, the consciousness conditioned by volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and the existence (*bhava*) produced through clinging (*upādāna*)—it would be impossible for it to be established. Why is this?

This consciousness is permeated by the three types of volitional formations; because it follows the four types of clinging, and because it is perfected through such permeation, consciousness becomes existence.

If this consciousness is either extinguished or interrupted by another consciousness, its substance having already perished and its functional capacity likewise having ceased, in what place could one establish the functional capacity for these two types of karmic activity?
Therefore, the defilement of karma is not established.

As for the term "defiled," this karma is called defiled because it is associated with afflictions (*kleśa*); it is also called defiled because it arises from defilement; and it is called defiled because it can induce the defiled retribution of birth and death within the six realms of existence.
Chapter Three: On the Impurity of Birth. The commentary states:
It is logically untenable for defilement to arise apart from the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
Since this point has not yet been established, it shall now be explained.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, how is it that defilement arises?
This [proposition] is not established, because the linking of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*) is not established.
The commentary states:

If this birth were to cease, then by the power of karma, the subsequent retribution would be bound and the preceding retribution would be connected; however, this principle would not be established. Why is that?
The Treatise says:
If a person, having fallen from a non-quiescent stage while in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), gives rise to a defiled mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), only then does one obtain birth.
The Commentary explains:
Because one retreats from the non-quiescent stage and falls into a subsequent birth, it is called "retrogression and falling.

There are two ways of taking birth: either with an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) or without an intermediate state; here, the discussion specifically concerns those who take birth via the intermediate state.
If one is in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and is about to undergo rebirth, one must first give rise to a defiled consciousness (*kliṣṭa-vijñāna*) before rebirth can occur.
The treatise says:
This defiled consciousness ceases within the intermediate state.
The commentary states:
Herein, this defiled consciousness of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) takes the conditioned phenomena of rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*) as its object.
This consciousness ceases within the intermediate state.
Why is this? Because the aggregates of birth are free from defilement.
The treatise states:
"This consciousness relies upon the *kalala* and undergoes transformation and union within the mother’s womb to take birth.
The commentary explains:
"This 'consciousness' is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); because it is associated with the *kalala* at that single moment, it is said to 'rely upon the *kalala*.'"
This retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) differs from the previously mentioned defiled consciousness; therefore, it is said to "transform" (*pariṇāma*).

Because the functional power of past karma gives rise to wind, which unites the red and white elements and causes them to become one with the consciousness, it is said to "combine" (*saṃyoga*); this very process is termed "taking birth" (*upapatti*).
The treatise says:

If it were the case that only the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) transforms to become the basis for the *kalala* and subsequent stages, then there would be no such principle as the arising of a distinct mental consciousness within the mother’s womb.
The commentary states:
If you maintain that this consciousness which enters the *kalala* stage is merely the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*),
then if it is indeed the mental consciousness, are its arising from sense faculties and objects identical to or different from other instances of mental consciousness?
If you say they are identical, then at the moment this consciousness ceases, the kalala must also perish.
If you say they are different, then it should not be called "mental consciousness" (manovijñāna).

Why is this? Because the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) universally takes all three natures as its roots, whereas this consciousness takes only the defiled consciousness (kliṣṭamanas) as its root;
the mental consciousness takes the three periods of time as its objects, whereas the objects of this consciousness are unknowable.
The mental consciousness (manovijñāna) sometimes arises and sometimes ceases, whereas this consciousness is ever-present and never ceases; therefore, it is not the same as the mental consciousness.
Furthermore, if they were the same, this consciousness would not exist within the stages where there is no consciousness (asaṃjñika-bhūmi).
If this consciousness did not exist, one could not say that when entering the mindless meditative attainments, consciousness does not depart from the body.
Furthermore, if consciousness were absent, the body would necessarily perish; therefore, it cannot be said that this is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
If you say that this mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is indistinguishable [from the sense consciousnesses],
and that it is upon this consciousness— arising based on the sense faculties and their objects— that a distinct mental consciousness arises within the mother’s womb,
this argument is not tenable.
Why is this? The treatise states:
Within the mother’s womb, two types of consciousness do not arise simultaneously; such a principle does not exist.
The commentary states:
These words serve as proof for the preceding point that there is no simultaneous consciousness.
This is because two consciousnesses of the same nature necessarily do not arise together, as they cannot attend to objects simultaneously.

This consciousness, relying upon the *kalala* and coalescing with the red and white [elements], serves as their common substratum; while this consciousness exists, a distinct mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises simultaneously with it, yet this consciousness of the *kalala* does not constitute the mental consciousness.

Why is this? Because it constantly takes the defiled consciousness as its support; this supported consciousness, being defiled by desire and so forth, arises by taking the objects of existence as its objective condition.

Since the supporting consciousness is a result of maturation (*vipāka*) and is therefore exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), and since its objective condition is unknowable, it cannot be established as the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
If this were established as the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), then there would be no possibility of simultaneous arising.
If there were simultaneous arising, they would have to cognize identically and would likewise perish together.

If they cognized identically, there could be no meditative absorption involving the cessation of mind (*nirodhasamāpatti*), because while one cognizing mind perishes, another cognizing mind would remain.
If [the mind] were to cease together with [the body] into non-existence, then there would be spontaneous nirvāṇa without effort, because the mind would not arise again.
The treatise says:
"The transformed consciousness has already ceased."
The commentary states:
The consciousness that first undergoes birth has already transformed into the *kalala*.
The treatise says:
It cannot be established as the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The commentary states:
There are three reasons why the consciousness at the moment of initial birth cannot be established as the mental consciousness.
The Treatise says:
Because the basis is not pure.
The Commentary explains:
Mental consciousness arises from a mind of the three natures.
The initial consciousness at the moment of rebirth must necessarily arise from a defiled consciousness; that is, it relies upon what is impure.
The treatise says:
"Because it takes objects for a long duration.
The commentary explains:

From beginning to end, the consciousness at the moment of initial birth maintains its continuity in taking objects without interruption; the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), by contrast, easily detaches from its objects and is unstable.
The treatise says:
Because the object of cognition cannot be known.
The commentary explains:

The objective referent of the consciousness at the moment of initial rebirth cannot be known; however, the objective referents of the mental consciousness—namely, those belonging to the three periods of time and those not belonging to the three periods of time—can be known.
Because of these three distinct meanings, it cannot be established as being the mental consciousness.
The Treatise says:
"If this mental consciousness has already undergone transformation.
The Commentary explains:

If, after birth has been conceived, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) unites with the red and white elements, it transforms the preceding consciousness into a subsequent consciousness; thus, the subsequent consciousness differs from the preceding one.
The treatise states:
at that time, the mental consciousness becomes the kalala.
The commentary states:
It undergoes transformation because it has become the *kalala*.
The treatise says:
Is this consciousness itself the seed of all dharmas, or does it serve as the basis upon which other consciousnesses arise as the seeds of all dharmas?
The commentary states:
Should the consciousness that undergoes rebirth be considered the seed of all dharmas?
Should one rely on the consciousness that arises through appropriation (*upādāna*) as the consciousness that produces other consciousnesses, serving as the seed for all phenomena?
The treatise says:

If you maintain that the consciousness which has already undergone transformation is called the "all-seed consciousness," then it is none other than the *ālayavijñāna*; you are merely establishing it under a different name and calling it the "mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*).
The commentary states:

If you maintain that the consciousness at birth is the seed-consciousness, then it is identical in meaning to what I have taught; that is to say, you are describing the *ālaya-vijñāna* as the seed-consciousness.
You yourself merely do not call it the *ālaya-vijñāna*, but instead establish a different name for it, "mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*).
The Treatise says:
If you maintain that the consciousness which serves as the support is the all-seed consciousness.
The Commentary explains:
The consciousness that arises based on the consciousness at birth gives rise to further consciousnesses; this is called the "supported consciousness" and is the consciousness containing all seeds.
The treatise says:
Therefore, this consciousness becomes the cause for others by virtue of being their support.
The commentary states:
Since a distinct consciousness arises from another, it cannot itself serve as its own seed.
Therefore, this consciousness becomes a seed only by depending on the appropriating consciousness (*ādānavijñāna*), thereby functioning as a cause for others.
The treatise states:

If this supported consciousness were not the consciousness containing all seeds, then that which depends upon it could not be designated as the consciousness containing all seeds; thus, this meaning would not be established.
The commentary states:
A distinct consciousness cannot serve as its own seed; it becomes a seed only by depending on something else.

Since the supporting consciousness that undergoes rebirth is not itself the seed, how can the dependent distinct consciousness be established as the seed-consciousness? This principle is surely untenable.
The Treatise says:
Therefore, it is this consciousness that, upon taking rebirth, undergoes transformation to become the *kalala*; it is not the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The Commentary explains:
This consciousness is precisely the ālayavijñāna; it cannot be designated as the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The treatise states:
"It is solely the fruition (*vipāka*), and it is also the storehouse of all seeds (*sarvabījaka*)."
This meaning is established.
The commentary states:
It is called the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) because it arises from seeds; it is also called the seed consciousness (*bījāvijñāna*) because it is capable of maintaining the seeds.
If this is asserted, the meaning is established.
The treatise says:

Furthermore, if sentient beings have already taken rebirth, their ability to maintain the remaining sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) would be impossible apart from the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).
The commentary states:
Previously, the meaning of correctly undergoing birth was clarified; now, the meaning subsequent to undergoing birth is further clarified.

Previously, it was clarified that sentient beings are within the womb; now, it is clarified that sentient beings have emerged from the womb, and thus it is said that "sentient beings have already taken up residence in a new life."
If sentient beings have already taken birth, they necessarily possess three characteristics:
first, they maintain existence without cessation; second, they universally sustain the various sense faculties; and third, their essence is the retributive neutral (avipāka-avyākṛta).
If one were to exclude the ālayavijñāna, these three meanings could not be established.
The treatise asks:
For what reason must the remaining consciousnesses necessarily have distinct supports?
The commentary states:
To cite reasoning as proof, it asks, "For what reason?
Among the six consciousnesses, any one consciousness is referred to as "the remaining consciousnesses."

Visual consciousness necessarily relies upon the eye-faculty as its support, and so on up to tactile consciousness, which necessarily relies upon the body-faculty; this clarifies their distinct supports and demonstrates that they cannot collectively maintain [the body].
The Treatise says:
"It does not endure for long.
The Commentary explains:

Among the five consciousnesses, whichever faculty serves as its respective support, if that consciousness can maintain it, this consciousness will not remain stable for long; for its continuity is easily disrupted—either because it is destroyed when within a state of non-consciousness, or because it is interrupted by the arising of other consciousnesses.
The Treatise says:
If these material sense-faculties were devoid of a supporting consciousness, they could not even be established.
The Commentary explains:
Just as the physical sense-faculties of a dead person rot and decay because they lack the sustaining power of consciousness;
if the sense-faculties were to exist apart from the sustaining consciousness, this same [process of decay] would apply to them as well.
This argument is also not established.
The Treatise says:

Furthermore, this consciousness and name-and-form depend upon one another; just as bundles of reeds stand together by leaning on each other, so too this consciousness would not be established [without them].
The Commentary explains:
In the sūtras, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, said:
"Consciousness arises dependent on name-and-form (nāmarūpa), and name-and-form arises dependent on consciousness.
Here, "name" refers to the four non-material aggregates (skandhas), and "form" refers to the kalala.
What is that which depends on name-and-form?

Consciousness takes this name-and-form as its basis; through moment-to-moment transmission, it arises in a continuous stream without interruption, capable of sustaining name-and-form so that it is accomplished and remains indestructible. This consciousness is called "that which depends on name-and-form."
If one were to deny the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) and take the six consciousnesses as the consciousness, this principle would not be established.
Apart from the ālayavijñāna, which among the six consciousnesses would it be?
What does this question intend to demonstrate?
It intends to demonstrate that other consciousnesses do not constitute the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*).
The treatise says:
Furthermore, if apart from the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), the consciousness-nutriment (*vijñānāhāra*) would not be established for all sentient beings seeking birth or already born.
The commentary states:
These words are intended to demonstrate that the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is capable of acting as the consciousness-nutriment for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

Why is this? The Buddha, the World-Honored One, has taught that there are four kinds of nutriment; these four nutriments are taught for the sake of enabling the continuity and subsistence of sentient beings who have been born or seek to be born.
What are the four?
There are four nutriments: first, the nutriment of physical food; second, the nutriment of contact; third, the nutriment of volition; and fourth, the nutriment of consciousness.
As for the nutriment of physical food, its characteristic is transformation. Why is this so?
If this "lump" (kavaḍa), when transformed, can perform the function of benefiting the body, it is called food by the mouthful (kavaḍīkārāhāra).
As for food by contact (sparśāhāra), its characteristic is that it depends upon sense objects.
Because it depends upon various objects such as forms (rūpa) and so forth, it can perform the function of benefiting the body; thus, it is called food by contact.
The nutriment of volition (*manosaṃcetanāhāra*) has the characteristic of aspiring for attainment.

This aspiration, when successful, can perform beneficial functions for the body; it is like a person suffering from hunger or thirst who reaches a place where food and drink are available, aspiring to obtain them so that the body does not perish—this is called the nutriment of volition.
The nutriment of consciousness has the characteristic of sustaining.

Because this consciousness sustains the body, it remains intact and does not perish; if there were no consciousness to sustain it, the body would immediately rot and decay like that of a dead person. This is called the nutriment of consciousness.
Therefore, you too should accept this meaning of the consciousness-nutriment (*vijñānāhāra*), for it is capable of performing beneficial functions for the body.

Among these four nutriments, the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*) belongs to the six consciousnesses; the nutriment of volition (*manaḥsaṃcetanāhāra*) belongs to the mental faculty’s aspiration for attainment; and the nutriment of edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) belongs to form and does not concern the mind. Within these three meanings, to which meaning does the nutriment of consciousness belong?
If you do not assert the existence of the *ālayavijñāna*, on what basis do you explain this consciousness as being "food"?

Furthermore, when a person is asleep without dreaming, or when the mind is fainting, or has entered the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the six consciousnesses have already ceased; and since the three kinds of food—edible food, volitional food, and contact-food—are also absent, what phenomenon sustains this body so that it does not perish?
If there were no ālayavijñāna to sustain it, this body would perish; therefore, one should know that the ālayavijñāna must certainly serve as the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*).
The treatise asks: Why is this so?

If one were apart from the retributive consciousness (vipākavijñāna), none of the individual consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and so forth, would be capable of performing the function of "nutriment" for sentient beings born within the three realms; therefore, such a capacity is not observed.
The commentary states:

If one were to exclude the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna), then among the six consciousnesses, in whichever single consciousness one might look for sentient beings already born within the three realms, one would not find any such consciousness possessing the functional capacity to perform the act of eating.
Therefore, it should be known that the claim that other consciousnesses constitute the nutriment of consciousness is not established.
The treatise says:
If a person dies from this life and is reborn in a higher, tranquil plane (*śāntabhūmi*), they take birth there by means of a distracted and defiled mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The commentary states:
Within the meditative stages (*dhyāna-bhūmi*), if one were to undergo rebirth apart from the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), this principle would not be established.
For a person to undergo rebirth necessarily depends upon a defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-citta*).

If one is born in a tranquil stage (śānta-bhūmi), it must necessarily be by means of an afflicted, distracted mind; "afflicted" means being defiled by the afflictions (kleśa) of that very tranquil stage.
What are the characteristics of these afflictions?
Regarding the "taste of meditative concentration" and so forth,
these afflictions necessarily exist in the tranquil stages (*śānta-bhūmi*).
If a person dies from a distracted stage (*vikṣipta-bhūmi*) and is reborn in a higher realm using a mind belonging to a lower, distracted stage, such a thing is logically impossible.
Why is this? Because all those who undergo birth necessarily exist in a state of distracted consciousness (*vikṣipta-citta*).
If one were separated from the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), this distracted and fluctuating consciousness could not be found.

If it is a person who has become free from desire, they will be reborn from this Desire Realm into the Form or Formless Realms. Regarding those who are defiled, it is the mind of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) that gives rise to the afflictions of the higher realms; regarding those who are distracted, it is the consciousness at the moment of actual birth. As for being born there, it consists of both the preparatory birth and the actual birth.
The treatise states:
It is not established that this defiled, distracted consciousness possesses seeds other than the retributive consciousness within the meditative stages.
The commentary explains:

If a sensation is currently arising, it necessarily possesses four characteristics: it takes defilement as its root, distraction as its state, retribution as its substance, and remaining seeds as its functional capacity.
Since these four meanings cannot be established apart from the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), one should believe that the *ālayavijñāna* exists. Why is this?

Within this consciousness, the perfuming of the mind belonging to the tranquil stages has existed since beginningless time with a remainder yet to be exhausted; by virtue of this functional capacity, there are seeds within the tranquil stages, and through them, the resultant consciousness of dispersion and movement (*vikṣepavipākavijñāna*) undergoes rebirth therein.
The Treatise says:
Furthermore, if sentient beings are born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
The Commentary says:
This demonstrates that one is already liberated from the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
The treatise states:
"Apart from the resultant consciousness containing all seeds (*sarvabījaka-vipākavijñāna*)."
The commentary states:
If the fundamental consciousness did not exist,
or if it truly exists but you deny its existence by asserting that it does not, this is therefore called "separation."
The treatise says:
"If one gives rise to an afflicted mind or a wholesome mind.
The commentary explains:

If, within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one gives rise to a defiled mind that relishes the flavor of concentration, or gives rise to a contaminated wholesome mind of a higher realm (*ūrdhvabhūmi*), the treatise states:
"Then there would be neither seeds nor a support; both the defiled and the wholesome consciousnesses would fail to be established."
The commentary states:
"Lacking seeds" means lacking causes; because there are no causes, there is no basis for support.
Furthermore, if there are no seeds, then there are no causes; if there are no causes, from what could anything arise?
If there were no basis of support, how could [the mental continuum] persist? Why is this?

These two minds are subsumed by the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna); therefore, they arise from their own seeds and, by depending upon the fundamental consciousness, they are able to persist in a continuous stream.
The Treatise says:
If one gives rise to an untainted mind within the formless realm, all remaining mundane minds have already ceased; thus, one should abandon this path.
The Commentary explains:
If a person has already been born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) and gives rise to a supramundane mind, their mundane mind must necessarily cease.

If they were devoid of the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna), they would have to abandon the retribution of the formless realm and enter nirvana without remainder (nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa) without any effort.
Since this meaning does not exist, one cannot deny the existence of this consciousness.
The treatise says:

If a sentient being is born in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) and gives rise to a mind of the Sphere of Nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana) or an untainted mind (anāsravacitta), they immediately relinquish both spheres.
The commentary states:

If a noble being is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), there are times when they give rise to an untainted mind based on the stage of the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana). This is because the mind of the sphere of nothingness is lucid, whereas the mind of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is obscure.

When this person cultivates the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) on the stage of clear comprehension, upon attaining the untainted mind, they immediately relinquish both the stages of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) and the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
The treatise says:

Why is this? Because the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) is a supramundane mind, the path of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is not its support, nor is the path of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) its support.
The commentary states:
Because the first and second paths are mundane phenomena (*laukika-dharma*), they cannot serve as the support for an outflow-free mind (*anāsrava-citta*).
When such a person is born in another stage (*bhūmi*) and takes up a mind belonging to that other stage, these two paths likewise do not serve as the support for this [new] mind.
Why is this? Because this mind is lucid and clear, it does not rely upon the first path;
having already abandoned the second path, the second path likewise cannot serve as a support for this mind.
The Treatise says:
Even proceeding directly toward nirvana is not a basis.
The Commentary explains:
Because there exists the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), yet the afflictions (*kleśa*) still remain;

since these three points demonstrate that a basis (*āśraya*) is thus not established, if one were to depart from the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), upon what dharma would such an untainted mind depend?
The Treatise says:
Furthermore, if a person has already performed wholesome or unwholesome karma.
The Commentary says:
If a person performs the ten wholesome actions, such as abstaining from killing, within this world, they will certainly receive the retribution of birth among humans or devas.
If they perform the ten unwholesome actions, such as killing, they will certainly receive the retribution of birth in the four realms of existence.
The treatise states:

When one properly relinquishes the life-force, it would be impossible for the process of sequential cooling to occur based on the ālayavijñāna, whether from the top down or from the bottom up, were it to be separated from the ālayavijñāna.
The commentary states:
At the time of death, if this person possesses determinate wholesome karma, they will certainly ascend; if they possess determinate unwholesome karma, they will certainly descend.

If you do not believe in the existence of the foundational consciousness (ālayavijñāna), how could the sequential occurrence of cold sensations—either descending from the top or ascending from the bottom—be established within this supporting body?
If the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) did not exist, how could it be established that this fundamental consciousness is able to maintain the five sense faculties?

If the fundamental consciousness were to abandon the body, then at the point where it is abandoned, tactile sensations of cold would arise in succession; that place of abandonment would then become a dead body.
The Treatise says:
Therefore, the arising of defilement cannot be established apart from the retributive consciousness that contains all seeds.
The Commentary explains:
Birth-defilement (*saṃkleśa*) refers to birth itself, the acquisition of birth, and the basis for its maintenance;
it is collectively termed "defilement" because these constitute the cause and fruit of defilement.
Furthermore, it is called "defilement" because saṃsāra stands in opposition to nirvāṇa.
Because the fundamental consciousness is the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*), it is called the "seed";
because it is the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), it is called "retribution.
Because it is the cause of others, it is called the "seed."
Because it is the fruit of that [other cause], it is called "retribution" (*vipāka*).
If one were separated from this consciousness, the arising of defilement would not be established.
Chapter Four: On Worldly Purity. The commentary states:
By such reasoning, the pure categories (*śukla-pakṣa*) of the world cannot be established; this shall now be explained.
The treatise says:
In what way are the pure categories of the world not established?
"If sentient beings have not yet abandoned desire for the desire realm and have not yet attained the mind of the form realm.
The commentary states:
"If a person wishes to abandon desire for the desire realm and attain the mind of the form realm, they therefore cultivate preparatory application (*prayoga*)."
There are two kinds of practitioners: first, those who are established in contemplation; second, those who have newly begun their practice.
Those established in contemplation are situated within the wisdoms of hearing and reflection.
The wisdoms of hearing and reflection each have three grades; because one cultivates them so that they increase, it is called "preparatory application" (*prayoga*).
One who first initiates practice is precisely one who first cultivates the wisdom of hearing.

These two individuals have not yet abandoned desire for the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), and neither has attained the "attainment of non-arrival" (*anāgamya-samādhi*), which is the mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
The treatise states:
First, they give rise to a wholesome mind of the desire realm, seeking to become free from desire for the realm of desire, and practice the contemplative mind.
The commentary states:

If a person has not yet attained the mind of the form realm (rūpadhātu-citta), they are said to have previously given rise to a wholesome mind of the desire realm (kāmadhātu) while within the wisdom derived from hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā).

Within that wisdom derived from hearing, seeking the contemplative mind that seeks detachment from the desires of the desire realm constitutes the wisdom of reflection and cultivation (cintāmayī- and bhāvanāmayī-prajñā).
In order to become detached from the desire realm, one practices the wisdom of reflection and the wisdom of cultivation.
The commentary states:
Because this preparatory mind of the desire realm does not arise and cease simultaneously with the mind of the form realm, it is not susceptible to perfuming (*vāsanā*).
The commentary states:
The wisdoms of hearing and reflection each have three grades, which constitute the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Why is it that this mind does not arise and cease simultaneously with the mind of the form realm?
Because they differ in (1) coarseness and subtlety, (2) movement and stillness, (3) intrinsic nature and cultivation, and (4) bondage and liberation, they cannot arise and cease simultaneously.
If they do not coexist, then a mind of the form realm cannot permeate a mind of the desire realm.
The treatise says:
Therefore, a wholesome mind of the desire realm is not the seed of a wholesome mind of the form realm.
The commentary states:
Since the mind of the desire realm is not perfumed by the mind of the form realm, it is not the seed of the mind of the form realm.
Consequently, when the mind of the form realm arises, it would lack any causal conditions.
If there were no causes and conditions, how could it arise?

If you say that within beginningless saṃsāra, a mind of the form realm has already arisen such that its retribution has not yet matured and this seed has not yet been extinguished, and is thus able to act as the cause for the present mind of the form realm.
This interpretation is not correct. Why?
The treatise says:
A past mind of the form realm, being separated by immeasurable other births and other mental states, cannot later be established as the seed of a tranquil consciousness, because it no longer exists.
The commentary states:
Within the beginningless cycle of birth and death, the mind previously produced in the form realm serves as the seed.
Since this seed is not sustained by any [substantial] entity, it perishes immediately upon arising.

Within the six realms of existence, there are immeasurable births; within each single birth, there are immeasurable moments of mind that separate it from the mind previously arisen. Since these seeds have long since ceased and perished, how can this [present mind] be established as the cause of a mind in the form realm?
The Treatise says:
Therefore, this meaning is established.
The Commentary says:
Since the thesis established by you is not proven, the thesis established by me is proven.
How is it proven?
The treatise says:

This refers to the seeds of all [phenomena] within the tranquil mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), which have been transmitted in succession as the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*); this is established as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
The commentary states:

Within beginningless saṃsāra, the perfuming (*vāsanā*) of the non-attained concentrations (*asamāpatti-samādhi*) and the four dhyānas has taken the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) as its seed. Being sustained by the fundamental consciousness, it has been transmitted in continuous succession down to the present without being extinguished; therefore, it can be established as the causal condition for the tranquil mind of the form realm.
If a tranquil mind of the form realm arises, it arises from its own seeds; therefore, it is not like what you maintain, which lacks causes and conditions.
If past-life seeds are taken as the causes and conditions, then what is the use of the wisdoms of hearing and reflection cultivated in the present?
The Treatise says:
This wholesome mind of preparatory application is established as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
The Commentary explains:
This preparatory mind is not devoid of effort; by the predominant power of this [effort], the mind of the form realm arises.
If this preparatory mind were absent, one would be unable to destroy the desires of the desire realm.
If the desires of the desire realm have not been extinguished, the seeds of the form realm cannot produce a present mind of the form realm.
Thus, while preparatory effort may serve as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for a mind of the form realm, it cannot serve as a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
The treatise states:
This principle should be understood to apply to all stages of detachment from desire (*vairāgya-bhūmi*).
Thus, the meaning of the worldly category of purification (*laukika-vyavadāna*) cannot be established apart from the retributive consciousness containing all seeds (*sarva-bījaka vipāka-vijñāna*).
The commentary states:

If one considers the detachment from the desire realm through the four dhyānas, or the detachment from the form realm through the four formless attainments, the causes and conditions (hetu-pratyaya) and dominant conditions (adhipati-pratyaya) for the mind of the form realm, as well as the causes and conditions and dominant conditions for the mind of the formless realm, should all be distinguished in this same manner.
Chapter Five: On Supramundane Purity. The Treatise says:
How can the supramundane category of purity be established if it is not found apart from the ālayavijñāna?
The commentary says:
The meaning of this shall now be explained.
The treatise states:
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, said:
"From hearing the voices of others and from one's own correct reflection—through these two causes, right view arises.
The commentary explains:
In the Chapter on Purification, right view is the foremost.
By what factors does this right view take its dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*)?
It is from hearing the voice of another and from correct reflection; these two causes constitute the dominant conditions for right view.
Each of these two causes has four meanings: first, there is right view subsumed under the wisdom of hearing, which takes hearing the voice of another as its cause;
second, there is right view subsumed under the wisdom of reflection, which takes correct contemplation as its cause.
Second, if it is the right view of a śrāvaka, it has the hearing of sounds from others as its cause;
if it is the right view of a pratyekabuddha or a bodhisattva, it has correct reflection as its cause.
Third, regarding those of dull faculties as the first phrase, and regarding those of sharp faculties as the second phrase.
Fourth, regarding wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) as the first phrase, and regarding wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) as the second phrase.
From these two causes, right view arises; these two causes serve as the dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for right view.
What is now termed "cause" is a general designation, wherein conditions are spoken of as causes.
The Treatise says:

This hearing of another's voice and correct reflection cannot permeate the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) and the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*), or both the ear- and mental consciousnesses together.
The Explanation says:
"Other sounds" refers to the Dharma-gates established by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
"Hearing other sounds" means understanding them as they are heard; this is the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
"Correct reflection" means discerning right from wrong according to what has been heard; this is the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).

These two types of wisdom do not have the sense of being perfumed individually by the ear-consciousness and the mental-consciousness, nor do they have the sense of being perfumed by them both together.
The treatise asks: Why is this so?
The commentary asks:
For what reason can these two types of wisdom not permeate the consciousnesses of the ear and so forth?
The treatise says:
If a person understands the Dharma as they have heard it and correctly contemplates it, at that time auditory consciousness cannot arise.
The commentary explains:

Once a person has heard the voice of another, subsequently there arises the wisdom resulting from hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī prajñā*). Since this wisdom of hearing and reflection belongs to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), auditory consciousness cannot arise at that time; therefore, the wisdom of hearing and reflection cannot perfume the auditory consciousness.
The Treatise says:
"Mental consciousness, too, cannot arise.
The Commentary explains:
Right view is about to arise, yet the mental consciousness associated with wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) cannot arise either.
The treatise states:
"Because it is interrupted by other distracted, discursive consciousnesses."
The commentary states: Why can it not arise?
Because intermediate states of distracted and discursive consciousness arise in between, this wisdom consisting of reflection cannot arise immediately.
The Treatise says:
"If it arises in association with right reflection.
The Commentary explains:
This clarifies the wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī prajñā*) at the moment when the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) is about to arise.
The treatise states:
"This mental consciousness has long since ceased."
The commentary states:
The previously arisen wisdom consisting of reflection has long since ceased and passed away.
The treatise says:
"Once that which is perfumed by hearing and the common perfuming have ceased.
The commentary explains:
"Previously, at the initial stage, the wisdom of reflection (cintāmayī-prajñā) perfumed by extensive learning, together with its perfuming, both pass away into the past."
The Treatise asks:
How is it that a subsequent consciousness arises with a preceding consciousness as its seed?
The Explanation states:
The wisdom of reflection (cintāmayī-prajñā) acquired at the initial stage cannot serve as the seed for the production of subsequent wisdom of reflection.

Since the preceding wisdom of reflection has long since ceased and been interrupted by other intervening mental states, its functional capacity cannot be transmitted from the prior wisdom of reflection into the subsequent one.
Later, when the wisdom born of reflection is weak, it can no longer induce right view to arise; furthermore, this cannot be said to be the seed that produces the consciousness of right view.
This section clarifies that there is no principle of mutual perfuming between preceding and succeeding moments; it does not yet discuss the absence of simultaneous mutual perfuming.
The treatise states:
Furthermore, the mundane mind associated with right reflection and the supramundane pure mind associated with right view can never arise together nor cease together.
The commentary states:

Right reflection and right cultivation of wisdom—from the four foundations of mindfulness up to the supreme mundane dharma—constitute this stage; because this mind has not yet realized the vision of the Four Truths, it is called a mundane mind.

Because one has already realized and seen the Four Noble Truths, it is called the supramundane dharma that is devoid of intrinsic nature; because it is a dharma attained through cultivation, it is called the pure mind.

Right view is the first factor among the Eightfold Noble Path, and this right view is inseparable from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. Because the pure mind is attained through cultivation, the thirty-seven factors arise; because the thirty-seven factors arise, one attains the supramundane.
Since beginningless time, there has been no sense of simultaneous arising and simultaneous ceasing between the mundane and supramundane minds, because their natures are mutually contradictory.
The treatise states:
"Therefore, this mundane mind is not subject to perfuming by the pure mind."
The commentary states:
Since they do not arise and perish simultaneously, there is no sense in which they can mutually perfuse one another.
The treatise says:
Since there is no perfuming, it cannot become a supramundane seed.
The commentary states:
If the wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) were perfumed by a supramundane mind, it could become a supramundane seed.
Since there is no sense of being perfumed, the doctrine of supramundane seeds cannot be established.
The treatise states:
"Therefore, if one is separated from the retributive consciousness containing all seeds, the supramundane pure mind also cannot be established."
The commentary states:
If one were separated from the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna), the supramundane mind would lack both cause and condition, and thus could not be established.
The treatise says:
Why is this? Because within this [state], the perfuming of hearing and reflection lacks the capacity to encompass the seeds of supramundane perfuming.
The commentary states:
Within this context, specifically within the wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), there is the cultivation through hearing (*śruta-vāsanā*).
If the cultivation of supramundane mind has already arisen from the beginning, it is possible for this wisdom of reflection to take up that supramundane cultivation as its seed.

Since one has never previously generated the mental cultivation of wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) that perfumes the transcendental mind, it is logically impossible to say that the transcendental perfuming, held by this wisdom of reflection, serves as its seed.
The Treatise says:
How does the retributive consciousness containing all seeds become the cause of the impure category?
If it can act as the cause for the supramundane pure mind that serves as the antidote to defilement.
The commentary states:
The fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) should not be established as the cause of the impure category.
If one posits the fundamental consciousness as the supramundane cause that serves as the antidote to defilement, then it cannot be taken as the cause of the impure category.

The category of impurity consists of the truth of origination and the truth of suffering; because it contains the seeds of karma and afflictions, it is the truth of origination, and because it can give rise to birth and death, it is the truth of suffering.
That which serves as the antidote to defilement is eliminated; alternatively, that which acts as the cause for supramundane mind gives rise to the Path and extinguishes delusion.

Since the arising of the Path is diametrically opposed to the category of impurity (*aśubha*), and since it has already been established as the antidote to defilement and the cause for supramundane mind, one should not further describe it as a cause for the category of impurity.
The Treatise says:
Since this supramundane mind has never previously arisen or been cultivated, it certainly lacks any perfuming.
The Commentary explains:
Since beginningless time, the supramundane mind has never arisen; since it does not arise, how much less can it be cultivated?
Therefore, it is certain and beyond doubt that the supramundane mind cannot infuse the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
The treatise says:
If there were no perfuming (vāsanā), from what cause would this supramundane mind arise?
The commentary explains:
If there were perfuming acting as a seed, the supramundane mind could have a cause.
Since there is no perfuming, the supramundane mind would arise without a cause.
The Treatise says:
You should now provide an answer.
The Commentary says:
Since the logical principle of its having a cause has not yet been seen, the author demands an answer.
The treatise states:
Because the seeds are the permeations of correct hearing that flow from the most pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the supramundane mind is able to arise.
The commentary states:
It is called the "most pure dharma-realm" (*suviśuddhadharmadhātu*) in order to distinguish it from the dharma-realm attained by those of the two vehicles.
In what way does it differ from that which is attained by the two vehicles?
Because the afflictive obscurations and cognitive obscurations within this dharmadhātu are extinguished without remainder, it is said to be "most pure.

As for the dharmadhātu, its essence consists of the three natures of non-essence (niḥsvabhāvatā), encompassing both the mode of being as it is (yathābhūta) and the full extent of phenomena (yāvadbhāva).
That which flows forth refers to the correct teaching of the True Dharma, namely the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
Correct hearing means listening with single-minded reverence and without error.

From this correct hearing, the meaning of the six kinds of perfuming arises within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*); if supramundane mind is to arise, it must necessarily be produced on account of this.
The Treatise says:
Is this perfuming of the wisdom derived from hearing of the same nature as the ālayavijñāna, or is it of a different nature?
The Explanation says:
If that were so, what would be the fault?
The treatise says:
If it were of the nature of the ālayavijñāna, how could it function as the seed for the antidote to this consciousness?
If they are not of the same nature, upon what dharma does this seed of the wisdom of hearing rely?
The commentary states:
If it were of the nature of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), how could that very nature act as its own antidote to destroy itself?
If they were of different natures, this perfuming of the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) would have to have a separate basis.
The treatise says:

Up until the stage of the Buddhas’ unsurpassed enlightenment, this arising perfuming of the wisdom derived from hearing resides in whichever basis it may occupy; therein, it arises together with the resultant consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).
The commentary states:
From what does this functional capacity of hearing arise?
To what stage does its continuity extend?

For all bodhisattvas, from the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) upward until the state of unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*), this functional capacity of hearing persists in succession without being lost.
That which has not yet arisen is "origination" (*jāti*); that which has already arisen and has not yet ceased is "abiding" (*sthiti*).

Regarding its arising and abiding: within the six realms of existence, depending upon whichever single realm one inhabits, it arises together with the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) within the five-aggregate body of that particular realm, continuing in succession without ceasing throughout the duration of that life.
Although it is of a different nature from the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), it arises simultaneously with it.
The treatise says:
"It is like water and milk."
The commentary states:
Although water and milk are blended together, their natures are different yet they can arise simultaneously.
The treatise says:
This perfuming by hearing is not the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), because it has already become the seed that serves as the antidote to this consciousness.
The commentary states:
Since this function of hearing is the antidote to the fundamental consciousness, it is of a different nature from the fundamental consciousness.
Although they do not share the same nature, because they are inseparable, they always arise together.
What serves as the antidote to the fundamental consciousness?
The treatise says:
In this context, based upon inferior-grade perfuming, medium-grade perfuming arises;
based upon medium-grade perfuming, superior-grade perfuming arises.
The commentary states:
Within this very basis and within the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna), there are three grades of the functional capacity of the perfuming of hearing (śrutavāsanā):

namely, inferior, intermediate, and superior. The inferior corresponds to the wisdom of hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā); the intermediate corresponds to the wisdom of reflection (cintāmayī-prajñā); and the superior corresponds to the wisdom of cultivation (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā).
Furthermore, there are three grades; within each of the three types of wisdom, these are further divided into three grades.

There are another three grades, namely: the grade of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*), the grade of the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), and the grade of penetration (*abhisamaya*).
There are three meanings of "hearing" (*śruta*): first, the equipment for hearing, which refers to the names, phrases, and syllables expressed by sounds;
second, the essence of hearing, which refers to auditory consciousness;
and third, the fruit of hearing, which refers to the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) and the Dharma-gates realized through that wisdom.
These three grades of perfuming through hearing arise according to their respective grades, each capable of counteracting one grade of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
If a lower grade arises, it can counteract an upper grade of the fundamental consciousness; likewise, if an upper grade arises, it can counteract a lower grade of the fundamental consciousness.
The Treatise says:
For what reason?
The Commentary says:
This involves three points:
first, for what reason are there three grades?
Second, for what reason do they arise from one another?
Third, why is it able to act as an antidote?
The treatise says:
Because of the repeated application of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
The commentary states:

The frequent mention [of "repeatedly"] reveals that the application (*prayoga*) is constant and uninterrupted; it shows that one exerts effort rather than practicing in a lax or intermittent manner. Because of this repeated application, because there are three grades, and because the characteristics of the stages arise, the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) is attained.
If it is established that three grades and their characteristics arise through repeated application, this point is beyond doubt.
How, then, does repeated application serve as the antidote to the fundamental consciousness?
The Treatise says:
It should be understood that these seeds of the Dharma-body consist of the perfuming of hearing, whether they be of inferior, middling, or superior grade.
The Commentary explains:
What dharma is called the dharmakāya?
The transformation of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti) is called the dharmakāya.
What are the characteristics of this transformation of the basis?

The maturation through the cultivation of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and the perfections (*pāramitā*), characterized by the merit of transcendence and the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), is accomplished through four factors resulting from the perfuming of hearing (*śruta-vāsanā*):

first, faith and delight in the Mahāyāna is the seed of great purity; second, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) is the seed of the Great Self; third, the vessel-like samādhi of space is the seed of great bliss; and fourth, great compassion is the seed of the Great Constant.

Eternity, bliss, self, and purity are the four virtues of the Dharma-body; these—the hearing-perfuming and the four dharmas—serve as the seeds for these four virtues, and when the four virtues are perfected, the fundamental consciousness is entirely exhausted.
Since the perfuming of hearing (*śruta-vāsanā*) and the four dharmas serve as the seeds for the four virtues, they are able to counteract the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*).

The perfuming of hearing is precisely the seed of the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*); as the practice of the Dharma, the perfuming of hearing brings about the fivefold Dharma-body where it did not previously exist.
Furthermore, because that which did not previously exist now exists, it is precisely the seed of the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañcadharmakāya*).

The perfuming of hearing (*śrutavāsanā*) is merely the seed for the path of the four virtues; while the path of the four virtues can bring about the manifestation of the four virtues, the four virtues themselves are primordially existent and do not arise from seeds. They are called "seeds" only by virtue of being designated as such based on their causes.
The Treatise says:
Because it arises as the antidote to the ālayavijñāna, it is therefore not included within the nature of the ālayavijñāna.
The Commentary explains:

This perfuming of hearing does not arise for the purpose of augmenting the fundamental consciousness; rather, it arises for the purpose of diminishing the power and momentum of the fundamental consciousness, and thus it is able to act as its antidote.
