Because it is contrary in nature to the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), it is not subsumed within the nature of the fundamental consciousness.
This demonstrates that the Dharma-body is the fruit of the perfuming of hearing (*śrutavāsanā*).
The treatise states:
"Because it flows forth from the most pure supramundane dharma-realm.
The commentary explains:
It is called "supramundane" because it transcends the seven kinds of the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and extinguishes the three kinds of the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).

This refers to the suchness of the three natures, which is fundamentally free from defilement; because it subsequently becomes separated from the stains of the three obstacles, it is called "most pure.
Since the paths of the three vehicles arise from this dharma, it is termed a "realm" (dhātu).
Because this perfuming of hearing flows forth from the most pure dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), it is not subsumed within the nature of the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna).

This demonstrates that the dharma-body is the cause of the perfuming of hearing; since the cause of the perfuming of hearing differs from the fundamental consciousness, its fruit likewise differs from the fundamental consciousness.
Is the essence of the permeation of hearing the same as or different from the fundamental consciousness?
The treatise states:
Although it is a mundane phenomenon, it gives rise to the supramundane mind.
The commentary states:

Although the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is a mundane phenomenon, it can penetrate the suchness (*tathatā*) of the Four Noble Truths; because it serves as the antidote to the obscurations of the Four Noble Truths, it becomes a supramundane mind.
The permeation of hearing is also like this: although it is a mundane dharma, because both its cause and its fruit are supramundane dharmas, it also becomes a supramundane mind.
The treatise asks: Why is this?
The commentary states:
Why is it that this dharma is exclusively supramundane and not a mundane dharma?
Because there are four kinds of remedies (*pratipakṣa*).
The Treatise says:
When this seed of the supramundane pure mind has not yet arisen, it serves as the antidote to all manifest afflictions (*paryavasthāna*).
The Commentary explains:
This first [category] is for the purpose of revealing the antidote to aversion.

Through this, the clear realization of correct principles via the permeation of hearing enables one to know the faults of all sense objects; thus, one develops aversion toward what is irrational and toward all sense objects. This mind of aversion can counteract the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*), and because it is the functional power of the permeation of hearing, it is called the "seed of the antidote to aversion."

This refers to the perfuming of hearing (*śruta-vāsanā*); it is called the supramundane pure mind (*lokottara-śuddha-citta*) of the bodhisattva who has not yet known what he seeks to know. Prior to the arising of this mind, it is the perfuming of hearing, belonging to the stage of wisdom consisting of hearing and reflection (*śruta-mayī-prajñā* and *cintā-mayī-prajñā*).

During the stages of hearing and reflection, prior to attaining the wisdom derived from hearing and reflection, afflictions to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation constantly arise as active mental states due to inverted views and inverted perceptions; these give rise to the four types of evil karma, which result in the retribution of the four miserable realms.
By attaining this dharma, afflictions that have not yet arisen, as well as karma and its retributive results, shall all fail to arise.
The Treatise says:
It is the antidote to birth in any of the evil realms.
The commentary states:
This second [point] reveals the counteractive agent that eliminates [afflictions].

Through the cultivation of hearing (*śruta-vāsanā*), which arises and adheres to the mental continuum, it causes the continuum to enter the stage of the correctly determined group (*samyaktva-niyāma*). As the cultivation of hearing arises and perishes in succession, it severs and blocks the arising of unwholesome dharmas, thereby preventing birth in the four evil destinies and inducing birth in the auspicious paths.
In the past, one may have committed evil karma that would have led to birth in the four miserable realms; by means of this Dharma, it is extinguished and will no longer be experienced.
The Treatise says:
"It is the remedy for the decay and destruction of all unwholesome conduct."
The commentary states:
This third [point] is for the purpose of revealing the antidote that brings about distancing.
The evil karma of retributive fruition created throughout beginningless saṃsāra can cause one to fall into the four miserable destinies at the time of that subsequent retribution.
This dharma is able to transform [the karmic process], causing future retribution to become non-retribution; this is precisely the meaning of "decaying.
The Treatise says:
It is able to lead the continuity [of consciousness] to be born in a place where one may accord with, meet, and serve the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
The commentary states:
This fourth [point] is intended to reveal the basis for the inclusion of the antidote.
It refers to that which can lead the continuity of the five aggregates to be born in a place where Buddhas and Bodhisattvas reside, thereby enabling one to accord with and attend upon them.
Meeting by chance is called "encountering"; serving from beginning to end without ever parting is called "attending.

This person relies upon a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); for the sake of generating roots of goodness, the spiritual friend practices the means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) of generosity and kind speech; for the sake of maturing those roots of goodness, they practice the means of attraction of beneficial conduct;
and for the sake of attaining liberation through those roots of goodness, they practice the means of attraction of purposeful action.
The cultivation of the gathering through common benefit relies on the gathering to manifest the four meanings of extensive learning (*bahuśruta*):

first, the basis of extensive learning, which is the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); second, the cause of extensive learning, which is the bodhicitta; third, the purification of extensive learning, which is practicing according to the teachings; and fourth, the fruit of extensive learning, which is self-benefit and the benefit of others.
The first one has the meaning of "encountering," while the latter three have the meaning of "phenomena.
Furthermore, the first three types of remedies depend upon the fourth type of remedy, and the fourth type of remedy subsumes the first three types of remedies.
Why is this? Because without a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), the preceding three cannot be accomplished.
The preceding three rely upon the fourth; since the preceding three are themselves the functional power of the spiritual friend, they are subsumed within the fourth.
The Treatise says:
Although this perfuming of hearing is a mundane phenomenon, it should be understood that the dharma obtained by a Bodhisattva when first practicing contemplation is subsumed within the Dharma-body.
The commentary states:

Auditory consciousness hears sounds and induces the arising of mental consciousness, which discerns their meaning based on words and phrases. Through repeated practice, a functional capacity is generated; this capacity, which maintains [the impressions] without forgetting, is called "hearing-perfuming" (*śruta-vāsanā*). For this reason, it is said to be a mundane dharma.
There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those in the stage of ordinary beings; second, those in the stage of sages.

From the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment down to the end of the ten stages of faith, all belong to the stage of ordinary beings; from the ten stages of understanding upward, all are included within the stage of sages.
Those who first practice contemplation are ordinary person bodhisattvas.
The perfuming of hearing attained by such beginner bodhisattvas is called a mundane dharma.
Although these are mundane dharmas, because they serve as the causes for the ultimate attainment of the Dharma-body, they are subsumed under the Dharma-body.
The treatise says:
Those attained by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are subsumed under the Body of Liberation.
The commentary states:

If even the hearing-perfuming (*śrutavāsanā*) possessed by those who have already attained the ultimate fruit of the two vehicles is still subsumed under the body of liberation (*vimuktikāya*), how much more so for śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas!
Why is this? These two individuals have attained only the body of liberation, but they cannot attain the Dharma-body of a Tathāgata.
It is because of their body of liberation that these two individuals are equal to a Tathāgata.
It is not by virtue of the Dharma-body that the Tathāgata is peerless among all sentient beings; rather, it is because he has attained the Dharma-body.

Although the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and the permeation of hearing (*śrutavāsanā*) arise and perish together in mutual correspondence, while the fundamental consciousness gradually diminishes, the continuity of the fundamental consciousness does not gradually increase. This meaning I shall now explain.
The treatise states:
This perfuming by hearing is not the ālayavijñāna; it is subsumed under the dharmakāya and the vimuktikāya.
In this manner, it gradually increases through the successive stages of inferior, medium, and superior.
"In this way, and so forth, the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) gradually diminishes in succession.
The commentary explains:

"The essence of the cultivation through hearing (*śrutavāsanā*) is a supramundane dharma; the cause and fruit of the cultivation through hearing are subsumed within the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and the Liberation-body (*vimuktikāya*)."

The essence of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is a worldly phenomenon; its cause is the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*), and its fruit is the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*). Therefore, these two phenomena are contradictory in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
For this reason, as the permeation of hearing (*śrutavāsanā*) gradually increases, the fundamental consciousness gradually diminishes.
When the inferior grade of the perfuming of hearing arises, the superior grade of the fundamental consciousness diminishes;
when the perfuming of hearing increases to the middle grade, the middle grade of the fundamental consciousness diminishes;
when the perfuming of hearing increases to the superior grade, the inferior grade of the fundamental consciousness diminishes.
The Treatise says:
"The basis is itself the transformation.
The Commentary explains:

Through the increase of the Truth of the Path and the decrease of the Truth of Origination, the Truth of the Path consists of merit and wisdom, while the Truth of Origination consists of the seeds within the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*); as merit and wisdom gradually increase and the seeds gradually diminish, one attains the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).
The Treatise says:

If that which relies upon the exclusively evolving [consciousness] possesses seeds, then the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) would be without seeds, and thus everything would be utterly exhausted.
The Commentary explains:
The basis is the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body.
The gradual increase of the Path-truth and the gradual decrease of the Truth of Accumulation (saṃudaya-satya) is called "exclusive relinquishment" (ekānta-prahāṇa).
From the first stage (bhūmi) through the second stage, and so on until the attainment of Buddhahood, this is called "transformation" (parāvṛtti).
Because the afflictions and karma have been extinguished, it is said that there are "no seeds"; this reveals *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Because all retributive fruits have been completely extinguished, it is said that "everything has reached its end"; this reveals *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
For this reason, although the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and the path arise together, there is a distinction between their increase and decrease.
The treatise says:

If the fundamental consciousness and that which is not the fundamental consciousness arise and perish together, like water and milk mixed together, how can it be that the fundamental consciousness perishes while that which is not the fundamental consciousness does not?
The commentary states:

Previously, the blending of water and milk was cited as an analogy for the blending of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) with non-fundamental consciousnesses; therefore, this very point is raised again as an objection.
Since the blending of water and milk necessarily involves their simultaneous arising and ceasing, there is no principle whereby either the water or the milk could perish alone.
The same should apply to the fusion of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and what is not the fundamental consciousness; how then could one cease while the other remains?
The treatise says:
It is like the milk drunk by a swan from water.
The commentary states:
This explains the objection by means of an analogy.
Although water and milk are mixed together, when a swan drinks, it drinks only the milk and not the water; thus, even though the milk is exhausted, the water is not depleted.
The same applies to the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and that which is not the fundamental consciousness: although they are in conjunction, when one ceases, the other remains.
The treatise says:

Just as in the world, at the time of detachment from desire, the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the non-quiescent stages cease and the latencies of the quiescent stages increase, so too is the meaning of the world’s transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) established.
The supramundane transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) is likewise so.
The commentary states:
The former citation uses what is understood by worldly people as an analogy; the latter citation uses what is understood by wise people of the world as an analogy.

Just as in the world, when a person who has become free from desire extinguishes the seeds of afflictions and karma belonging to the non-quiescent stages within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), and brings to completion the perfuming of the roots of goodness that are the merits of the quiescent stages, they transform the basis of the lower realm into the basis of the upper realm.

The supramundane transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) is likewise: as the functional capacity of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) gradually diminishes, and the cultivation through hearing (*śrutavāsanā*) and so forth gradually increase, one abandons the basis of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and effects the basis of a noble one (*ārya*).
The "basis of the noble ones" refers to the harmonious integration of the perfuming of hearing and the nature of understanding.
Taking this as their basis, all the paths of the noble ones arise in dependence upon it.
*Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, Fascicle Three.
Commentary on the Mahāyānasaṃgraha, Scroll Four.
Explained by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu;
translated by Paramārtha, the Tripiṭaka Master from India during the Chen Dynasty.
Chapter Two of the Section on Citing Scriptural Authority: Chapter Six, on Accordance with Reasoning. The Treatise says:

If a person enters the meditative attainment of the cessation of mind (*nirodhasamāpatti*), because it is taught that consciousness does not depart from the body, it follows that the resultant consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) must remain non-departed from the body during that attainment.
The commentary states:
This chapter further cites what does not contradict reason in order to demonstrate that the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) truly exists.

If someone were to claim that the third and fourth fruits, the pratyekabuddhas, and the bodhisattvas cultivate the meditative absorption that extinguishes the mind (*cittanirodha-samādhi*) for the sake of attaining a state of peaceful abiding and to avoid the fault of falling back, [it would follow that they do so] because of the existence of this fundamental consciousness.

It is not that the substance of the mind itself is called "extinguished mind"; rather, it is called "extinguished mind" because the mental factors have been extinguished. The designation "mind" is established based on what depends upon it, following its support.
Thus, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, said:
"At the time of entering meditative absorption, consciousness does not depart from the body."

This consciousness is exclusively the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*); if one were to claim that any one of the other six consciousnesses—not this [retributive] consciousness—remains inseparable from the body, this principle would not be established.

Why is this? One cultivates this meditative absorption of the cessation of mind as an antidote to the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), because one perceives that the evolving consciousnesses possess the fault of being non-quiescent.
As for what is called "fault," it means that the six consciousnesses take external objects as their conditions and give rise to improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*).
The first fault is that through improper mental attention, one falls away from meditative concentration.
The second fault is that by the arising of consciousness during a state of distraction, one is obstructed from attaining the most subtle state of tranquility.

Having already attained [attainments] and then lost them, or not yet having attained what should be attained— because one cultivates the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) as an antidote to these two faults,
it should be understood that if consciousness is established as not departing from the body, it must be the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
The Treatise asks:
For what reason?
The Commentary explains:
Furthermore, by what reasoning is it proven that consciousness does not depart from the body, but is merely the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*)?
The treatise states:
Because the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is not the antidote to this [fundamental] consciousness.
The commentary states:

If a person desires to attain abiding in tranquility, yet does not contemplate the faults of this consciousness nor cultivate the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) as an antidote to it, then at the time of correctly entering that absorption of cessation, this consciousness is not extinguished; thus, it is said that this consciousness does not depart from the body.
The Treatise asks:
How is this known?
The Commentary explains:
How can this meaning be understood?
Why is it not said that at the time of entering the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), there is truly no mind remaining?
Since the mind is not permanently extinguished and arises again later, it is said that consciousness does not depart from the body.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, said:

"If a person enters the fourth dhyāna, bodily formations (kāya-saṃskāra) cease; if a person enters the second dhyāna and so forth, verbal formations (vāk-saṃskāra) cease; if a person enters the cessation of mind (nirodha-citta-samāpatti), mental formations (citta-saṃskāra) cease."

Just as bodily formations cease while the body does not perish, so too should it be with the mind: mental formations cease while the mind does not perish; therefore, it is said that consciousness does not depart from the body.
Why was it not stated in this way?

If one maintains that when a person enters the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), the mind arises again upon emerging from it, and that for this reason consciousness does not depart from the body—
this argument is incorrect.
Why is this? The treatise says:
If one were to emerge from this meditative absorption, consciousness should not arise again.
The commentary states:

If, within this meditative absorption, the continuity of consciousness is severed and nothing remains, then there is no possibility of emerging from this absorption nor of consciousness arising again.
The Treatise asks:
For what reason?
The Commentary explains:
Wishing further to establish this meaning by means of reasoning,
the treatise says:
Once this retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) has been severed from its continuity, it cannot arise again unless it relies upon the moment of rebirth (*pratisandhi*).
The commentary states:

Just as when a person’s retribution for a single lifetime has been exhausted, the continuity of the resultant consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) is severed forever, and there is no possibility of rebirth.
If consciousness were to arise again, it would necessarily depend upon another embodied existence.
If the resultant consciousness were to depart from the present body and then return to arise within that same body, such a thing is impossible.

Therefore, we know that when one enters the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), the statement that "consciousness does not depart from the body" refers exclusively to the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna).
The Treatise says:
If a person asserts that there is mind within the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), what that person says does not constitute [a valid] mind.
The Explanation says:
To say that there is a sixth consciousness and thus it is called "having mind" (sacittaka), and to claim that based on this sixth consciousness consciousness does not depart from the body—
according to what they have said, this does not constitute "mind.
The treatise says:
Why is this? The commentary states:
To further employ reasoning to refute the sixth consciousness and establish the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) as being inseparable from the body.

If one were to set aside the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) characterized as previously established, and instead claim that any one of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) exists within the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*),
this interpretation would be incorrect.
Why is this? The treatise states:
Because the definition cannot be established.
The commentary states:
Below this, ten points are used to demonstrate the fallacies in the position that the mind exists during the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

This is the first fallacy: it has never been observed that the mind and its mental factors (*caitta*) exist apart from one another, just as one mental factor is not seen apart from another mental factor; for example, there is no time when perception (*saṃjñā*) is separated from feeling (*vedanā*), nor is there any time when feeling is separated from perception.
The same applies to the mind and its mental factors; they can never be separated from one another.

If they were not inseparable, the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*) and the meditative attainment of the cessation of mind (*citta-nirodha-samāpatti*) would both be impossible to achieve.
This meditative absorption is accomplished by the cessation of three factors; since these three factors have not ceased, this absorption is not accomplished.
If one maintains that there is a foundational consciousness (ālayavijñāna), asserting that consciousness does not depart from the body, then this fault does not arise.
Why is this? While all other consciousnesses cease, this consciousness alone does not cease.

For those who cultivate the meditative absorption of the cessation of mind (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and seek to attain a state of peaceful abiding, it serves as the antidote to the mind and mental factors that obstruct such peaceful abiding.

When the meditative absorption that extinguishes the mind arises, because it is not practiced as an antidote for the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) but rather for the purpose of extinguishing [the active] minds, the other consciousnesses are extinguished while this [fundamental] consciousness does not cease.
Furthermore, within this absorption, if one were separated from the fundamental consciousness, the other consciousnesses could not be established.
The Treatise says:
Because the characteristics of cognition and its objects cannot be apprehended.
The Commentary explains:
This is the second fault.
If one maintains that the mind and mental factors exist, then this existence must necessarily possess a mode of apprehension (*ākāra*) and an object (*ālambana*).
There are two kinds of modes of apprehension:
There are two types: non-conceptual and conceptual.
Non-conceptual refers to the five sensory consciousnesses; the mental consciousness may be either conceptual or non-conceptual.
If it is non-conceptual, all six consciousnesses equally constitute direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); if it is conceptual, it constitutes inference (*anumāna*).
This is because the objective spheres (*viṣaya*) consist of the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) and the suchness (*tathatā*) of those six sense-objects.
Since both the mental states (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*), as well as their characteristics (*nimitta*) and objective spheres,

can all be discerned [in other states], and since neither the characteristics nor the objective spheres can be apprehended within this meditative concentration, one knows that there is certainly no other consciousness present within this concentration.

If it is said that the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) exists within this meditative absorption, then this objection does not apply, because this consciousness is manifested by its capacity to produce the basis [of existence].
The treatise states:
"Because it would entail the fault of being associated with wholesome roots."
The commentary states:
This is the third fault.

Furthermore, if one maintains that when this concentration occurs there arises another consciousness, this consciousness cannot be outside the three natures—namely, the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate.
This mind cannot be established as having a wholesome nature (*kuśala-svabhāva*), because it would entail the fault of being associated with the roots of wholesomeness (*kuśalamūla*).

Since this [mind] is contrary to those [roots], if consciousness were not associated with the roots of wholesomeness yet its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) were wholesome, such a case would be impossible; therefore, this wholesome mind is necessarily associated with the roots of wholesomeness.
If it is argued that concentration is said to be wholesome because the concentrated mind is wholesome, this meaning is not tenable;

for it would follow [absurdly] that it is not associated with wholesome roots such as non-attachment, since you have lost the definition of concentration as being the state of a mind that has attained cessation.
Why is this? Because a wholesome mind is universally present without distinction, as all mental factors are inseparable from one another.
If they are inseparable, then feeling and perception would likewise not cease; therefore, it is impossible to establish this mind as being wholesome.
The Treatise says:
Because it is not associated with the unwholesome (*akuśala*) or the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
The Commentary explains:
This is the fourth fault.
Furthermore, it is also impossible to establish that this mind is of an evil or indeterminate nature, because those two natures are not established.
Since all unwholesome dharmas are extinguished when one becomes free from desire for the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), it is not of an evil nature.
Because this concentration is necessarily wholesome, it cannot be established that this mind is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*).
The treatise states:
"Because of the fault of the arising of perception (*saṃjñā*) and feeling (*vedanā*)."
The commentary states:
This is the fifth fault.
Furthermore, it cannot be said that this mind is wholesome, because there is the fault of the arising of perception, feeling, and so forth.
If one is separated from the roots of goodness, the nature of goodness cannot be established; therefore, a wholesome mind must necessarily be associated with the roots of goodness.
Just as it must necessarily be associated with the roots of goodness, it should also necessarily be associated with feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), for there is no differing cause.
This argument is not established; for if that which is to be countered exists, that which counters it must also exist.
For example, when desire and so forth are actively arising, the contemplation of impurity and the like cannot exist.
If you do not accept this principle, then it follows that [the contact] does not constitute a wholesome mind.
The treatise states:
Because there must necessarily be contact when the three [factors] come together, and because it necessarily possesses efficacy with respect to the others.
The commentary states:
This is the sixth fault.
Furthermore, if one accepts the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna), there would be the fault that contact does not arise within this meditative absorption, just as in other absorptions.

If, within the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), a distinct wholesome mind were to arise apart from the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), this mind would necessarily not be devoid of contact (*sparśa*).

Since the characteristic of this state is the tranquility born of concentration, it would have to give rise to pleasant contact capable of producing feelings of pleasure, as well as contact that is neither painful nor pleasant.
Therefore, with this peaceful contact, pleasant feeling and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling must necessarily arise.
Why is this? Because it has already been observed that, in other meditative attainments, this contact possesses the functional capacity to produce both pleasant and equanimous feelings.
This meditative absorption is likewise so, because there is no obstruction.
Therefore, this absorption should also give rise to feeling based on contact.
This argument is not correct.
Why is this? The treatise states:
It is because the cessation of perception alone constitutes a fault.
The commentary states:
This is the seventh fault.

Furthermore, if one believes that because there is contact (*sparśa*), this meditative absorption necessarily possesses feeling (*vedanā*), then it follows that this absorption must be entirely devoid of perception (*saṃjñā*).
This interpretation is not correct.
Why? Because the Blessed One has taught that both perception and feeling are absent [in that state].
The treatise says:
Because it transcends the arising of wholesome roots such as attention and faith.
The commentary explains:
This is the eighth fault. Furthermore,
this contact should not exist,

because at other moments of consciousness, when contact arises together with its associated mental factors, there would be the fault that attention, faith, and other roots of goodness would arise simultaneously.

If there is contact that arises in association with the mind, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, taught that attention (*manasikāra*), feeling (*vedanā*), and so forth necessarily arise together with contact.
Since the presence of attention necessarily gives rise to wholesome states of mind and the like, the wholesome roots such as faith (*śraddhā*) arise accordingly following that attention.
This argument is not tenable, as it does not avoid the faults previously mentioned.

If you wish to avoid both those aforementioned faults and the fault of contradicting the Āgamas by asserting that [the mind] arises from a state of aversion toward mental factors (caitta), then because you are merely eliminating mental factors, this meditative concentration would consist of mind alone, devoid of mental factors.
This interpretation is not correct.
Why? Because it is illogical to extract the dependent from its basis.
The Treatise says:
One must uproot that which depends [on a basis], for it cannot be found apart from its basis.
The Commentary explains:
This is the ninth fault.

Furthermore, if you say that because one loathes contact, feeling, perception, and so forth within this meditative method, these mental factors are extracted, such that there is only mind and no contact and the rest; [this is not so].
This argument is not tenable. Why?
Because it is impossible to extract the dependent from its basis.

The basis is the mind, and that which depends upon it is the mental factors; the mind and its mental factors constitute the entities of the basis and the dependent. Since beginningless saṃsāra, they have been constantly inseparable from one another, mutually inducing each other; therefore, the mind must be established as being associated with wholesome roots such as non-attachment.
If you say that when concentration (*samādhi*) and the means to concentration arise, they necessarily conflict with wholesome roots such as non-attachment (*alobha*),
and thus non-attachment and the other wholesome roots do not arise but only a wholesome mind arises— this principle has never been seen elsewhere.
If all phenomena were to possess association by virtue of their causes possessing association, then their similar effects would likewise possess association;
this position is incorrect.
The treatise states:
Because there is an analogy.
The commentary states:
This is the tenth fault.

Furthermore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has taught that within this meditative concentration, all bodily formations (*kāya-saṃskāra*), verbal formations (*vāk-saṃskāra*), and mental formations (*citta-saṃskāra*) are extinguished and do not arise.

Bodily formations refer to the two breaths of inhalation and exhalation; verbal formations refer to vitarka and vicāra (applied and sustained thought); and mental formations refer to volition, perception, feeling, and so forth.
Just as when vitarka and vicāra are extinguished through contemplation, speech does not arise;
so too, if mental activity (*citta-saṃskāra*) were to cease, the mind itself would likewise cease.

If you argue that just as when bodily activity ceases, a person remaining in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) does not have their body destroyed, so too in concentration, although mental activity ceases, the mind does not cease—[this is not so].
This interpretation is also incorrect. Why?
The treatise says:
"Just as it is not the case that all formations [are so], for all formations are not like this.
The commentary states:
At the time when bodily formations cease, there is a distinct sustaining cause capable of maintaining this body so that it does not perish.
As the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has said:
"Apart from the two breaths of inhalation and exhalation, food, life-force, consciousness, and so forth are able to sustain this body and prevent it from decaying and perishing.
Just as when bodily activity ceases, there is a distinct dharma that sustains the body and causes it to remain."
When mental activities cease, there is no separate dharma that sustains the mind so as to prevent its cessation.
Therefore, what you have established does not accord with this principle; thus, by this reasoning, it is certain that there is no mind in this state.
If there were no mind, why did the Buddha, the World-Honored One, say that consciousness does not depart from the body?
It is this retributive mind that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, designated as "consciousness.
When one emerges from meditative absorption, the mental consciousness arises from this all-seed consciousness.

Because the subsequent consciousness has a cause, and because the body in meditative absorption possesses the nutriment of consciousness, we know that the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) must certainly exist.

If that [fundamental consciousness] were originally the basis for the dependent consciousnesses and performed the great function of uprooting the dependent to separate it from its basis, such a principle would not hold true.
Why is this? Because it is established by way of analogy.

Within the world, from its primordial beginning until its ultimate end, these factors have arisen together constantly and are mutually inseparable; there is no principle by which the supported could be extracted and separated from its support.

Just as it is impossible for the four great elements and the matter derived from them to exist apart from those elements that produce them, so too it is with mental phenomena; they cannot be separated from their basis.
Therefore, the claim that in the mindless attainments there exists only mind and no mental factors is incorrect.

If you maintain that the supported [mind] is extracted from its support [the body], this argument fails; for it is only because of aversion toward feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) that these two factors alone cease.
The claim that within this meditative concentration two dharmas cannot function while other dharmas can is incorrect. Why is this so?
If it were not the case that all formations (*saṃskāra*) could undergo such cessation, then such cessation would not exist within all formations.

If there were a universal cessation of formations, the mind would necessarily cease along with them; thus, the Blessed One, the Buddha, would not have said that consciousness does not depart from the body.
Because this consciousness exists, we know that the Tathāgata established the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) as being present within this meditative absorption.

Furthermore, the Sūtra states that "consciousness does not depart from the body"; if this were understood apart from the fundamental consciousness and applied only to the other [evolving] consciousnesses, it would be untenable.

Why is this? This meditative absorption of the cessation of mind arises as an antidote to the evolving consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*), because one perceives that this evolving consciousness is not tranquil.
If someone maintains that the mind arises again at the time of emerging from concentration, it is with reference to this meaning that the expression "not separated" is used.
This is also not the case.
Why? Because if such were the principle, the mind of one who has emerged from meditative absorption would not arise again.
If the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) were to be severed from its continuity, there would be no possibility of it being reborn when taking up a subsequent birth.

If a person, apart from the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), maintains through the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that there is a mind during the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the "mind" they grasp at would not constitute a true mind, because the natures of good, evil, and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) could not be established therein.
Since this meditative absorption is stated to be virtuous by nature, it is not unwholesome.
The same applies to the indeterminate: the minds of deportment, craftsmanship, and transformation cannot exist within this absorption.
If you say that there is a resultant indeterminate mind, it must be the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna), because there is no fifth category of indeterminate mind.
If you say this mind is wholesome, then it should be associated with wholesome roots such as non-attachment.

Why is this? Since the defiled mind has already ceased and the wholesome mind is currently arising, the faculty of mind (manas-indriya) likewise possesses its object and there is likewise the conjunction of the three factors; why, then, would contact (sparśa) not arise?
If there is contact (*sparśa*), how could there be no feeling (*vedanā*)?

If that were the case, the definition of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) could not be established, because the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) would not have ceased therein.

If someone maintains that this meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is necessarily wholesome by virtue of its projecting cause (*ākṣepaka-hetu*), [it is argued that] while the mental application of a wholesome mind during the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) can project this mind of absorption, the mind of absorption itself—though it is a similar result (*niṣyanda-phala*) and thus wholesome—is not associated with wholesome roots such as non-attachment (*alobha*).
Therefore, because the Tathāgata wishes to demonstrate that contact gives rise to feeling, he first seeks to distinguish their conjunction.
Based on the sense faculty and conditioned by the object, consciousness arises; through the capacity of these three being conjoined, contact gives rise to feeling.
If the three are conjoined but lack this capacity, then only contact arises and no feeling is produced.
Therefore, although this concentration is wholesome, it cannot bring about the synthesis [of rebirth]; thus, it is devoid of feeling and perception.
This expedient mind is associated with the three wholesome roots, whereas its corresponding fruit is not like this.
This meaning is not so.
Why? Because it is impossible to extract the dependent from its basis.
These difficulties are fully as previously explained.
The treatise says:
If there are those who maintain that the sequential arising of form and mind constitutes the seeds of all phenomena.
This position is incorrect.
The commentary states:

If someone maintains that the matter of a preceding moment is the cause of the matter of a subsequent moment because it can serve as the seed for that subsequent matter, and that the consciousness of a preceding moment is the cause of the consciousness of a subsequent moment because it can serve as the seed for that subsequent consciousness.
This position is incorrect.
The treatise asks: Why is this so?
Having already incurred the previous fault, there is yet another further error.
The commentary states:
The previous fault refers to the fact that if the continuity of consciousness were severed, the subsequent consciousness would lack a cause and thus could not arise.
Furthermore, when the retribution of a single lifetime is exhausted, there is no principle for being born again once one has departed from the subsequent womb.
Such a flaw has already been fully explained above.

As for those who hold such a view: if a person were to fall back from the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) and be reborn in a lower realm possessing form (rūpadhātu), [this would contradict their position].
If a subsequent form were to arise while its preceding seed has long since ceased, from what cause would this form arise?
The treatise states:

As for the specific fallacy, if a person falls from the Heaven of Non-conception or emerges from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), that which was maintained therein is not established.
The commentary states:
For one born in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*) or who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the mind has long since ceased.
Later, when such a person falls away from that state and is reborn, or emerges from that absorption, how can they achieve the accomplishment of a prior mind as the cause for a subsequent future mind?
If it were necessarily so,
the treatise states:
even the final mind of an Arhat would not be established [as such].
The commentary states:
An Arhat does not possess the principle of entering nirvana without remainder. Why is this?
Because subsequent form and subsequent mind do not cease to serve as causes,
this meaning should be understood.
The treatise says:
If one were to exclude the condition of immediate succession (*samanantarapratyaya*), this thesis would not be established.
The commentary states:
"The matter of the preceding moment, by virtue of the condition of immediate succession, is connected with the subsequent matter."
Consciousness is likewise; it does not correspond between preceding and succeeding moments by virtue of causes and conditions.

Therefore, if this position were to establish the meaning of "causal condition" (hetu-pratyaya) apart from the "condition as immediate antecedent" (samanantara-pratyaya), this position would be untenable, as it contradicts liberation.
The treatise says:
Thus, if one were separated from the consciousness that contains all seeds, neither the pure nor the impure categories of the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) could be established.
Therefore, it should be understood with faith that this mind possesses the established meaning [of being the storehouse consciousness].
Based on the characteristics previously explained, I shall now further compose verses.
The commentary states:
This meaning is fully as explained before.

If a person were to abide only in the arising consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) and not in the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), the meaning of the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) would not be established.
To clarify this point, three verses of practice are spoken.
The treatise says:
When a bodhisattva abides in wholesome consciousness, they are then separated from the other five consciousnesses;
since there is no further transformation of the basis of the mind, by what means is this accomplished?
If the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) were the antidote [itself], it would not be established because it is not a cessation;
there would be no distinction between cause and fruit, and thus there would be a fault regarding cessation.
If one asserts that the transformation of the basis consists of the absence of seeds and the absence of dharmas, [this is untenable].
"Because non-duality does not exist, the meaning of the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) is not established.

Commentary: There are two kinds of bodhisattvas: namely, ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) and noble ones (ārya). Those at the stage of the ten faiths (daśa-śraddhā) and below are ordinary beings; those from the ten understandings (daśa-adhimukti) upward are noble ones. Here, one wishes to clarify the transformation of the basis of an ordinary being into the basis of a noble one.
In which consciousness is this transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) accomplished?
It is accomplished only within the fundamental consciousness (mūla-vijñāna).
Without the fundamental consciousness, it cannot be accomplished in any other consciousness.
How is this known to be so?
This meaning is revealed sequentially by three verses.
It is called "wholesome" because it is free from the unwholesome and the neutral.
Because it is the sixth consciousness, it is called "consciousness.
This wholesome state is a supramundane mind that is associated with the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and other auxiliary dharmas of the path; thus, it is termed "wholesome consciousness."

This wholesome consciousness is free from the five kinds of distracted movements; since it is never associated with the five sensory consciousnesses, it is said to be separated from the other five consciousnesses.
How, then, can it arise in dissociation from them?
Because it arises in this manner at all times.
The treatise says:
there is no other mind.
The commentary states:

Apart from the defiled mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and the wholesome consciousness associated with outflows (*sāsrava-kuśala-vijñāna*), if one speaks only of "wholesome consciousness" without specifying that no other minds are excluded, then the wholesome consciousness associated with outflows is included therein.
The Treatise asks:
By what means is the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) effected?
The Commentary explains:

Because all seeds of defilement and turbidity have been extinguished and abandoned, only the fundamental consciousness remains; this is called the characteristic of the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).
By what means is it accomplished?
As stated in the subsequent verse.
The treatise says:
If it is the transformation of the basis through the application of remedies.
The commentary explains:
If you say that because the antidote arises, the basis undergoes transformation, and thus the antidote is called the "transformation of the basis" (āśraya-parāvṛtti),
this interpretation is incorrect.
The treatise says:
"It is not established because it is not a cessation.
The commentary states:
Taking cessation as the basis of transformation (āśraya-parāvṛtti) is not established for two reasons.

First, if the antidote arises while the seeds are not yet extinguished, the basis remains as it was according to its original meaning; this is not called "transformation of the basis" (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).
Second, the antidote is the revealing cause (*vijñapti-hetu*) of the transformation of the basis, not the essence (*svabhāva*) of the transformation of the basis itself.

The antidote is the Truth of the Path (mārgasatya), while the transformation of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti) constitutes liberation and the Dharma-body, which is the Truth of Cessation (nirodhasatya); therefore, the transformation of the basis should consist in the extinction of the seeds.

If you maintain that when the antidote arises, the seeds of defilement are extinguished, and these two meanings coexist simultaneously, why is extinction taken as the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) rather than the Path?
This position is flawed.
The treatise states:
"If there were no distinction between cause and effect, there would be a logical fallacy regarding cessation."
The commentary states:
The fruit is the truth of cessation, which is termed *nirvāṇa*;
the cause is the truth of the path, which is termed the "antidote."
If the antidote were the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*), then cause and effect would become one.
If they were to become one, what further fault would there be?
If the antidote were attained, one would immediately enter parinirvāṇa.

If someone posits the Truth of Cessation as the basis of transformation (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), should it be by the cessation of seeds that the transformation occurs, or should it be by the cessation of consciousness?
The treatise says:
Without seeds, there is no phenomenon.
If it is asserted that this constitutes the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*),
the commentary states:
If someone says that the cessation of both the supported (*āśrita*) and the support (*āśraya*) is called the transformation of the basis.

Within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the seeds that serve as the basis for dependence (*āśraya-bīja*) are extinguished; once these seeds of dependence have been extinguished, the mental consciousness which serves as their support (*āśrita*) is also extinguished, and this is therefore called "transformation of the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
If one were to maintain that these two meanings constitute the transformation of the basis, it would not be so.
The Treatise says:
Because duality does not exist, the meaning of the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) is not established.
The Commentary explains:

If the sixth evolving consciousness were absent during the state of meditative equipoise, there would be no seeds, and since there would be no activity, the meaning of the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) could not be established.

If there is the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), and the seeds produced by the perfuming of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) abide within that fundamental consciousness, then even though the evolving consciousnesses are no longer present, it is possible to cause those seeds to cease and the evolving consciousnesses to cease; this is called the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).

If one were separated from the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), then because the two [aspects] would not exist, the meaning of the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) would not be established.
For this reason, one must certainly believe that the fundamental consciousness exists.
Chapter Four: Explanation of the Distinctions Section One: Discourse Commentary: [The text begins with the explanation of the first section on discourse.]
This chapter consists of two general sections and seven specific sections.
Regarding the two general sections: first, habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*); second, functional activity (*kārya-kriyā*). Regarding the seven specific sections: first, verbal expression;

second, the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*); third, the constituent parts (*bhāga*); fourth, projection and production (*ākṣepa-utpatti*); fifth, retributive fruit (*vipāka-phala*); sixth, the characteristics of conditions (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*); and seventh, appearances (*nimitta*).
The first three chapters have already established that the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) exists; its specific categories and distinctions shall now be further explained.
The treatise says:
What are the distinctions of this *ālayavijñāna*?
The commentary says:
This question concerns whether the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) has distinctions in its nature (*svabhāva*) or distinctions in its functional entities (*vastu*).
The treatise states:
Briefly stated, there are either three or four types of distinctions.
The commentary says:
Here, the distinctions are explained in terms of their actual entities.
The single fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) is non-different in its nature;
however, in terms of phenomena, it is distinguished as being of three kinds, four kinds, or seven kinds.
The treatise says:

Regarding the "three kinds," they are so called because of the differences among three types of perfuming (*vāsanā*): namely, the distinctions between the perfumings of verbal expression, the view of self, and the existence-constituent (*bhavāṅga*).
The commentary states:
The reason these three are not explained in the root treatise is that their superior characteristics should be understood through the subsequent explanation.
Since these three meanings were already individually analyzed at the outset, they will not be explained here.
Regarding the distinction of verbal熏習 (vāsanā): there is only the single fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), which, due to the distinctions in its *vāsanās*, manifests in three forms.
Verbal expression has "name" (*nāman*) as its essence.
There are two kinds of names: namely, names for verbal expression and names for mental reflection.
These two kinds of names take sound as their basis; with respect to the sense organ capable of seeing form, it is called "eye" based on the presence of sound.

Through the repeated practice of such verbal expressions, one generates within the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) the perfuming of craving; this perfuming is the cause for the arising of the eye-faculty, and thus the retributive eye-faculty is produced.

From within this fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), the perfuming of attachment to verbal expression arises; therefore, the perfuming of verbal expression is established as the cause of the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*).
Just as with the eye-faculty, it should be understood that for all the faculties, such as the ear, the perfuming of verbal expression arises in the same manner.
This is the first differentiation of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
Chapter Two: The Chapter on the View of Self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). The treatise states:
It is due to the differentiation of the habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) by the view of self.
The commentary states:

There is a defiled consciousness which, by virtue of relying upon the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and so forth, engenders the perfuming (*vāsanā*) of "self" and "mine" within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*).
Due to this perfuming, conceptualization arises, whereby one regards oneself as "I" and that which is other than oneself as "another."
This is called the second differentiation of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
Chapter Three: On the Divisions of Existence (*bhavāṅga*). The treatise states:
Due to the specific distinctions in the perfuming (*vāsanā*) of the divisions of existence.
The commentary states:
Due to the influence of wholesome, unwholesome, and immovable karma, there are distinctions among the six sense faculties experienced within the six realms of existence.
Therefore, the fundamental consciousness possesses three types and the distinctions of the six realms.
This is called the third differentiation of the fundamental consciousness.
Chapter Four: On Inducing and Producing. The Treatise says:
There are four kinds, namely, the differentiations of inducing and producing, retributive maturation, objective conditions, and formal characteristics.
Regarding the distinction of "producing": this refers to the new arising of perfuming (*vāsanā*).

If this did not exist, the principle that consciousness arises conditioned by formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*) arises conditioned by grasping (*upādāna*) would not be established.
The commentary states:
Regarding the differentiation of the projecting cause (*ākṣepaka-hetu*), what are its characteristics?

It is the newly produced perfuming (*vāsanā*). If there were no differentiation within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) that projects [the result], then the consciousness perfumed by the formations (*saṃskāra*) arising and ceasing—being comprised by grasping (*upādāna*)—would give rise to birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*); yet this existence could not be established.
Because arising occurs from this, it is said that this is the "existence-factor" (*bhava-dharma*) and the grasping (*upādāna*), as well as the fruits of what was repeatedly practiced in past lives.
Chapter Five: On Retribution (*Vipāka*). The Treatise states:
Regarding the distinctions of retribution, these phenomena mature within the six realms of existence (*ṣaḍ-gati*) based upon one's formative actions (*saṃskāra*).
If this did not exist, the arising of all phenomena at the time of taking birth in a future life would be untenable.
The commentary states:

Formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*) act as the projecting causes; they project the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) into maturation within the six realms of existence, and thus are called "projection."
If this dharma of "re-arising" did not exist, the re-arising of the sense organs such as the eye and the objects such as visible forms could not be established.
This dharma is precisely the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*).
Chapter Six: The Characteristics of Conditions (*Pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*). The treatise states:
Regarding the distinctions among the characteristics of conditions, within this mind there are characteristics capable of giving rise to the grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha*).
If this did not exist, the apprehension of the object characterized as "self" within other states of consciousness would be untenable.
The commentary explains:

This fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) serves as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the self-grasping of the second consciousness (the *manovijñāna*) and the self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) of the sixth consciousness.

If this fundamental consciousness lacked the differentiation of objective conditions, then the objective referent for the grasping of a self—which has the view of a self-body as its cause—could not be established.
This is called the "concordant fruit."
Chapter Seven: On Characteristics The treatise states: Regarding the differentiation of characteristics, this consciousness possesses both common characteristics and uncommon characteristics;
it possesses the characteristic of seeds that do not result in rebirth and the characteristic of seeds that do result in rebirth.
The commentary states:
There are many varieties of distinctions in characteristics; briefly stated, there are four types.
The treatise says:

The common characteristic (*sādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*) refers to the seeds of the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*); the uncommon characteristic (*asādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*) refers to the seeds of the individual internal bases (*ādhyātmika-āyatana*).

Furthermore, the common characteristic refers to the seeds of birth without sensation (*anupabhoga-janman*); the uncommon characteristic refers to the seeds of birth with sensation (*sopabhoga-janman*).
The commentary states:
The fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) possesses a function common to all sentient beings; it is the cause for the arising of the receptacle world (bhājanaloka) shared by these beings.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the common characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) is the seed for the arising of that which is without sensation," this fundamental consciousness is a dharma devoid of conscious feeling.

That is to say, regarding the external causes for the arising of the four great elements and the five sense objects, if such a fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) with these characteristics did not exist, it would be impossible for it to serve as the common cause for the receptacle world and its sentient beings.

Regarding the statement that "the unique characteristics (*asādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*) are the seeds of the respective internal bases (*ādhyātmika-āyatana*)," "respective" is established in relation to self and others; they are called "respective" because their objects differ, their types differ, and the apprehension of their characteristics differs.
Furthermore, with respect to oneself as "internal" and others as "external," these internal faculties, objects, and so forth are the uncommon causes for their arising.

As for that which possesses the seeds for the arising of sensation, this fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is the cause for the arising of dharmas involving perception; if it did not possess this second characteristic, the world of sentient beings could not be established.
If they were established by other causes, such as wood or stone, which lack sentience and sensation,
then of these two types of seeds, which seed would be destroyed by the Noble Path?
The Treatise says:
When the antidote arises, that which is uniquely opposed by it ceases.
The Commentary says:
These unique seeds, when the Path arises, are contrary to the Path and must necessarily be destroyed by it.
Why is this? Because there is not a single person who attains the Path while others simultaneously attain liberation.
What function does the Path have regarding the common seeds?
The treatise says:
Regarding the consciousness of common seeds, it is purified by the right view maintained by the conceptualization of others.
The commentary states:
Regarding the common seeds, the Path is both effortless and effortful.
Just as there is effort regarding the uncommon seeds, such effort is absent here; therefore, it is said to be "effortless."
After attaining the Path, what is perceived is pure and differs from what was previously perceived; therefore, it is said that there is also functional efficacy (*sābhisamskāra*).
How does the Path function differently with respect to the common seeds?
Because it is sustained by the conceptualization of others.
If that is so, what function does the path have regarding the common seeds?
It is simply that, by removing conceptualization, one gives rise to non-conceptualization with respect to objects.
The Dharma-eye is pure regarding its objects because it takes only the absence of intrinsic nature as its object.

If one further engages in conceptual differentiation based on compassion and prajñā, this differentiation—arising from reliance upon suchness—results in the purified land that is the object of that differentiation.
If the objective realm is one and only, why do sentient beings perceive it differently?
The treatise states:
It is like a practitioner of meditation who, toward a single type of object, forms various aspirations and various observations; these are established according to the mind.
The commentary states:
Due to the transformative mind (*nirmāṇa-citta*) of the practitioner, there arise different perceptions of sentient beings regarding a single class of objects.
Since such an objective sphere is maintained by the conceptualization of others, the practitioner attains a pure vision therein.
The treatise says:
A verse here states:
"That which is difficult to extinguish and difficult to unravel is called the common fetter."
The minds of those practicing contemplation differ; because they perceive signs as substantial, they become externalized.
For those who have not yet extinguished their impurities, they see purity within this [world];
they achieve a pure buddha-field because the Buddha sees it as pure.
The commentary states:
There are two kinds of fetters: first, the fetter of signs (*nimitta-bandhana*); second, the fetter of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya-bandhana*).
The fetter of signs is difficult to unravel; the fetter of coarse heaviness is difficult to extinguish.

The mind’s conceptualization of various objects as signs and characteristics is called the "bond of signs" (*nimitta-bandhana*). From this conceptualization, afflictions such as desire and hatred arise, which are termed the "bond of heavy dysfunction" (*dauṣṭhulya-bandhana*).

If one attains non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), one is immediately liberated from the bond of signs; once the bond of signs does not arise, the bond of heavy dysfunction is likewise extinguished.
Furthermore, the difficulty of extinguishing refers to the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*), because this path is difficult to attain;

the difficulty of liberation refers to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), because the path of uninterrupted realization is difficult to attain, and consequently, the path of liberation is also difficult to attain.

Because they give rise to fetters (*saṃyojana*) within a common objective sphere, they are called "common fetters" (*sādhāraṇa-saṃyojana*); however, if considered in relation to one's own personal continuum (*svasaṃtati*), they are not termed "common.
Why are these afflictions so difficult to extinguish and so difficult to unravel?
The Treatise says:
The mind of one practicing contemplation differs [from ordinary mind], because it manifests externally through the great characteristics.
The Commentary says:

Apart from consciousness, there is no separate external object; therefore, the practitioner of contemplation observes only that internal phenomena are non-existent and does not observe external phenomena, which is why it is said that the mind is distinct.
Its pervasive characteristic extends throughout the worlds of the ten directions, which is why it is called the "Great Characteristic."
The observation of the mind is directly contrary to internal seeds and has no relation to external objects; therefore, it is said that [the view of] externality is established.
Due to these three meanings, the external fetters are difficult to unravel and difficult to extinguish.

If these fetters possess three characteristics that make them difficult to extinguish and difficult to unravel, what efficacy does the practice of contemplation and the cultivation of the path have regarding these fetters?
The treatise says:
"The pure person has not yet extinguished them; herein, one perceives purity."
The commentary states:

When the seeds that are not shared [with afflictions] are extinguished at the moment the path of counteraction arises, the practitioner of contemplation is either partially purified or fully purified.
Although external appearances have not yet been extinguished, within them the Dharma-eye and the Wisdom-eye are pure and free from attachment.
The Commentary says:
"One accomplishes a pure Buddha-field."
The commentary states:
If there is wisdom and compassion that give rise to discernment for the sake of benefiting others, the accomplishment of a pure Buddha-field is its capacity.
By what causes and conditions is this pure Buddha-field accomplished?
The Treatise says:
"By means of the Buddha’s vision being pure.
The Commentary explains:

The first stage (*bhūmi*) is the bodhisattva’s stage of vision; within this first stage, purity is the purity of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*). This purity of the path of vision is called the purity of the Buddha’s vision. Because of this purity, one is able to attain the purity of the buddha-field (*buddhakṣetra*); how much more so, then, for the stages of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhāgama*).
Furthermore, the contemplation of *tathatā* (suchness) is called the "Buddha-vision. Why is this?
Because when one reaches the ultimate stage, the contemplation of *tathatā* attained does not differ from this; therefore, it is called the Buddha-vision.
Furthermore, because one can attain this vision by practicing in reliance upon the Buddha’s true teaching, it is called the "Buddha-vision.
Moreover, a bodhisattva may also be designated as a "Buddha" because they are certain to attain Buddhahood; thus, by applying the name of the result to the cause, it is termed the "Buddha-vision."
Furthermore, when the bodhisattva’s path of counteraction arises and the non-common seeds are extinguished, they then possess three purities:
first, the purity of the Dharma-eye; second, the purity of the Buddha-field; and third, the purity of seeing the Buddha, which refers to seeing the three bodies (*trikāya*).
Because a bodhisattva gives rise to a vision by taking the Buddha as an object, it is called "the vision of the Buddha.
The treatise states:
Furthermore, there is another verse.
The commentary says:
What does this verse intend to reveal?
It reveals two meanings:

First, a bodhisattva cultivates internal contemplation without relying on external objects; second, by means of this contemplation, one realizes that there is only consciousness and no external sensory realms.
These two meanings mutually clarify one another.
The Treatise says:
Various vows and views can be accomplished by the practitioner through contemplation.
The Explanation says:
Whether the practitioner desires to achieve mastery for themselves, or wishes to lead others to accept the true teaching, whatever various transformations they aspire to, all shall be accomplished.
If one’s vow has been fulfilled, whether seen by oneself or by others, it is accomplished exactly as vowed.
Does this vow have distinct objects, or does it have a single object?
The Treatise says:
Within a single category of objects.
The Commentary explains:
If many practitioners of meditation, through their respective vows, were able to cause a single object to undergo transformation, this transformation would be established.
Why would it be established?
The treatise says:
"Because they are accomplished according to their respective intentions.
The commentary explains:
Since there is truly no external object and only consciousness exists, each [object] is accomplished through transformation according to its respective intention.
If external objects truly existed, the practitioner’s aspiration would not be fulfilled.
Because the cause is not established, the transformation of what is seen by oneself and others could likewise not be established.
The Treatise says:
Because various perceptions are established, that which is grasped exists only as consciousness.
The Commentary explains:
Because the consciousness of the practitioner serves as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), the consciousnesses of other persons undergo transformation.
Just as the practitioner’s vow manifests [objects], one knows that there are certainly no external objects; there is only the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*).

It has already been clarified that the cause of manifest perception is necessarily an uncommon seed, while the cause of non-manifest perception is necessarily a common seed; now, it shall further be explained how common and uncommon causes together produce a single fruit.
The treatise says:
This is a specific differentiation of the non-common fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which possesses the seeds for the arising of sensation and birth.
If this were absent, the conditions for the arising of the world of sentient beings would not be established.

This [ālayavijñāna] contains the seeds for the production of the shared [receptacle world] and the unshared [personal existence]. If this did not exist, the conditions for the arising of the receptacle world would not be established.
The commentary states:

The two causes—the shared and the unshared—produce the five internal sense faculties and the five internal sense objects; because they serve as the bases for one's own six consciousnesses, they function as the unshared cause [of experience].
Because they serve as the objects of the six consciousnesses of others, they are produced by common causes.
If they were not produced by both types of causes, then there would be no aggregate of form, nor would there be mutual seeing.
The Treatise says:
Furthermore, there are consciousnesses characterized by grossness and heaviness, and consciousnesses characterized by subtlety and lightness.
The Commentary explains:

This passage clarifies that the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is the concordant fruit of both wholesome and unwholesome karma, and it is also the generative cause for both wholesome and unwholesome karma.
The treatise states:
"The consciousness characterized by *dausthulya* (coarseness) refers to the seeds of the two types of afflictions, both gross and subtle."
The commentary states:
Because the mind lacks functional capacity regarding both principle and phenomena, it is termed "coarse heaviness" (*dausthulya*).
Since all future afflictions and karmas arise from this consciousness, it is termed "seed."
The Treatise says:
"The subtle and light characteristic consciousness" refers to the seeds of all contaminated (*sāsrava*) wholesome dharmas.
The Commentary explains:
Because the mind possesses functional capacity regarding both principle and phenomena, it is called "subtle and light.
Since all future wholesome factors, such as the five faculties beginning with faith, arise from this consciousness, it is called the "seed."
The Treatise says:

If this did not exist, the distinction between the bases [of consciousness]—namely, those possessing superior capacity and those lacking superior capacity due to the results of prior karma—could not be established.
The Commentary explains:
If this portion of consciousness did not exist, neither the fruit of habituation nor the fruit of retribution could be established.

The fruit of habituation is a concordant fruit, while the fruit of retribution is the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) of the six realms of existence; within this fundamental consciousness, there further exist both coarse and heavy characteristics as well as subtle and light characteristics.
The fruit of practice is also called the "fruit of resemblance," for superior capacity is the basis of the fruit of resemblance.

This fruit of retribution differs within the wholesome realms between humans and devas, and within the unwholesome realms between those in hell, animals, and so forth; therefore, it is said that there is a distinction in their bases.

The basis for the wholesome paths possesses superior capacity, whereas the basis for the unwholesome paths lacks such capacity; if the fundamental consciousness did not exist, these two aspects—the meaning of cause and effect—could not be established.
The Treatise says:

Furthermore, there are two kinds of fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna): that which possesses the characteristic of being appropriated (upātta) and that which does not possess the characteristic of being appropriated.
The Commentary says:
To clarify whether the functional capacities within the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) are exhausted or not,
the treatise states:
"That which possesses the characteristic of being experienced" refers to the consciousness of the seeds of wholesome and unwholesome karma whose retributive results have already matured.
The commentary states:

This fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) previously possessed seeds of both good and evil; when the fruits of retribution have all matured and the seeds have been exhausted, yet the fundamental consciousness alone remains, this fundamental consciousness is said to possess the characteristic of "having reception" (sopādāna).
The Treatise says:
"That which does not possess the characteristics [of a real entity] refers to the seeds of the perfuming of names and words.
The Commentary explains:

This fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) is inexhaustible in its enjoyment within the cycle of birth and death; because the seeds of common karma thereby possess a cause for continuous succession, it is termed "the aspect of non-experiencing."
What is the nature of the characteristic of non-apprehension?
It refers to the seeds of the perfuming of names and words (*nāma-vyañjana-vāsanā*).

First, one designates all phenomena with sounds as "words" (*vyañjana*); subsequently, without uttering words, the mind directly takes those prior sounds as "names" (*nāman*). These names have conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) as their intrinsic nature.

If one discriminates internal phenomena by means of these names, either increasing or decreasing them, thereby subverting correct principle and establishing what is irrational, it is called "fleshly affliction.
If one discriminates external objects by means of these names, giving rise to desire, hatred, and so forth, it is called "skin-like affliction."

If one uses these names to differentiate between all mundane and supramundane phenomena, this constitutes the mental affliction of "discrimination" (vikalpa), which is distinct from the two aforementioned types of discrimination.
Therefore, all afflictions have discrimination as their essence; they obstruct the non-discriminative object and non-discriminative wisdom.
Why is this described as having the characteristic of non-appropriation?
The treatise says:
Because it is the seed from which the proliferation of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) arises throughout immeasurable time.
The commentary states:
The four kinds of worldly discourse are called conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), namely: seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
These four exist merely through the discrimination of names and conventions; because they do not take actual reality as their object, they are termed conceptual proliferation.
Because conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) regarding the past and future limits is inexhaustible, it is said to be "conceptual proliferation throughout immeasurable time.

Whether this conceptual proliferation arises or manifests, it does so due to the perfuming of linguistic designations (*nāma-vyañjana-vāsanā*); therefore, the perfuming of linguistic designations is taught to be the seed of conceptual proliferation.
If these two parts did not exist, what fault would there be?
The treatise says:
