If this consciousness did not exist, then the principle that the two types of karma—good and evil—whether performed or unperformed, are exhausted through the experience of their maturation, would not be established.
The commentary states:

If there were no fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) characterized by appropriation, then since the two types of karma—wholesome and unwholesome—are repeatedly performed or not performed, and because the functional capacity for bestowing retribution would be extinguished such that one would no longer experience retribution, it could not be called "appropriation" (upabhoga). This point would be untenable, as it would result in the loss of the meaning of liberation.
If there were no "non-appropriation" (anupāttatva), what further fault would there be?
The treatise states:
The arising of the perfuming of names and phrases (*nāma-vyañjana-vāsanā*) at the moment of initial birth could not be established either.
The commentary states:
If one were separated from the prior perfuming of names and expressions, then this perfuming of names and expressions—which has never existed in the present or future—could not be established.
Why is this? If the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) were to lack a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), it could not arise.
If it were to arise, then even when Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas have completely severed their afflictions (*kleśa*), those afflictions would arise once again.

If [the afflictions] do not arise, there would be no root afflictions; if there are no root afflictions, there is no karma; if there are neither afflictions nor karma, there would be no existence or differentiation. Consequently, the two truths of origination and suffering would naturally cease and be exhausted, and one would enter nirvana without the need for the arduous cultivation of the path.

Because these two meanings do not exist, there would be neither liberation nor spontaneous liberation; therefore, one knows that the two characteristics of being "appropriated" (*upātta*) and "non-appropriated" (*anupātta*) must certainly exist.
The Treatise says:
Furthermore, there is the characteristic of consciousness as a metaphorical illustration.
The commentary states: For example,
just as a magical illusion serves as the cause for the distracted mind [perceiving] elephants,

horses, and so forth, so too does this illustrative characteristic— the fundamental consciousness— serve as the cause for all inverted and distracted minds, because it is the seed of false discrimination.
The Treatise says:
Just as with magical illusions, mirages, dream-images, and cataracts, the primary consciousness is like these phenomena.
The Commentary explains:
These four matters are analogies for the four inversions (*viparyāsa*).

The illusory phenomenon is an analogy for the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*); the mirage is an analogy for craving for a self (*ātma-tṛṣṇā*); the dream-image is an analogy for pride (*māna*); and the cataract-induced darkness is an analogy for ignorance (*avidyā*).
These four analogies collectively illustrate the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*); the fundamental consciousness itself manifests as these four phenomena.

Just as illusory objects give rise to the false attachments of sentient beings, a mirage gives rise to their craving and desire, dream-images give rise to their distracted minds, and cataracts obstruct sentient beings from clearly perceiving their objects.

If the ādāna-vijñāna has not yet ceased, it can transform the fundamental consciousness (mūla-vijñāna) to produce the six consciousnesses and give rise to the four kinds of active mental perversions; therefore, it is said that the fundamental consciousness appears as these phenomena.
The Treatise says:
"If these seeds of false discrimination did not exist, this consciousness would not constitute the causal condition for inversion.
The Commentary explains:

If a portion of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) were not associated with the appropriating consciousness (*ādānavijñāna*), then the fundamental consciousness would not constitute the causal condition for the four perversions (*viparyāsa*). Why is this?
Because this fundamental consciousness is the causal condition for the seeds of false discrimination (*abhūtaparikalpa*); all false discriminations arise from this fundamental consciousness.
The Treatise says:
Furthermore, there are the characteristics of being complete and incomplete.
The Commentary explains:
Based on this analogy, the fundamental consciousness further constitutes two aspects: first, the aspect of being fully bound; second, the aspect of not being fully bound.
The treatise states:
"If there are sentient beings bound by all fetters who possess the complete characteristics," the commentary explains:
"This refers to sentient beings in the desire realm who have not yet abandoned desire; because they possess the three types of afflictions, they are said to possess the complete characteristics."
The Treatise says:
If one attains worldly detachment from desire, there is the characteristic of harm.
The Commentary says:

If sentient beings have abandoned desire for the realm of desire and the realm of form, yet possess the afflictions of the flesh and the mind in their entirety, there is the sense that the afflictions of the skin are gradually being damaged.
These two [categories] refer to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
The Treatise says:
If there are śrāvakas in training and various bodhisattvas, they possess the characteristic of partial cessation and detachment.
The Commentary says:
The afflictions of the flesh are partially exhausted, while the afflictions of the skin are either impaired or not yet impaired.
The treatise says:
Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Tathāgatas possess the characteristic of complete cessation and detachment.

Why is this? Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas extinguish only the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), whereas the Tathāgata extinguishes both the obstacles of afflictions and the obstacle to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
The commentary states:

Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas have extinguished and abandoned only those afflictions to be eliminated by the paths of seeing and meditation; therefore, they possess no obstacle to liberation (*vimokṣāvaraṇa*).

The Tathāgata has completely extinguished and abandoned all three types of afflictions; thus, the Tathāgata’s fundamental consciousness is forever free from all obstacles to liberation as well as obstacles to omniscience (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). This consciousness is sometimes called non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and sometimes called post-non-conceptual wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
If one gives rise to even a single portion of activities for the benefit of sentient beings, it is called conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*);

if one gives rise to even a single portion by taking the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) of all phenomena as its object, it is called the knowledge of suchness (*tathatā-jñāna*). These two combined are termed the *sāmbhogika-kāya*.
The Treatise says:
If these afflictions did not exist, their successive extinction could not be established.
The Commentary says:

If these [cessations] with and without specific characteristics did not exist, the sequential cessation of ordinary beings, noble learners (śaikṣa), and noble non-learners (aśaikṣa) would be untenable.
Among the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), why is the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) exclusively of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*)?
Because it is a maturation (*vipāka*).
The treatise says:
For what reason are the fruits and retributions of the two dharmas—wholesome and unwholesome—exclusively non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*)?
The commentary explains:
Because they are not defiled by afflictions (*kleśa*), they are called non-obscured neutral.
The afflictions of the upper realms are different in that they are obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*). Why are they different?
Because their causes are wholesome or unwholesome, while their fruits are neutral.
The Treatise says:
This indeterminate nature is not incompatible with its co-arising alongside both wholesome and unwholesome dharmas.
The Commentary explains:
Because the nature of non-obscured neutral [states] is not incompatible with the two natures of good and evil, both good and evil karma can arise within neutral retribution.
Because of the arising of karma, there exist the two paths of good and evil.
The Treatise says:
The two dharmas of good and evil are mutually contradictory.
The Commentary explains:
If the retribution were itself good or evil, then the natures of good and evil would be mutually contradictory.
If it were good, evil could not arise, and thus there would be no evil realms;
if it were evil, good could not arise, and thus there would be no good realms. Consequently, of the two paths of good and evil, one path would necessarily cease to exist.
The Treatise says:
If the nature of retribution were established as being either wholesome or unwholesome, there would be no means by which one could attain liberation from the afflictions.
The Commentary says:
If retribution were of a virtuous or non-virtuous nature, then from virtue a further virtuous retribution would arise, and from non-virtue a further non-virtuous retribution would arise.
Since retribution would give rise to further retribution, birth and death would never cease; thus, there would be no possibility of attaining liberation.
The Treatise says:
Furthermore, there is no skillful means by which either virtue or afflictions can arise.
The Commentary explains:
If meditative concentration (*samādhi*) were exclusively wholesome, afflictions (*kleśa*) could not arise;
if it were exclusively unwholesome, the wholesome could not arise.
The treatise states:
Therefore, there is neither liberation nor bondage.
The commentary states:
if there is no goodness, there is no liberation; if there are no afflictions, there is no bondage.
The Treatise says:
Because these two meanings do not exist, the retributive consciousness (vipākavijñāna) is necessarily of the nature of non-obscured indeterminate (anivṛtāvyākṛta).
The Commentary explains:
There is no sense of liberation through non-existence, nor is there a sense of bondage through non-existence;
since liberation and bondage are both established as existing, it is known that the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) is necessarily of an indeterminate nature (avyākṛta).
Commentary on the Mahāyānasaṃgraha, Scroll Four;
Commentary on the Mahāyānasaṃgraha, Scroll Five.
Exegesis by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha from Central India. 2.
Commentary on the Chapter on the Superior Characteristics of What Should Be Known (Jñeyalakṣaṇaviśeṣanirdeśa). Part One of Two. This treatise consists of four sections: first, the characteristics;
second, the distinctions; third, the analysis; and fourth, the clarification of the basis for the intended meaning.
The Treatise says:
Thus has been explained the superior characteristic of the object of knowledge (jñeya) as its basis.
How should the superior characteristic of the object of knowledge itself be understood?
The commentary states:

It was previously stated that there are ten points in the sequential order; the first, the superior characteristic of the basis (*āśraya*), has already been explained. Next, the second, the superior characteristic of what is to be known (*jñeya*), should be explained.
How many categories does this meaning have?
What is its name?
What are its characteristics?
How are these three to be understood?
The treatise says:
These characteristics of what is to be known should be understood as being, in brief, of three kinds.
The commentary states:

The following answers the three preceding questions, clarifying that the second superior characteristic, when explained briefly, consists of three numbers; that is, three names and three characteristics.
What are these three?
The treatise states:
First, the characteristic of the dependent nature; second, the characteristic of the imagined nature; third, the characteristic of the perfected nature.
The commentary explains:
This statement first clarifies the number three and the names designated by that number; the characteristics of the three natures will be explained separately in the subsequent text.
One, two, and three are the numbers; the dependent, the imagined, and the perfected are the names.
The Treatise says:
"The characteristic of the dependent nature.
The Commentary explains:
The following explains the three characteristics.
The treatise says:
"With the fundamental consciousness as their seed, they are the various distinctions among all consciousnesses subsumed under false discrimination."
The commentary states:

Because the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is capable of transforming and manifesting as the eleven consciousnesses, the fundamental consciousness is itself the seed of the eleven consciousnesses.
Since these eleven consciousnesses are distinct from one another, they are said to be "differentiated."
Discrimination is the nature of consciousness.
What does the nature of consciousness discriminate?
It discriminates the non-existent as existent; therefore, it is called false and illusory.

Discrimination is the cause and false imagination is the fruit; by means of the fruit of false imagination, the cause of discrimination is revealed. Thus, this nature of discrimination encompasses all consciousnesses without exception.
The Treatise asks:
What constitutes the distinction?
The Commentary explains:
This does not inquire into their common nature, but rather into the distinctions among the various consciousnesses.
The treatise says:

namely, body-consciousness, the consciousness of the body-possessor, the consciousness of the experiencer, the consciousness of the object to be experienced, the consciousness of the actual experience, world-consciousness, number-consciousness, location-consciousness, linguistic-consciousness, the consciousness of the distinction between self and others, and the consciousness of birth and death within the two paths of good and evil.

The body-consciousness, the consciousness of the self, the consciousness of the experiencer, the consciousness of the object to be experienced, the consciousness of the actual experience, the consciousness of time, the consciousness of number, the consciousness of place, and the consciousness of speech—such consciousnesses as these arise from the seeds of the perfuming of speech.
The consciousness that discriminates between self and others arises from the seeds of the habitual perfuming of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
The consciousness of birth and death within the two paths of good and evil arises from the seeds of the habitual perfuming of the [view of] existence (*bhava-aṅga*).

The commentary states: "Body-consciousness" refers to the five elements beginning with the eye; "body-possessor consciousness" refers to the afflicted consciousness (*kliṣṭa-vijñāna*); "experiencer consciousness" refers to the mind-element (*manodhātu*); "object-of-experience consciousness" refers to the six external objects such as form; "consciousness of actual experience" refers to the six consciousness-elements; "temporal consciousness" refers to the consciousness of the uninterrupted succession of birth and death; "numerical consciousness" refers to the consciousness of counting from one up to the *asaṃkhyeya*; "locational consciousness" refers to the consciousness of the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*); and "verbal consciousness" refers to the consciousness of seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing. These nine consciousnesses are the bases that should be known, having the differentiation of verbal habitual tendencies (*abhilāpa-vāsanā*) as their cause.

The consciousness of the distinction between self and others refers to the consciousness of the distinction between the bases of self and others, which has the habitual tendencies of the view of self as its cause.

The consciousness of birth and death within the two paths of good and evil refers to the consciousness of the various distinctions within the path of birth and death, which has the habitual tendencies of the *bhavāṅga* (existence-element) as its cause.
The Treatise says:
By means of such consciousnesses as these, all realms, paths, and afflictions are subsumed.
The Commentary explains:
"All realms" refers to the three realms and the eighteen realms; "all paths" refers to the six paths.

Within these realms and paths, there are three types of afflictions: namely, delusion, karma, and karmic retribution. These three are also termed "afflictions" (*kleśa*) and are further called "turbidities" (*kaṣāya*); within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), no phenomena transcend these.
These dharmas are subsumed by the aforementioned eleven consciousnesses; because they share the same nature, they can be mutually subsumed.
The treatise states:
"The dependent nature serves as the characteristic, and through it, false discrimination is manifested."
The commentary states:
It is intended to show that false discrimination has the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) as its essential characteristic.
The disordered consciousness and the transformations of disordered consciousness are precisely what constitute false discrimination.
Discrimination (*vikalpa*) is precisely the distracted consciousness (*kṣipta-vijñāna*); falsity (*abhūta*) is precisely the transformation of the distracted consciousness.

If explained extensively, false discrimination consists of eleven kinds of consciousness; if explained concisely, there are four kinds of consciousness: first, consciousness resembling objects (*viṣaya*); second, consciousness resembling sense organs (*indriya*); third, consciousness resembling a self (*ātman*); and fourth, consciousness resembling consciousness itself (*vijñāna*).
All false conceptualizations within the entire triple world do not transcend this meaning, for it is by means of such consciousness that they are manifested.
Although it is said that this consciousness exhaustively encompasses all false conceptualizations, among these false conceptualizations, what is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)?
What is the nature of the imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva)?
The treatise states:
These various consciousnesses are subsumed under false discrimination and have representation-only (vijñapti-mātra) as their essence.
The commentary states:
Such consciousnesses thus manifest eleven consciousnesses and four consciousnesses.
Among all phenomena, there is only consciousness and no other dharmas; therefore, consciousness-only (vijñapti-mātra) constitutes their essence.

This essence, by virtue of its existence, differs from the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); and because it is subsumed under the nature of false discrimination (*abhūta-parikalpa*), it differs from the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Since this nature is neither truly existent nor truly non-existent, it cannot escape being false.
Because this false nature is its very essence, it is said to be comprised within unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*).
The treatise states:
"The appearance of non-existent, false objects as a basis is called the characteristic of the dependent nature (*paratantrasvabhāva*)."
The commentary states:
Because there is definitively nothing that exists, it is said to be "non-existent.
Since that which is non-existent serves as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the six consciousnesses, it is called a "false object" (*abhūta-viṣaya*).
Because the transformations of the mind—such as the arising, abiding, and ceasing of what resembles the sense organs, objects, self, and consciousness—are clearly manifest, they are said to "appear.
Since this appearance has the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) as its cause, it is said to be "dependent" (*āśrita*).

For example, when one grasps at a self as an object, this object is in fact non-existent. Because the self does not exist, and because it appears as a self through the transformations of the mind, it is said to be a non-existent, false object.

This manifestation occurs because it arises from the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); since the dependent nature serves as the basis for the manifestation of unreal objects, this is described as the characteristic of the dependent nature.
The treatise says:

Regarding the characteristic of the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), there are in reality no external objects; rather, it is only the substance of consciousness that manifests as objects. This is called the characteristic of the nature of discrimination.
The commentary states:

Just as the objects such as the self (*ātman*) have no separate substance and take consciousness-only as their essence, yet consciousness itself is not the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

It is the transformations of consciousness that manifest as the self and so forth; these objects do not exist but appear to exist, being grasped by consciousness, and are thus called the nature of discrimination.
The treatise states:
As for the characteristic of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), it is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Because the appearances of objects are eternally non-existent, yet this [dependent nature] is not non-existent in reality, it is called the characteristic of the perfected nature.
The commentary states:
The object of false construction never exists as a cause for manifestation, because its manifesting essence does not exist and thus cannot be apprehended.

For example, although objects such as "self" and so forth appear to exist substantially, their essence cannot be found when sought through the three means of valid cognition—direct perception, inference, and authoritative testimony—based on those very appearances.

Just as the object of the self (*ātman*) is without essence, so too is the object of phenomena (*dharma*); because they are eternally without substance, both persons and phenomena are without self (*anātman*).

This absence of self truly exists and is not non-existent. Because these two kinds of objects lack intrinsic nature, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is ungraspable, yet it truly exists and is not non-existent; this is called the characteristic of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The treatise states:
By means of the body-consciousness, the consciousness of the body, and the consciousness of the experiencer, one should know that the six internal bases, such as the eye, are subsumed.
By means of the consciousness of what is to be experienced, one should know that the six external bases, such as form, are subsumed.
By means of the consciousness of correct realization, one should understand that it subsumes the six consciousness-elements, such as the eye-consciousness and so forth.
With these types of consciousness as the basis, all other consciousnesses are merely specific manifestations of this consciousness.
The commentary says:
What meaning does this statement intend to reveal?
It intends to reveal the meaning of true reality (*tathatā*).
If it were not definitively clarified that all phenomena are consciousness-only, the nature of ultimate reality would not be manifested.
If the eleven types of consciousness were not fully explained, the conventional truth would not be exhaustively described.
If one speaks only of the first five consciousnesses, one attains only the fundamental level of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), but not its differentiated meanings.

If conventional truth is said to be non-pervasive, then ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) will not be clearly understood; if ultimate truth is not clearly understood, then conventional truth cannot be fully eliminated. Therefore, it is taught that all eleven consciousnesses together encompass conventional truth.
Are the eighteen elements (dhātus) possessed of faculties (indriya), objects (viṣaya), and consciousness (vijñāna), or is it not so?
The treatise says:
These various consciousnesses are merely consciousness (vijñaptimātra), because there are no objects and so forth.
The commentary states:

Although the transformations of consciousness manifest as internal and external phenomena with differing characteristics, in reality there is only a single consciousness; since there are no separate entities such as external objects, all are designated by the name "consciousness."
If there were no objects, how could the experience of attachment, aversion, and so forth be established for this consciousness when it is separated from objects?
The treatise says:

For example, in dreams and the like, even though one is entirely devoid of external objects and it is merely consciousness-only, various objects such as forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, houses, forests, lands, and mountains appear as if they were real; yet among these, not a single object exists as a reality.
The commentary states:
The various differences seen within a dream have no real objects; they are all produced by consciousness.
Thus, the principle that the experience of attachment, aversion, and so forth is likewise established is also proven.
The Commentary says:
By means of this analogy, one should understand that in all cases there is only consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*).
By the phrase "and so forth," one should understand the analogies of magical illusions, mirages, and cataracts.
If one awakens from the perception of objects seen by others, then in all places there is only consciousness, just like objects in a dream.
Just as when a person awakens from a dream, they discern that dream-objects are merely consciousness, why is it not the same upon waking from this [present] state?
It is not that this principle does not exist.
If a person has already attained the awakening to the wisdom of *tathatā*, this awakening is certainly present.
It is, for example, like a person who is still in the midst of a dream and has not yet awakened; in that state, this awakening does not arise.
If a person has already awakened, only then does this awakening exist.

Likewise, if a person has not yet attained the awakening of the wisdom of *tathatā*, this awakening is likewise absent; if a person has already attained the awakening of the wisdom of *tathatā*, this awakening necessarily exists.
If a person has not yet attained the awakening of true suchness-wisdom, how can they give rise to inferential knowledge regarding consciousness-only?
It is through sacred teaching and the nature of reality that such inference is possible.
Regarding the sacred teaching, as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, stated in the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*:
"O Son of the Buddha!
The three realms consist of nothing but consciousness."
Furthermore, as it is said in the *Viniscayasamgrahani* (Exegesis on the Sections):
The commentary states:

"By means of this analogy of a dream, one should understand that within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) and other such categories, there is only consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*) and no external objects (*artha*)."
For what reason are two Āgamas cited to clarify the sacred teaching?
The former is a brief exposition, while the latter is an extensive exposition; thus, the former serves as proof for the latter.
The treatise says:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya asked the Buddha, the World-Honored One:
"World-Honored One!
Is this form-characteristic (rūpa-lakṣaṇa), which is the object of focus for a concentrated mind, different from the mind, or is it not different from the mind?"
The commentary states:
At this time, there are three meanings: first, the time of equality, meaning the absence of sinking, floating, or inversion;
second, the time of harmony, meaning that which causes hearing, the capacity for hearing, and correct hearing.
At the time of the three turnings of the Wheel of Dharma, it is said that there is correct teaching and correct reception.
Regarding "form-characteristics" (rūpa-nimitta), this refers to the first eight bases among the ten universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana).
These form-characteristics are the objects of focus for the concentrated mind; are they distinct from the mind, or are they the mind itself?
The treatise states:
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, said:
"Maitreya!"
It is not different from the mind.
Why? Because I teach that there is only consciousness; these objective appearances of form are manifested by consciousness.
The commentary states:
The Buddha taught that there is only consciousness (vijñapti) because there are no external objects (artha).
If this is so, what kind of phenomenon is this form (rūpa) that is perceived by the practitioner of meditation?
As the Sūtra says:
"This objective sphere of form-phenomena is manifested by consciousness.
In reality there is no objective sphere; it is produced by the transformation of consciousness."
First, consciousness-only (vijñapti-mātra) is explained; subsequently, objective-consciousness (viṣaya-vijñapti) is explained. What is the difference between these two types of consciousness?
To reveal that there are two aspects: the former consciousness is the determinate essence, while the latter consciousness is the determinate object.

This essence and its object are fundamentally a single consciousness; one appears as the arising of the subject that discriminates, and the other appears as the arising of the object that is discriminated.
The Treatise says:
Maitreya Bodhisattva stated:
“World-Honored One!
If the color-form (*rūpa-nimitta*) of the meditative object is not different from the concentrated mind, how can this consciousness take that very consciousness as its object?
The commentary states:
If there were a distinct consciousness that took [another] as its object, then the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) would not be established.
Nor could it be established if one were to take its own self-substance as an object, for such a thing does not exist in the world.
The treatise says:
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, said:
"Maitreya!"
There is no dharma that can apprehend another dharma.
Although it cannot so apprehend, this consciousness arises through such a transformation as to manifest like an external object (*viṣaya*).
Commentary:
This consciousness arises with such characteristics that, within meditative concentration, two kinds of aspects emerge:

first, differences arising from the aspect of the grasper (*grāhaka*), and second, differences arising from the aspect of the grasped (*grāhya*). These two aspects manifest simultaneously from a single consciousness.

These forms, such as blue and so forth, are objects of meditative concentration (*samāhita-viṣaya*), not objects of the consciousness that recollects and maintains them. For this reason, these forms do not exist within the state of concentration; it is impossible for something previously realized to be recollected and maintained later in the manner described.
When dust arises and appears before one, it is clearly manifest; this consciousness that retains the memory is defiled, whereas what arises and appears now is seen with clear purity.

If you say that the objects of hearing and reflection have been repeatedly practiced and, though the time has now passed, they are again contemplated through recollection, just as what was seen in the past is seen again now.
This interpretation is not correct. Why?

Because these two objects of hearing and reflection, being past, do not exist now. Since they do not exist at this time, if [cognition] arises resembling them without having been previously seen, then the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) is all the more clearly demonstrated; thus, the doctrine of consciousness-only and the doctrine that external objects (*viṣaya*) are non-existent are established.
The Treatise says:
For example, when one looks at a face and perceives it as a reflection, saying "I see a shadow," this shadow appears as something similar yet distinct from the face.
The Commentary explains:
This analogy is intended to show that there is only one's own face and no separate reflection. Why is this?
The principle of the conjunction of all dharmas is difficult to conceive; it causes that which cannot be seen to become visible.
It is just as with reflections in water or mirrors: although there is no separate entity in the reflection, one sees one's own face and thinks there is a distinct reflection.
The treatise says:
the concentrated mind is likewise; it manifests appearing like an object, yet this is thought to be something other than the concentrated mind itself.
The commentary states:
The concentrated mind has two aspects; one aspect resembles consciousness and the other resembles objects. These two types are in reality nothing but consciousness.
The treatise says:
By means of this scripture (*āgama*) and the reasoning (*yukti*) it establishes, the meaning of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only) is revealed.
The commentary states:

"Scripture" refers to the two preceding sūtras; "reasoning" refers to the principles such as the recollection of past forms by consciousness and the analogy of the reflection on a face, which reveal the meaning of consciousness-only.
The Treatise asks:
Why is it so? The Commentary explains:
Regarding the question, "How can it be said that there is only consciousness?
the treatise states:

At that time, when the practitioner’s mind is precisely within meditative observation, if they perceive pervasive color-forms such as blue or yellow, they are seeing their own mind and not perceiving external objects such as blue or yellow colors.
The commentary states:

If it occurs within the five consciousnesses of a distracted mind, one may say that it arises by taking present external objects as its conditions; if it occurs within the mental consciousness of a distracted mind, it arises by taking past objects as its conditions; however, if it occurs within meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*), it can by no means take external form as its object.

Since form is present before one and does not take a past object as its condition, it should be known that when the concentrated mind takes form as its object, one sees only one's own mind and does not see a separate external object.
The Treatise says:
By this principle, within all consciousnesses, a bodhisattva should apply such analogical inference regarding representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*).

Regarding consciousnesses of blue, yellow, and so forth, they are not recollective consciousnesses because their objects are perceived as being present before one. In the two stages of hearing and reflection, there is a recollective mental consciousness; this consciousness takes a past object as its condition and arises as if it were that past object. Therefore, the principle of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only) is established.

By means of this inference, a bodhisattva, even if they have not yet attained the awakening of the wisdom of *tathatā*, can give rise to inferential knowledge regarding the principle of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
The commentary states:

Previously, it was explained that the eleven consciousnesses collectively comprise the eighteen *dhātus*; within these eighteen *dhātus*, there are both sense faculties (*indriya*) and sense objects (*viṣaya*).

A bodhisattva should contemplate the meaning of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*): since there are no separate objects within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), by analogy with the forms within concentration, one should know that external forms as well have no separate objects.
The Treatise says:
These various consciousnesses have already been explained previously.
The Commentary says:
The eleven consciousnesses have already been fully explained above.
Since one is about to establish a critique, it is necessary first to clarify those eleven consciousnesses previously mentioned.
The treatise says:
For example, in cases such as illusions and dreams, the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) can be established regarding the visual consciousness and other cognitions therein.
The commentary states:

Previously, illusions and the like were cited as analogies for the absence of distinct sense organs and objects; now, because one wishes to challenge whether the doctrine of *vijñapti-mātra* is established or not, it is necessary to cite the previously mentioned analogies.

Within the eleven consciousnesses, eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are fully present. The preceding explanation of the consciousness of meditative attainment refers to the six consciousness-elements, through which the meaning of "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*) can be explained.
The treatise asks:
Since the consciousnesses of the eye, form, and so forth possess material form (*rūpa*), how can the meaning of "consciousness-only" be perceived?
The commentary states:
This objection implies that the remaining ten elements (*dhātu*) should not be described as consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
Previously, it was clarified that bodily consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) consists of the five sense faculties, namely, from visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) up to bodily consciousness.

The consciousness that was previously explained as that which should be experienced refers to the five sense objects, namely, visual consciousness up to tactile consciousness; therefore, it is called "consciousness of the eye, form, and so forth.
Regarding the existence of form (*rūpa*), there are three meanings: first, form already exists prior to the arising of visual consciousness;
second, when consciousness transforms into form, that too is considered form.
Third, because there are material objects as domains, visual consciousness arises resembling those forms and is thus called "discerning form.
If there were no material objects as domains, what would it discern?
Based on these ten elements, the principle of Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra) would fail to be established.
The Treatise says:
These consciousnesses should be understood as previously explained, based on both scripture (āgama) and reasoning (yukti).
The Commentary says:
This answers the previous question.
Based on the two preceding sūtras and the principles of the analogies cited above, one should understand it in this way.
The treatise says:
If form (*rūpa*) is consciousness, how is it that it manifests as if it were form?
The commentary explains:
This question asks, if one says there is no separate objective realm of form and that it is merely the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), why does it manifest as if it were form and so forth?
The treatise asks:
What is meant by "continuity that is firmly established and characterized by similarity between preceding and succeeding moments"?
The commentary explains:

If this question were produced by a transformation of consciousness, then it should arise and perish suddenly, changing and shifting without constancy; how then could a single form persist continuously for a long duration across many moments, remaining uniform from beginning to end without any alteration?
Therefore, one should know that there must be a distinct form (*rūpa*).
The treatise says:
"Because it serves as the basis for afflictions such as inversion."
The commentary states:
Perversion is the root of the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Through the transformation of consciousness, various conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) arise; these conceptual constructions are themselves perversions, and because of perversion, the various afflictions are produced.
The dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is associated with the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), which is the locus of inverted afflictions.

Through inverted afflictions, the dependent nature is made to correspond with the imagined nature; furthermore, these inverted afflictions are themselves the locus upon which the transformation of consciousness (vijñāna-pariṇāma) depends.
The Treatise says:
If it were not so, the inversion regarding what is non-meaningful as being meaningful could not be established.
The Commentary explains:
If there were no sense of mutual dependence, then consciousness would not undergo transformation; thus, the conceptualization of non-entities as entities would not constitute such an error.
The treatise states:
If there were no error regarding objects, the two kinds of afflictions—the afflictive obscurations and the cognitive obscurations—could not be established.
The commentary states:
If consciousness does not undergo transformation and discrimination, and thus does not take what is non-objective as an object, how could there be inversion?
If there is no inversion, then afflictions do not arise; if there are no afflictions, then Śrāvakas have no obstruction to liberation and Bodhisattvas have no obstruction to omniscience.
The treatise states:
If the two obstacles did not exist, the category of the purified (viśuddha-pakṣa) could likewise not be established.
Therefore, that these various consciousnesses arise in this manner can be accepted as real.
The commentary states:
If there were no afflictions, how could there be the Noble Path?
Therefore, this argument is also untenable.
Therefore, one should believe that there are no dharmas distinct from consciousness.
The treatise says:
Herein, a verse is spoken:
The causes of confusion and the essence of confusion— whether it be consciousness of form or consciousness of the formless—
if the preceding consciousness does not exist, the subsequent consciousness cannot arise.
Commentary:
To grasp at existence within non-existence is confusion.
From what dharma does this confused consciousness arise?
It arises from form (rūpa).
What constitutes the consciousness of form (*rūpa-vijñāna*)?
If we consider it in relation to the five consciousnesses, the five sense organs and the five sense objects are termed the consciousness of form.
This consciousness of form can give rise to the eye-consciousness and the other sensory cognitions; to cognize this consciousness of form is itself the cause of delusion.
If this consciousness does not arise, one cannot grasp at existence within non-existence.
What dharma is called the substance of confusion?
It is formless consciousness.
If categorized according to the five sense organs, these are the five consciousnesses; if categorized according to the mind organ, they are simply the mental consciousness.
Neither the consciousness of dharmas nor the consciousness of form and the consciousness of the formless are anything other than causes of distraction.
The Treatise says:
If the preceding consciousness does not exist, the subsequent consciousness cannot arise.
The Commentary explains:

The preceding consciousness is the cause of confusion; if it did not originally exist, then the essence of confusion—which is the subsequent consciousness as its effect—could not arise, as there would be no cause.
Chapter Two: On Differentiation. The Treatise says:

How is it that the body-consciousness (*deha-vijñāna*), the consciousness of the body-possessor (*dehin-vijñāna*), the consciousness of the experiencer (*bhoktṛ-vijñāna*), the consciousness of the object to be experienced (*bhojana-vijñāna*), and the consciousness of the actual experience (*bhoga-vijñāna*) arise in all places of birth, mutually and intimately conjoined?
The commentary states:

These five consciousnesses are themselves the eighteen elements (*dhātus*). Within the three realms, the six destinies, and the four modes of birth—across all places of birth—how can these eighteen types arise in mutual, close conjunction?
The Treatise says:
Because it is manifested by the fullness of taking birth.
The Commentary says:
In every place of birth, within a single moment, the eighteen elements (dhātus) are fully present.
Since these eighteen elements are not mutually separated and can act as causes for manifestation, they manifest by arising in mutual, close conjunction.

Furthermore, the faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are necessarily inseparable; there is no arising of sensation (*vedanā*) where the faculty exists but the object and consciousness do not, and the same applies to the other two.
Since one must necessarily possess the other two, the presence of the other two serves to manifest this one. Because they are inseparable, they arise in mutual, intimate conjunction.
The Treatise says:
How is it that worldly consciousness and so forth arise with various distinctions as previously described?
The Commentary explains:
This further questions the first five consciousnesses.
Since the phenomena subsumed within the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*) are already exhaustive, what is the purpose of further explaining the subsequent arising of the six consciousnesses?
The treatise states:
"Because birth and death have continued in succession without interruption since beginningless time.
The commentary states:

In order to clarify that the karmic retribution of sentient beings has been a continuous succession of birth and death throughout the three periods of time since beginningless time, it is necessary to establish the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness).
The Treatise says:
Because it is subsumed within the immeasurable realm of sentient beings.
The Commentary explains:

In order to clarify that the karmic retributions of sentient beings involve various realms (dhātus) in differing quantities—such as the four realms, the six realms, the eighteen realms, and so forth—it is necessary to establish the "consciousness of number" (saṃkhyā-vijñāna) to encompass all such enumerations.
The Treatise says:
Because it is subsumed within the immeasurable receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).
The Commentary explains:

In order to clarify the dwelling places of sentient beings—since there are immeasurable distinctions among humans, devas, and the evil realms—it is necessary to establish the "consciousness of various locations" (*pradeśa-vijñāna*) to encompass all such places.
The Treatise says:
Because immeasurable activities are mutually inclusive in their manifestation.
The Commentary explains:
To clarify that seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing each have many kinds of causes—

and because these immeasurable verbal expressions and activities mutually manifest one another with seeing and the other senses— it is necessary to establish a "verbal expression consciousness" (*abhilāpa-vijñapti*) that subsumes all such verbal expressions.
The treatise says:
Because they are subsumed under the distinctions of the immeasurable [qualities], the encompassing, and the enjoyment.
The commentary explains:
The inclusion [of the self and others] refers to the inclusion of oneself and others; the enjoyment refers to the enjoyment of what is experienced by oneself and others.

Because it is to clarify that sentient beings each conceive of a "self" in various ways, and likewise conceive of "what belongs to the self" (ātmīya) in various ways, one must establish the distinction between self and other as a form of consciousness that includes all such distinctions between self and other.
The Treatise says:
Because immeasurable enjoyments are comprised within the karmic retribution of love and hatred.
The Commentary says:
The fruit of wholesome karma is love, and the fruit of unwholesome karma is hatred; sentient beings experience these two types of karmic fruits in immeasurable varieties.
The treatise states:
This is because they are subsumed under the distinctions of the attainment of immeasurable births and deaths.
The commentary states:
Within these two fruits, there is birth and death.
The initial reception [of the fruit] is birth; the subsequent continuity after birth is attainment; the approach to death is realization; and the severance of life is death.
To clarify that sentient beings experience the fruits of two types of karma— birth and death— which encompass the birth and death of all paths of both good and evil,
the treatise says:
How is it correctly argued that these various consciousnesses establish the principle of *vijñapti-mātratā* (consciousness-only)?
The commentary states:

It has already been established that the previously discussed five consciousnesses are *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). How, then, can it be established that the subsequently discussed six consciousnesses are also *vijñapti-mātra*?
The treatise says:
If briefly stated, there are three characteristics by which all consciousnesses are established as *vijñapti-mātra*.
The commentary states:
There are three principles for establishing these six consciousnesses so that they become *vijñapti-mātra*.

The principle consists of three stages: first, entering the stage of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*); second, entering the stage of the two [natures]; and third, entering the stage of various kinds of natures.
"Entering" (*praveśa*) means the sense of thorough penetration.
What is meant by entering the stage of representation-only?
The treatise says:
"There is only the measure of consciousness.
The commentary explains:
Among the six consciousnesses, if one investigates according to reason, one perceives only consciousness and no other phenomena. Why is this?
The treatise says:
"Because external objects do not exist.
The commentary explains:
Since all dharmas that are cognized are devoid of consciousness and do not truly exist, it is said that the six consciousnesses consist of nothing but the measure of consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*).
What is meant by "entering into the two alone"?
The treatise says:
There are only two, namely the image (*nimitta*) and the vision (*darśana*), because they are subsumed within consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The commentary states:

If one can thoroughly penetrate that a portion of each of the six consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and so forth, constitutes the aspect (*nimitta*) and a portion constitutes the seeing (*darśana*), this is called "entering the two-only" (*dvaya-mātra*).
What is the meaning of this?

Among the various consciousnesses, one portion of any given consciousness transforms into the aspect of form and so forth, while another portion transforms into the aspect of vision; therefore, they are said to be "only two.
Since the six consciousnesses—such as those of the eye and so on—do not transcend these two natures of consciousness, it is taught that they are subsumed within these two alone.
What is meant by "entering into various kinds"?
The treatise states:
Because it is subsumed under the arising of various characteristics.
What is the meaning of this?
All these consciousnesses are established as "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*) because they lack external objects (*artha*).

The various consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, possess both an aspect (*nimitta*) and a seeing-part (*darśana*): they take form and so forth as their aspect, and these visual and other consciousnesses take [other] consciousnesses as their seeing-part. Furthermore, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) takes all consciousnesses, from the visual consciousness up to the consciousness of mental phenomena (*dharmavijñāna*), as its aspect, and it takes the mental consciousness itself as its seeing-part.
Why is this so? Because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is capable of conceptual discrimination, and because it arises as if divided into all the objects of the various consciousnesses.
The commentary states:
This single visual consciousness, as it is established, has one part that can give rise to various appearances and another part that can apprehend those various appearances;
that which apprehends is precisely what is called "seeing."

If the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) takes as its objective aspect all eye-consciousnesses and so forth, as well as the consciousness of phenomena (dharmavijñāna), then the mental consciousness is that which sees.
Furthermore, regarding the arising of various aspects: it is only the mental consciousness that gives rise to various aspects, because the objects it perceives are not fixed.
The remaining consciousnesses necessarily take only a single type of object as their condition and are incapable of discrimination.
When there is discrimination, it constitutes "seeing" (darśana-vijñāna); when there is no discrimination, it constitutes "image" (nimitta).

By means of these three characteristics, it is established that the six consciousnesses, such as those of the world and so forth, are mere consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*); this meaning is thus revealed.
The treatise says:
Herein, a verse is spoken:
Entering into the "measure-only" and the "two-only," various people have explained it as such;
this refers to the stage of penetrating vijñapti-mātra and the stage of suppressing and departing from consciousness.
Commentary:

This verse reveals three ways of penetrating the meaning of representation-only (*vijñapti-mātra*): first, penetrating that there is only measure (*mātra*), because external objects do not exist in reality;
second, penetrating that there are only two, because the image (*nimitta*) and the vision (*darśana*) are both representation-only;
and third, penetrating the arising of various forms, because there are merely various appearances while there is no difference in their substance.
Who is it that can thoroughly comprehend these three characteristics?
Only the practitioner of contemplation.

There are two kinds of practitioners of contemplation: first, bodhisattvas who have entered the stage of seeing; second, those who have attained the four formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) and so forth.
The practitioner first attains thorough penetration and subsequently explains it to others.
At what stage are this penetration and this explanation accomplished?
The treatise says:
"At the time of penetrating vijñapti-mātra, and at the stage of suppressing and abandoning consciousness.
The commentary states:
From the first bhūmi up to the stage of perfect enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) constitutes the stage of penetrating vijñapti-mātra.

From the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, as well as the attainment of non-conceptualization and the attainment of cessation, these constitute the stages for suppressing and detaching from consciousness.
If the grasped objects do not exist, how can consciousness be said to be the grasper?
In that case, the meaning of "only cognition" would not be established.
This interpretation is incorrect. Why is this so?
The meaning of Vijñapti-mātra (consciousness-only) is not lost, nor is the meaning of the grasped (grāhya) and the grasper (grāhaka) non-existent.
To establish this principle, the three characteristics are revealed.
For those who enter into "representation-only" (vijñapti-mātra), it is to reveal that there is consciousness-only and no external objects.
Since that which is cognized does not exist, how can "consciousness-only" be established?
To establish this principle, it is said that there are "only two" and "various kinds.
"Only two" refers to the image (nimitta) and the vision (darśana); the image is the apprehended object, and the vision is the apprehending subject.
The various [aspects] are likewise so.
Therefore, the principles of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) and the grasper and the grasped are all established.
The latter half of the verse is explained as before.
The Treatise says:
Various masters state that this mental consciousness arises in accordance with various bases and thus receives various names.
The Commentary explains:
The various masters maintain that for all bodhisattvas, a single mental consciousness arises in succession.

Although the mental consciousness is one, when it arises in dependence upon the eye-faculty, it receives the name "eye-consciousness," and so on, up to when it arises in dependence upon the body-faculty, it receives the name "body-consciousness. Within this process, there is no other consciousness distinct from the mental consciousness.
Apart from the ālayavijñāna, this fundamental consciousness is subsumed within the manovijñāna because they belong to the same category.
This manovijñāna receives a distinct name based upon its support (*āśraya*).
The treatise states:
For example, it is like how mental action (manas-karman) receives the names of bodily and vocal actions.
The commentary states:
although this mental action is but one, when it arises based on the gateway of the body, it is called bodily action; when it arises based on the gateway of speech, it is called vocal action.
The mental consciousness is likewise; it receives different names according to its respective basis.

If someone were to say that the five faculties, such as the eye, are devoid of discrimination, then they would also have to say that the mental consciousness is devoid of discrimination when it arises based upon them.
For example, when the mental faculty (*manas*) is defiled by afflictions, because its basis is defiled, the consciousness that arises supported by it is also defiled.
The mental consciousness is also like this.
The treatise says:
This consciousness arises in dependence upon all bases.
The commentary says:
This means it arises depending upon the various faculties, such as the eye.
The treatise says:
Various appearances manifest as two kinds of phenomena: first, they manifest as resembling objects; second, they manifest as resembling conceptualization.
The commentary states:
Consciousness arises in dependence upon the six sense faculties and manifests as resembling these two kinds of phenomena.
There are two types of phenomena: those of multiple categories and those of a single category.
Phenomena of multiple categories belong to the objective field (*viṣaya*), while phenomena of a single category belong to the discernment (*vikalpa*).

By means of these two statements, although consciousness is a single phenomenon, one part appears as the objective field and another part appears as the discernment of the objective field; therefore, what was stated previously is without fault.
The treatise says:
"In all places, there is the manifestation of what resembles tangibility.
The commentary explains:
"In all places" refers to those places where there is form.
Wherever there is form, there must be a body; and wherever there is a body, it necessarily manifests as something resembling tangibility.
The treatise says:
If one is in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises in dependence upon the body.
The commentary asks:
For what reason is the sphere of the body (*kāyāyatana*) necessarily similar to tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*)?
Because mental consciousness necessarily arises in dependence upon the body, it manifests as if it were contact.

Since this mental consciousness arises in dependence on the body as if it were contact, when a practitioner correctly enters meditative absorption, although the five sensory consciousnesses do not arise, a feeling of joy and bliss nevertheless arises within the physical body during that interval.
The Treatise says:
For example, the various material sense faculties arise in dependence upon the body.
The Commentary explains:
The material faculties—namely the eye and other faculties—are distinct from the material body, yet they depend upon the body.
Because these faculties depend upon the body, the body may be either harmed or benefited by them.
Consciousness is likewise; because it relies upon the body, it manifests as if it were contact, and thus there is benefit or harm to the body.
Furthermore, just as the body-faculty relies upon the body, when there is the condition of external contact, the body-faculty arises as if it were contact.
If it arises resembling contact, it either harms or benefits its own basis.
Consciousness is likewise; because it relies upon the body, it arises resembling contact.
The treatise says:
A verse is spoken herein.
The commentary says:
The various Bodhisattvas maintain that there is only mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and no separate fivefold sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*).
To establish this point, they cite a verse from the *Dharmapada-sūtra*.
The treatise states:
Traveling far and wandering alone, bodiless and dwelling in the empty cave,
taming that which is difficult to tame— one is then liberated from the bonds of Māra.
The commentary states:
It is called "Far-Reaching" (dūrangama) because it is able to take all objects as its cognitive domain.
It is called "Solitary" (ekākin) because there is no second consciousness.
Regarding the absence of a body, there are two meanings: first, the absence of a material body (rūpakāya); second, the absence of a birth-body (upapattikāya).
The interior of the body is called the "empty cave" (*khaṇḍa*); because consciousness resides within the body, it is said to "dwell in the empty cave.
Furthermore, among the five internal organs, the heart-organ has a cavity within it; since the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) resides in this cavity, it is said to "dwell in the empty cave."

Third, although all phenomena are in reality non-existent, one clings to them as being existent; because consciousness dwells within this state of non-existence, it is called "dwelling in an empty cave.
Because its original cause is base and evil affliction, it is called "difficult to subdue."
If a person can subdue this consciousness, causing it not to follow along with afflictions and karma and thereby attaining mastery, it is called "subduing.
The obstacles of affliction within the three realms are termed the "bonds of Māra"; when such a person subdues that which is difficult to subdue, they attain liberation.
Furthermore, there is another authoritative scriptural statement that serves as proof for this meaning.
The treatise says:
As the Sūtra states:

Regarding the objects of perception for these five faculties, such as the eye: each individual object is grasped and discriminated by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which serves as the cause for their arising.
The commentary states:
When the consciousness perceives an object such as form (*rūpa*) that is the objective domain of these five faculties, it is established as "eye-consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
Since the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is capable of apprehending each and every object and can also perform discrimination, the five sensory consciousnesses would be rendered useless.
Furthermore, if the mental consciousness is distracted, the visual and other sensory consciousnesses do not arise.

Because the transformation of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) gives rise to the sense faculties such as the eye and their corresponding consciousnesses, the mental consciousness is the cause for their production.
The treatise states:
Furthermore, there is another explanation:
In the detailed exposition of the twelve *āyatanas*, this collection of the six consciousnesses is designated as the *manāyatana*.
The commentary states:
This further cites the words of the Sage to prove that there is only mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and no other distinct consciousnesses exist.
In the sūtras, the Tathāgata distinguishes the twelve bases (*āyatana*), combining the collection of the six consciousnesses to form the mind base (*manāyatana*).
By these three meanings, it is known that there is only mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and no other distinct consciousnesses.
The treatise says:

In this context, the foundational consciousness (mūlavijñāna) is established as the object-consciousness (arthavijñapti); all other consciousnesses herein are called the appearance-consciousness (nimittavijñapti); and the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), along with its supporting consciousness, should be known as the seeing-consciousness (darśanavijñapti).

Why is this? This aspect-consciousness (*nimitta-vijñāna*) is the cause for the arising of the seeing-consciousness (*darśana*); because it manifests as resembling an object (*viṣaya*), it performs the function of being the support for the arising of the seeing-consciousness.
The commentary states:

Within these two types of consciousness, the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) can be established as the object-consciousness (nimittavijñāna) and the perceiving-consciousness (darśanavijñāna); it is not established as the consciousness of the sense-object (viṣayavijñāna).
Herein, all consciousnesses are termed object-consciousness.
The fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) can be established as abiding within the two aspects of the object-aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and the seeing-aspect (*darśanabhāga*).

This fundamental consciousness takes the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and the supporting consciousnesses (*āśrayavijñāna*) as the seeing-aspect, and takes the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) and so forth, along with all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), as the object-aspect. It serves as the cause for their arising; because it acts as the objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*), it is the cause for the arising of the seeing-aspect within those [object-aspects].

Regarding those phenomena, it performs the function of being the support for this consciousness because it manifests appearing as objects and because it serves as the cause for the uninterrupted continuity of the mental consciousness's perception.
The treatise says:
In this way, these various consciousnesses establish the nature of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
How is it that when objects appear before one, they are known to be non-existent?
As the Buddha, the World-Honored One, said:
"If a bodhisattva is endowed with four dharmas, they are able to seek out and enter into the fact that all consciousnesses are devoid of external objects.
Commentary:
The four dharmas are wisdom.

If a bodhisattva is endowed with these four wisdoms, they are able to seek out principles within skillful means and attain correct understanding, thereby entering into reality; thus they know that all things are representation-only (vijñapti-mātra) and devoid of external objects.
The treatise says:
What are the four? First, knowing the characteristics of contradictory cognitions.
For example, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and gods perceive the same objective realm differently due to differences in their consciousness.
The commentary states:

because there are differing conceptualizations regarding a single objective realm, they are called "contradictory"; the object of such contradictory consciousnesses is termed "characteristic" (*nimitta*).
This object does not exist in reality at all; it is merely that because it undergoes transformation according to consciousness, its conceptualizations differ.
If a bodhisattva penetrates this principle, they will understand that there is only consciousness (vijñapti-mātra); therefore, this is called wisdom (jñāna).
The Commentary states: Second,
[consciousness exists] by virtue of seeing consciousness that lacks an objective realm,
as in the case of the past, the future, dreams, reflections, and sensory objects.
The commentary states:
At times, consciousness arises even when separated from its object, as for example, when consciousness takes past objects as its domain.
The treatise says:
Third, because it is known that [cognition] is free from effortful activity, non-perversion would necessarily follow.

For example, when consciousness arises in dependence upon an object that truly exists, it does not constitute perversion, because it knows the object as it truly is without depending on effortful activity.
The commentary states:

When a bodhisattva forms such an understanding, if objects were truly existent as they appear, then even without cultivating the remedies, they would naturally attain non-erroneous knowledge by virtue of knowing things as they truly are.
Since this [external] object does not exist, we know that there is truly no external realm; rather, it is because one clings to existence within non-existence that error arises.
The Treatise says:
Fourth, by knowing that objects conform to the three types of wisdom.
The commentary says:
All objects of the sensory realms follow along with the three types of wisdom; the Bodhisattva is able to know them in this way.
The treatise says:
Why is this so? The commentary states:
In what way do all objects follow along with the three types of wisdom?
The Treatise says:
All noble ones enter meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*).
The Commentary says:
The "sages" refer to śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas.
When these sages are currently in a state of meditative concentration, it is called "entering contemplation.
The treatise states:
"Attaining mastery over the mind.
The commentary explains:
one has already attained mastery such that the mind acts in accordance with one's will throughout the stages of entering, abiding, and emerging [from meditative absorption].
The treatise says:
"By virtue of mastery over aspiration and delight.
The commentary explains:
All objects transform according to one's wishes and inclinations.
The commentary states:
This is because objects manifest in various ways in accordance with one's wishes and inclinations.
The commentary states:
If one wishes to transform the earth element into the water element, it is accomplished as soon as one intends;
the same applies to the fire element and others.
The Treatise says:
If a practitioner has already attained śamatha.
The Commentary says:

There are two types of practitioners: first, those who have attained right reflection; second, those who have attained right cultivation. Here, we clarify the person who has attained right cultivation.
The treatise states:
"One cultivates the preparatory application of the contemplation of dharmas."
The commentary states:
"Dharma" refers to the twelve divisions of the scriptures, such as the Sūtras and so forth.
Based on the characteristics of phenomena revealed by these twelve divisions of scripture, one brings the practice of vipaśyanā to maturity.
The treatise states:
Because objects manifest in accordance with mere mental attention (*manasikāra*).
The commentary explains:

Within a single set of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), one contemplates according to the mind, such that they manifest as impurity, suffering, impermanence, emptiness, non-self, and so forth, up to the sixteen aspects of the truths (*ṣoḍaśākāra-satya*) all manifesting through contemplation; and it is the same for all other dharmic characteristics as well.
The Commentary states:
If a person attains non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and has not yet emerged from non-conceptual contemplation (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*), no objects (*viṣaya*) manifest at all.

Since the meanings of "objects" and so forth accord with the three types of wisdom, and since the meaning of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) has been established by the preceding scriptural citations, one knows that there are no external objects, only consciousness.

In this context, there are six verses that reiterate the preceding meaning; these will be explained in detail later, within the section on the training in wisdom (*jñāna-śikṣā*), concerning such beings as hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and gods.
The commentary states:

If a bodhisattva has already attained non-conceptual wisdom and is currently in the state of meditative observation, if objects were to exist as they appear, then non-conceptual wisdom could not be established.
Since non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna) truly exists, it is known that, according to the principle of reality, nothing at all exists [independently].
Chapter Three: The Chapter on Discrimination. The Treatise says:
If the manifestation of consciousness-only as resembling an object is its basis of dependence, it is called the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva).
How is it established as the dependent nature?
By what causes and conditions is it called "dependent"?
The commentary states:

Apart from objects, there is only consciousness; this consciousness is able to produce transformations that manifest as if they were objects. This essence, characteristic, and functional capacity of the deluded consciousness is called the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

If one perceives only that the disordered consciousness possesses its own intrinsic nature and does not perceive anything else, how can this consciousness be established as the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature)?

If you say that it can produce transformations and that these transformations depend upon this consciousness such that it serves as their support (*paratran-āśraya*), then why is this consciousness itself called the dependent nature?
The treatise says:
Because it arises from seeds of its own habitual perfuming, it is bound to causes and conditions and lacks independence.
Furthermore, because it has no power to persist for more than a single moment once it has arisen, it is called "dependent on others" (*paratantra*).
The commentary states:

Because it arises from its own causes, once arisen, it lacks the inherent capacity to remain for even a single moment; because it is apprehended by itself, it is called "dependent" (paratantra) insofar as it is designated in dependence upon other [conditions].
The treatise says:

If the nature of discrimination (parikalpita-svabhāva) depends upon the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), being in reality non-existent yet appearing as if it were an object, how does it constitute "discrimination"?
For what reason and by what conditions is it called "discrimination"?
The commentary states:

This question has three parts. First, it asks about the basis: since this nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) relies upon another, it should be the nature of dependence (*paratantra-svabhāva*); why then is it called "discrimination"?
Next, he asks about "non-existence": since this discrimination is truly non-existent, what kind of discrimination could there be within that non-existence?
Subsequently, he asks about "resembling objects": since this discrimination manifests as resembling objects, how can it be called "discrimination"?
For what reason is it called the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)?
The treatise says:
Because immeasurable marks are discriminated by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), serving as the cause for the arising of inversion, it is therefore termed "discrimination."
The commentary states:
All appearances of objects are conceptual constructions, which are termed the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Because the mental consciousness arises with inverted objects, it is called the "cause of arising."
By this principle, it is therefore established as "discrimination" (*vikalpa*).
The treatise says:
Because there is no intrinsic characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), and one perceives only discrimination, it is called "discrimination."
The commentary states:
Since the intrinsic nature does not exist and one perceives only a confused consciousness, it is called "discrimination.
The treatise says:
If the nature of reality (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) is characterized by the absolute non-existence of the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), how does it become "reality"?
For what reason and by what causes is it called "reality"?
The commentary states:

The nature of discrimination is eternally absent within one portion of the dependent nature; if its characteristic is defined as non-existence, why is it established as the perfected nature (the real) rather than as that which is not real?
The explanation is likewise.
The treatise states:
Because it is as it is and not otherwise, it constitutes reality.
The commentary states:

The following three points answer two questions; this is the first, which reveals the ultimate reality through the sense of non-contradiction, as when it is said in the world that one has a "true friend."
The Treatise says:
"By virtue of accomplishing the pure realm.
The Commentary explains:
This is the second [point], which reveals reality by means of the meaning of non-perversion.
Because the object is non-perverted, one attains the fourfold purity, just as the world speaks of a "real entity."
The Treatise says:
Because it is the most supreme among all wholesome dharmas.
The Commentary explains:

This is the third [point], which reveals reality by means of the meaning of non-conceptuality; that is, the five kinds of non-conceptuality refer to the five kinds of reality, as when it is said in the world that one practices according to reality.
The Treatise says:
It is called "ultimate reality" because it is established in the ultimate sense.
The Commentary explains:
Because the three preceding excellences are without destruction or loss, they are said to be "accomplished"; because they are accomplished, they are "real.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, if there is both the conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and that which is conceptualized (*vikalpya*), the nature of conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is established.
The commentary states:
Because one wishes to inquire into the meaning of these three types of conceptualization, the names of these three conceptualizations are first set forth.
The treatise says:
In this context, what dharma is called "discrimination"?
What dharma is that which is discriminated?
And what dharma is termed "the nature of discrimination" (parikalpita-svabhāva)?
The commentary states:
Each is asked individually to seek out their distinct characteristics.
The Treatise states:
"Mental consciousness is conceptualization, because it possesses three types of conceptualization.
The Commentary explains:
The following answers three questions; this specifically answers the first question.

Among the six consciousnesses, it is only the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that is considered "discrimination," because the mental consciousness possesses the three types of discrimination—namely, intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), recollection (*anusmaraṇa*), and manifesting (*nidarśana*)—whereas the five [sensory] consciousnesses do not.
The Treatise asks:
For what reason?
The Commentary explains:
For what reason does the mental consciousness possess three types of discrimination?
The treatise states:
This consciousness takes its own verbal熏習 (vāsanā) as its seed.
The commentary states:

As it is said regarding the names for the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), the repeated practice of these names perfumes the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), serving as its seeds.
From these seeds, at a later time, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises appearing as the faculties and appearing as the objects; this is termed "form-consciousness" (*rūpavijñāna*).
There are two meanings for "intrinsic" (*sva*):
first, just as the name "eye" refers to a perfuming that produces only the eye and not other dharmas, so it is with other perfumings; therefore, they are called "intrinsic."
The two [aspects] lack the substance of dharmas; because language is produced by one's own conceptual discrimination, it is called "self.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, all verbal expressions serve as the seeds for perfuming consciousness.
The commentary states:
