first, to eliminate delusions; second, to give rise to the Buddha-dharmas; and third, to bring sentient beings to maturity.
By eliminating delusions, one attains benefit for oneself in the present.
By giving rise to the Buddha-dharma and maturing sentient beings, one attains benefit for both self and others in the future.
If delusions have been eternally extinguished, then one dwells in peace and happiness in the present.
Why is this? Because there is no need to exert further effort to extinguish these afflictions or to prevent them from arising again; thus, one attains personal benefit in the present life.
Once the obstacles of delusion have been extinguished, one will necessarily possess the Buddha-dharma in its full perfection in future lives.
Furthermore, by being able to bring sentient beings to maturity, one attains the benefit of both self and others.
The Commentary states:
In order to counteract the causes for failing to initiate the resolve [for awakening], the two pāramitās of generosity and ethical discipline are established.
The causes for failing to initiate the resolve are attachment to wealth and property, as well as to one's household.
The commentary states:

Attachment to wealth and possessions obstructs generosity; attachment to one's household obstructs ethical discipline. Due to such attachments, one is unable to give rise to the mind of spiritual practice.
The treatise says:
If one has already generated the mind for practice, the two pāramitās of patience (*kṣānti*) and diligence (*vīrya*) are established as antidotes to the causes of mental withdrawal and weakness.
The commentary states:
although one may already be able to practice giving (*dāna*) and ethical discipline (*śīla*), if one cannot endure painful circumstances, the resolve for giving and ethical discipline will weaken.

Although one may be able to endure suffering, if one does not diligently cultivate various virtues and cease all evils, then the mind of generosity, ethical discipline, and patience will all decline and weaken.
Therefore, as an antidote to this declining and weakening mind, these two perfections must be established.
The Treatise says:
"The causes for the regression and weakening of the mind refer to the adverse and painful circumstances encountered by sentient beings within saṃsāra.
The Commentary explains:
Those who cannot be reasoned with are called sentient beings in birth and death.
To act in opposition to the Bodhisattva’s teaching is defiance; to invade and destroy the Bodhisattva’s body is rebellion; both of these are matters of suffering.
If one cannot endure these painful matters, then a mind of aversion arises; such aversion is a cause for the weakening of the mind.
The treatise states:
"It is weariness resulting from long-term application to the cultivation of wholesome dharmas."
The commentary states:

Although one practices all virtues over a vast expanse of time with diligent application, if one lacks compassion for sentient beings and cherishes only oneself, and fails to perceive the superior merit of the practice undertaken, one will give rise to a mind of weariness and indolence regarding that very practice.
Because one possesses this mind, one is unable to apply oneself with diligence; this is precisely laziness (*kausīdya*), and laziness is the cause for the mind’s regression and weakness.
The treatise states:

If one has already initiated the practice and possesses a mind that does not regress or weaken, then, in order to counteract the causes for the loss and destruction of the mind, the two pāramitās of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are established.
The causes for the ruin and loss of the mind are distraction and false knowledge.
The commentary states:
through distraction, the tranquil mind is ruined; through false knowledge, correct understanding is lost.
The Commentary says:
Therefore, in order to counteract the six kinds of afflictive obstacles, the perfections (pāramitās) are established as being six in number.
Regarding the phrase "because they serve as the basis for the arising of all Buddha-dharmas":
The commentary states:
The six perfections are the causes for the growth and development of the Buddha-dharma.
The treatise says:
The first four perfections are the causes for non-distraction.
The commentary states:

there are four obstacles that serve as causes for distraction: first, the obstacle of abandonment; second, the obstacle of withdrawal; third, the obstacle of acceptance; and fourth, the obstacle of repeated application.

Due to attachment, one is unable to relinquish; due to the arising of the ten unwholesome actions from greed, hatred, and delusion, one is unable to distance oneself from them; due to malice, one is unable to accept [the teachings] with composure; and due to the afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion, one is unable to apply frequent remedies. Because of these four obstacles, the mind becomes distracted.
Because the first four perfections can counteract these four obstacles, the four perfections are the causes for non-distraction.

Furthermore, with respect to the five hindrances as obstacles to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), four hindrances obstruct the causes of concentration, while one hindrance obstructs right concentration and the wisdom arising from concentration.
The four hindrances—sensual desire, restlessness and remorse, ill-will, and sloth-and-torpor—are causes of distraction and obstruct the first four perfections.
Because these four perfections serve as the antidotes to these four hindrances, they are the causes of non-distraction.

Because doubt involves indecision regarding its object, the mind becomes distracted; since meditative concentration (*samādhi*) resolutely maintains a single object, doubt obstructs right concentration.
Because one does not perceive the truth due to doubt, and because it obstructs the wisdom (*prajñā*) produced by concentration, concentration and wisdom serve as the antidotes to doubt.
The Commentary states:
The next pāramitā is the essence of non-distraction.
By relying upon this non-distraction, one is able to realize the true reality of all phenomena as they truly are, and thus all the True Dharma of the Tathāgatas is brought into being.
Therefore, as the basis for the arising of all Buddha-dharmas, the perfections (pāramitās) are established as being six in number.

Regarding their function as the support for maturing all sentient beings in accordance with their needs: through the perfection of giving, one benefits sentient beings; through the perfection of ethical discipline, one does not harm or afflict them; through the perfection of patience, one is able to accept their insults and slanders without giving rise to a mind of retaliation; and through the perfection of diligence, one generates their roots of virtue and eliminates their roots of evil. By means of these causes of benefit, all sentient beings are brought to subdual.

Next, for the sake of bringing that mind to tranquility when it has not yet attained it, and for the sake of bringing about liberation once tranquility has been attained, the two pāramitās of concentration (dhyāna) and wisdom (prajñā) are established.
"By means of these six perfections, the bodhisattva skillfully instructs sentient beings.
The commentary states:
"Skillful instruction has two meanings: first, it is called 'instruction' because it is taught in accordance with reason; second, it is called 'skillful instruction' because it is taught constantly."
The Commentary says:
Therefore, maturation is attained.
For this reason, in order to serve as the basis for maturing all sentient beings in accordance with their needs, the perfections (pāramitās) are established as being six in number.
By this meaning, it should be understood that the establishment of the perfections (pāramitās) consists of six in number.
Chapter Three: Characteristics. The Treatise says:
How are the characteristics of these six perfections to be seen?
The commentary states: Why is this question asked?

Both worldly beings, followers of the two vehicles, and bodhisattvas all possess the six practices such as giving; if the characteristics of the six pāramitās practiced by bodhisattvas were not clarified, how could one distinguish which of these are pāramitās and which are not?
Therefore, one must inquire into the characteristics of the *pāramitās*.
The treatise states:
"By virtue of six kinds of supremacy."
The general characteristics of the six pāramitās are sixfold:
first, they have an incomparable basis, meaning they arise based upon the unsurpassed bodhicitta.
The commentary states:
This clarifies that there is a difference in their basis.

The practice of giving and so forth by worldly beings and those of the two vehicles does not arise based upon the unsurpassed bodhicitta; only the practice of giving and so forth by Bodhisattvas necessarily arises based upon the unsurpassed bodhicitta. Therefore, having an incomparable basis is the characteristic of the six perfections practiced by Bodhisattvas.
The treatise says:
Second, they are peerless by way of their categories; that is to say, each and every pāramitā is briefly said to have three grades, all of which the bodhisattva fully practices.
The commentary states:
This clarifies that the objects of focus (ālambana) differ and are not equal.

Neither worldly beings nor those of the two vehicles possess the complete categories for practicing giving and the other perfections—namely, the external, the internal, and both external and internal. Since a bodhisattva’s practice of giving and the others necessarily encompasses all these categories, the absence of such equality in categories constitutes the characteristic of the six perfections practiced by a bodhisattva.
The Commentary states:
Third, they are peerless in terms of their activities, namely, the activities for the peace, happiness, and benefit of all sentient beings.
This is because all the perfections practiced by Bodhisattvas are undertaken solely to accomplish these two purposes.
The commentary states:
This clarifies that there is a difference in the practice of the deeds.
What is the capacity of the bodhisattva’s practice of the six perfections?

First, one brings about the happiness of sentient beings in the present, past, and future worlds; subsequently, according to their faculties and natures, one brings them to the fruits of the paths of the Three Vehicles.

As for the practice of giving and so forth by those in the world or the Two Vehicles, since they do not even achieve the peaceful benefit of themselves alone, how much less could they bring peace and benefit to sentient beings?
Therefore, the practice of deeds constitutes the characteristics of the six perfections practiced by bodhisattvas.
The treatise states:
Fourth, they are peerless due to skillful means, which refers to non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
"Because all the perfections practiced by Bodhisattvas are subsumed under non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
The commentary explains:

This clarifies that there is a distinction in skillful means (*upāya*). That which is called the "Bodhisattva's skillful means" refers to purity regarding the three spheres (*trimandala-pariśuddhi*); this very purity regarding the three spheres is non-conceptual wisdom.
By means of this wisdom, the bodhisattva does not discriminate between the giver, the recipient, and the material object given.

Worldly beings and those of the two vehicles are unable to relinquish discrimination regarding the three spheres; consequently, they give rise to self-love and attachment to material wealth, and thus cannot maintain equanimity toward others. Therefore, through skillful means, these constitute the characteristics of the six perfections practiced by bodhisattvas.
The three wheels of ethical discipline are free from the conceptual distinctions of sentient beings, objects, and time.
The three wheels of patience are free from the conceptual distinctions of self, others, and faults.
The three wheels of diligence are free from the distinctions of sentient beings, high and low, and purposeful activity.
The three wheels of meditative concentration are free from the distinctions of objects, sentient beings, and afflictions.
The three wheels of *prajñā* are free from the conceptual distinctions of object, cognition, and sentient beings.
The Commentary states:
Fifth, by way of incomparable dedication, which means dedicating [merit] toward unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
The various perfections practiced by Bodhisattvas are so called because they resolutely turn toward and lead to the fruit of omniscience.
The commentary states:
If a Bodhisattva practices giving and the other perfections, they first form this thought:
I give these things as alms to all sentient beings of the six realms.
These are the wealth and possessions of those beings; I practice giving on their behalf, wishing that they may all attain unsurpassed bodhi.
Because this giving is dedicated so as to cause others to attain unsurpassed enlightenment, this practice of giving is never exhausted.
If one practices the other perfections, they likewise all involve dedication.
Since worldly beings and those of the two vehicles lack dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), dedication is established as the characteristic of the six perfections practiced by Bodhisattvas.
The treatise states:
"The sixth [perfection] is due to its purity and peerlessness," meaning that both the afflictive and cognitive obstructions (*kleśa-jñeya-āvaraṇa*) are forever extinguished without remainder.
Because the various perfections practiced by Bodhisattvas eliminate the two obstacles part by part until they are completely exhausted.
The commentary states:
This passage reveals two kinds of purity: first, it reveals the cause of purity; second, it reveals the stage of purity.
Regarding the cause of purification: because the two obstacles—the afflictive and the cognitive—are eliminated through their causes, the practices such as giving become purified.

Regarding the stage of purification: first, prior to the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*), one gradually eliminates the obstacle of afflictions; subsequently, upon ascending to the first stage, one gradually eliminates the obstacle of cognition.
These two stages are called "purity of distinct parts," which refers to the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*).
If one reaches the fruit of Buddhahood, the six perfections are fully perfected; this is called "purity of complete parts," which refers to the resultant stage (*phala-bhūmi*).
The treatise asks:
Is giving itself the pāramitā, and is the pāramitā itself giving?
The commentary explains:
What is intended to be revealed by this question?
It is intended to distinguish the characteristics of that which is a *pāramitā* from those that are not.
The treatise says:
There is giving that is not a *pāramitā*.
The commentary explains:

this refers to practicing giving while remaining apart from the six characteristics of relying on the "unequaled with the unequaled" (*asamasama*); because such giving is not subsumed within the six perfections, it is merely giving and not a *pāramitā*.
The Treatise says:
There are those that are perfections (pāramitā) but not giving (dāna).
The Commentary explains:
This refers to possessing the practice of the remaining perfections, such as ethical discipline (*śīla*), based upon the six aspects of "equality with the unequaled.
The treatise states:
There are instances that are both giving (*dāna*) and a perfection (*pāramitā*).
The commentary says:
This refers to practicing giving while fully relying upon the six aspects of the peerless (asama-sama).
The treatise says:
There is that which is neither giving nor a pāramitā.
The commentary states:

this refers to actions other than those mentioned in the first three cases—namely, those that are indeterminate (avyākṛta) or unwholesome (akuśala), and so forth—all of which are subsumed under the fourth case.
The Treatise says:
Just as there are four permutations regarding generosity, it should be understood that the other perfections likewise possess four permutations.
The Commentary explains:
Just as giving is distinguished in terms of what is appropriate and inappropriate, the remaining perfections should likewise be distinguished in this manner.
Chapter Four: On the Sequence. The treatise asks:
Why are the six pāramitās taught in this particular order?
The commentary states:
This question may arise either from doubt or from a lack of understanding. Regarding questioning out of doubt:

all undertakings must first be preceded by knowledge that understands cause and effect before one initiates right effort; because of these two causes, one is able to act according to one's desire. Therefore, there should be both a reversed order and no fixed order.
Because of these doubts, it is necessary to ask. Regarding asking because of a lack of understanding:

if a person wishes to cultivate various practices, they do not yet know which are shallow or deep, or which are difficult or easy to perform. That which is shallow is easy to perform, while that which is deep is difficult to perform; the easy should be studied first, and the difficult should be studied later.
To understand this meaning, it is therefore necessary to ask.
The treatise says:
Because each preceding pāramitā accords with and gives rise to each subsequent pāramitā.
The commentary states:
A bodhisattva cannot bear to see sentient beings suffering from poverty and hardship; thus, they repeatedly practice the relinquishing of wealth.

Because they have become habituated to such relinquishment, they do not wish to perform acts that would harm or afflict sentient beings. Consequently, they leave the household life and uphold the precepts; therefore, morality arises from generosity.

Because a bodhisattva cherishes and protects the precepts they have received, and does not wish to violate those pure precepts through acts of anger or resentment toward sentient beings, they practice patience; thus, patience arises from the precepts.
Because afflictions may or may not be exhausted, the bodhisattva practices diligence in order to protect this patience; thus, diligence arises from patience.

If a person constantly practices diligence, they are able to cultivate the mind. Through this diligence, if the mind sinks into dullness, it is uplifted; if the mind becomes agitated, it is suppressed so that it does not arise; and if the mind is balanced, it is maintained in continuity. Because the mind becomes harmonized, concentration is attained; thus, concentration arises from diligence.
If the mind attains concentration, it can penetrate *tathatā* (suchness); therefore, wisdom arises from concentration.
This is precisely the former producing the latter.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, each preceding perfection is purified by each subsequent perfection.
The commentary explains:

generosity is purified by ethical discipline; if a person does not maintain ethical discipline, their actions of body, speech, and mind are impure, and thus the generosity they practice is also impure because its basis is impure.
Because one is able to maintain the precepts and relies upon purity, giving becomes pure.
Precepts become pure through patience; if a person is able to be patient, their actions of body, speech, and mind all attain purity.
Patience is purified by means of diligence, because diligence can give rise to the wholesome and eliminate the unwholesome.
Diligence is purified by means of meditative concentration, for if diligence does not abide in the state of cultivation, it cannot eliminate afflictions.

Concentration is purified by means of wisdom; if one does not discern suchness (*tathatā*), then even if concentration is attained, it remains a phenomenon of birth and death because it is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*).
However, if one perceives suchness, the concentration thus attained becomes free from outflows (*anāsrava*) and constitutes the path to nirvāṇa.
This means that the latter is able to purify the former;
because of these two meanings, there is a sequential order.
Chapter Five: Establishing Names. The Treatise says:
By what meaning are the names of the six perfections established?
How is this meaning to be understood?
The commentary states:

In the world, there are many causes for establishing names: there are names established based on species, names established based on characteristics, names established based on conventional designation, names established based on contempt, and names established based on veneration.
Among these five causes, from what sense are the names of the six perfections established?
They are established from two causes:
because their spiritual lineages (*gotra*) differ, they are named according to their class of birth; and...
Because their merit is vast, they are named according to the respect accorded to them.

The names thus established have both general and specific aspects: all six are called *pāramitās*, which is the general name; that they are "generosity," "precept-keeping," and so forth, constitutes their specific names.
For what reason are they collectively termed *pāramitās*?
The treatise states:
Because they are the most supreme and peerless among all the roots of virtue—such as generosity and so forth—of all worldly beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.
The commentary states:
There are six kinds and three kinds of supreme peerlessness.
The six kinds are as explained previously in the section on the six characteristics.
The three kinds of peerlessness are: first, peerlessness in time; second, peerlessness in application; and third, peerlessness in fruit.
Because each and every perfection (pāramitā) is practiced for three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, they are peerless in time.
Regarding the "unequaled preparatory application" (*prayoga*), there are four kinds, five kinds, another five kinds, and another six kinds.
The four kinds are precisely the four types of cultivation explained previously.
The five kinds are the five kinds of purity explained previously.
Furthermore, there are five kinds, which are the five cultivations.
Additionally, there are six kinds, which are the six intentions.
The five cultivations and six intentions will be explained in the subsequent text.
Regarding "the fruit is peerless," this refers to the unsurpassed bodhi manifested by the three bodies (*trikāya*).
The treatise states:
Because they are able to reach the other shore, they are collectively termed *pāramitās*.
The commentary states:
There are three ways of reaching the other shore: first, reaching the other shore by bringing the practice to ultimate completion without remainder.
The worldly and those of the two vehicles also have practices that ought to be cultivated; however, because they do not cultivate them to completion, they do not reach the other shore (*pāramitā*).

Just as all rivers take the ocean as their ultimate destination, so too with generosity and the other perfections: they take the entry into *tathatā* (suchness) as their final consummation, and it is precisely this entry into *tathatā* that constitutes reaching the other shore.
Although worldly beings and those of the two vehicles practice giving and other perfections, they cannot enter into suchness; therefore, they have not reached the other shore.
Third, reaching the other shore consists in attaining the peerless fruit that ought to be attained.
There is no other fruit superior to this fruit; because it is the most excellent among all fruits, it is called the "Other Shore" (pāra).
Although those in the world and those of the two vehicles practice generosity and other virtues, they do not seek this fruit, and therefore they have not reached the Other Shore.
The perfections (pāramitā) cultivated by Bodhisattvas all possess these three meanings; therefore, they are collectively termed "pāramitā.
Why, then, are they given specific names such as *dāna* (giving), and so forth?
The treatise says:
Because it can destroy stinginess, jealousy, and the suffering of poverty and low status, it is called *dha*.
The commentary states:
stinginess is an obstacle to abundant wealth; jealousy is an obstacle to noble status.
Because at the time of the cause one is able to eliminate the obstacle of stinginess, and at the time of the fruit one obtains abundant wealth, one is freed from the suffering of poverty.
Because at the time of the cause one is able to eliminate the obstacle of envy, and at the time of the fruit one attains a position of honor and dignity, one is freed from the suffering of lowliness.
Why is this? If a person has not yet destroyed the mind of stinginess and envy, they are unable to practice giving; therefore, it is said that one must be able to destroy these obstacles.
If a person practices giving and is able to destroy these obstacles, it is impossible for such a person to subsequently undergo the suffering of poverty and low status.
The Treatise says:
Furthermore, because one attains the status of a great lord of wealth and is able to draw forth the provisions of merit, it is called *na*.
The Explanation says:
One who is able to give and able to utilize [wealth] is called a great master of riches.
Because of being such a master, one is able to attract the provisions of merit (*puṇya-saṃbhāra*).
Since it possesses this meaning, it is termed *dāna*.
The Treatise says:
Because it can pacify wrong conduct and the evil destinies, it is called *śīla*.
The Commentary explains:
At the time of the cause, one is able to destroy wrong precepts; at the time of the fruit, one is able to leave the evil realms.
It is impossible for a person to maintain the precepts without abandoning evil karma; therefore, one first destroys wrong precepts.

If a person who has broken wrong precepts yet maintains right precepts were to fall into the four miserable destinies, such a thing is impossible; therefore, at the time of fruition, they are able to remain free from the evil paths.
The Treatise says:
Furthermore, because they are able to attain the good paths and samādhi, they are called "Ara."
The commentary states: By virtue of having previously observed the precepts, one subsequently receives the fruits of the wholesome paths of humans and devas.

Whether in the state of the cause or the state of the fruit, because of the observance of the precepts, body and speech are purified; because they are purified, there is no remorse; because there is no remorse, the mind is at peace; because the mind is at peace, joy is attained; because of joy, pliancy is attained; because of pliancy, bliss is attained; because of bliss, concentration is attained; because of concentration, one sees reality as it is; because one sees reality as it is, disenchantment is attained; and because of disenchantment, liberation is attained.
Therefore, one attains samādhi by means of upholding the precepts.
Because it possesses this meaning, it is called śīla.
The treatise says:
Because it can eliminate ill-will (*vyāpāda*) and the mind of resentment and anger (*krodhopanāha*), it is called *kṣānti*.
The commentary states:
During the stage of causal practice, by means of contemplating five meanings, one eliminates ill-will and the resentment and anger produced by that ill-will.
The five meanings are: first, contemplating that all sentient beings have been kind to oneself since beginningless time;
second, contemplating that all sentient beings are constantly perishing from moment to moment—what person could cause harm, and who could be harmed?
Third, contemplating that there are only phenomena and no sentient beings, what is there that can cause harm, and what is there that is harmed?
Fourth, contemplating that all sentient beings are already suffering their own pains, how could one wish to further inflict suffering upon them?
Fifth, one contemplates that all sentient beings are one's own children; how then could one wish to inflict harm upon them?
By means of these five contemplations, one is able to extinguish anger; since anger is extinguished, one is able to eliminate resentment and hostility.
The Treatise says:
Furthermore, because it can produce matters of peace and harmony for oneself and others, it is called "ti" (supporting).
The Commentary says:
This matter thoroughly penetrates cause and effect.
This patience enables one’s own person not to be defiled by the fault of anger, which is peace toward oneself;
since one neither harbors resentment nor inflicts suffering upon others, this is peace toward others.

As the Sūtra says: "If one practices patience, there are five virtues: first, being free from resentment; second, being free from reproach; third, being beloved by the multitude; fourth, having a good reputation; and fifth, being reborn in the happy realms."
These five virtues are called "the matter of peace.
Because they possess this meaning, they are termed *kṣānti*.
The treatise says:
Because it eliminates indolence and all unwholesome dharmas, it is called *vi*.
The commentary states:
one is said to be "indolent" because of being submerged in unwholesome states.
Furthermore, because one does not loathe unwholesome conduct, one is called "lazy.

Due to this laziness, one abandons all wholesome practices and gives rise to various unwholesome dharmas; since the three types of action (trikarma) constantly give rise to transgressions, they are termed "unwholesome dharmas."
Because of the cessation of laziness, one is able to eliminate all evils produced by laziness; this is called the diligence of extinguishing unwholesome dharmas (*kṛṣṇadharma*).
The treatise says:
Furthermore, by practicing heedfulness (*apramāda*), one causes immeasurable wholesome dharmas to grow and flourish; therefore, it is termed *laya*.
The commentary states:
This explains diligence by way of faith in and delight in cause and effect.
Because one has faith that the cause can be practiced and delights in the fact that the fruit can be attained, one practices constantly and with reverence; this is called non-negligence (*apramāda*).
By practicing reverence, one causes unarisen wholesome states to arise and causes already arisen wholesome states to increase; this is the diligence (*vīrya*) acquired through birth.
Because it possesses this meaning, it is called *vīrya*.
The Treatise says:
It is called *dhikāra* because it is able to extinguish and eliminate distraction.
The Commentary explains:
There are five types of distraction: first, intrinsic distraction, which refers to the five sense-consciousnesses;
second, external distraction, which refers to the mental consciousness racing toward external objects;
third, internal distraction, which refers to the mind’s fluctuation between elation and depression, as well as attachment to sensory flavors and so forth.
Fourth is the distraction of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*), which refers to conceiving of "I" and "mine" and so forth;
fifth is the distraction of reflection (*manasikāra*), which refers to an inferior mind, wherein a bodhisattva abandons the Mahāyāna and reflects upon the Hīnayāna.
The Treatise says:
Furthermore, it is able to lead the mind to abide within its internal object; therefore, it is called "na.
The Commentary explains:
Drawing the mind to abide in five kinds of tranquility is called the "internal object.
Because it possesses this meaning, it is termed *dhyāna*.
The treatise says:
Because it can extinguish all modes of view and eliminate false wisdom, it is called *prā* (般羅).
The commentary states:
"modes of view" refers to the sixty-two views; "false wisdom" refers to the deluded understandings of the world.
The conduct of views is the afflictive hindrance, and false wisdom is the cognitive hindrance.
The treatise states:
"It is able to take the true nature as its object."
The commentary states:
This refers to taking True Suchness as the object, which is precisely the wisdom that accords with reality.
The treatise says:
"According to their categories.
The commentary explains:
There are two types of categories, namely the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), as well as the fivefold inclusion of names (*nāman*) and so forth.
If one knows this dharma, it is precisely the wisdom of suchness (yathābhūta-jñāna).
The treatise says:
because it knows all dharmas, it is termed "if" (cet).
The commentary states:
The characteristics and categories of suchness are called "all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*).
Wisdom that accords with reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) is called *prajñā*; wisdom that accords with the measure of reality (*yathāmātra-jñāna*) is the fruit of *prajñā*, and is also called *prajñā*.
These two types of wisdom are manifested through three meanings:
first, their antidotes, which are the two obstacles;
second, their objects, which are the true nature.
The third fruit is the wisdom of suchness (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).
Because it possesses this meaning, it is called *prajñā*.
Chapter Six: On Cultivation (*Bhāvanā-varga*). The Treatise says:
How should one understand the cultivation of the various pāramitās?
The commentary states:
Both worldly beings and those of the two vehicles possess the cultivation of giving and the other perfections.
How can it be known that the bodhisattva’s cultivation of giving and so forth differs from that of worldly beings and those of the two vehicles?
The treatise says:
Briefly stated, one should know that there are five kinds of cultivation.
The commentary states: If explained in detail, there are twelve kinds of cultivation (*bhāvanā*):

first, cultivation of manifestation; second, cultivation of diminution; third, cultivation of remedial accomplishment; fourth, cultivation of subsequent practice; fifth, cultivation of association; sixth, superior cultivation; seventh, progressively superior cultivation; eighth, cultivation of the initial limit; ninth, cultivation of the middle limit; tenth, cultivation of the final limit; eleventh, cultivation with something superior; and twelfth, unsurpassed cultivation.
The cultivation of manifestation refers to the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), because they are able to manifest the meaning of the Four Noble Truths.
The cultivation of diminution refers to the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), because they are able to gradually eliminate all unwholesome dharmas.

"Cultivating the factors conducive to mastery" refers to the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), because they can bring meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to mastery by eliminating the five faults and maintaining the provisions for the eight cessations.
Cultivation through subsequent practice refers to the cultivation of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*), because they possess the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
Cultivation through correspondence refers to the cultivation of the five powers (*pañcabala*), because they correspond to the continuous progression toward the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Superior cultivation refers to the seven factors of enlightenment, because they involve entry into the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths.
Supreme cultivation refers to the Eightfold Noble Path, because it excels the Path of Seeing.

Cultivation at the initial stage refers to the cultivation of the precepts up to the attainment of the contemplation of impurity and the contemplation of counting the breath while in the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), because these are in accordance with inversion.
Cultivation at the intermediate stage refers to the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), because within this stage, there is no inversion, whereas inversion was previously present.
Cultivation regarding the future limit refers to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), because therein there is neither error nor being erroneously inverted.
Cultivation with something superior refers to the cultivation of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as well as those at equivalent stages.
"Unsurpassed cultivation" refers to the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of a bodhisattva and so forth, because they are the most excellent.
The treatise says:
First, cultivation by means of the preparatory method (*prayoga*).
The commentary states:
This refers to the fact that the actions of body, speech, and mind are capable of accomplishing that which is vast, pure, and most excellent.
The treatise says:
Second is cultivation through faith and aspiration.
The commentary states:
This is explained according to the hearing of the teachings, as in the first chapter.
The Treatise says:
"Threefold cultivation through reflection.
The Commentary explains:

Within the cultivation of reflection (*cintā-bhāvanā*), there are three types: cherishing (*adhimukti*), sympathetic joy (*anumodana*), and aspiration (*prārthanā*). These together are termed the "cultivation of reflection," as explained in the first chapter.
The Treatise says:
Cultivation of the four superior wisdoms of skillful means.
The Commentary explains:
This is non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which possesses three meanings:
first, vastness; second, purity; and third, rapid accomplishment.
Because it is endowed with these three meanings, it is designated by the name "superior wisdom of skillful means" (*upāya-viśiṣṭa-jñāna*).
The treatise states:
There are five types of cultivation for the benefit of others.
Among these, the first four types of cultivation should be understood as previously explained.
"Cultivating for the benefit of others" refers to the Buddha’s effortless mental activity (*anābhoga-citta*), which does not abandon the deeds of a Tathāgata.
The commentary explains:
This clarifies that according to the teachings of the Mahāyāna, although the Buddhas have already entered parinirvāṇa, they nevertheless further give rise to [compassionate] minds.
Parinirvāṇa is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
When the mind arises again, there are the two bodies of the Response (*nirmāṇakāya*) and Transformation (*sambhogakāya*).

Although all Buddhas already abide in the Dharma-body and, by the power of their original vows, are free from the three types of karma, the two bodies of Response and Transformation manifest spontaneously in accordance with the task of benefiting sentient beings. They never abandon the true work of the Tathāgata nor the practice of the various *pāramitās*; therefore, all Buddhas possess the cultivation of the *pāramitās*.
The Treatise says:
One cultivates the various pāramitās and, upon reaching the stage of perfection, further cultivates the various pāramitās.
The Commentary explains:

Whether Buddhas or Bodhisattvas possess the perfections either partially or fully, when they practice the various pāramitās at this stage of perfection, they do not act for their own sake because their own welfare is already accomplished.

Rather, seeing that sentient beings may thereby leave the four miserable destinies and enter the fruits of the paths of the three vehicles, they further cultivate the various pāramitās; this is precisely acting for the benefit of others.
The Treatise says:

Furthermore, regarding the cultivation through reflection, it consists of cherishing, sympathetic joy, and aspiring for attainment; this reflection is comprised of six intentions that encompass what is cultivated.
The Commentary explains:
This chapter generally clarifies the meaning of cultivation.
Previously, the five types of cultivation were explained, but the distinctions among the stages of cultivation were not yet analyzed.
How is this known?
The cultivation of the stages of aspiration and practice differs from the cultivation of the stage of purity.
If the six mental engagements encompass the three types of contemplative cultivation of the *pāramitās*, one should know that these belong to the stage of purity.

In the stage of the practice of vows (*praṇidhāna-caryā-bhūmi*), this meaning does not apply; for these three types of reflection are the foundation of cultivation, and they are adorned and sustained by the six mentalities.

The treatise states: The six mentalities are: first, the expansive mentality; second, the long-term mentality; third, the joyful mentality; fourth, the mentality of having merit and virtue; fifth, the mentality of great resolve; and sixth, the excellent mentality.
Regarding the "vast intention": if a bodhisattva can attain unsurpassed enlightenment over the course of several *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
The commentary states:
this refers to the total number of kalpas, which is without limit as to how many; therefore, it is said to be "several."
Because the various Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras describe different numbers of kalpas, the specific duration of kalpas is not fixed.
The Hīnayāna explains that one attains Buddhahood after three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, whereas the Mahāyāna explains that one may attain Buddhahood after three, seven, or thirty-three asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
The treatise says:
This duration of time constitutes one *kṣaṇa*.
The commentary explains:
Alternatively, three asaṃkhyeya kalpas may be combined into a single kṣaṇa, or thirty-three asaṃkhyeya kalpas may be combined into a single kṣaṇa; for this reason, it is again termed a "kṣaṇa."

In this manner, from one moment to immeasurable moments, there are one day, one month, and so forth, up to one asaṃkhyeya kalpa; from one asaṃkhyeya to thirty-three asaṃkhyeyas, one finally attains buddhahood.
In order to demonstrate that the bodhisattva’s intention is never satiated, this long duration is taught.
The treatise states:
During this period, the bodhisattva constantly relinquishes body and life at every single moment (*kṣaṇa*).
The commentary states:
"At this time" refers collectively to the long duration.
"Moment" (kṣaṇa) clarifies what is conventionally designated as a moment in the world.

Throughout the long duration previously described, just as "a moment" (kṣaṇa) is spoken of in the world, in each and every moment he constantly relinquishes his body, life, and external wealth until the attainment of Buddhahood, never having a mind of weariness or satiety.
The Treatise says:

Furthermore, one might fill worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges with the seven treasures and offer them as gifts to the Tathāgata, from the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment until entering and abiding in the ultimate, cool state of Bodhi.
The commentary states:
*Sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* is called "pure" (*śīta*) because it is free from the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa*).
*Nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* is called "cool" (*śītala*) because it is free from the burning distress of all sufferings.
Furthermore, bodhi has purity and bliss as its essence; to manifest the virtue of purity it is called "clear," and to manifest the meaning of bliss it is called "cool.
The Treatise says:
This bodhisattva’s intention for giving is still not yet satisfied.

For such a long duration, moment by moment, throughout a great trichiliocosm filled with blazing fire, the Bodhisattva performs the four modes of conduct—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—devoid of all necessities for sustaining life.
The commentary states:
Hereafter, it is intended to clarify the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the remaining five perfections.
Throughout this long duration, in each and every moment, he constantly remains in places of extreme suffering and hardship, where the necessities for sustaining the body are never sufficient.
Although the Bodhisattva undergoes this suffering, during this time he practices the various *pāramitās* without ever becoming weary or satisfied.
The Commentary says:

The Bodhisattva constantly practices the mind of ethical discipline (*śīla*), patience (*kṣānti*), diligence (*vīrya*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) until he enters and abides in ultimate, cool enlightenment (*bodhi*). Even then, his intention regarding ethical discipline, patience, and so forth, remains unsatisfied. This lack of weariness or satisfaction is called the Bodhisattva’s vast intention (*udāra-āśaya*).

If a bodhisattva, from the first generation of the mind of awakening until the attainment of Buddhahood, does not abandon the mind of insatiable diligence, this is called the bodhisattva’s long-term intention (*dīrghakālika-āśaya*).

If a bodhisattva constantly gives rise to incomparable joy regarding the beneficial deeds for others performed through the six perfections—a joy that cannot be matched by the joy felt when sentient beings actually receive those benefits—this is called the bodhisattva’s joyful intention (*pramuditā-āśaya*).

If a bodhisattva, having benefited sentient beings by practicing the six pāramitās, perceives that sentient beings have rendered him great kindness and does not perceive himself as having rendered kindness to them, this is called the bodhisattva’s mind of gratitude and virtue.

If a bodhisattva gives the roots of merit and goodness arising from the six pāramitās to all sentient beings, dedicating them with a mind free from attachment so that they may obtain desirable and weighty retributions, this is called the great resolve of a bodhisattva.

If a bodhisattva causes all sentient beings to equally attain the merit and roots of goodness from the six pāramitās they practice, dedicating them toward unsurpassed enlightenment, this is called the bodhisattva’s wholesome and excellent intention.
By means of these six types of contemplation characterized by affection and esteem, the bodhisattva practices cultivation.
The commentary states:
To manifest the mind that seeks attainment, seeing that there are great merits therein, one desires to attain them.
The Treatise says:

If a bodhisattva rejoices in the roots of merit and wholesome qualities arising from the six intentions through which immeasurable bodhisattvas practice their preparatory applications, this is called the bodhisattva’s mental cultivation of rejoicing as subsumed under the six intentions.
The commentary states:
To manifest a mind free from doubt, since one has already rejoiced in the deeds performed by superior persons, one is thus certain and without doubt.
The treatise says:

If a bodhisattva vows that all sentient beings shall practice the six perfections as subsumed by the six intentions, and also vows for themselves to practice the six perfections as subsumed by the six intentions, cultivating these preparatory applications until the attainment of Buddhahood, this is called the bodhisattva’s contemplation on the vow subsumed by the six intentions.
The commentary states:
This is to reveal that great compassion is not characterized by a mind that seeks for itself alone.

These three reflections eliminate three types of mental states: first, they eliminate the state of non-action; second, they eliminate the state of vacillation between advancing and retreating; and third, they eliminate the state of one-sided advancement.
The Treatise says:

If a person hears of the bodhisattva’s contemplative cultivation subsumed under the six intentions and gives rise to even a single thought of faith, that person shall obtain an immeasurable and boundless accumulation of merit, and all their evil karmic obstructions will be destroyed and extinguished without remainder.
The commentary states:
There are two meanings to the "extinction of karmic obstructions. First, it is the ability to destroy karma so that it is exhausted.

Second, although the karma still exists, because the power of the wholesome [roots] is great, it can obstruct the retribution of the evil realms such that one never again experiences it; thus, this also carries the meaning of destruction and extinction.
If even those who merely hear [of these perfections] obtain immeasurable and boundless merit, how much more so for a bodhisattva who is able to practice them fully.
Chapter Seven: On Distinctions. The treatise asks:
How should one understand the distinctions among the various pāramitās?
The commentary says:
What does this question intend to reveal?
Since the categories of the various pāramitās are incalculable, this question is posed in order to reveal their true essence.
Because the distinctions among the various *pāramitās* are clarified, the true essence manifests.
The Treatise says:
Their distinctions are known by virtue of each having three grades.
The commentary states:
This provides a general enumeration to answer the question.
The treatise says:
The three types of giving are: first, the gift of Dharma; second, the gift of material wealth; and third, the gift of fearlessness.
The commentary states:
The gift of Dharma benefits the minds of others, for through the gift of Dharma, the virtues of the roots of goodness—such as the wisdom derived from hearing—arise in others.
The gift of material wealth benefits the bodies of others;
the gift of fearlessness benefits both the bodies and minds of others.
Furthermore, through the gift of material wealth, those who are heading toward evil are drawn back and led toward the good.
Through the gift of fearlessness, one gathers others and causes them to become one's retinue.
Through the gift of Dharma, one generates roots of goodness in them and brings them to maturity for liberation.
Because it possesses these meanings, it is said that there are three grades of giving.
The treatise states:

Regarding the three categories of ethical discipline (*śīla*), they are: first, the ethical discipline of restraint; second, the ethical discipline of gathering virtuous dharmas; and third, the ethical discipline of benefiting sentient beings.
The commentary explains:
The morality of guarding [the precepts] is the basis for the other two types of morality.
If a person does not abandon evil, they will not attain the morality of gathering wholesome qualities or the morality of benefiting others.

If a person abides in the morality of guarding [the precepts], they can induce the morality of gathering wholesome qualities, which serves as the basis for the arising of the Buddha-dharma and enlightenment.
If one abides in the first two types of ethical discipline, they can induce and encompass the ethical discipline of benefiting sentient beings, serving as the basis for maturing them.
Furthermore, by guarding the ethical discipline through the avoidance of evil, one is free from remorse and affliction, thereby attaining a state of peaceful dwelling in the present life.

By virtue of this dwelling in peace and happiness, one is able to cultivate the ethical discipline of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*) for the sake of maturing the Buddha-dharmas.

If a person dwells in the first two types of ethical discipline, they are able to cultivate the ethical discipline of gathering the welfare of sentient beings (*sattvārtha-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*) for the sake of maturing others.
These three categories of precepts are the causes for the four fearlessnesses.

Why is this? The first category of precepts constitutes the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*); the second, the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*); and the third, the virtue of beneficence (*anuśaṃsā-guṇa*).
The four fearlessnesses do not transcend these three virtues; therefore, it is said that they are the causes of the four fearlessnesses.
Because it possesses this meaning, it is taught that there are three grades of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
The treatise says:
The three grades of patience are: first, patience regarding insults and humiliation; second, patience in accepting suffering; and third, patience through the observation of dharmas.
The commentary states:
by means of patience regarding insults and humiliation, one is able to endure the faults committed by others.
Why is this? Because the bodhisattva generates the mind of awakening and practices for the sake of benefiting others;
thus, even when reviled or insulted by others, they do not, due to attachment to these faults, regress from their original resolve to practice.

Through the patience of accepting suffering, although one may fall into the various hardships and sufferings of saṃsāra, one does not retreat from the mind of the fundamental practice because of such suffering.
Through the patience of observing phenomena, a bodhisattva is able to enter into the true reality of all phenomena.
This patience (*kṣānti*) serves as the basis for the preceding two types of patience, because it is capable of eliminating the dualistic grasping at persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-grāha*).
Since it possesses this significance, it is said that patience has three grades.
The treatise states:
There are three grades of diligence: first, diligent vigor; second, applied vigor; and third, undaunted, indestructible, and insatiable vigor.
The commentary says:
How is it known that diligence has these three essences?
Because the Blessed One, the World-Honored One, spoke this sūtra passage in the sūtras:
This person possesses integrity, possesses superior capability, possesses valor, possesses coercive power, and does not abandon the yoke of the wholesome.
These five phrases are spoken to manifest these three natures.
The term "steadfastness" (*dhṛti*) is taught to manifest diligent and courageous effort; the term "supreme capacity" (*vīrya*) is taught to manifest applied effort (*prayoga-vīrya*). Why is this?
Because at the time of application, this person possesses supreme capacity, being able to carry out everything exactly as previously intended.
To manifest diligence that is undaunted, indestructible, and insatiable, three phrases are taught in succession: being courageous, possessing coercive power, and not abandoning the yoke of virtue.

Why is this? Because there may be someone who, at the outset, for the sake of attaining unsurpassed bodhi, first possesses earnest and authentic preparatory application (*prayoga*) and possesses superior capability; yet, because the duration of time is so vast and the signs of the sought-after fruit have not yet manifested, they give rise to an inferior mind during this interim period.
To counteract this mind and to manifest unflagging diligence, "valiance" is taught.

Even if a person possesses a valiant mind free from weakness, if they encounter the hardships and sufferings of birth and death that impair their resolve, they will then retreat from their bodhicitta vow.
To counteract this, the mind manifests an indestructible diligence; therefore, it is said to possess coercive power.
Because it possesses coercive power, the sufferings and hardships of saṃsāra cannot cause one to retreat.

If a person, though encountering suffering, does not retreat, yet conceives the notion of sufficiency upon attaining only a small measure of gain, they will be unable to attain supreme enlightenment due to this contentment with little.
To counteract this mind and to manifest tireless diligence, it is said that one does not abandon the yoke of the wholesome.
Because it possesses this meaning, diligence is said to have three grades.
The Treatise says:

Regarding the three categories of meditative concentration, they are: first, concentration for dwelling in peace and happiness; second, concentration for inducing supernormal powers; and third, concentration that accords with benefiting others.
The Commentary explains:
There is a concentration that results in dwelling in happiness in the present life. Why is this?
Because it is able to abandon all defiled phenomena.
Relying on this concentration, one gives rise to that which benefits oneself, namely the three types of higher knowledge (*vidyā*).

It is capable of inducing the causes for accomplishing the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and it induces the concentration of the supernormal powers that gives rise to concentrations benefiting others.
Benefiting others consists of three wheels:

first, the wheel of supernormal powers (ṛddhi), which refers to the power of the body, the divine eye, and the divine ear; this wheel serves to lead those who have gone astray back to the correct path.

The second is the wheel of knowing the minds [of others], which refers to the supernormal power of knowing others' minds, the supernormal power of the divine eye, and the supernormal power of the divine ear; this wheel serves to lead those who have already returned to the correct path, as well as those who have not yet accepted the teaching, to bring them to faith and acceptance.

The third is the wheel of the correct teaching, which refers to the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsābhijñā*) and the supernormal knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayābhijñā*). By means of the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives, one recognizes the dispositions and faculties of others; by means of the supernormal knowledge of the destruction of the outflows, one imparts the correct teaching according to what one has realized oneself, causing them to plant the seeds [of liberation], bring them to maturity, and attain deliverance.
Because it possesses these meanings, it is said that there are three grades of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The treatise states:
Regarding the three grades of *prajñā*: first, non-conceptual preparatory *prajñā*; second, non-conceptual *prajñā*; and third, non-conceptual subsequently attained *prajñā*.
The commentary states:

From hearing the Mahāyāna teachings on signlessness (*animitta*), one attains the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation; entering into the emptiness of conceptualized perception is collectively termed the non-conceptual preparatory *prajñā*.
Having entered the three natures of non-substantiality, there is non-conceptual wisdom, which is called non-conceptual *prajñā*.

After attaining non-conceptual wisdom and emerging from meditative observation (*vyutthāna*), one either reflects for oneself or explains it to others according to what was previously realized; this is called subsequently attained non-conceptual *prajñā*.

Furthermore, there are three grades of *prajñā*: namely, the faculty of "desiring to know what is not yet known," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "having already known," which function for the sake of producing, abiding in, and employing supramundane phenomena.
Because it possesses these meanings, it is said that there are three categories of *prajñā*.
Chapter Eight: On Compendium. The treatise asks:
How should one understand the meaning of the compendium of the various *pāramitās*?
The commentary states:
Regarding the meaning of how all other wholesome dharmas mutually encompass the various pāramitās,
how should this be understood?
The Treatise says:
All wholesome dharmas are subsumed within the six pāramitās.
The Commentary explains:

All wholesome dharmas—namely, from aspiration up to the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and all the Tathāgata’s secret treasuries of Dharma—are entirely subsumed within the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).
The treatise says:
"Because it is that nature.
The commentary explains:
Because the pāramitās have the nature of these dharmas such as aspiration,
these aspirations and so forth also encompass all the pāramitās, since aspiration and so forth have the nature of the pāramitās.
All the pāramitās share the same nature, which is non-conceptual wisdom; therefore, they are mutually inclusive.
The treatise states:
"Because they are the outflowing fruits of those six pāramitās."
The commentary states:

Those very qualities—the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), and even the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikadharma*)—are all fruits flowing from the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), because they share the same nature as the perfections.
The Treatise says:
Because it is that which all wholesome dharmas follow and thereby accomplish.
The Commentary explains:

Faith, pliancy, and other such wholesome dharmas are subsumed within the bodhisattva path; they enable the fulfillment of all the perfections (pāramitās) that the bodhisattva wishes to practice. Since the perfections are the outflowing fruits of those [wholesome dharmas], they are mutually inclusive.
Chapter Nine: The Chapter on Antidotes (Pratipakṣa) The Treatise asks:
How should one understand that the various perfections (pāramitās) encompass all the afflictions (kleśas) through their respective antidotes?
The Commentary explains:

Just as the pāramitās are able to encompass all categories of purity in their entirety, so too should that which is counteracted by the pāramitās be able to encompass all categories of impurity in their entirety.
How should this be understood?
The treatise says:
Because it has that as its nature.
The commentary states:
Just as the *pāramitās* encompass all wholesome phenomena (*kuśaladharma*) because their essential nature is non-attachment,
so too do the factors opposed to the *pāramitās* encompass all unwholesome categories because their essential nature is attachment.
The Treatise says:
Because it serves as the cause for their arising.
The Explanation says:

Factors such as lack of faith, wrong views, and the view of a self can produce results such as stinginess, envy, misconduct, and malice; because they share the same nature, they function as their causes.
The Treatise says:
Because it is the outflow-result (*niṣyanda-phala*) of that.
The Commentary explains:

This stinginess, envy, misconduct, anger, and so forth arise from attachment to self and others; thus, various unwholesome actions—namely, the ten non-virtues and the like—are also established as their results by virtue of having the same nature.
By virtue of these various meanings, they are thus mutually inclusive.
Chapter Ten: On Merit. The Treatise says:
How should one understand the merits of the various pāramitās?
The commentary states:
The practice of worldly acts such as giving also possesses merit; how, then, should one understand the merit of the bodhisattva’s pāramitās?
The merit of the bodhisattva’s pāramitās shares both similarities and differences with the worldly; there are six kinds of similarity and four kinds of difference.
Regarding the sixfold commonality,
the treatise states:
If a bodhisattva revolves within saṃsāra, they are comprised within the state of great wealth and mastery.
The commentary states:
Universal Monarchs (*cakravartin*), the Lord of Gods (*devendra*), the Brahmā King, and others constitute the state of great wealth.
Because they are masters therein, they are called "sovereigns" (*vaśin*).
Whether a bodhisattva or an ordinary person practices giving, they both equally obtain this retribution.
The Treatise says:
It is comprised within "great birth."
The commentary states:
Great birth is of three kinds: first, excellence of the path; second, excellence of nature; and third, excellence of majestic power.
Whether they be bodhisattvas or ordinary persons, those who maintain the precepts equally obtain this retribution.
The Treatise says:
"It is comprised of a great retinue of followers.
The Commentary explains:
Relatives are called "retinue" (*kula*), while those who are governed and led are called "disciples" (*gaṇa*).
Both retinues and disciples also possess three kinds of excellence as previously described; for this reason, they are termed "great."
All are mutually affectionate and do not give rise to hatred or envy; they always gather together in joy and never part.
Whether Bodhisattvas or ordinary persons practice patience, they equally obtain this retribution.
The Treatise says:
It is comprised within the accomplishment of the great activities for the production of livelihood.
The Commentary says:
There are four types of livelihoods: first, agriculture; second, animal husbandry; third, commerce; and fourth, service to the king.
"Service" refers to engaging in activities that involve either harmony and cooperation or discord and contention.
Because whatever one desires is accomplished without fail, it is called "attainment" (*siddhi*).
Whether Bodhisattvas or ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) practice diligence, they equally obtain this fruit.
The treatise says:
It is comprised of freedom from illness and affliction, few desires, and so forth.
The commentary states:

The meditative concentration (samādhi) comprised by the four immeasurables (apramāṇa) results in a body free from all diseases and a mind detached from all afflictions; therefore, one is constantly joyful.

Regarding the fruits of retribution obtained through the other meditative concentrations, although they may be householders, they are no different from sages who have abandoned desire because their afflictions are few.
"Equal" refers to obtaining excellent physical features, long life, and so forth.
Whether Bodhisattvas or ordinary persons cultivate meditative concentration, they equally attain this fruit.
The Treatise says:
All fields of knowledge concerning arts and crafts are subsumed under intelligence.
The commentary states:

In order to establish the means of livelihood, one requires the field of knowledge of crafts and arts; that is, the eighteen fields of knowledge can establish the dharmas of the present, the future, and liberation.
Within this, there are two principles: establishment and refutation.
One who possesses wisdom is able to accomplish these matters.
Whether they be bodhisattvas or ordinary persons, if they cultivate prajñā, they equally obtain this retribution.
Regarding the four kinds of difference,
the treatise says:
it is as with the mind.
The commentary states:

When a bodhisattva practices generosity and so forth, they obtain rewards such as wealth and happiness; within these, they always remain free from faults, meaning they act for the benefit of both themselves and others without defilement.
In the worldly practice of giving and so forth, although there is merit, this [state] does not exist.
This is called the first distinct characteristic.
The Treatise says:
"There is no loss of wealth and happiness.
The commentary explains:
When a bodhisattva practices generosity and so forth, they obtain the retribution of wealth, happiness, and so on.
In this regard, "according to one's wish" means that whether for one's own use or for the use of others, one constantly gives rise to three kinds of joy;
although there are merits in worldly acts such as giving, they do not compare to this.
This is called the second distinct characteristic.
The treatise says:
because benefiting sentient beings constitutes the primary objective.
The commentary states:

When a bodhisattva practices generosity and other perfections, the merit produced thereby constantly serves to bring about mundane and supramundane benefits for sentient beings, and not for their own sake.
Although there are merits in worldly practices such as giving, they do not compare to this.
This is called the third distinct characteristic.
The treatise says:
Because the merit of a bodhisattva’s cultivation of the six perfections remains constant and unchanging from the initial entry into and abiding in ultimate, cool enlightenment.
The commentary states:

The merit generated by a bodhisattva’s practice of giving and so forth remains as it was from the first production of the thought of enlightenment until the ultimate fruit; because its benefit to others is no different [from its original state], this is the eternally abiding merit.
The practice of giving and so forth in the world, though it possesses merit, is not like this.
This is called the fourth distinct characteristic.
Chapter Eleven: Mutual Elucidation. The Treatise says:
How should one understand that the various *pāramitās* mutually illuminate one another?
The commentary states:
As explained in the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sūtras through thirty-six phrases, the exposition of each individual *pāramitā* simultaneously explains the remaining five *pāramitās*.
How should this be understood?
The treatise states:

The Blessed One sometimes teaches the various pāramitās under the name of "giving" (dāna), or under the name of "ethical discipline" (śīla), or under the name of "patience" (kṣānti), or under the name of "vigorous effort" (vīrya), or under the name of "meditative concentration" (dhyāna), or under the name of "wisdom" (prajñā).
The commentary states:
The five pāramitās are subsumed within one pāramitā; thus, all six are present within a single pāramitā, yet they are designated by the singular names such as "giving" (dāna) and so forth.
The Treatise says:
With what intention did the Tathāgata speak thus?
It is because within the skillful means of practicing each of the pāramitās, all the other pāramitās are gathered together to provide assistance and bring them to fulfillment.
This is the intended meaning of what the Tathāgata has said.
The commentary states:
If a bodhisattva practices the application of effort toward each individual pāramitā, all the other pāramitās assist and bring that one to completion.

When Bodhisattvas practice giving correctly, they guard their body and speech and remain free from the seven types of unwholesome conduct; this is precisely the observance of the precepts of right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
Because of this morality, giving achieves fulfillment; thus, morality can perfect giving.

When a bodhisattva practices giving correctly, they are able to peacefully accept the contrary speech and contrary demeanor of the recipient, even to the point of peacefully accepting the hardships involved in the act of giving.
Because of this patience (*kṣānti*), giving (*dāna*) achieves fulfillment; thus, patience can perfect giving.

When a bodhisattva practices giving correctly, the intention to give eliminates greed and attachment; through great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), it eliminates anger; by humbling the body and mind, it eliminates pride; by wishing to bring peace and happiness to the recipient, it eliminates stinginess, envy, and jealousy; and by knowing that giving has causes and effects, it eliminates ignorance and false views. Diligence (*vīrya*) gives rise to such virtues and counteracts such evils.
Because generosity is accomplished through diligence, diligence is able to perfect generosity.
When a bodhisattva correctly practices generosity, they maintain a continuous one-pointed mind focused on the task of benefiting and bringing happiness to sentient beings.
Because of this meditative concentration (*samādhi*), giving becomes perfected; thus, concentration can accomplish giving.
When a bodhisattva practices giving correctly, because they discern cause and effect and do not cling to the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*), wisdom (*prajñā*) can accomplish giving.
This is called the assistance of the other pāramitās in the fulfillment of a single pāramitā; therefore, the six pāramitās are collectively termed "giving" (dāna).
As it is with giving, so it is with morality (śīla) and the others as well.
Because each [category] possesses six [aspects], thirty-six propositions are formed.
The treatise says:
Herein, an uddāna verse is stated.
The sequence of the stages and their characteristics, Is called the differentiation of cultivation and inclusion;
Through the remedies and the virtues, The meanings of the various perfections are mutually revealed.

In the ninth fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, on the fifteenth line of the ninth sheet, immediately after the phrase "laziness is the cause of the weak and regressive mind," there should be the passage concerning the two perfections of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Furthermore, these three [sections] were originally missing from all three versions of the canon, which resulted in the subsequent text being corrupted and lost.
As for the "causes of the mind," they refer to distraction and false wisdom.
Regarding the statement that the *pāramitās* are established as a remedy for the six kinds of afflictive hindrances, the mention of the number six and so forth has no source whatsoever.
Now, examining the original treatise, it states therein:

"If one has already initiated the practice and possesses a mind that does not retreat or weaken, then, for the sake of counteracting the causes of mental decline and loss, the two pāramitās of meditative concentration (dhyāna) and wisdom (prajñā), along with twenty-five other characters, are established."
Now, based on the root treatise, this is added.
*Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, Fascicle Ten,
Commentary by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha from Central India. Chapter Five:

Explaining the Superior Characteristics of the Differentiations in the Cultivation of Entering Cause and Effect (Part One). Section One: The Chapter on Antidotes. Commentary: This treatise consists of five sections:
first, the antidotes; second, the establishment of names; third, the characteristics of attainment; fourth, the characteristics of cultivation; and fifth, the timing of cultivation.
The Treatise says:
Thus far, the superior characteristics of entering into cause and effect have been explained. How should one understand the distinctions in the cultivation for entering into cause and effect?
The Explanation says:

Previously, the distinctions between the causes and results of the six perfections were explained in general terms: they constitute the cause during the stages of aspiration and application, and the result during the stage of purity. Since the specific differences in their cultivation according to the *bhūmis* have not yet been analyzed, they are here presented in this summary fashion.
The wisdom of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) is called "entry.
The three natures (*tri-svabhāva*) are its supreme characteristics.
The six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) are themselves the wisdom of *vijñapti-mātra*.
Regarding the entry into the cause and fruit of the three non-natures, in order to manifest the distinctions in the cultivation of the various *pāramitās*, it is asked: "How should this be known?
The treatise says:
"By means of the ten bodhisattva stages."

What are the ten? First, the Stage of Joy; second, the Stainless Stage; third, the Radiant Stage; fourth, the Blazing Stage; fifth, the Difficult to Conquer Stage; sixth, the Manifest Stage; seventh, the Far-Reaching Stage; eighth, the Immovable Stage; ninth, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence; and tenth, the Cloud of Dharma Stage.
The commentary states:
If one wishes to know the distinctions in cultivation, by observing the distinctions among the ten stages (*bhūmi*), one will understand the distinctions in the cultivation of cause and effect.
The treatise says:
How should one understand that these grounds are established as ten by means of this principle?
The commentary states:
What meaning does this question seek to clarify?
If a bodhisattva enters the first stage (bhūmi), their vision of suchness (tathatā) is immediately exhausted. Why is this?
Because suchness has no divisible parts.
If the vision of *tathatā* were not exhaustive, then *tathatā* would possess distinct parts.
If it possessed distinct parts, it would be identical to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
If the vision is already exhaustive, for what reason do you speak of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*)?
The Treatise says:
"In order to counteract the ten kinds of ignorance that constitute obstacles to the stages.
The Commentary says:
True Suchness (tathatā) is in reality without the numerical distinction of one or two.
If considered from the perspective of the essence of True Suchness, it is impossible to establish ten distinct varieties.
Nevertheless, True Suchness possesses ten kinds of merit, which can give rise to ten kinds of correct practice.
Because they are shrouded by ignorance, they do not perceive these merits; because they do not perceive these merits, correct practice is not accomplished.
Since there are ten kinds of merits that are obstructed, there are likewise ten kinds of ignorance that can act as obstructions.
The Treatise says:
Regarding the dharma-realm as manifested by ten characteristics.
The Commentary explains:
The ten characteristics refer to the ten kinds of merit and the ten kinds of correct practice; these characteristics are all capable of manifesting the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
The treatise states:
there are ten kinds of ignorance that still remain as obstacles.
The commentary states:
Although these ten aspects are indeed real, they cannot manifest because they are shrouded by ignorance (*avidyā*).
Therefore, it is known that when a bodhisattva first enters the contemplation of *tathatā* (suchness), which obstructs the vision of the path, ignorance is immediately extinguished.
Because the remaining ignorance still persists and has not yet been extinguished, ten types of ignorance shroud the ten virtues and obstruct the ten right practices.
What are these ten kinds of ignorance?
First, the ignorance of the nature of ordinary beings;
second, the ignorance that gives rise to wrong conduct toward sentient beings based on bodily actions and so forth;
third, the ignorance of mental sluggishness and suffering, which is the ignorance of forgetting what has been heard, reflected upon, and cultivated.

Fourth, the ignorance that arises together with the subtle afflictive activities, such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); this is called "subtle affliction" because these afflictions are of the lowest grade, arise in accordance with conceptualization, and have already distanced themselves from the objects of their original habitual tendencies.
Fifth, the ignorance regarding parinirvāṇa in the Lesser Vehicle;
sixth, the ignorance regarding coarse characteristics and activities.
7. Ignorance regarding the activity of subtle characteristics;
8. Ignorance regarding the mental application of effort toward the signless;
9. Ignorance regarding the spontaneous accomplishment of activities for the benefit of sentient beings.
Tenth is the ignorance that lacks mastery over the various phenomena.
The ignorance of the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is the obstacle to the first stage; this ignorance is precisely the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
The view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is of two kinds: first, the cause; second, the result.
Grasping at a self in phenomena (*dharmātmagrāha*) is the cause, while grasping at a self in persons (*pudgalātmagrāha*) is the result.
The cause is precisely the nature of ordinary beings who are deluded regarding the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*); therefore, it is termed ignorance (*avidyā*).

The followers of the two vehicles can only eliminate the fruit but cannot sever the cause; if they do not sever this ignorance, they cannot enter the first stage (bhūmi). Therefore, this ignorance constitutes the obstacle to the first stage.
Ignorance regarding the commission of improper conduct toward sentient beings through physical actions and so forth is the obstacle to the second bhūmi.
When a bodhisattva has not yet entered the second bhūmi, they give rise to this notion: that there are three distinct types of practice for those of the three vehicles.
Because they are deluded regarding the principle of the One Vehicle, it is called ignorance.
Furthermore, it is explained that all the wholesome deeds performed by sentient beings are nothing other than the great, pure skillful means of the Bodhisattvas.
Why is this? Because purity is already one, yet until the stage of Great Purity is reached, there is no sense of abiding.
