If all should equally return to the Great Path of the Bodhisattva, why would one cultivate skillful means instead of cultivating the True Path?
As long as one has not entered the second bhūmi, this wisdom is absent; because of delusion regarding this meaning, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
If this ignorance is not severed, one cannot enter the second bhūmi; therefore, this ignorance constitutes the obstacle to the second bhūmi.
Sluggishness of mind and suffering-ignorance, as well as the forgetfulness of hearing, reflection, and cultivation-ignorance, constitute the obstacles of the third stage.

"Sluggishness" refers to the state where the faculties have not yet reached the level of knowledge (*jñāna*); "suffering" refers to the failure to attain the subtle and supreme meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) of a bodhisattva; and these are termed "ignorance-obstacles" because they obstruct the faculties and the practice of cultivation.
Because dhāraṇīs such as "hearing and retaining" cannot be accomplished, and because what has been heard, contemplated, and cultivated is subject to forgetfulness, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
If this ignorance is not severed, one cannot enter the third stage; therefore, this ignorance constitutes the obstacle to the third stage.
The subtle afflictions that arise concomitantly with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and other forms of ignorance constitute the obstacle to the fourth stage.

Regarding these "afflictive formations" (*kleśa-saṃskāra*): their essence consists of the seeds of conceptual attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha-vikalpa*); they are called "formations" because they proceed incessantly through arising, abiding, and ceasing.

This seed is the cause of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); the essence of this seed is also the view of a self-identity itself, because it is a category of conceptual differentiation regarding these phenomena.
As for the phrase "because this affliction is of the lowest grade," this explains its subtle nature.
Because this is of the lowest grade, it cannot defile the bodhisattva’s mind; therefore, it is called "subtle.
As for the phrase "arising in accordance with thought," this explains the meaning of its co-arising.

Although it cannot defile the mind of a bodhisattva, because it arises in accordance with right reflection and is associated with right reflection, it cannot be said not to exist; for it can obstruct the omniscience of a bodhisattva.
"Having already distanced oneself from the activities that accord with one's former conduct" explains the meaning of "separation from companions.

Previously, while in the common stage of ordinary beings and prior to the [bodhisattva] stages, one followed all afflictive activities that accorded with one's former conduct; now, having practiced the fourth stage, one has distanced oneself from them. Because of the failure to realize the emptiness of the self of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*), this is termed ignorance (*avidyā*).
If one does not sever this ignorance, one cannot enter the fourth stage; therefore, this ignorance constitutes the obstacle to the fourth stage.
Regarding the ignorance concerning parinirvāṇa in the Lesser Vehicle, this is the obstacle to the fifth stage.

If a person, relying on the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths, practices through the five stages, they see that birth and death are being scorched by the fires of immeasurable faults, and they see that nirvana is supremely cool, tranquil, and perfected in merit. Yet, they do not wish to abandon birth and death—this practice is difficult to perform;
nor do they wish to grasp at nirvana—this practice is likewise difficult to perform.
If a person practicing the fifth stage has a mind that frequently seeks parinirvāṇa, it is therefore called ignorance (*avidyā*).
If one does not sever this ignorance, one cannot enter the fifth stage; thus, this ignorance constitutes an obstacle to the fifth stage.
The coarse aspect of the activity of ignorance is the obstacle to the sixth stage.

When a person practices the sixth stage and has realized, according to their measure and according to the principle, that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise in continuous succession, they dwell predominantly in a mind of revulsion toward these formations, yet are not yet able to dwell extensively in a signless (*animitta*) mind; therefore, it is called ignorance.
If one does not sever this ignorance, one cannot enter the sixth stage; therefore, this ignorance constitutes the obstacle to the sixth stage.
The ignorance characterized by subtle marks and activities constitutes the obstacle to the seventh stage.

If a person practices the seventh stage, because their mind has not yet been able to leave behind the characteristics of the continuity of conditioned phenomena—namely, arising and ceasing—over the course of a million great eons, they cannot penetrate the dharma-realm as being characterized by neither defilement nor purity.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"O Dragon King!
That which is dependently originated through the twelve links may arise, or it may not arise."
How is there arising?
By way of conventional truth.
How is there non-arising?

From the perspective of ultimate truth, because one has not yet been able to depart from the characteristic of arising within the twelvefold dependent origination and abide in the characteristic of non-arising, one cannot enter the seventh stage; therefore, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
If one does not sever this ignorance, one cannot enter the seventh stage; therefore, this ignorance constitutes the obstacle to the seventh stage.
The ignorance regarding the mental effort applied toward the signless constitutes the obstacle to the eighth stage.

If a person practices the eighth stage, although they employ effortful application to eliminate the ignorance of subtle mental formations and to abide in a mind free of signs (*animitta*), they are as yet unable to dwell spontaneously and continuously in a mind free of signs without interruption; therefore, this is called "ignorance."
If one does not sever this ignorance, one cannot enter the eighth stage; therefore, this ignorance constitutes the obstacle to the eighth stage.
Regarding the benefit of sentient beings, the ignorance that does not function through effort is the obstacle to the ninth stage.

If a person practices the nine stages, their mind naturally and constantly abides in the signless; however, regarding the four kinds of mastery in the work of benefiting sentient beings, they are not yet able to spontaneously and constantly initiate such beneficial activities. Therefore, this is termed ignorance.
If one does not sever this ignorance, one cannot enter the ninth stage; therefore, this ignorance constitutes the obstacle to the ninth stage.
The ignorance regarding the lack of mastery over all phenomena is the obstacle to the tenth stage.

If a person practices the ten stages (bhūmi) but has not yet attained mastery over the activities of the three bodies (trikāya), nor over the subtle and secret dhāraṇī-samādhi-gates, they are therefore called "ignorant" (avidyā).
If one does not sever this ignorance, one cannot enter the ten stages; therefore, this ignorance constitutes an obstacle to the ten stages.
The treatise asks:
What is it that can manifest the ten aspects of the dharma-realm?
The commentary states:
This question is intended to reveal that *tathatā* (suchness) possesses ten aspects of merit.
These ten merits can give rise to ten types of correct practice and ten types of uncommon fruits, thereby manifesting the essence of the *dharmadhātu*.
These ten virtues manifest the fundamental nature of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu); therefore, the characteristics of these ten virtues are first inquired about.
The treatise states:
"In the first stage (bhūmi), one should understand the dharma-realm by means of the sense of its universal pervasiveness."
The commentary states:
The *dharmadhātu* of true suchness (*tathatā*) pervades all phenomena without exception. Why is this so?
Because among all phenomena there is not a single phenomenon that is not without self,
the conceptualization arising from the dualistic grasping at persons and phenomena obscures the meaning of the dharmadhātu’s universal pervasiveness.
Due to these hindrances, those at the stages of aspiration and practice cannot enter the first bhūmi.
If these hindrances are eliminated, one perceives the meaning of the all-pervading nature of True Suchness (tathatā), and the two attachments to persons and phenomena are forever purified.
By contemplating this meaning, one enters the first stage (*bhūmi*).
The Treatise says:
"In the second stage, by means of the most excellent meaning."
The commentary states:
The meaning of "pervasive" is that the two emptinesses of person and phenomena exhaustively encompass all dharmas; this meaning is the most supreme and pure among all dharmas.
By contemplating this meaning, one enters the second stage (*bhūmi*).
The Treatise says:
"In the third stage, by way of the meaning of 'superior outflow' (śrutamaya).
The Commentary explains:

Tathatā is the most supreme among all phenomena; because non-conceptual wisdom arises by taking Tathatā as its object, and this non-conceptual wisdom flows from Tathatā, it is the most supreme among all forms of wisdom.
Therefore, from this wisdom flows the great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) produced by subsequent non-conceptual wisdom; this great compassion is the most supreme among all meditative concentrations.
By means of this great compassion, the Tathāgata, wishing to establish the True Dharma to rescue and deliver sentient beings, has preached the twelve divisions of the Mahāyāna sūtras.

This Dharma flows from great compassion; this Dharma is the most supreme among all teachings. To attain this Dharma, Bodhisattvas are able to practice all that is difficult to practice and endure all that is difficult to endure.
By contemplating this dharma, one enters the third stage.
The treatise states:
"In the fourth stage, it is by way of the meaning of non-appropriation."
The commentary states:

Regarding the supreme *tathatā* and the phenomena that flow from *tathatā*, the bodhisattva perceives therein the meaning of non-appropriation; that is to say, these phenomena are not appropriated by him, nor are they appropriated by others.
Why is this? Because the three meanings of self, other, and phenomena cannot be apprehended.
For example, the people of Uttarakuru do not give rise to the conceptualization of "self" and "other" with respect to external objects.
The Bodhisattva is likewise with respect to the dharma-realm; therefore, attachment to dharmas cannot arise.
By contemplating this meaning, one enters the fourth stage.
The Treatise says:
Regarding the fifth ground, it is explained by way of the meaning of non-differentiation in the continuum (*saṃtāna*).
The commentary states:

Although this dharma is not comprised [within categories], the Buddhas of the three times are non-differentiated in their continuum therein; it is not like the continua of the sense organs such as the eyes, the objects such as forms, or the sentient beings of the six realms, which possess differentiation.
Why is this? Because these dharmas are produced through conceptual differentiation, their continuities differ;
because the true thusness (tathatā) manifested by the Buddhas of the three periods of time is undifferentiated, their continuity does not differ.
If one contemplates this meaning, one enters the fifth stage.
The Treatise says:
In the sixth stage, it is by virtue of the meaning of the absence of defilement and purity.
The commentary states:
Although the Buddhas of the three periods of time are continuous and non-different within this Dharma, this Dharma is unstained for future Buddhas because its intrinsic nature is pure;
it is not "pure" for past and present Buddhas because its intrinsic nature is already unstained. By contemplating this meaning, one enters the sixth stage.
The Treatise says:
"In the seventh stage, there is no distinction among various phenomena.
The Commentary explains:
The Dharma-gates revealed by the twelve divisions of the scriptures appear distinct due to their various meanings;
yet, because they are of one flavor in practice, one flavor in realization, and one flavor in attainment, no distinction is perceived.
By contemplating this meaning, one enters the seventh stage.
The treatise says:
"In the eighth stage, by means of the meaning of neither increasing nor decreasing."
The commentary states:

When a bodhisattva perceives all phenomena, they neither increase when the Path is accomplished nor decrease when it ceases; such wisdom is the basis for mastery over signs (*nimitta-vaśitā*) and mastery over the field (*kṣetra-vaśitā*).
Mastery over signs means that whatever signs one desires to seek, they immediately appear before one by virtue of such mastery.

Mastery over lands means that if a bodhisattva gives rise to a conceptual vow, wishing for this land to become entirely made of crystal and so forth, it is accomplished exactly as vowed by virtue of such mastery.
Mastery in the first stage is for the sake of maturing the Buddha-dharma; mastery in the subsequent stage is for the sake of maturing sentient beings.
These two masteries are accomplished through the wisdom of neither increase nor decrease, and thus take that very wisdom of neither increase nor decrease as their basis.
By contemplating this meaning, one enters the eighth stage.
The Treatise says:

In the ninth stage, there is the sense of reliance upon mastery over meditative concentration, the sense of reliance upon mastery over the buddha-field, and the sense of reliance upon mastery over gnosis.
The commentary states:
The meaning of the first two supports has been explained as before.

Regarding "mastery of wisdom" (*jñāna-vaśitā*): that which is manifested by the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) is termed "wisdom," and this wisdom has non-conceptual subsequent knowledge (*nirvikalpa-pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) as its essence.
Why is this? Because all dharma-gates are entirely without error.
By attaining this wisdom, one becomes a great Dharma-master, capable of leading sentient beings throughout the infinite trichiliocosm to enter into the profoundly deep meaning.

Because it can accomplish all that is wished for, it is called "mastery" (*vaśitā*); this mastery takes non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) as its basis, and by attaining this mastery, one enters the ninth stage (*bhūmi*).

Furthermore, it is explained that thorough penetration of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) serves as the basis for mastery over knowledge (jñāna-vaśitā), whereby one attains the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid).
By contemplating this meaning, one enters the ninth stage.
The treatise says:

On the ten stages, the dharmadhātu should be understood by way of the sense of being the basis for mastery over karma, and by way of the sense of being the basis for mastery over the doors of dhāraṇī and the doors of samādhi.
The commentary states:
By penetrating the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), one performs deeds for the benefit of sentient beings.

If one attains the three karmas of all Buddhas and the gateways of dhāraṇī and samādhi, one is then able to penetrate the entire secret treasury of the Tathāgata’s teachings and enter the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

Furthermore, it is explained that penetrating the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) serves as the basis for mastery over karma; penetrating the dharma-realm serves as the basis for mastery over the gates of dhāraṇī and the gates of samādhi. Because this penetration enables the transformation and deliverance of sentient beings throughout the ten directions and results in the attainment of the three bodies and the three types of action, it is called "mastery over karma."
Because one attains the gates of dhāraṇī and samādhi, one penetrates all the Tathāgata’s secret treasuries of Dharma with sovereign mastery; therefore, it is called "sovereignty.
These three sovereignties both take True Suchness (tathatā) as their basis.
By contemplating this meaning, one enters the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
If one penetrates the ten kinds of merit of the *dharmadhātu-tathatā*, what fruit is obtained?

By penetrating the merit of the pervasiveness of the *dharmadhātu*, one attains the realization of the meaning of the emptiness of all obstructions and obtains the fruit of the cessation of all obstructions.
If one penetrates the supreme merit of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), one attains the fruit of the supreme, peerless enlightenment for all sentient beings.

If one penetrates the merit of the sublime flow of the dharma-realm’s words and phrases, one attains the fruit of infinite Dharma-sounds and the ability to fulfill the intentions and desires of all sentient beings.
Why is this? Because this sound of the Dharma is boundless and non-erroneous.
If one penetrates the merit of the non-appropriation of the dharma-realm, one attains the fruit of performing all beneficial deeds for sentient beings as they ought to be done.

If one penetrates the merit of the continuity of the dharma-realm being non-different, one attains the fruit of the dharma-body that is indistinguishable from that of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.

If one penetrates the merit of the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the twelvefold dependent origination being neither defiled nor pure, one attains the fruit of the purification of one’s own continuum as well as the ability to purify the defilements and turbidity of all sentient beings.
If one penetrates the fact that various phenomena have no distinct qualities, one attains the fruit of the permanent abiding in signlessness, wherein all signs are extinguished.
If one penetrates the quality of neither increasing nor decreasing, one attains the karma-fruit of wisdom and majestic power equal to that of all Buddhas.
If one penetrates the merit that serves as the basis for the four kinds of mastery, one attains the fruit of the three bodies:
by penetrating the basis of non-conceptuality, one attains the fruit of the Dharma-body;

by penetrating the bases of mastery over the realm and mastery over wisdom, one attains the fruit of the Enjoyment-body (*saṃbhogakāya*); through this Enjoyment-body, within the great assembly, one attains the fruit of experiencing the joy of the Dharma together with sentient beings.
If one penetrates the basis of karma, one attains the fruit of the transformation body; by means of this fruit, one is able to perform immeasurable benefits for infinite sentient beings.
The treatise says:
A verse is spoken herein.
Pervasive, supreme meaning, Supreme flow, and non-appropriation;
Without distinction, without defilement or purity, The various phenomena are without difference.
These four kinds—non-increase and non-decrease, Mastery, and the sense of reliance—[constitute the nature of the Tathāgata].
The basis for mastery over karma, dhāraṇī, and samādhi—
these two verses should be understood according to the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*.
Furthermore, it should be understood that this ignorance is non-defiled for the followers of the two vehicles, whereas it is defiled for the bodhisattvas.
The commentary explains:
since the practice of the two vehicles is not for the purpose of entering the ten stages (*bhūmi*), this ignorance does not obstruct them.
Because it is not that which is destroyed by the paths of the two vehicles, it does not defile the two vehicles.
Bodhisattvas practice in order to enter the ten stages (*bhūmi*), yet this ignorance constitutes an obstruction to the bodhisattva’s ten stages.
Because it is destroyed by the path of the bodhisattva, it defiles the bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva, at the first stage (*bhūmi*), is able to penetrate all stages, why are the distinctions between the various stages established in a sequential order?
By virtue of this dwelling, the bodhisattva practices the ten perfections through both general and specific modes of conduct.
Because the specific modes of conduct are cultivated within this dwelling, the distinctions of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are established in successive order.
Chapter Two: On Establishing the Names The Treatise says:
Why is the first stage named "Joyful" (*pramuditā*)?
It is because one has, for the first time, attained the functional capacity to benefit both oneself and others.
The commentary states:

When a bodhisattva first ascends to the [first] stage (*bhūmi*), they immediately attain the capacity for both self-benefit and the benefit of others—a capacity previously unattained which is now acquired for the first time; therefore, they rejoice.

When a śrāvaka first realizes suchness, they attain only the capacity for self-benefit and lack the capacity for benefiting others; although the śrāvaka also possesses the sense of joy, it does not equal that of a bodhisattva. Therefore, the name "Joyful" (Pramuditā) is established only for the first stage of a bodhisattva, whereas this name is not established for the first fruit of a śrāvaka.

Furthermore, regarding the supramundane dharmas that were previously unattained but are now for the first time realized, immeasurable causes and conditions give rise to a great sense of jubilation that flows continuously; therefore, it is called "joy."
The Commentary says:
Why is the second stage called "Stainless"?
Because this stage is far removed from the stains of violating the bodhisattva precepts.
The commentary states:

In this stage, the bodhisattva possesses naturally pure ethical discipline (*śīla*); because it is not obtained through correct deliberation as was the case in the first stage, it is called "stainless" (*vimalā*).

Furthermore, because all subtle stains of the transgressions of the precepts have been abandoned and distanced within this stage, and because the naturally pure precepts flow in constant succession, it is called "Stainless" (vimalā).
The Commentary says:
Why is the third stage called the "Blazing Radiance" (Arciṣmatī)?
Because it is based upon non-retrogressive *samādhi* and *samāpatti*, and because it is based upon the radiance of the Great Dharma.
The commentary states:
In this stage, the bodhisattva has never been separated from *samādhi* and *samāpatti*, because they do not regress from these concentrations.
The Mahāyāna teachings that have been expounded are the basis for these concentrations; "great Dharma" refers to the Mahāyāna Dharma.

Non-conceptual wisdom and the subsequently attained non-conceptual wisdom are called "light"; the bodhisattva also never departs from this wisdom, and the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining serves as its basis.
Taking concentration as its light and wisdom as its flame, it is called "Light and Flame" (Jyotis).
Furthermore, concentration is explained as the root of wisdom, and thus it is termed the "basis";
wisdom is the root of concentration, and thus it is also termed the "basis."
Furthermore, because this stage is the basis for immeasurable light of wisdom, immeasurable samādhis, and the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining, it is called "Blazing Radiance."
The Treatise says:
Why is the fourth stage called "the Blazing"?
Because the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) are able to incinerate and extinguish all hindrances.
The commentary states:
Because a bodhisattva constantly abides in the factors conducive to enlightenment within this stage, it is called "blazing" (*jvalana*);
because by abiding in these factors one incinerates all afflictions, both great and small, it is called "burning," and is thus termed "the Blazing One" (*jvalana*).
Furthermore, because the fire of the Path blazes intensely and is able to burn away the fuel of the afflictions (*kleśa*), it is called "blazing.
The treatise asks:
Why is the fifth stage named "Difficult to Conquer" (*sudurjaya*)?
The two wisdoms of the ultimate and the conventional are mutually contradictory, yet they are able to unite what is difficult to unite and bring them into correspondence.
The commentary states:

Ultimate wisdom is non-conceptual, while conventional wisdom possesses conceptualization, such as that found in the fields of arts and crafts (*śilpa-vidyā-sthāna*). The union of these two—conceptualization and non-conceptualization—which are mutually contradictory, so as to bring them into correspondence, is a difficult task.
Because a bodhisattva is able to bring [the factors] into correspondence within this stage, it is called "Difficult to Conquer" (Sudurjaya).
The treatise asks:
Why is the sixth stage called "Manifest" (Abhimukhī)?
Because it relies upon the knowledge of dependent origination through twelve links, it enables the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) to manifest and abide.
The commentary states:

In this stage, the bodhisattva dwells in the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination; by the power of the knowledge of these twelve links, they attain non-conceptual abiding, and this non-conceptual abiding is itself the perfection of wisdom.
Because this *prajñāpāramitā* dwells in constant clarity, it is called "manifest" (*abhimukhī*).
The treatise asks:
Why is the seventh stage called "Far-Going" (*dūraṅgamā*)?
"Because it reaches the final limit of the stage of effortful practice.
The commentary explains:
Having practiced with effortful mental application within this stage, the bodhisattva ultimately deliberates upon and definitively realizes that all signs are [empty].
This contemplation is accomplished through effort; because it occurs at the very end of the mind of applied effort (*prayoga-prayoga-citta*), it is called "Far-Reaching" (*dūramgamā*).

Furthermore, it is called "Far-Reaching" because it consists of uninterrupted reflection on the characteristics of all phenomena, enters long-term cultivation, and is adjacent to the pure stages (*viśuddha-bhūmi*).
The Treatise says:
Why is the eighth stage called "the Immovable"?
Because it cannot be moved by any mental images (*nimitta*) or the effort of volitional attention (*manasikāra*).
The commentary states:

Because they apply effort toward the signless and all signs, and because they cannot be moved by afflictions, the Bodhisattva has two kinds of objects on this stage: first, the ultimate object; second, the conventional object.
The true realm is called "signless"; when a bodhisattva abides in this realm, it cannot be overturned by any signs or by effortful activity.
The conventional realm is called "all signs," which refers to the activities that benefit sentient beings; in this realm, no delusions can defile the bodhisattva.
Because of these two meanings, the bodhisattva’s mind is called "unshakable.
Furthermore, no mental images, no phenomena, and no functional activities can turn back the non-conceptual mind of a bodhisattva.
Why is this? Because this non-conceptual mind naturally continues in a constant flow, it is called "immovable.
The treatise says:
Why is the ninth stage called "Excellent Intelligence" (*sādhumatī*)?
Because it is based upon the most excellent knowledge of the unimpeded analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
The commentary states:

The four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) attained by the Bodhisattva on this stage are called "wisdom" (*jñāna*); because this wisdom is perfected, irreversible, and stainless, it is called "excellent" (*sādhu*), and thus the stage is termed "Excellent Wisdom" (*Sādhumatī*).

Furthermore, on this stage, the Bodhisattva is able to fully expound all dharmas; because he has attained vast, infallible wisdom, he possesses this capacity, and thus it is called "Excellent Wisdom."
The Commentary says:
Why is the tenth stage called the "Dharma Cloud" (*dharmameghā*)?

Because it takes as its object the universal realm and knows all phenomena, and because it has all *dhāraṇī* gates and *samādhi* gates as its treasury; therefore, it is likened to a cloud. This is because it can cover the coarse obstructions that are like space, and because it can bring the *dharmakāya* to full completion.
The commentary states:
In this stage, the bodhisattva attains such wisdom that it is able to take all phenomena as a single, unified object.
This wisdom possesses a superior efficacy, which is illustrated by the three meanings of a cloud: namely, its ability to store, its ability to cover, and its ability to benefit.
Just as pure water within a cloud is contained by the cloud, which constitutes the sense of "that which can contain" (nibandhana), so too is this wisdom.
The gates of dhāraṇī and the gates of samādhi are like the pure water within this wisdom; because they are contained by this wisdom, it possesses the sense of "that which can contain."
Just as a cloud can cover one portion of the sky, so too is this wisdom:

it can cover all coarse and gross afflictive obstructions because it acts as their antidote; thus, it functions as the path of cessation for its own stage and as the path of non-arising for other stages.
Furthermore, just as clouds are able to pervade the entirety of space, so too is this wisdom;
it is able to fulfill the *dharmakāya*, the basis upon which the bodhisattva transforms.
For these two reasons, there is the sense of being able to cover.

Because Bodhisattvas possess this wisdom, they are like great clouds that constantly rain down the Dharma upon all sentient beings according to their faculties and dispositions. They are able to remove the scorching heat of the afflictions of sentient beings, to free them from the dust and grime of the three obstructions, and to cause the seeds of the goodness of the Three Vehicles to grow; thus, it possesses the meaning of being beneficial.
The Dharma designates this wisdom; because it compares wisdom to clouds, it is called "Dharma-Cloud" (Dharmameghā).
There are four meanings for the general designation "ground" (bhūmi):
first, the meaning of abiding; second, the meaning of place; third, the meaning of encompassing; and fourth, the meaning of remediation.
Because these eleven are states of abiding in the superior, untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), they have "abiding" as their meaning.
Because they are the locus for enjoying the blissful dwelling of the present life, maturing the Buddha-dharmas, and maturing sentient beings, they have "locus" (*sthāna*) as their meaning.
Because it encompasses all merit and wisdom, its meaning is "comprehension" (*saṃgraha*).
Because it can counteract the flow of afflictions, its meaning is "remedy" (*pratipakṣa*).
Chapter Three: On the Characteristics of Attainment. The Treatise states:
How should one understand the characteristics of attaining the various stages (*bhūmi*)?
The commentary states:

If a bodhisattva has already attained the true reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*) obtained on the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), this characteristic can initiate the bodhisattva’s own mind of diligence, can give rise to the sentient beings’ mind of faith and delight, and can cause the bodhisattva to abandon the mind of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
The characteristics of the stage attained must be explained; therefore, it is asked: "How should this be known?
The treatise says:
"By means of four kinds of characteristics."
The commentary states:
When any one of the four characteristics manifests, it is verified that this person has already entered the bodhisattva stages. Why is this?
These four characteristics are absent elsewhere except for those who have ascended the stages (*bhūmi*).
The treatise says:
First, by virtue of having attained the characteristic of faith and delight, because they generate decisive faith and delight in each and every stage.
The commentary states:
There are five kinds of faithful devotion, as explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*:
first, freedom from negligence;
Second, for sentient beings who encounter suffering and hardship and have no rescue or reliance, one acts as their savior and place of refuge;
third, one gives rise to a mind of supreme respect toward the Triple Gem and exhausts all means of making offerings;
fourth, one recognizes all transgressions and reveals them all immediately without concealing them for even a single thought-moment.
Fifth, one first generates the bodhicitta regarding all activities and in the course of reflection and cultivation.
If any one of these five appears, it is verified that one has already entered the bodhisattva stages.
For example, a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) attains the four kinds of indestructible faith. Why is this?
Because these five are the dharmas constantly practiced by bodhisattvas; therefore, they can manifest the signs that a bodhisattva has already entered the stages (bhūmi).
The Treatise says:
Second, by means of the aspects already attained, because one attains the ten kinds of correct practice that correspond to the stages (*bhūmi*).
The Commentary explains:
If a bodhisattva practices the ten stages (*bhūmi*), they do not transcend ten kinds of correct practice (*samyak-pratipatti*); these ten kinds of correct practice are the basis for the ten stages.
Regarding the ten kinds of correct practice in the Dharma, as explained in the *Saptadaśabhūmika-śāstra*:

"Within the Mahāyāna, there are ten kinds of wholesome dharmas of correct practice by which bodhisattvas bring sentient beings to maturity; they are in accord with the Mahāyāna and are subsumed within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka of the twelve divisions of the Vaipulya sūtras."

What are the ten? First, writing and maintaining [the text]; second, making offerings; third, giving it to others; fourth, listening with reverence when others correctly expound it; fifth, reading it oneself; sixth, teaching others so that they may attain it; seventh, single-mindedly practicing and reciting it as it has been taught; eighth, providing extensive and reasoned explanations for others; ninth, dwelling alone in a secluded place, correctly reflecting upon, weighing, and discerning it; and tenth, entering the mind through the cultivation of its signs.
Among these ten kinds of correct practice, how many constitute the path of great merit?
How many constitute the path of application?
And how many constitute the path for purifying hindrances?
All these constitute the path of great merit; the ninth is the path of preparatory application (*prayoga-mārga*), and the tenth is the path of purifying obstructions (*āvaraṇa-viśuddhi-mārga*).
The treatise states:

Thirdly, by virtue of having attained the characteristic of penetration, because when one first penetrates the *tathatā* dharma-realm in the first stage (*bhūmi*), one is simultaneously able to penetrate all stages.
The commentary states:
The suchness (tathatā) attained through the four investigations and the four cognitions of reality as it is is not different from stage to stage.
The treatise says:
Fourth, by the characteristic of having already attained accomplishment, for these ten stages have all reached the ultimate stage of cultivation.
The commentary states:
there are four kinds of accomplished mind, and there are likewise four kinds of objective referents.

Once the bodhisattva has fully increased their roots of goodness within the stage of aspiration and delight, they rely upon the path to enlightenment to transcend the two attachments; thus, the bodhisattva’s mind arises taking four kinds of objects as its focus.
What are the four?

First, the swift fulfillment of the provisions for enlightenment in future lives; second, the fulfillment of performing deeds that benefit sentient beings; third, the fulfillment of the fruit of unsurpassed enlightenment; and fourth, the fulfillment of the buddha-deeds endowed with all marks of the Tathāgatas.

Based on these four objects, there are four corresponding states of mind: first, the mind of diligence; second, the mind of great compassion; third, the mind of virtuous aspiration; and fourth, the mind of virtuous conduct.
Chapter Four: On the Characteristics of Cultivation. The Treatise asks:
How should one understand the characteristics of cultivating the various stages (*bhūmi*)?
The commentary states:
Having already explained the characteristics of attaining the various stages (*bhūmi*), by what means (*upāya*) should one cultivate them so as to attain those stages?
Therefore, it asks: "How should this be understood?"
The treatise states:
All bodhisattvas first cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā within each respective stage (bhūmi), attaining perfection through five distinct modes of cultivation for each.
The commentary states:
The practices of Bodhisattvas throughout the three periods of time are entirely identical, as they prioritize the attainment of what has never been attained before.
This indicates that the time of practice occurs within the stage of the purified intention; therefore, it is said to take place "in each and every stage."
The ten pāramitās that are cultivated have two general natures: first, non-distraction as their nature; second, non-perversion as their nature.
Non-distraction belongs to śamatha, while non-perversion belongs to vipaśyanā.
Each of the stages (*bhūmi*) is cultivated through five distinct aspects, whereby one attains the bodhisattva stages.
Without these five cultivations, one cannot enter the bodhisattva stages.
The treatise says:
What are the five?
First, the cultivation of collective synthesis.
The commentary states:

Based on the various phrases, various principles, and various dharma-gates of the Mahāyāna’s authentic teachings as expounded by the Buddha, one investigates names, objects, and dharma-gates through the four types of thorough investigation (*paryeṣaṇā*) and the four types of knowledge of reality (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*), finding that neither intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) nor specific difference (*viśeṣa*) can be apprehended.
This cannot be apprehended and cannot be said to exist, because it is free from the three natures;
nor can it be said to be non-existent, because it is the fruit of pure brahmacarya.
What the Tathāgata has taught is universally of one single flavor; therefore, it is called "universal cultivation."
This cultivation relies on the practice of wisdom.
The treatise says:
it is the twofold cultivation of signlessness.
The commentary states:
It is called "signless" (animitta) because it possesses the five kinds of purity, such as non-attachment, as previously described.
Furthermore, it is called signless because one does not cling to the karmic retribution of repaying one's own body.
This cultivation relies upon the practice of great compassion.
The treatise states:
"Third, effortless cultivation."
The commentary states:
A bodhisattva does not rely on the application of effortful mental activity (*manasikāra*), but naturally abides in the practice of enlightenment (*bodhicaryā*).
If effortful mental activity is required for other matters, this cultivation depends upon mastery (*vaśitā*) and the practice of right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).
The Treatise says:
The cultivation of the four blazing [elements].
The Commentary explains:

A bodhisattva does not cultivate the path with a distracted mind; rather, when they abandon inferior and middling states of mind and rely upon a superior state of mind in their practice, they have no stinginess regarding body, life, or wealth, and for this reason it is called "blazing."
This cultivation relies on the practice of vigor.
The treatise states:
Fifth is the cultivation of non-contentment.
The commentary states:
As previously explained, one does not give rise to weariness or fatigue while practicing acts such as generosity over a long period; therefore, this is called "lack of contentment.
This cultivation is based upon faith and conduct.
As the Sūtra says:
"If a person possesses faith, they will never grow weary of the wholesome.
The Commentary states:
One should know that these five types of cultivation exist within all the stages (*bhūmi*).
The commentary states:
there are two reasons why all stages require these five cultivations: first, to cause what has not yet been attained to be attained; second, to ensure that what has already been attained is not lost.
The Treatise says:
These five cultivations produce five dharmas as their fruit.
The Commentary says:
The five cultivations are the cause, and the five dharmas are the fruit.
There are two kinds of fruit: first, the real fruit; second, the nominal fruit.
The five dharmas are the real fruit, while the stages (bhūmis) are the nominal fruit.
Because the stages (*bhūmi*) are established by means of five factors, the stage is a conventional designation for the fruit.
The treatise asks:
What are these five?
"In each and every moment, it is able to destroy all coarse and heavy dharmas.
The commentary explains:
the afflictive obscurations are "coarse," while the cognitive obscurations are "heavy."
All seeds of impure dharmas within the fundamental consciousness serve as the basis for these two obstacles.
The first moment constitutes the path of application (*prayoga-mārga*), and the second moment constitutes the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
In the first moment, it destroys present afflictions, causing them to cease; in the second moment, it obstructs future afflictions, preventing them from arising.

Furthermore, through the wisdom of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, which takes universal phenomena (*dharmas*) as its object, it is able to destroy the mass of afflictions moment by moment; that which is to be countered is caused to cease, while that which is not to be countered is rendered weak.
The non-arising of the fruit through the extinction of these afflictions is what is obtained through general cultivation.
The treatise states:
"Both [types of cultivation] can bring about the attainment of the blissful state free from various conceptual proliferations."
The commentary states:
One is able to attain liberation from various conceptualized signs and experience the joy of the Dharma in the present. Why is this?

The Tathāgata establishes various Dharma characteristics according to the faculties, natures, afflictions, and behaviors of sentient beings; yet if one were to judge the meaning solely by the literal text, these various Dharmas would appear to be contradictory from beginning to end.
If one clings to these signs without being free from doubt, there is no possibility of attaining a state of peaceful dwelling within the True Dharma in this present life.

If, however, one practices according to signlessness, one transcends the various conceptualizations of established signs within the True Dharma; by contemplating this correctly taught teaching as having the single flavor of true suchness (*tathatā*), the mind becomes free from doubt and weariness. Thus, because one acts with spontaneous mastery within the True Dharma, one attains a state of peaceful dwelling in this present life.
This ripening of the fruit of the Buddha-dharma is attained through the cultivation of signlessness (*animitta*).
The treatise states:
"Third, one is able to perceive in all places the immeasurable light of wholesome dharmas that are free from conceptual differentiation (*avikalpa*)."
The commentary states:

"The term 'all places' is explained in relation to the three vehicles; it is also explained in relation to internal and external phenomena; and it is further explained in relation to the ultimate and conventional truths."
In this way, in all places, the bodhisattva is able to perceive immeasurable characteristics.

Just as the Buddha has taught the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and as the characteristics of phenomena established in the world are, the bodhisattva is able to thoroughly comprehend them all; this is precisely the knowledge of things as they are (*yathābhūtajñāna*).
According to their respective numbers, bodhisattvas penetrate non-conceptual characteristics through the wisdom of suchness.
Because these two types of wisdom can illuminate and comprehend both the ultimate and conventional realms, they are called the "Light of Virtuous Dharmas."
The fruits of these two knowledges are obtained through effortless cultivation (*anābhoga-bhāvanā*).
The treatise states:

"The four aspects of phenomena as they are conceptually differentiated undergo transformation to attain the pure portion, arising in constant succession to bring about the full perfection of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*)."
The commentary states:

As previously heard, within the context of deliberative reflection and investigation (*vitarka-vicāra*), *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* have not yet reached fulfillment or greatness, nor do they proceed in accordance with their objects, because there has as yet been no intense cultivation.

Having attained this cultivation, one further attains the purified portion due to the abandonment of hindrances; one attains fulfillment due to its continuous arising; one attains contact with the *dharmakāya* due to that fulfillment; and one attains accomplishment due to reaching the ultimate stage—namely, at the time of arising, the time of fulfillment, and the time of culmination.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata has two kinds of bodies: first, the body of liberation (vimukti-kāya), and second, the dharma-body (dharma-kāya).
Because delusions are extinguished, the body of liberation is perfected; because the body of liberation is perfected, the dharma-body is accomplished.
This fruit of renunciation is obtained through fervent cultivation.
The treatise states:
"The five [faculties] increase further within the superior grade, serving as the causal conditions for the supreme-superior grade."
The commentary states:

Once a bodhisattva has ascended the stages (*bhūmi*) and attained the superior grade, because they remain insatiable regarding wholesome dharmas, they further cultivate and practice them. Thus, they progress from the first stage to touch upon the second stage, and so on, until they progress from the tenth stage to touch upon the fruit of Buddhahood, thereby achieving the most supreme superior grade.

The previously cultivated accumulations of merit and wisdom, with non-conceptual wisdom as the cause and the various factors conducive to enlightenment as the conditions, are fulfilled simultaneously; therefore, it is said that the causes and conditions have converged.
This perfection of the fruit is obtained through the cultivation of non-contentment.

As for the meaning of the remaining stages, one should understand them as explained in the *Saptadaśabhūmi-śāstra*, namely, the distinctions between those who possess capability and those who do not, and so forth.

Within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), how many kinds of dharmas are there such that, for the sake of extinguishing what has not yet been extinguished and attaining what has not yet been attained, the bodhisattva cultivates the practices of the ten stages?

Previously, while in the stage of practice through aspiration (*praṇidhāna-caryā-bhūmi*), the bodhisattva cultivates the ten types of dharma-practices and achieves the perfection of aspirational patience (*praṇidhāna-kṣānti*). By virtue of achieving this aspirational patience, they transcend the stage of practice through aspiration and enter the bodhisattva’s state of correct determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
The aspirant has ten great vows:
first, the vow of offering, which is the aspiration to make offerings to the supreme conditions, the field of merit, the teachers, and the masters of the Dharma;
second, the vow of upholding, which is the aspiration to receive and uphold the supreme and wondrous True Dharma.
The vow of turning the wheel of Dharma three times: the vow to turn the unprecedented wheel of Dharma within the great assembly.
The vow of practice: the vow to practice all the correct conducts of bodhisattvas exactly as they have been taught.
Fifth is the vow of maturation, which is the aspiration to mature the roots of goodness of the sentient beings within this vessel-world through the three vehicles.
Sixth is the vow of service, which is the aspiration to go to all buddha-fields to constantly see the Buddhas, always to receive their veneration and service, and to hear and receive the true Dharma.
Seventh is the vow for the pure land, which is the aspiration to establish the True Dharma in one’s own purified land and to enable sentient beings to practice it there.
Eighth is the vow of non-separation, which is the aspiration to never be separated from all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in any place of birth, and to attain identical conduct with them.
Ninth is the vow of benefiting others, which is the aspiration to constantly perform deeds that benefit sentient beings at all times, without any failure.
Tenth is the vow of perfect enlightenment, which is the aspiration to attain unsurpassed bodhi together with all sentient beings and to perpetually perform the work of a Buddha.
These ten vows are established only upon ascending to the first bhūmi.
Why is this? These vows take true thusness (tathatā) as their essence, and it is at the first bhūmi that one is able to perceive true thusness.
Patience (*kṣānti*) is none other than non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
Because patience is perfected through aspiration, it possesses two kinds of superior capacities: namely, the capacity to eliminate and the capacity to attain. What are these?
There are twenty-two types of ignorance, eleven types of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*), and eleven stages of retribution-obstructions.
Each stage is able to extinguish three types of obstructions and each attains superior merit.

Regarding the ability of the first stage (*bhūmi*) to extinguish the three obstacles: first, the ignorance of conceptualizing a self in phenomena (*dharma-ātman-vikalpa-avidyā*); second, the ignorance of karma leading to the evil realms (*durgati-karma-avidyā*).
These two types of ignorance induce the *saṃvṛti-saṃsāra* (conventional birth-and-death), which is termed the "heavy burden" (*dausthulya*) retribution.

One practices right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*) for the sake of extinguishing the three obstacles; having extinguished the three obstacles through the practice of right effort, one enters the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) and attains the ten perfections in their entirety.
First, one enters the correct state of determination of a bodhisattva (*bodhisattva-samyaktva-niyāma*), because one has entered the first untainted stage (*anāsrava-bhūmi*) of a bodhisattva.
Second, birth into the family of the Buddha, like that of the various bodhisattvas who are born into the royal house of the Dharma, because they are endowed with supreme excellence.
Third, their lineage is beyond reproach, as it surpasses the lineages of the two vehicles and the mundane world.
Fourth, they have already turned away from all worldly conduct, because they are definitively committed to not engaging in wrong actions such as killing.
Fifth, they have already reached supramundane conduct, because the stages (bhūmis) they attain are necessarily free from outflows (anāsrava).
Sixth, they have already attained the suchness of the bodhisattva-dharma, because they have realized the equality of self and others.
Seventh, they have already well established themselves in the station of a bodhisattva, because they have realized the true reality of the bodhisattva-dharma.
Eighth, they have already attained equality with the three periods of time, because they have realized the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena as being devoid of self.
Ninth, they are definitively established within the nature of the Tathāgata, for they will certainly attain Buddhahood in the future.
Tenth, one has already abandoned the matter of breaking eggs, because by means of the Buddha-way one has shattered the shell of ignorance and attained parinirvāṇa externally.

At the first stage (*bhūmi*), the Bodhisattva, by virtue of perceiving the meaning of the pervasiveness of the *dharmadhātu*, attains these ten parts; just as a Śrāvaka at the first fruit possesses tenfold merit, it is through these parts that the first stage is perfected.
In the first stage (*bhūmi*), the bodhisattva does not yet possess superior capability, as they have not yet fully realized the subtle transgressions and infractions within the bodhisattva precepts.
The reason they are unable to do so is due to three obstacles: first, ignorance regarding subtle transgressions; second, ignorance regarding the karmic activities of various characteristics.
Because these two types of ignorance induce the *saṃskāra-bhava* (birth through effort), they are termed "coarse heaviness" (*dauṣṭhulya*) as retribution.

In order to extinguish the three obstacles, one practices right effort; having extinguished the three obstacles by means of practicing right effort, one enters the second stage and attains eight kinds of pure merit.

First, purity of faith and joy; second, purity of mind; third, purity of compassion; fourth, purity of the pāramitās; fifth, purity of seeing and serving the Buddhas; sixth, purity of maturing sentient beings; seventh, purity of birth; eighth, purity of majestic power.

Excluding the stage of the Tathāgata, these eight kinds of merit become increasingly superior and more excellent in each successive higher stage; by virtue of these factors, the second stage is perfected.

Regarding this second stage, the bodhisattva has not yet attained superior capability, nor has he yet acquired the four worldly dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*samāpatti*), or the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining, which is endowed with perfect power of mindfulness.

The reason why [the fruit] has not yet been attained is due to three obstacles: first, the ignorance of desire and craving; second, the ignorance regarding the *dhāraṇī* of perfect hearing and retention.
The retribution of heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) resulting from these two types of ignorance is termed the "birth-and-death of expedient means."

One cultivates the cause of right effort in order to extinguish the three obstructions; having extinguished the three obstructions through right effort, one enters the third stage (*bhūmi*), attaining eight kinds of increasingly superior purity, the four concentrations (*dhyāna*), and so forth, up to the realization of the meaning of the supreme flow of the *dharmadhātu*. By virtue of these factors, the third stage is perfected.

In the third stage, the bodhisattva has not yet attained superior capability; he is unable to dwell for as long as he desires within the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) according to his own attainment, nor is he able to dwell in the purity of mind that has abandoned attachment to the states of meditative absorption (samāpatti).

The reason one has not yet attained this is due to three obstacles: first, the ignorance of craving for meditative absorption (*samāpatti*); second, the ignorance of craving for the practice of the Dharma (*dharmacaryā*).
The retribution of these two types of ignorance is the coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*) of the *saṃskṛta-bhava* (birth-and-death) resulting from preparatory effort (*prayoga*).

In order to extinguish these three obstacles, one practices right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*). Having extinguished the three obstacles through the practice of right effort, one enters the fourth stage (*caturthī bhūmi*), attaining eight kinds of increasingly superior purity, as well as dwelling at will for long periods within the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), and so forth, up to the thorough penetration of the meaning of the non-appropriation of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). By virtue of these factors, the fourth stage is perfected.

At the fourth stage (*bhūmi*), the bodhisattva has not yet attained superior capability; while correctly practicing the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths, they have not yet been able to abandon the mind that either exclusively turns away from or exclusively seeks toward saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, nor have they been able to attain the bodhisattva’s factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) as subsumed by the four kinds of skillful means (*upāya*).

The reason why they have not yet attained it is due to three obstacles: first, the ignorance of conceptualizing nirvana and saṃsāra as being exclusively opposed to one another; second, the ignorance regarding the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) subsumed under skillful means.
The birth and death resulting from these two types of ignorance as causes and conditions is called the retribution of *dausthulya* (coarseness).

To extinguish these three obstacles, one practices right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*). Having extinguished the three obstacles through the practice of right effort, one enters the fifth stage and attains eight kinds of increasingly superior purity, as well as the abandonment of the mind that turns away from or grasps at [phenomena], up to the thorough penetration of the meaning of the continuity of the *dharmadhātu* without differentiation. By virtue of these factors, the fifth stage is perfected.

In the fifth stage, the bodhisattva has not yet attained superior capability because he has not yet realized, in accordance with reality, the continuous arising of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); because he has extensively practiced the loathing of the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*); and because he is as yet unable to dwell for a long duration in signless mental attention (*animittamanasikāra*) at will.

The reason one has not yet attained this is due to three obstacles: first, ignorance regarding the arising and continuous succession of all conditioned phenomena; second, ignorance regarding the frequent arising of perceptions of signs.
These two types of ignorance that induce the cycle of birth and death through causes and conditions are termed "heavy burdens" (*dausthulya*) as their retribution.

To extinguish these three obstacles, one practices right effort; having extinguished the three obstacles through the practice of right effort, one enters the sixth stage and attains eight kinds of increasingly superior purity, as well as the non-realization of the signs of the arising and continuity of conditioned phenomena, up to the thorough penetration of the meaning of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) being neither defiled nor pure. By virtue of these factors, the sixth stage is perfected.

In the sixth stage, the bodhisattva has not yet attained superior capability; he is unable to abandon the arising of subtle marks of conditioned phenomena, nor is he able to dwell for long periods at will within uninterrupted, outflow-free, and markless contemplation.

The reason they have not yet attained it is due to three obstacles: first, the ignorance that arises from the activity of subtle marks; second, the ignorance regarding the skillful means of one-pointed contemplation on the signless.
The cycle of birth and death, induced by the causal conditions of these two types of ignorance, is termed the "retribution of heaviness" (*dausthulya*).

To extinguish the three obstacles, one practices right effort; having extinguished the three obstacles through the practice of right effort, one enters the seventh stage and attains eight kinds of increasingly superior purity. Furthermore, one becomes detached from the subtle arising of signs associated with conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), and even penetrates the meaning of the non-differentiation of the various phenomena within the *dharmadhātu*. By virtue of these factors, the seventh stage is brought to completion.

In the seventh stage, the bodhisattva has not yet attained superior capability; he is unable to dwell in the cultivation of the signless while free from effortful application, nor is he able to attain mastery over the mental states associated with the signs of self-benefit and benefit for others.

The reason one has not yet attained this is due to three obstructions: first, the ignorance that exerts effort in the contemplation of signlessness; second, the ignorance regarding mastery over signs and activities.
The birth and death resulting from these two types of ignorance is called the retribution of *dausthulya* (coarseness).

One practices right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*) in order to extinguish the three obstacles; having extinguished the three obstacles through the practice of right effort, one enters the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*) and attains eight kinds of increasingly superior purity, as well as the dwelling in signless cultivation through the attainment of non-effortful mind, and so forth, until reaching the penetration of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) in its sense of being without increase or decrease. By virtue of these factors, the eighth stage is perfected.

In the eighth stage, the bodhisattva has not yet attained superior capability; he has not yet attained mastery over the characteristics, distinctions, names, and categories within correct exposition, nor has he attained the skillful eloquence of dhāraṇīs.

The reason why they have not yet attained it is due to three obstacles: first, ignorance regarding the *dhāraṇī* of mastery over skillful speech that provides difficult answers to immeasurable, correctly taught Dharma with its immeasurable names, phrases, and syllables; second, ignorance regarding the resolution of doubts and the generation of understanding through reliance on the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
The existence and non-existence of birth and death brought about by these two types of ignorance are called the retribution of *dausthulya* (gross dysfunction).

To extinguish these three obstacles, one practices right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*). Having extinguished the three obstacles through the practice of right effort, one enters the ninth stage and attains eight kinds of increasingly superior purity, as well as mastery over the characteristics of perfect teaching and so forth, up to the meaning of the reliance upon mastery of wisdom that penetrates the *dharmadhātu*. By means of these factors, the ninth stage is perfected.

In the ninth stage, the bodhisattva has not yet attained superior capability; he has not yet realized the perfectly expounded dharmakāya, nor has he attained the unattached and unimpeded perfection of the six supernormal knowledges (ṣaḍabhijñā).

The reason they have not yet attained it is due to three obstructions: first, ignorance regarding the wisdom of the six supernormal powers; second, ignorance regarding entry into the subtle and secret Buddha-dharmas.
The existence and birth-and-death produced by these two types of ignorance are called the retribution of *dausthulya* (coarseness).

To extinguish these three obstacles, one practices right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*). Having extinguished the three obstacles through the practice of right effort, one enters the tenth stage (*daśamī bhūmi*) and attains eight kinds of increasingly superior purity, as well as the ability to attain the perfectly expounded *dharmakāya*, and so forth, up to the realization of the meaning of the basis for mastery over karma within the *dharmadhātu*. By means of these factors, the ten stages are brought to completion.

The Bodhisattva, while on the ten stages, has not yet attained superior capability, has not yet realized the pure and perfect Dharmakāya, and has not yet attained unattached and unimpeded vision and knowledge regarding all objects of cognition.

The reason why it has not yet been attained is due to three obstacles: first, the subtle attachment-ignorance regarding all objects of knowledge; second, the subtle obstruction-ignorance regarding all objects of knowledge.
The birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) experienced as a result of these two types of ignorance is called the "retribution of coarse heaviness" (*dauṣṭhulya*).

To extinguish these three obstacles, one practices right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*); having extinguished the three obstacles through the practice of right effort, one enters the stage of the Tathāgata (*tathāgatabhūmi*), attaining the seven kinds of supreme purity, the purity of being free from birth, as well as the pure and perfect *dharmakāya*, and unattached, unimpeded vision and knowledge. Through these factors, the stage of the Tathāgata is perfected.
The merits of the ten stages are all surpassed, whereas the merits of the Tathāgata stage are entirely unsurpassed.
The pāramitās are the training grounds of bodhisattvas; for what reason are they sometimes said to be six and sometimes said to be ten?
There are two general meanings for why six [perfections] are taught:
first, the first three accomplish the benefit of others in future lives;
second, the latter three serve as antidotes to the afflictions of others.
By practicing generosity, the bodhisattva establishes the means of subsistence for sentient beings, thereby causing others to be free from the suffering of poverty.
By practicing ethical discipline, the bodhisattva refrains from harming or afflicting sentient beings, thereby causing others to be free from fear.

Because the Bodhisattva practices patience, refraining from retaliating against the harms, injuries, and afflictions inflicted by sentient beings, he causes others to be free from doubt and find peace of mind.
These three constitute the accomplishment of worldly benefit for others.

When a bodhisattva practices diligence, if others have not yet subdued their afflictions or have not yet severed them, he is able to establish such persons in what is wholesome and in the conditions that assist the wholesome.
By virtue of this diligence, various afflictions are unable to cause them to regress from the wholesome and the conditions that assist the wholesome.
When a bodhisattva practices meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they are able to subdue and extinguish the afflictions of others;
when a bodhisattva practices wisdom (*prajñā*), they are able to sever and eliminate the afflictions of others.
Therefore, the latter three [perfections] serve as the remedies for the afflictions of others.

Some say there are ten, establishing the latter four perfections (*pāramitā*) in addition to the former six; these latter four are established because they assist in the accomplishment of the former six.
That which is benefited by the first three perfections is manifested through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
Because the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*) is able to establish them in wholesome states, the perfection of skillful means is the companion to the first three perfections.

If, in the present life, a bodhisattva—whether due to an abundance of afflictions, or by virtue of having taken birth in a lower realm through the power of a vow, or because of mental weakness—is incapable of constant cultivation and mental abiding, they will lack the capacity to generate a concentration that takes the words and phrases of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka as its object, nor will they have the capacity to bring forth supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-prajñā*).

When a bodhisattva practices with meager roots of goodness and merit, yet vows that in future lives their afflictions shall likewise be meager and powerless, this is the power of the bodhisattva’s perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*).

By thinning out the afflictions and so forth, one is able to give rise to the bodhisattva’s perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*); since this applies both to oneself and to others, the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*) is the auxiliary companion to the perfection of diligence.

This bodhisattva who has already attained diligence hears the true Dharma by attending upon spiritual friends; because he reflects correctly upon what he has heard, he is able to eliminate the feeble state of mind and attain a powerful and superior state of mind regarding sublime objects—this is the bodhisattva’s perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*).

By the power of this cultivation, the bodhisattva is able to draw the mind and cause it to abide within internal objects; therefore, the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*) is the auxiliary companion to the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).

This bodhisattva who has already attained power possesses the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation arising from the words and phrases of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, as well as the wisdom pertaining to the five types of knowledge (*vidyā*); through this wisdom, one can correctly discern the objects of both the ultimate and conventional truths.
This wisdom may exist either prior to non-conceptual wisdom or subsequent to non-conceptual wisdom; it is the Bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-pāramitā*).

Because this wisdom can produce meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and bring forth insight (*prajñā*), the perfection of wisdom is an auxiliary companion to the perfection of insight (*prajñā-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, what is the sequence of the ten bodhisattva training rules?
Each preceding perfection (pāramitā) is able to encompass and bring about the succeeding perfection, serving as its basis.

If a bodhisattva, without begrudging the six sense objects or his own personal pleasure, undertakes and upholds the prohibitive precepts, then for the sake of protecting and cherishing those precepts, he endures the insults and humiliations of others. Because he is able to endure them, he exerts diligence without slackening; through this diligence, evil is stilled and goodness is produced, whereby he touches samādhi. If concentration is perfected, he is then able to bring forth supramundane prajñā.
By means of *prajñā*, one turns the first six perfections toward the attainment of great enlightenment so that giving and the other virtues become inexhaustible.

*Prajñā* can induce the causes of skillful means (*upāya*), and these skillful means give rise to various virtuous vows capable of encompassing favorable places of birth, such that in all places of birth one always encounters the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world.
Therefore, because one constantly practices giving and the other perfections, skillful means can induce aspiration.

By virtue of this aspiration, one attains two kinds of power—namely, the power of analytical discernment (*cintā-bala*) and the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bala*)—which destroy the opposing factors to giving and the rest, ensuring that one is always able to practice giving and so forth. Thus, aspiration is able to induce these powers.

By the power of this, when one grasps the meaning according to the words, ignorance is extinguished; one obtains the superior condition of the joy of the Dharma through receiving offerings and so forth, and because this joy of the Dharma can mature the roots of goodness in sentient beings, its power is able to induce wisdom.

On the first stage (*bhūmi*), one penetrates the meaning of universal pervasion and attains supramundane wisdom; the Bodhisattva perceives the *dharmadhātu* as subsumed within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), namely the two kinds of emptiness, and is thus able to realize the equality of self and others.

Because one attains equanimity—neither loving oneself nor hating others—one is able to practice for the benefit of both self and others with impartiality; therefore, on the first bhūmi, the perfection of giving is fulfilled.
On the second bhūmi, one penetrates the supreme meaning, namely, intrinsic purity.
The Bodhisattva forms this thought:
"As the Sūtra says, 'We shall likewise attain this purity and thereby achieve liberation,' therefore one should cultivate only the true path.
This Sūtra reveals two meanings:
First, it reveals that the self-nature of the *dharmadhātu* is supremely pure and without distinction; second, it reveals that the true path leads to the *dharmadhātu*.
Since one perceives no grades of superior, middling, or inferior within the *dharmadhātu*, one does not seek the fruits of the two vehicles, but seeks only unsurpassed *bodhi*.
This path of purification is precisely the bodhisattva precepts; therefore, on the second bhūmi, the practice of morality is perfected.
On the third bhūmi, one practices patience by means of penetrating the meaning of the "excellent flow" (viśeṣa-mukha).
Why is this? The twelve divisions of the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata are the supreme outflow of the dharmadhātu, for they arise from the thorough penetration of the dharmadhātu.
If a person practices according to the text in accordance with the principle, they shall attain realization of this rare dharma.
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"As it is said in the sutras, there is no suffering that is difficult to endure which he cannot endure for the sake of attaining this teaching.
Even if the great trichiliocosm were filled with blazing fire, the Bodhisattva would cast himself into that fire for the sake of seeking this Dharma."
Therefore, on the third stage, the practice of patience is perfected.
On the fourth stage, by means of penetrating the meaning of non-appropriation, one contemplates that the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is without any attachment or dependence.
Because this is the object of non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna), as the sūtra says:
By means of this, one penetrates the dhyānas, samādhis, and samāpattis, as well as the cessation of craving for wholesome dharmas so that they do not arise again.
Within this stage, all meditative concentrations and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are fully perfected; one takes such delight in them that they cannot be relinquished.
Why is this? Because faults are difficult to perceive.
Without supreme right effort, this craving cannot be extinguished.
When this craving is extinguished, one knows that right effort has been accomplished; therefore, on the fourth stage, the practice of diligence is perfected.

On the fifth stage, through the realization of the meaning of the non-differentiation of the continuum—that is, the fact that the self-nature of the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas is without distinction—the Bodhisattva attains the ten kinds of equality of the pure mind.
This equanimity of mind is precisely the meditative concentration of a bodhisattva. Why is this?
Because the object of a bodhisattva’s concentration is equanimous, as it takes both suchness and sentient beings as its focal objects.

Because the equality of practice universally encompasses the six perfections; because the equality of skillful means is free from the mind of superiority or inferiority; and because the equality of the path is free from the two extremes of existence and non-existence—these ten kinds of equality of intention constitute the essence of meditative concentration. Therefore, the practice of concentration is perfected in the fifth stage.

The sixth stage, by virtue of penetrating the meaning of the absence of defilement and purity, involves the bodhisattva observing the twelvefold dependent origination; within this observation, not a single dharma is seen to be either pure or defiled.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is pure.

The twelve links of existence, such as ignorance, have conceptualization (*vikalpa*) as their nature; since conceptualization has the absence of characteristics (*animitta*) as its nature, one does not perceive any defilement in phenomena. Since defilement is not established, one does not perceive any purity in phenomena.
As the Sūtra says:
"O Dragon King!
The twelvefold dependent origination is both produced and non-produced."
Birth is spoken of in terms of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), while non-arising is spoken of in terms of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Furthermore, within the twelve links of dependent origination, there is no dharma that can be called defiled and no dharma that can be called pure, because the nature of dharmas (*dharmatā*) is without differentiation.
Therefore, the practice of Prajñā is perfected in the sixth stage.

In the seventh stage, through the thorough penetration of the meaning that various dharmas are without distinction—namely, that the immeasurable Dharma-gates of the Three Vehicles taught by the Tathāgata share the single flavor of True Suchness (tathatā)—the various conceptualizations of characteristics described in the twelve divisions of scripture never arise again.

By knowing that all phenomena have no distinct meaning, one takes all conditioned activities of both the ultimate and conventional truths and directs them exclusively toward unsurpassed enlightenment. This is the dedication of skillful means; its essence is superior wisdom as the means, its function is to benefit others, and its activity is that the roots of goodness such as generosity neither diminish nor exhaust.

This skillful means is solely for the benefit of others and not for one's own benefit; because it is inexhaustible, the benefit of others is infinite. Therefore, at the seventh stage, the practice of skillful means is perfected.

In the eighth stage, by means of penetrating the meaning of neither increase nor decrease, the bodhisattva contemplates that when afflictions cease there is no decrease, and when the path arises there is no increase.
The dharma-realm has two states: first, the state with stains; second, the state without stains.
The Bodhisattva does not perceive an increase in the state of defilement within the dharma-realm, nor does he perceive a decrease in the state of purity within the dharma-realm.
Furthermore, he does not perceive an increase in the arising of the path in the state of purity, nor does he perceive a decrease in the non-arising of the path in the state of defilement.
Because not a single dharma is seen to increase or decrease, the supreme vow based upon this *dharmadhātu* is accomplished.

In the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), the Bodhisattva encounters the mutual opposition of the two wisdoms that take the ultimate and conventional objects as their respective domains; were it not for the power of the vow, there would be no possibility of their simultaneous realization.
Why is this? Taking the ultimate truth as the object is mastery over non-conceptual wisdom, because it functions without effortful application;
taking conventional reality as the object is mastery over the pure land, because it functions with pure effortful application.
These two masteries must necessarily be accomplished by relying on the power of vows.
What dharma constitutes the essence (*svabhāva*) of this vow?

The essence of the vow is the seeking of what has not yet been attained; its function (*karman*) is that what was previously sought is spontaneously accomplished; and its activity (*vṛtti*) is that in all places of birth one constantly encounters the Buddhas and perpetually practices roots of goodness such as giving, thereby establishing them without interruption.

This vow is solely for the benefit of others and not for one's own benefit; because it is uninterrupted, the benefit of others is inexhaustible in all places of birth. Therefore, the practices and vows of the eighth stage are perfected.

The ninth stage, by virtue of its basis in mastery through the wisdom of thorough penetration, attains two kinds of power within that stage: namely, the power of analytical investigation and the power of cultivation.
By virtue of this power, one is able to subdue all counteractive factors to right practice and can bring virtuous conduct to certainty.
What constitutes the essence of this power?
