This samādhi takes true suchness as its object; because it is truly existent, easily attained, and possesses immeasurable merit, it can destroy the habitual tendencies of icchantikas. This is precisely the means by which the obstacle of birth-and-death is overcome regarding great purity; by destroying this obstacle, one attains the fruit of great purity.
The treatise says:
"The samādhi of the King who Accumulates Merit.
The commentary says:
All wholesome dharmas, with the sole exception of *prajñā*, are collectively termed "merit.
This merit consists of four categories, namely: that of ordinary beings, that of the two vehicles, and that of bodhisattvas.

Because the bodhisattva, by means of this meditative concentration, is able to produce those four merits that have not yet been produced, to increase those that have not yet increased, and to perfect those that have not yet been perfected, it is called "accumulation."
He is called a "King" because he possesses mastery over the three stages of arising, growth, and perfection.
By virtue of this mastery, he is able to practice the ten perfections, such as generosity.

Because he brings to completion the accumulations for enlightenment through the cultivation of merit, he is able to destroy the habitual tendencies of the non-Buddhists' view of a self; this very [view] constitutes the obstacle of dependent origination that obstructs the Great Self.
By destroying these obstacles, one attains the fruit of the Great Self (*mahātman*).
Furthermore, all wholesome dharmas rely upon *tathatā* (suchness); since *tathatā* can gather all wholesome dharmas, *tathatā* is termed the "accumulation of merit."
Because this concentration attains mastery within *tathatā* (suchness), it is called "King.
The treatise says:
"The Samādhi of Bhadrapāla."
The commentary states:
"Worthy" (*bhadra*) has two meanings: first, the ability to dwell in manifest peace and happiness; second, the ability to attract and gather all meritorious qualities.

Regarding "dwelling in manifest peace and happiness": this samādhi enables the Bodhisattva’s body not to abandon the nature of space, and by being free from the three periods of time, one attains dwelling in peace and happiness.

Regarding "attracting and gathering all merits": it is able to attract and gather immeasurable concentrations that are beyond the hearing or knowledge of those of the two vehicles; because of each of these concentrations, immeasurable supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) arise.

By virtue of these two meanings, the bodhisattva is able to abandon the habitual tendencies of fear associated with the śrāvakas; that is, there is the obstacle of conditioned existence (*bhava*) within saṃsāra that obstructs great bliss.
By destroying this obstacle, one attains the fruit of great bliss.

Because this concentration takes true suchness (*tathatā*) as its essence for the bodhisattva, and because it does not depart from wisdom (*jñāna*), it can induce various concentrations and supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*); therefore, concentration is taken as its essence.
The treatise says:
"The *śūraṅgama-samādhi* and so forth."
The commentary states:
This samādhi is so named because it is practiced by Bodhisattvas of the ten stages and by Buddhas. Why is this?
Bodhisattvas of the ten stages and Buddhas possess four kinds of superior virtues, and for this reason it is called Śūraṅgama.
First is fearlessness, because they have attained all-knowledge;
second is freedom from doubt, because they see no one among pure beings who is their equal.
Third, it possesses the merit of being firm and substantial, because it remains constantly in contemplation without distraction;
fourth, it possesses superior capability, because it can shatter the obstacle of the dwelling-place of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*), which is otherwise difficult to destroy.
A person endowed with the four virtues is able to attain and practice this samādhi; therefore, it is called *gamā*.

This samādhi frequently performs deeds for the benefit of others and can destroy the habitual tendencies of self-love characteristic of the pratyekabuddhas; thus, there is no obstruction of saṃsāra regarding the Great Permanence.
Because this hindrance is destroyed, one attains the fruit of great permanence.
The word "etc. collectively refers to all meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*).
The treatise states:
"Because it encompasses various categories of samādhi.
The commentary states:
"The five hundred types of concentration are termed 'various'; they are all categories of the four dhyānas, and are entirely subsumed within the four dhyānas."
The Treatise says:
Regarding the distinction of the antidote, it is the wisdom that takes all phenomena as its universal object.
The Commentary says:
Non-conceptual wisdom takes as its single object the suchness (tathatā) of all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena; this wisdom and its object are no longer subject to differentiation.
The Treatise says:
It is like the skillful means of using a wedge to extract a wedge.
The Commentary explains:
Just as in the world, when one wishes to split wood, one first uses a fine wedge and subsequently uses a coarse wedge;
so too it is for the practitioner who destroys afflictions: they first employ an inferior path, then a middling path, and finally a superior path.
The Treatise says:
Because all heavy impediments (*dausthulya*) and obstructions are extracted from within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
The Commentary explains:

Within the continuity of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), there exist seeds of the three categories of afflictions, karma, and retribution—defiled and turbid—which are termed "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*). These are said to obstruct the four virtues.

Because of this [consciousness], that which has not yet been extinguished is caused to be extinguished, and that which has already been extinguished is prevented from arising. Since its capacity for counteraction, the objects of counteraction, and the results obtained through counteraction differ entirely from those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), it is described as being "distinct."
The Commentary states:
Regarding the distinction of its function, while dwelling for a long time in the bliss of samādhi in the present life, one is able to take birth in superior realms at will.
The commentary states:
The Bodhisattva employs various skillful means to cultivate the mind until it is matured, just as a goldsmith refines gold to make it pure.
Once the mind has been matured through cultivation, this is termed "conformity with function."

Why is this? Because by means of this concentration, if a bodhisattva wishes to bring the Buddha-dharmas to maturity, they can dwell for as long as desired upon a single object; that which is not yet attained they cause to be attained, that which has been attained they cause to be fulfilled, and that which has been fulfilled they cause not to decline.

Possessing such capacity in the present life, one will be able to extensively perform deeds that benefit sentient beings in future places of rebirth, and encounter the appearance of a Buddha in the world to hear the True Dharma; this is called a "superior place of rebirth."

By virtue of this meditative concentration (*samādhi*), a bodhisattva is able to exercise the three functions of grasping, abiding, and relinquishing within superior states of existence according to their will, without regression or exhaustion; since such a concentration does not exist within the Śrāvaka vehicle, it is said to be distinctive.
The treatise says:
Regarding the distinction of what is drawn forth, it is able to draw forth unimpeded supernormal knowledge throughout all worlds.
The commentary explains:
Bodhisattvas possess the "great matter samādhi," which means they encounter no obstruction whatsoever regarding any matter or in any place.
There are two meanings for "inducing":
first, that which can induce, which refers to the power of the samādhi.

Whether following the person, the object, or the cultivation, if a person of sharp faculties takes the unconditioned as their object, they attain the three kinds of mastery: entering, abiding, and emerging.
The second is "that which is induced," referring to matters accomplished through meditative concentration, such as shaking the earth or emitting light.

Regarding these matters, superior supernormal wisdom cannot take them away; all manifested phenomena correspond exactly to the mind. Since delusions cannot obstruct them and karma cannot hinder them, they are called "unimpeded inductions."
There is only the essence, but no function; "function" refers to the differentiation of phenomena.
Since only Bodhisattvas possess this samādhi and it is not cultivated by those of the Two Vehicles, it is said to be "differentiated."
The treatise says:
"By way of the differentiation of entities.
The commentary explains:
Based on these matters, one should understand that there is a definitive distinction between the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of a bodhisattva and that of the two vehicles (*dvaya-yāna*).
What are these matters?
The treatise says:
"Causing movement.
The commentary states:
"The power of *rddhi* can move the worlds of the ten directions."
The Treatise says:
Emitting light.
The Commentary explains:
The wish-fulfilling gem can illuminate the worlds of the ten directions.
The treatise says:
it is all-pervasive.
The commentary states:
Radiance, the sound of the Dharma, and emanated bodies can, through the power of *rddhi*, pervade the worlds of the ten directions.
The treatise says:
This is shown.
The commentary states:

Other sentient beings, by relying on the supernormal wisdom (*abhijñā*) of the Bodhisattva, are able to see immeasurable worlds as well as Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; whatever they ought to see, they behold accordingly, just as they wish.
The Treatise says:
"Transformation.
The Commentary explains:
The natures of the four great elements and so forth cause one another to undergo transformation and alteration.
The treatise says:
"Going and returning."
The commentary states:
Within a single moment, one can travel to and return from immeasurable worlds.
This supernormal power (abhijñā) itself is of three kinds:
First is the supernormal power of swift mental penetration, whereby whatever the mind focuses upon arrives immediately at the mere thought;
second is the supernormal power of bodily movement, like that of a flying bird;
third is the supernormal power of transformation, which refers to contracting the long into the short.
The Treatise says:
"It shortens the distant to make it near.
The Commentary explains:
It causes what is distant to become near, such that there is no longer any interval between them.
This consists of three things: namely, seeing, hearing, and proceeding.
The treatise says:
"Transforming the coarse into the subtle.
The commentary explains:
it causes countless worlds to become subtler than an atom (paramāṇu), such that they enter within a single atom while the atom remains as it was.
The Treatise says:
"Transforming the subtle into the coarse.
The Commentary explains:
It causes a single atom (*paramāṇu*) to envelop countless worlds, yet the worlds remain as they were before.
The treatise says:
It causes all forms (*rūpa*) to enter within one’s own body.
The commentary states:
All manner of rare and marvelous phenomena are manifested within the body.
The treatise says:
"Resembling those of their own kind, they enter the great assembly.
The commentary explains:

Just as the various bodhisattvas go to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, assuming the same physical appearance, ornaments, and voices as the inhabitants, they enter the great assembly to teach and deliver them.
The Treatise says:
"Either manifest or hidden.
The Commentary says:
It is able to manifest one or many within non-existence to reveal [the nature of phenomena], and able to render one or many characteristics non-existent within existence to conceal [it].
The treatise says:
It possesses the eight masteries (*vaśitā*).
The commentary states:
The number eight is as previously explained.
Furthermore, as when the Buddha, the World-Honored One, caused Māra to practice the Buddha-way and later attain Buddhahood, this too is called mastery (*vaśitā*).
The Treatise says:
"It subdues the supernatural powers of others.
The Commentary explains:
By the power of the Bodhisattva’s meditative concentration, he causes others' supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) to remain unaccomplished.
The treatise says:
Or he bestows eloquence (*pratibhāna*) upon others.
The commentary states:
If there is a person who wishes to pose difficult questions but whose speech and eloquence are clumsy and stammering, the Bodhisattva can bestow upon them the gift of *pratibhāna* (eloquence).
The treatise says:
"And recollection.
The commentary states:
If a person holds wrong views, [the practice] causes them to know their past lives, thereby personally verifying the law of cause and effect.
The Treatise says:
"Joy and bliss.
The Commentary explains:

Whether a bodhisattva enters hell, is born into an age of famine, or dwells in a place of illness, they cause all these sentient beings to experience exactly the same joy and bliss as that which the bodhisattva themselves experiences.

Either he merely grants them bliss, or first grants them meditative concentration, or at the very moment they hear the Dharma, causes them—by means of this joy and bliss—to perceive sixty minor kalpas as being like the duration of a single kṣaṇa.
The Treatise says:
"Or they emit rays of light.
The Commentary explains:
In order to attract bodhisattvas from other directions so that they all assemble,
the Treatise says:
"He is able to attract those endowed with the marks of great pervasive wisdom."
The commentary states:

Just as the noble supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) of the Śrāvakas can perform one hundred and one types of deeds, the deeds manifested by the supernormal knowledges of a Bodhisattva are beyond calculation.
Furthermore, because he wishes to reveal matters not yet mentioned, he first sets forth this general statement.
The Treatise says:
It is capable of inducing all difficult practices and correct conduct.
The Commentary explains:
Having already explained the accomplishment of the welfare of others as previously stated, what follows below further clarifies the bodhisattva’s own practice.
This meditative concentration can induce the correct conduct of a bodhisattva; it is not something that can be practiced by those of the two vehicles.
The Treatise says:
Because it is able to encompass ten kinds of difficult-to-cultivate practices.
The Commentary says:
These ten kinds of correct practice are of the nature of meditative concentration; therefore, concentration is able to encompass these correct practices.
The treatise asks: What are the ten?
First, it is difficult to practice because one personally undertakes the virtuous vows for enlightenment.
The commentary states:
If one were to generate the ten vows based on another, this would not be a difficult practice, as they have not yet been established by oneself.
A bodhisattva possesses three inherent capacities:
first, the wisdom capable of discerning skillful means; second, the compassion capable of gathering in sentient beings; and third, the right diligence capable of fulfilling the ten vows.
These three are difficult to attain, yet a bodhisattva is able to attain them; because they possess these three capacities, they are able to generate vows independently, without relying on others.
Furthermore, if one were to take up virtuous vows for one's own sake alone, this would not be difficult.
If one receives [the precepts] for another's sake alone without a causal basis, this constitutes a difficulty.
The Treatise says:
These two are difficult to turn back and difficult to cultivate, because the manifold sufferings of birth and death do not cause one to regress.
The commentary states:

The eight sufferings of beginningless saṃsāra, as well as the eight sufferings that will be endured for a long duration after the arousal of the bodhicitta, cannot obstruct the compassion of a bodhisattva or cause them to retreat from their bodhisattva practice.
The detailed explanation is as found in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*; therefore, it is difficult to practice.
The treatise states:
"The three [practices] that do not turn away are difficult to practice."
"Because sentient beings commit evil and [the Bodhisattva] is constantly directed toward them.
The commentary explains:

Sentient beings constantly give rise to unwholesome conduct within the cycle of birth and death; yet, the Bodhisattva does not dwell upon their faults, but instead constantly directs wholesome actions toward them for the sake of their liberation. Therefore, this practice is difficult to cultivate.
The Treatise says:
The fourth is difficult to practice when facing others; it consists in performing all manner of beneficial deeds for sentient beings who harbor enmity toward oneself.
The Commentary explains:
If sentient beings commit extremely grave evils against a bodhisattva, yet the bodhisattva repays them with great kindness and virtue, it is therefore difficult to practice.
The Commentary says:
The fifth is the difficulty of practicing without defilement; for although a bodhisattva is born into the world, they are not defiled by worldly dharmas.
The commentary states:
Because of their affection, Bodhisattvas enter into saṃsāra; having entered saṃsāra, they are not defiled by the eight worldly dharmas.
To love without being defiled—this is why it is difficult to practice.
The Treatise says:
"Sixth, faith and delight are difficult to cultivate, because one practices the bottomless Mahāyāna and is able to believe in and delight in its vast and profound meaning.
The Commentary explains:

The "bottomless" has three meanings: first, the teaching is difficult to conceive; second, the path is difficult to practice; and third, the fruit is difficult to attain—because its majestic virtue is perfect, and because its vast principle is subtle.

Profound majesty has three aspects: first, accordance with intention; second, purity; and third, the principle of non-alteration, which is the principle of the three natures of non-essence (*tri-niḥsvabhāva*).
It is not the domain of lower stages; therefore, it is difficult to cultivate.
The Treatise states:
The seven [stages] are difficult to cultivate because they enable one to penetrate the two kinds of selflessness—of persons and of phenomena.
The Commentary explains:

Previously, during the stage of the ten understandings (*daśa-avabodha*), one had already thoroughly realized the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*); now, at the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), one further realizes the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).

These two types of emptiness are free from the nature of existence and non-existence; if one can thoroughly realize them, one becomes identical with this Dharma, and for this reason, it is difficult to cultivate.
The Treatise says:
The eighth is the difficult practice of discerning according to reality, because one is able to correctly judge the profound sūtras of provisional meaning belonging to the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
The Commentary explains:
The True Dharma taught by the Tathāgata does not transcend the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and the non-definitive meaning (*neyārtha*).

If sentient beings possess only the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) but have not yet developed the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), the Tathāgata speaks with non-definitive meaning in order to establish their faculty of faith, as in the teachings for the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
Furthermore, in order to subdue sentient beings who are arrogant, he provides teachings of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*), as explained at length in the *Saptadaśabhūmi-śāstra*.
To give rise to the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, he speaks the sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
The sūtras of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) contain secret言辞 (words) that can only be correctly discerned; therefore, they are difficult to practice.
The Treatise says:
The ninth is the difficulty of practicing without being separated from or defiled by [saṃsāra], because one does not abandon saṃsāra, yet is not defiled by it.
The commentary states:
Because of compassion, one does not abandon saṃsāra; because of prajñā, one is not defiled by it.
Being without attachment or dwelling in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa, this practice is therefore difficult to cultivate.
The Commentary states:

The ten preparatory practices are difficult to cultivate. The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, abide in liberation from all obstacles; without exerting effort, they are able to perform deeds for the benefit of all sentient beings, continuing even until the very end of saṃsāra.
The commentary states:
It is called "all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas" because it fully manifests the three bodies (*trikāya*).
"All obstacles" refers to the three obstacles, the four obstacles, the thirty obstacles, and so forth.
The Dharma-body has already attained stainless purity; therefore, it abides in liberation from all obscurations.
The Dharma-body eternally dwells in liberation until the very end of saṃsāra.
Based on the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) arises; it spontaneously and constantly flows toward all correct activities without the exertion of effort.

Based on the Response-body, the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) arises; it performs deeds that benefit all sentient beings, causing them to plant the seeds of goodness according to their faculties and natures, until they attain liberation.
The Treatise says:
Because one delights in cultivating such preparatory practices (*prayoga*).
The Commentary explains:

Desiring to attain joy, one arouses right effort as cultivation; constantly practicing respectful cultivation constitutes the preparatory application (*prayoga*). Therefore, it is difficult to cultivate.
The Treatise says:
Regarding the difficulty of cultivation in accordance with awakening, what is the meaning of the *neyārtha* (provisional) sūtras spoken by the Buddhas and Tathāgatas?
"A Bodhisattva should examine according to principle.
The commentary states:
Among the ten points difficult to practice, nine meanings are easy to understand; therefore, they are not explained again.
The eighth [point] is difficult to understand because a bodhisattva must follow it through introspection; therefore, its characteristics must be further demonstrated.
The treatise says:
As the Sūtra states:
How is it that a bodhisattva neither diminishes a single thing nor bestows anything upon a single person?
It is because the bodhisattva is skillfully able to practice giving immeasurably and incalculably, continuously generating the practice of *dāna-pāramitā* throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
The commentary states:

A bodhisattva relinquishes self-love and takes all sentient beings as his own body; since all practices and all material goods belong entirely to sentient beings, wealth is not one's own and its users are not others—how could those objects or their use concern me?
If one can direct the mind in this way, then one is truly capable of practicing giving.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva relinquishes self-love and embraces all sentient beings as their own body, the act of all sentient beings giving is itself the bodhisattva’s practice of giving. Therefore, by generating a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), the bodhisattva obtains immeasurable merit from giving; yet, without losing a single thing or bestowing anything upon a single person, this is called being truly capable of practicing giving.
The treatise says:
How does a bodhisattva delight in practicing generosity?
If a bodhisattva does not delight in practicing all forms of giving.
The commentary states:

If a bodhisattva does not delight in practicing the eight types of giving, such as "giving that follows" (*anuprāpta-dāna*) and so forth, but instead delights in practicing the pure-minded giving of a bodhisattva;
furthermore, if a bodhisattva does not delight in worldly giving that clings to the three spheres (*tri-maṇḍala*), but delights in practicing giving that does not cling to the three spheres.
Furthermore, attachment is called "delight. If a bodhisattva is attached to the cause of giving or attached to the fruit of giving, this is called "delighting in the practice of giving.
If a bodhisattva is not attached to the practice of giving, this is called "not delighting in the practice of giving."
The Treatise says:
What is the bodhisattva’s mind of practicing the giving of faith?
It is when a bodhisattva does not practice the faith of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
The commentary states:
A bodhisattva practices giving because of self-realization through giving, not because of faith in another.
The former faith has a root and thus constitutes faith; the latter faith lacks a root and therefore does not constitute faith.
The treatise says:
How does a bodhisattva practice the cultivation of giving?
If a bodhisattva does not exert themselves within the act of giving.
The commentary states:

If a bodhisattva possesses the natural capacity to practice giving, being free from obstacles such as greed, stinginess, and envy, they do not need to exert themselves through self-exhortation to be able to give.
The treatise says:
How does a bodhisattva constantly sport in giving?
It is when there is no time when the bodhisattva is not practicing giving.
The commentary states:
"A bodhisattva does not give at an improper time, nor does he give away even a single object.
The treatise says:
How is it that a bodhisattva is able to practice giving on a grand scale?
If a bodhisattva is free from the notion of *sāra* (solidity/essence) regarding giving.
Explanation:
The name *sāla* has two meanings: first, it signifies "steadfastness" (*ṛju*), and second, it signifies "dispersion" (*vikṣepa*).
Steadfastness is the explicit meaning (*nītārtha*), while dispersion is the implicit meaning (*neyārtha*).
If one takes the explicit meaning and departs from steadfastness, it would contradict the nature of great giving.
If one grasps the esoteric meaning and remains free from distraction, it accords with the "great gift.
When one practices giving after having detached from the desires of the three realms, it is called a great gift.

Why is this? Because the giving practiced by a bodhisattva who has abandoned desire cannot be equaled, even by a hundred thousand million times, by the giving practiced by an ordinary person bound by all fetters.
If giving were fixed such that it mutually obstructed one another, it would not be called "great giving"; it is because they do not obstruct one another that it receives the name "great."
The treatise says:
How is it that a bodhisattva is pure in giving?
If a bodhisattva suppresses greed and stinginess.
The commentary states:
The term *udvartana* has two meanings: first, it signifies "arising," and second, it signifies "uprooting and abandoning.
"Arising" is the explicit meaning (*nītārtha*), while "uprooting and abandoning" is the implicit meaning (*neyārtha*).
If one takes the literal meaning and gives rise to greed and stinginess, it contradicts pure giving;
if one takes the esoteric meaning and uproots and abandons greed while turning away from stinginess, it accords with pure giving.

To "uproot" means to eliminate the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); since the view of a self-identity is the root of greed and stinginess, to "turn away from it" means to eliminate the substance of greed and stinginess.
Because the Bodhisattva is able to sever the view of a self-identity and extinguish greed and stinginess, his giving is pure.
The treatise says:
How is it that a bodhisattva is able to abide in giving?
If a bodhisattva does not abide in the ultimate limit of the future.
The commentary states:
There are two senses of "the ultimate limit" (*paryanta*). First, regarding giving, there are three stages—beginning, middle, and end—and it is the final stage that constitutes the ultimate limit.
If one follows this sense, how could one who does not abide even in the final portion of giving be said to be able to abide in giving?
This, however, is contradictory.
If the nirvana with remainder is called the ultimate and the nirvana without remainder is called the ultimate limit,

then if a śrāvaka abiding in the nirvana without remainder no longer gives rise to the mind [of awakening], there would be no activity for the benefit of sentient beings, and thus he would be unable to abide in giving.
Because Bodhisattvas rely on great compassion and do not abide in the nirvana without remainder like the Śrāvakas, they constantly give rise to the six perfections without end.
If one relies on this meaning, it accords with the capacity to abide in generosity.
The treatise says:
How does a bodhisattva attain mastery over giving?
If a bodhisattva does not attain mastery over giving, [he is not yet established].
The commentary states:
If a bodhisattva does not encounter obstacles to the mastery of giving, the bodhisattva attains mastery over giving.

While formerly on the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), because the two types of afflictions—those innate and those acquired through cultivation—lacked the antidote of the Path, they would arise whenever one wished them to; thus, [the bodhisattva] attained mastery.

Now, having entered the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*), for the sake of applying the remedies (*pratipakṣa*) to the path, the bodhisattva does not attain mastery over afflictions (*kleśa*), yet attains mastery over generosity (*dāna*).
The treatise asks:
How is it that the bodhisattva’s generosity is inexhaustible?
"If a bodhisattva does not abide in the inexhaustible.
The commentary explains:
"Nirvana without remainder is called the inexhaustible."
The Bodhisattva differs from the Śrāvaka in that, upon entering inexhaustibility, he does not lack the activity of benefiting others; therefore, the Bodhisattva’s generosity is inexhaustible.
The treatise says:
As it is with generosity, so it should be understood according to principle for ethical discipline, and so forth, up to wisdom, as set forth in the *Dānasūtra*.
The commentary states:

As the *Dānasūtra* explains that there are words of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) regarding generosity, so too there are words of provisional meaning regarding the other perfections; all must be correctly analyzed and distinguished according to principle.
The treatise states:
Furthermore, a sutra says:
"How does a bodhisattva practice killing?"
"If a bodhisattva were to sever the continuity of a sentient being who possesses life.
The commentary states:
"If there is life, one knows that there is karma; if there is karma, one knows that there is affliction (*kleśa*)."
Because these three exist, the continuity of the six realms and four modes of birth remains uninterrupted.

If a Bodhisattva, according to their faculties and natures, teaches the noble paths of the Three Vehicles to them, enabling them to practice so as to sever these three dharmas and attain the fruit of *nirvāṇa* without remainder—thereby ending that continuity—it is equivalent to taking life; therefore, it is called "killing."
The treatise says:
What is meant by a bodhisattva seizing that which has not been given by another?
It refers to when a bodhisattva seizes for himself sentient beings who have not been given by another.
The commentary states:
The Bodhisattva, through great compassion, gathers all sentient beings as his own retinue and causes them to leave behind the perils of birth and death.
This is not something bestowed by their parents or sovereigns; therefore, it is called "taking away what was not given by others."
The treatise says:
What is a bodhisattva’s practice of sexual misconduct?
It is when a bodhisattva gives rise to improper thoughts and so forth toward objects of desire.
The commentary states:

The three karmas of a bodhisattva are the opposite of sexual desire. In his mind, he knows it to be false and unreal, the root of all evils; in speech, he likewise speaks thus; and in body, he does not engage in such acts—this is what constitutes being the opposite.
This refers to giving rise to improper intentions and so forth regarding sensual objects; therefore, it is called committing sexual misconduct.
The treatise asks:
How can a bodhisattva speak false words?
"If a bodhisattva is delusory, they are able to speak of things as delusory.
The commentary states:
All phenomena are indeed illusory; because the bodhisattva speaks in accordance with their illusoriness, they are said to be "able to speak of delusory speech."
The treatise says:
What is the bodhisattva’s practice of divisive speech?
It is when a bodhisattva constantly dwells in a state of ultimate emptiness and stillness.
The commentary states:
Divisive speech causes discord between this party and that.
When a Bodhisattva contemplates emptiness and speaks of emptiness, they cause themselves and others not to perceive "this" or "that," let alone to achieve harmony.
Therefore, this is called practicing divisive speech.
The treatise asks:
How is it that a bodhisattva is able to abide in *pāruṣya* (harsh speech)?
"If a bodhisattva abides on the further shore of what is to be known.
Commentary:
According to the direct meaning of the words, *pāruṣya* (harsh speech) refers to abusive language.
Those who dwell in harsh speech are not approached or befriended by others.

The Bodhisattva dwells in the "other shore" of what is to be known—that is, the principle of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*)—and likewise is not approached by sentient beings, because this principle is not the domain of practice for ordinary persons or those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). For this reason, it is called "dwelling in harsh speech."

Furthermore, if one relies on the esoteric terminology, the term *pāruṣya* (harsh speech) refers to dwelling on the further shore (*pāra-sthita*); thus, the esoteric terminology reveals the literal meaning.
The treatise asks:
How is it that a bodhisattva can speak words that are inconsistent?
"If a bodhisattva can analyze and break down all phenomena, explaining them according to their respective categories.
The commentary states:

A bodhisattva can analyze and break down all phenomena, meaning that the sense faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are all non-existent. This non-existence is neither definitively non-existent nor definitively existent, because both existence and non-existence are ultimately unapprehendable; therefore, this is called "speaking words of non-correspondence."
The treatise says:
What is the bodhisattva’s practice of *abhiṣekaloka*?
It is when a bodhisattva repeatedly causes his own person to attain supreme meditative absorptions (*samādhi*).
The commentary states:
If one follows the literal meaning, *abhidhyā* (covetousness) refers to desire; one who practices desire necessarily delights in external objects.
However, because a bodhisattva constantly delights in causing his own self to attain the most excellent meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is called "practicing desire."
Furthermore, if one relies on the esoteric terminology, the term *abhiṣaṃhāra* refers to repeatedly attaining meditative concentration; thus, the esoteric term is used to clarify the direct meaning.
The treatise asks:
How does a bodhisattva give rise to a mind of malice and harm?
If a bodhisattva is able to destroy all afflictions within the mental grounds of both self and others.
The commentary states:
Hatred has the characteristic of malice and harm; because a bodhisattva forms the intention to sever all afflictions of both self and others, it is called "arousing a mind of malice and harm."
The treatise says:
How does a bodhisattva give rise to wrong views?
It is when a bodhisattva correctly observes the nature of pervasiveness of error in all places.
The commentary states:

In the Mahāyāna, conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) is considered false nature; the fact that the nature of conceptual discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) pervades the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) constitutes its falsity.
If one is free from conceptual discrimination, this is called the true nature of the emptiness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā-tattva*).

In the Hīnayāna, the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is considered a false nature, because it gives rise to all various delusions; if one is separated from this view of a self-body, all false attachments will fail to arise, and one attains the true nature of the emptiness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*).
A bodhisattva is able to examine this nature of falsity according to reality; because they see it as false, it is called "arising of wrong view.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, there is a sutra that states, "The Buddha-dharma is extremely profound."
The commentary states:
First, the six perfections are elucidated; next, the ten non-virtues are revealed; hereafter, the path and the fruit of the path are elucidated; therefore, it is said to be "profound.
The treatise says:
What is profound?
Within this treatise, it is extensively analyzed that all Buddha-dharmas have permanence as their nature, because the Dharma-body is permanent.
The commentary states:

The Dharma-body of all Buddhas is eternally abiding; all Buddha-dharmas rely upon the Dharma-body, for the Dharma-body is their foremost. Thus, the eternally abiding Dharma-body is the nature of all Buddha-dharmas.
The Treatise says:
All Buddha-dharmas have severance as their nature, because all obstacles are completely severed.
The Commentary says:

Because each and every Buddha-dharma is entirely free from both the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the obscuration of knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), the complete severance of these obscurations constitutes the nature of all Buddha-dharmas.

The extinction of present afflictions is "severance" (*prahāṇa*), and the non-arising of future afflictions is "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*); this is precisely the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising (*kṣayānutpādajñāna*).
The Treatise says:
All Buddha-dharmas have arising as their nature, because the nirmāṇakāya constantly arises.
The Commentary says:

Because the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) arises from the fundamental vow of compassion and its continuity is inexhaustible, the arising of the emanation body constitutes the nature of all Buddha-dharmas.
The treatise states:
All Buddha-dharmas can function as their nature because they are able to serve as the common antidotes for the eighty-four thousand afflictive tendencies of sentient beings.
The commentary states:
All Buddha-dharmas have non-apprehension as their nature; this is the correct teaching, because the three natures of non-existence cannot be definitively described as either existent or non-existent.
Although its nature is non-attainment, it nonetheless possesses the sense of being able to attain.

For if one were apart from the Buddha-dharma, one could not attain the discernment of the afflictions to be countered, nor could one attain the establishment of the path that serves as the counteragent.
The Treatise says:
All Buddha-dharmas have desire as their nature, because they are embraced by the craving of sentient beings with desire and thereby brought to form their own essence.
All Buddha-dharmas have hatred as their nature; all Buddha-dharmas have delusion as their nature.
"All Buddha-dharmas have the dharmas of ordinary beings as their nature.
The commentary states:
This has two meanings. First, the Bodhisattva takes all sentient beings possessed of desire as his own essence; since all Buddha-dharmas rely upon this very essence.

Second, great compassion is love; love is precisely desire. Because a bodhisattva gathers in all sentient beings through great compassion, they give rise to the practices of merit and wisdom based upon that great compassion.
The same applies to hatred, delusion, and the dharmas of ordinary beings.
The *Śāstra* says:
All Buddha-dharmas have non-attachment as their nature; they realize true suchness (*tathatā*), for no obstacles can defile them.
The commentary states:
After the Path, True Suchness (tathatā) has severed all obstacles completely; it is thus stainless purity, and is therefore called "accomplishment" (*niṣpanna*).
It cannot be defiled by any obstacle, because all Buddha-dharmas take this True Suchness as their essential nature (*svabhāva*).
The Treatise says:
All Buddha-dharmas are incapable of being defiled by attachment, for when the Buddhas appear in the world, they cannot be defiled by worldly dharmas.
The Commentary explains:
The preceding section elucidated the realm of *tathatā* (suchness); this section elucidates the wisdom of *tathatā*.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas take the wisdom of *tathatā* as their essence, which is precisely the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body).

This essence is manifested by the *tathatā* of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only); it does not arise from the discrimination of sense organs and objects, nor can it be defiled or attached to by the eight worldly dharmas or the afflictions such as desire and hatred that arise from those worldly dharmas.
Why is this? Because it is the antidote to that [obscuration].
The attainment of the accomplishment of non-conceptual wisdom through cultivation is called the appearance of the Buddhas in the world.
The Treatise says:
For this reason, it is said that the Buddha-dharma is profoundly deep.
The Commentary says:
This statement concludes the preceding meaning, demonstrating that it is profound because it possesses three characteristics: being inconceivable, difficult to practice, and difficult to attain.
The treatise states:

One should understand that the distinctions in the activities of a bodhisattva’s samādhi are for the sake of practicing the pāramitās, for the sake of maturing sentient beings, for the sake of purifying Buddha-fields, and for the sake of attracting and gathering all Buddha-dharmas.
The commentary states:
This treatise elucidates the samādhis of bodhisattvas; it does not explain them by way of distinct categories of phenomena, but rather explains them generally through their functional distinctions.
The meditative concentrations cultivated by bodhisattvas include both general and specific types: there are these four general types, and specifically, there are five hundred.
These four are the karmas of the various meditative absorptions and supernormal powers. Why is this?

Once bodhisattvas have cultivated and attained meditative absorption, they rely upon this absorption to practice the ten perfections and rely upon this absorption to bring sentient beings to maturity.
How does one bring sentient beings to maturity?
By relying on this meditative concentration, one gives rise to supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) to lead them into the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Furthermore, by relying on the power of this concentration, one purifies the Buddha-field (*buddhakṣetra*).
Why is this? Because through mastery over the mind, one can, according to one's wish, manifest pure lands such as those of gold and jewels.
Furthermore, by relying on this meditative concentration, one attains a state of dwelling in present happiness, and is able to attract, gather, and bring to maturity all Buddha-dharmas.
These four matters are the distinct activities of all meditative concentrations and supernormal powers;
they should be understood in this way. *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, Fascicle 11 and Fascicle 12.
The Commentary by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Chen Dynasty.
Chapter Eight: Explaining the Distinguished Characteristics of the Differentiation of Training in Wisdom. The treatise states:
Thus, having already explained the distinctions of training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*), how should one understand the distinctions of training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*)?
The commentary states:

Since there is a distinction between the concentration of a bodhisattva and that of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas), and since concentration serves as the basis for wisdom—wisdom being accomplished by relying upon concentration—there must likewise be a distinction between the wisdom of a bodhisattva and the wisdom of the two vehicles.
How is this to be known?
By what dharma is the training in wisdom (prajñā-śikṣā) designated?

Non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna) is designated as the training in wisdom; it should be understood that the specific distinctions of this non-conceptual wisdom are themselves the specific distinctions of the training in wisdom.
This non-conceptual wisdom is of three kinds:
first, preparatory non-conceptual wisdom, which refers to wisdom such as investigative inquiry (*vitarka*) and so forth, being the cause of the path;
second, non-conceptual wisdom itself, which is the actual essence of the path.

The third is non-conceptual subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), which is precisely the knowledge that emerges from meditative absorption (*vyutthāna-jñāna*); it refers to the fruit of the path.
These three types of knowledge all constitute the essence of the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*).

Regarding how the knowledge of investigation (*vitarka-jñāna*) serves as the basis for the training in wisdom: the practitioner of meditation relies upon future non-conceptual knowledge to cultivate the knowledge of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*). Because one seeks the fruit of future non-conceptual knowledge, the knowledge of skillful means is accomplished in the present life.
Because it is that upon which one relies, it is called the training in wisdom based on reliance (*prajñā-śikṣā-niśraya*).

Furthermore, this skillful means (*upāya*) can induce future non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*); since the arising of non-conceptual wisdom must necessarily depend upon this skillful means for its accomplishment, it is called the training in wisdom based on reliance because it is the basis (*niśraya*).

Regarding the statement that the true essence of the Path is the training in wisdom based on internal [states]: this refers to the arising of knowledge within through meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*). Because it is free from distraction and movement, it is called "internal.
Since this knowledge arises based on observation, it is termed the "training in wisdom based on internal states."

Furthermore, when the self-substance (*svabhāva*) is internal, and the cause has already ceased while the fruit has not yet arisen, the continuum of the path’s own substance persists; this is what is called the "internal" self-substance.
Because it arises based upon this self-substance, it is termed "training in wisdom based on the self-substance."

Regarding "the wisdom of emergence from contemplation being the basis for the training in wisdom": one accomplishes this wisdom by relying on non-conceptual wisdom; thus, it is called the training in wisdom. Why is this?
Because when one enters contemplation, the object of focus subsequently becomes the object of the wisdom attained after contemplation (prsthalabdha-jñāna).
Among these three types of knowledge, which one should be established?
Only non-conceptual knowledge (nirvikalpa-jñāna) should be established.
If this knowledge is established, the other types of knowledge are thereby established as well.

If the former wisdom is established, only the meaning of the cause is manifested while the meaning of the fruit is not; thus, the nineteen distinct meanings, such as self-nature and so forth, are also not established.

If the latter wisdom is established, only the meaning of the fruit is manifested while the cause is not; thus, the nineteen distinct meanings, such as self-nature and so forth, are also not established.
Why is this? This wisdom takes the wisdom of investigation as its cause, and this wisdom is the fruit of the wisdom of investigation;
this wisdom is the cause of subsequent wisdom, and subsequent wisdom is the fruit of this wisdom.
Since this wisdom is established, the preceding and succeeding wisdoms are also established; therefore, it is sufficient to establish only this wisdom.
Within that establishment, one should first explain the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
Intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the very essence and characteristic.
The treatise states:

One should understand the distinctions of training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*) by way of the profound meaning of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), including its intrinsic nature, basis, causal origination, objective sphere, characteristics, establishment of rebuttals, sustenance, companions, retribution, outflow, renunciation, culmination, cultivation of virtue, preparatory application, the virtues of non-conceptual wisdom and subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), the distinct preparatory applications of non-conceptual wisdom, and the majestic power of non-conceptual and subsequently attained wisdom in performing effortless deeds.
One should understand the distinctions of non-conceptual wisdom through the distinctions of the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*).
The commentary states:
that is to say, one should understand the distinctions of the training in wisdom by means of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of non-conceptual wisdom.

Regarding the statement that "the distinctions in non-conceptual wisdom should be understood through the distinctions in the training in wisdom," this phrasing must be applied to all nineteen points when they are explained in sequence.

Now, for the sake of brevity, I have first indicated the beginning by means of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), followed by the enumeration of the nineteen meanings; finally, it is stated in summary that one should know the distinctions of the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*).

One should understand that the distinctions in non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna) arise from the distinctions in the training in wisdom (prajñā-śikṣā). Non-conceptual wisdom is established through nineteen meanings; this wisdom is the very essence of the training in wisdom, and the distinctions within the training in wisdom are precisely the distinctions of this wisdom. One should understand it in this way.
What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*)?
The treatise states:
It should be understood that the intrinsic nature of non-conceptual wisdom is free from five kinds of characteristics.
The commentary states:
If one possesses the abandonment of the five characteristics, that is non-conceptual wisdom; if one does not possess the abandonment of the five characteristics, it is not non-conceptual wisdom.
The treatise says:

The five characteristics are: first, being free from non-contemplation; second, being free from the stage of non-investigation and non-analysis; third, being free from the tranquility of the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling; fourth, being free from the intrinsic nature of form; and fifth, being free from divergent conceptualization regarding the true meaning.
The commentary states:
If this wisdom is called non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna) because it is free from discursive thought (vitarka),
then since deep sleep, negligence, and intoxication are likewise free from discursive thought, should they also be considered non-conceptual wisdom?
If it were because one has transcended the stage of vitarka and vicāra that it is called non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*),
then from the second dhyāna upward, having already transcended the stage of vitarka and vicāra, one should attain non-conceptual wisdom.
If one were to rely on these two meanings, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) should attain non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).

In those states where the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) can be abandoned—namely, the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha-samāpatti*) and so forth—one should designate them as non-conceptual wisdom.
If a person were to attain non-conceptual wisdom while in this state, it would not constitute wisdom.
Why? Because in states such as the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), there is neither mind nor mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
If it is said that just as the intrinsic nature of form is such, so too is the intrinsic nature of wisdom;
and just as form is insentient and devoid of cognition, this wisdom should likewise be insentient and devoid of cognition.

Furthermore, if [wisdom] were to manifest through conceptualization regarding the ultimate reality (*tattvārtha*), then that conceptualization would have to become non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
Why is this? Because this discrimination is able to discern the true meaning, namely, that "this meaning is true.
The treatise says:
This wisdom that is free from these five characteristics should be understood therein as non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
The commentary states:
if wisdom is free from the five characteristics and arises by taking true reality as its object, it is non-conceptual wisdom.
If one does not conceptually differentiate from the true reality (*tattvārtha*), meaning that this dharma is the true reality and merely takes the true reality as its object—
just as visual consciousness does not have conceptual differentiation as its intrinsic nature— this is called the characteristic of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
The Treatise says:
Within this context, regarding the nature of non-conceptual wisdom as it has been described, a verse is therefore spoken.
The Commentary explains:

Within this training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*), regarding the nature of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) as manifested by the nineteen meanings previously explained, this verse is further spoken to establish that meaning.
What does this verse intend to manifest?
To reveal that non-conceptual wisdom is supreme and the foremost among all practiced deeds,
the treatise says:
"The essential nature of all Bodhisattvas is free from five kinds of characteristics."
"The nature of non-conceptual wisdom is non-conceptual with respect to reality.
Commentary:

The Bodhisattva has non-conceptual wisdom as his essence; non-conceptual wisdom is not different from the Bodhisattva, for the self-nature of non-conceptual wisdom is itself the self-nature of the Bodhisattva.

Non-conceptual wisdom is free from five characteristics; this is precisely the Bodhisattva’s freedom from the five characteristics. Because it is truly non-conceptual, by being free from these five characteristics, it receives the name "non-conceptual."
Sentient beings are provisional designations, while dharmas are substantially existent. Apart from this wisdom, there is no other dharma that should be designated as a "Bodhisattva.

The knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising is bodhi; these sentient beings take bodhi as their essence. Bodhi is none other than non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), and non-conceptual wisdom is itself the Bodhisattva.

In order to demonstrate that non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is itself the bodhisattva, it is said that the self-nature of the bodhisattva is free from five characteristics; it does not speak of non-conceptual wisdom [as something separate]. The same principle applies to the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
Having thus explained the intrinsic nature of the bodhisattva, and since this nature arises based upon a certain support, that support shall now be explained.
Previously, it was stated that this wisdom is called "non-conceptual. Does this wisdom arise dependent upon the mind, or does it arise without depending upon the mind?
If it arises depending on the mind (*citta*) and is capable of volition (*manasikāra*), it is therefore called "mind"; this volition is itself discrimination (*vikalpa*).
If this wisdom arises depending on discrimination, it cannot be said to be non-discriminative.
If it were not dependent on the mind for its arising, it would be identical to dharmas such as form and so forth, and furthermore, it should not be called "wisdom.
To demonstrate that it avoids these two faults, the verse is repeated.
The treatise says:
The support of all bodhisattvas is neither mind nor non-mind;
it is non-conceptual wisdom, because it does not belong to the category of rapid thought.
The commentary states:
This wisdom does not take the mind as its support, because this wisdom is inconceivable.
Nor does it take what is not mind as its support, because it takes the continuous succession of swift and sharp mental types as its support.
Since the category of swift penetration is the seed-nature of this mind, and because it takes this as its support, it cannot be said that it does not take the mind as its support.
To clarify how this wisdom arises through causes and conditions, the verse is repeated.
The treatise says:
The causal conditions for all bodhisattvas consist of what is called the permeation of hearing,
which is non-conceptual wisdom and correct reflection in accordance with reality.
The commentary says:
Among the four conditions, excluding three conditions, one takes only the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
What are the characteristics of the causal condition?
If a cause and its fruit are of the same category, it is called a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). For example, a preceding wholesome mind acts as the causal basis for a subsequent wholesome mind.
From hearing the sound of the Dharma from others, the impression of hearing (*śruta-vāsanā*) arises as a cause; this impression subsequently gives rise to right reflection (*samyak-manasikāra*).
This right reflection arises from hearing the correct teachings of others; therefore, it is said to "possess words.
The causal conditions for this wisdom consist precisely of the permeation of hearing those words and right reflection as its essence.
For this reason, it is said that the cause of non-conceptual wisdom consists of verbal expressions, which cause what has not yet arisen to arise and cause what has already arisen to remain firm.
Without this perfuming, non-conceptual wisdom could not arise.
Therefore, this is explained as the causal condition (*nidāna*).
This wisdom arises from the perfuming of hearing (*śruta-vāsanā*); what dharma does it take as its object?
The treatise says:
The sphere of all Bodhisattvas is the ineffable nature of phenomena;
it is non-conceptual wisdom, the suchness of the two-fold selflessness.
Commentary:
The preceding verse explained the conditions (*pratyaya*) of a bodhisattva; this verse explains the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) of a bodhisattva.
The objective sphere (*viṣaya*) is precisely the object-condition.
What are the characteristics of the object-condition?
If a phenomenon arises conditioned by this, it is like a weak person who is able to stand up because of a cane.
Because that phenomenon can arise through the observation of this phenomenon, this serves as the condition for that, just as the five sense objects give rise to the five consciousnesses.
This object has two meanings:
first, the object as a basis for inference; second, the object as an object of inference.
For example, based on the characteristic of the impermanence of the mind, one infers that other phenomena such as form and so forth are all impermanent.
The ineffable nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is the object-condition for Bodhisattvas; all phenomena are inexpressible by virtue of their imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Why is this?
Because all phenomena lack intrinsic existence (*svabhāva*) and manifest through the conceptual construction of the mind, all phenomena cannot be said to exist, nor can they be said not to exist.
It appears in this way, yet it does not exist in that way; therefore, it cannot be said to exist.
It does not exist in this way, yet its appearance is not non-existent; therefore, it cannot be said to be non-existent.
Just as the objects of consciousness do not exist in the manner in which they appear, discrimination likewise lacks any intrinsic nature or characteristic.
Since this discrimination lacks an intrinsic nature or characteristic, does it exist or does it not exist?
If non-existence lacked a nature, then existence would possess one.
If existence possessed a nature, it could not be said to be non-existent.
For this reason, regarding the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it cannot be described as either existent or non-existent in terms of either the ultimate or the conventional truth.
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) has as its essence suchness (tathatā), which is characterized by the two kinds of selflessness.

Because of the nature of conceptual construction (parikalpita-svabhāva), the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is devoid of both persons and phenomena; this is termed the "two kinds of selflessness."
In order to eliminate the view of nihilism, it is taught that this selflessness is not non-existent; therefore, it is called *tathatā* (suchness).
This *tathatā* is the objective domain of the bodhisattva. Why is this so?
Since this non-conceptual wisdom, when it arises, must necessarily arise by taking this object as its condition,
and since this wisdom arises by taking ineffable *tathatā* (suchness) as its object, what is the manner in which it apprehends that object?
The treatise says:
The characteristics of all bodhisattvas, within the realm of suchness,
are non-conceptual wisdom— without marks and without differentiation.
The commentary states:
This wisdom arises in a state of perfect equality within the realm of *tathatā* (suchness); its characteristic is being without differentiation and without marks—this is precisely its characteristic.
It is, for example, like visual consciousness apprehending form: although appearances such as blue manifest, they are not distinct from the blue color itself.
This wisdom and its object, True Suchness (tathatā), are likewise so.

Furthermore, it is not like the relationship between visual consciousness and form; for while form has no intrinsic substance yet possesses appearance, visual consciousness possesses intrinsic substance yet lacks appearance.
This wisdom corresponds to the object of suchness (tathatā) and cannot be said to be different from it.
If all phenomena have the nature of being ineffable, what phenomenon could there be that is subject to conceptual discrimination?
The Treatise says:
"The meaning of the nature of correspondence is that which is discriminated, not something other.
The Commentary explains:

All verbal expressions possess three kinds of association (*saṃprayoga*), namely: habitual practice (*abhyāsa*), continuity (*prabandha*), and sequence (*anukrama*). Because these three are inseparable, they are termed "association."
Furthermore, the conjunction of three factors is able to denote an object; therefore, it is called "correspondence" (*saṃprayoga*).
This correspondence has the meaning of "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*), and this meaning is precisely that which is conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*).
If there were no other meaning apart from this meaning, then all phenomena would be inexpressible.
How is it known that there is no other meaning apart from this nature?
To establish this meaning,
the treatise says:
Because the syllables are in continuous succession, they are established through the sense of association.
The commentary states:
The continuous succession of each and every syllable constitutes the first conjunction (*yoga*).
Through this conjunction, the other two conjunctions are also fully established.
Because these three are associated (*saṃprayukta*), they can designate an object.
This meaning is established through their association, just as in the case of the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) and so forth.
Within the continuous flow of verbal expression, sentient beings grasp it as an object; therefore, it is called "association."
This meaning is that which is conceptually constructed; therefore, that which is conceptually constructed exists only as verbal expression, and its meaning likewise exists only as verbal expression.
If all phenomena are inexpressible, how can this meaning be established?
The Treatise says:
Wisdom that is free from verbal expression does not arise with respect to the objects of knowledge.
The Commentary explains:
If a person has not yet discerned a particular dialect, wisdom does not arise regarding the object expressed by that speech.
If you say: "Wisdom arises regarding the object expressed within the act of speaking," [we reply:]...
This interpretation is not correct. Why?
The treatise states:
"Because speech and its object are not identical, everything is inexpressible.
The commentary explains:

This speech and that which is spoken are not identical because their characteristics differ; thus, the characteristic of the speech differs from the characteristic of the spoken object. Therefore, all speech and all that is spoken are equally inexpressible.
What phenomena are sustained by non-conceptual wisdom?
The treatise says:
The sustenance of all bodhisattvas is this non-conceptual wisdom.
"Subsequently, one attains the practice, which serves as the growth for the ultimate.
The commentary states:
This is the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) following non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which is able to attain the two practices of merit and wisdom of a Bodhisattva.
The two practices rely upon this wisdom because they attain growth, continuity, and even ultimate perfection through it.
Subsequent non-conceptual wisdom can cause the bodhisattva’s correct practice to grow; thus, subsequent non-conceptual wisdom is that which sustains, and the bodhisattva is that which is sustained.
What are the factors that accompany non-conceptual wisdom?
The treatise states:
"The factors accompanying all bodhisattvas are said to be these two kinds of paths."
This non-conceptual wisdom is the category of the five perfections.
The commentary states:
"Companions" means they assist one another as their counterparts.
They are called "mutual assistance" because they assist one another in accomplishing a single task.
This single task is the fruit of enlightenment (*bodhi*).
The two types of paths are the companions of the Bodhisattva, namely the path of accumulation (*sambhāramārga*) and the path of reliance (*niśrayamārga*).
The four pāramitās beginning with generosity constitute the path of accumulation; the pāramitā of meditative concentration constitutes the path of reliance. Why is this?
From the wholesome dharmas produced by the [first] four pāramitās, this prajñāpāramitā arises; and this prajñāpāramitā arises in reliance upon meditative concentration.

The Prajñāpāramitā is non-conceptual wisdom; until one attains unsurpassed enlightenment, one is able to constantly give rise to non-conceptual wisdom throughout the interval leading up to the ultimate fruit.

When separated, there are five perfections; when combined, they constitute two paths. Because they can assist the sixth perfection to together achieve the single ultimate fruit, they are described as "associates.
If non-conceptual wisdom is established by relying on these two paths, what kind of fruition is obtained?
The treatise says:
The fruition of all bodhisattvas, within the two perfect accumulations of the Buddha, is non-conceptual wisdom;
it is attained through the stage of application.
The commentary states:
There are things that are merely results (*phala*) but not retributions (*vipāka*), and there are things that are both results and retributions.
That which arises from a cause and is shared by others is called a result; that which arises from a cause and is experienced individually is called a retribution.
"Phala" (fruit) has the meaning of arising, while "vipāka" (maturation) has the meaning of ripening.
The two bodies—the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*)—are called the Buddha's two perfect accumulations (*puṇyajñānasaṃbhāra*).
Within these two perfect accumulations of the Buddha, the fruit and maturation of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpajñāna*) reside.
If the fruit arises within the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), this fruit belongs to the Nirmāṇakāya;
if the fruit arises within the attainment (*prāpti*) of non-conceptual wisdom, this fruit belongs to the Saṃbhogakāya.
How is this known?
The treatise says:
It is known by virtue of the progression from application to attainment.
The commentary states:
It was previously explained that non-conceptual [wisdom] is of three types: first, preparatory; second, fundamental; and third, subsequently attained.
Preparatory non-conceptual [wisdom] itself is of two kinds: first, that which exists prior to the stages (*bhūmi*); and second, that which exists from the entry into the stages onward.
If one relies on the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) of these two bases, the fruit obtained is the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), while its essential nature is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*).
From the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the fruit of Buddhahood, all are termed "attainment" (*prāpti*).
If one relies on the non-conceptualization of the true essence (*dharmatā*), the resulting retribution is the *saṃbhogakāya*.
If such is the case for the fruit of retribution, what then is the fruit of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*)?
The treatise states:
The Bodhisattva’s result of natural outflow, throughout successive future births,
is this non-conceptual wisdom, which becomes increasingly superior through continuous progression.
Commentary:
The fruit may be equal to its cause or superior to its cause; when this fruit takes a similar type as its cause, it is called a fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).

Regarding the fruit of uniform outflow of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), within the two accumulations, one transforms the first stage into the second, and so on up to transforming the tenth stage into Buddhahood, becoming increasingly more exalted and superior in each successive state.
Just as the first stage (*bhūmi*) is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for the second stage, and the second stage is the outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the first stage,
so it is for all stages.
These are superior in terms of benefiting others and preeminent in terms of benefiting oneself.
Furthermore, the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) is the increase, while the stage beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is the excellence.
Regarding the meaning of the accomplishment of the attainment of liberation through non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*),
the treatise says:
Because all bodhisattvas attain the state of union through their departure [from saṃsāra],
this non-conceptual wisdom should be understood as existing throughout the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Commentary:
The cessation of afflictions and karma is "emergence," and the cessation of retributive results is "separation"; these constitute the two kinds of nirvana: with remainder and without remainder.
Since "emergence" has the meaning of "separation" and "separation" has the meaning of "emergence," why are they stated redundantly?
Because there are three meanings of "separation," the term is used in its intensive form: first, permanent separation; second, superior separation; and third, definitive separation.
Non-conceptual wisdom corresponds to two of these meanings within the context of transcendence (*niḥsaraṇa*): first, it corresponds with attainment; second, it corresponds with accomplishment.
Regarding these two types of correspondence, one should know that they do not transcend the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Attaining non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) for the first time in the first stage is called "correspondence of attainment.
From after the first stage up through the tenth stage, cultivating non-conceptual wisdom throughout incalculable eons until its ultimate consummation is called "correspondence of accomplishment."
This non-conceptual wisdom relies upon two paths and is cultivated for three asaṃkhyeya kalpas; by what dharma is its culmination attained?
The treatise says:
The culmination of all bodhisattvas is achieved through the attainment of the pure three bodies.
"This is non-conceptual wisdom, because it reaches supreme mastery.
The commentary states:
There are two kinds of culmination: first, the culmination of purity; second, the culmination of mastery.

Regarding ultimate purity: one first attains purity at the first stage (*bhūmi*), thereafter becoming increasingly pure through each successive stage until reaching ultimate purity at the tenth stage, just like the refining of gold.
Due to this purification, the bodhisattva’s attainment of the three bodies becomes increasingly purified in each successive stage.

Regarding "ultimate mastery," it refers not only to the ultimate attainment of these three types of pure bodies, but also to a further distinct ultimate, namely the ten masteries (*daśavaśitā*), as explained later in the treatise.
These ten masteries become progressively more excellent;
these two types of dharmas are ultimately supreme and represent the final consummation attained through non-conceptual wisdom, which is termed the "sovereign fruit" (adhipati-phala).
What are the merits of non-conceptual wisdom?
There are three kinds of non-conceptuality: first, preparatory non-conceptuality; second, fundamental non-conceptuality; and third, subsequently attained non-conceptuality.
How is it that this preparatory practice (prayoga) receives the name "non-conceptual" (nirvikalpa)?

Previously, having heard from others that non-conceptual wisdom is the true state of a bodhisattva, the bodhisattva, though not yet having personally realized the true principle, merely gives rise to a mind of faith and delight toward this wisdom.

By relying upon this mind of faith and aspiration, one subsequently enters and traverses the principle of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*); because non-conceptual wisdom arises from this faith and aspiration, this faith and aspiration is called "preparatory non-conceptuality" (*prayoga-nirvikalpa*).
Regarding these qualities of non-conceptual application, they are said to be "untainted.
What is the analogy for this?
The treatise states:
Untainted like space, this non-conceptual wisdom [is attained] through the power of mere faith and aspiration, even regarding various heavy and evil karmas.
Commentary:
This non-conceptual wisdom is pure and unstained, just as space is not defiled by the four types of dust.
What phenomena cannot defile it?
They are the various heavy and evil karmas arising from body, speech, and mind.
There are differences in views and the path of cultivation, and there are distinctions among the ten unwholesome actions; therefore, they are called "various.
With extremely heavy afflictions as conditions, one constantly engages in [unwholesome] action.
If one acts without remorse, the mind lacks any counteractive remedy.
It is called "heavy" because it has companions; therefore, one cannot be defiled by such evil karma.

If a person, through hearing the correct teaching, gives rise to faith and delight in non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), by means of this faith and delight, they destroy the karma of the four evil destinies.
Why is this? Evil karma arises based on what is unreasonable, whereas faith and delight arise from what is reasonable.
Because it arises based on the unreasonable, it is false; because it arises from the reasonable, it is real.
The unreal cannot withstand the real; therefore, it is destroyed.
This verse demonstrates that the non-conceptual wisdom of application (*prayoga-nirvikalpa-jñāna*) can counteract the karma of the four evil destinies, because it is not mixed with such evil karma.
This constitutes the merit of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*).
What are the merits of the fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (*mūla-nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and its purification?
The treatise says:
Pure like space, this non-conceptual wisdom Liberates one from all obscurations Through its attainment and its perfection.
Commentary:
Just as space is said by the world to be pure when it is free from the four obstructions such as smoke and clouds,
so too is non-conceptual wisdom pure.
By being free from what phenomena does it attain purity?
The treatise says:
"Liberated from all obstacles.
The commentary explains:

"All obscurations" refers to the three obscurations of skin, flesh, and heart, or alternatively, the four obstacles to virtue consisting of icchantikas, non-Buddhists, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas; it is purified by means of liberation from such obscurations.
By what cause is this liberation accomplished?
The treatise says:
It is by means of acquisition and realization.
The commentary states:

Because of being endowed with the supreme virtues of the various stages, because of the accomplishment of the cause in the tenth stage, and because of the accomplishment of the fruit in the Buddha-stage, one attains liberation from all obscurations.
This verse reveals that fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (*mūla-nirvikalpa-jñāna*) can serve as the antidote to all obscurations; this is the fundamental merit.
How then are the merits of the subsequently attained non-conceptual wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and its freedom from defilement (*asaṃkleśa*) to be understood?
The treatise says:
Just as space is untainted, so is this non-conceptual wisdom;
when it appears in the world, it is not defiled by worldly phenomena.
The commentary states:
Just as space cannot be moistened by water, ignited by fire, or moved by wind,
so too is non-conceptual wisdom free from defilement.
It is called "unstained" because it is without change. Why is this?
Because the bodhisattva, relying on this wisdom, contemplates the work of benefiting all sentient beings.
By virtue of this power of knowledge, the bodhisattva intentionally enters the triple world and manifests various jātaka tales.
Although born within the world, he is not altered by the eight worldly dharmas.
There are eight worldly dharmas: gain and loss, fame and ill-repute, praise and blame, pleasure and pain.
Because of these eight dharmas, desire and aversion arise.
Desire and aversion cannot transform desire and aversion; fundamental ignorance cannot cause them to waver.
Why is this? Because falsehood cannot confront reality.
This wisdom arises from non-conceptual wisdom; therefore, it is called "non-conceptual."
This verse reveals that the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) can avoid the obstacle of karmic retribution.
It does not abide in either of the two states—saṃsāra or nirvāṇa—but acts solely for the benefit of others; this is precisely the merit of subsequently attained wisdom.
Regarding these three types of non-conceptuality, what is their distinction?
To clarify this distinction so that they do not become confused, an analogy is established.
The treatise says:
Like a mute person seeking to perceive an object, like a mute person actually perceiving an object,
