and like a non-mute person perceiving an object— the three types of knowledge are illustrated by these analogies.
The commentary states:
For example, just as a mute person seeking various objects cannot describe those objects, so too is non-conceptualization through preparatory application:
while within the path of expedient means, one investigates suchness but is unable to express it.
For example, it is like a mute person who correctly perceives various sensory objects; although he has apprehended the objects, he cannot describe them.
Fundamental non-conceptuality is likewise: while one is directly in the contemplation of suchness, one cannot describe what is realized and seen therein.

For example, just as a person who is not mute correctly perceives various objects and is also able to describe those objects, so too is subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*): according to what has been seen, it can establish the true teaching and explain it for others.
Initially, when one has not yet attained but is directed toward the state free from conceptual discrimination, there is no causal basis for expression; therefore, it cannot be expressed.
Subsequently, when one has correctly attained the state free from conceptual discrimination, there is no causal basis for expression; therefore, it cannot be expressed.
Having subsequently attained it through emerging from meditative absorption, one is able to speak without error regarding what was previously perceived.
This verse clarifies the distinction between the three types of non-discursiveness and discursiveness; therefore, there is a difference.
The Treatise says:
Just as a fool seeks to receive objects, just as a fool is currently receiving objects,
and just as one who is not a fool receives objects— the three types of knowledge are illustrated by these analogies.
The commentary states:
Not recognizing the categories of things is called ignorance (*moha*).
Ignorance is analogous to sequence; the three meanings are explained as before.
This verse clarifies that there is a distinction between the non-conceptual and the conceptual; thus, they differ.
Non-verbal expression has non-conceptuality as its cause, for it is by virtue of non-conceptuality that there is no verbal expression.
It is said that verbal expression has conceptual discrimination as its cause; because of conceptual discrimination, there is verbal expression.
The analogy of the fool serves to illustrate the absence of conceptual discrimination.
Regarding these three objects of knowledge, how are they characterized in terms of being unreal or real?
The Treatise says:
Just as the five [senses] seek to receive objects, just as the five correctly receive objects,
and just as that which is not the five receives objects— the three types of knowledge are illustrated by these analogies.
The commentary states:
The term "five" refers to the five non-conceptual consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness and so forth.

For example, when a person seeks out the five objects within these five consciousnesses, they may apprehend either what is real or what is unreal, because the mental consciousness arises interspersed with the five consciousnesses.
The preparatory non-conceptual wisdom (*prayoga-nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is likewise: it may be real when it realizes a portion [of the object], or it may be unreal when it does not realize it.
It is, for example, like a person who, while in the midst of the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), attains a truly real object that is non-conceptual and beyond verbal expression.
Fundamental non-conceptual wisdom is likewise: it attains the true object, being without conceptualization or verbal expression.

For example, when a person is within the mental consciousness, they merely take as their object a sensory field previously experienced; this is called "taking a false object," and it involves conceptualization and verbal expression.
The subsequent non-conceptual wisdom is likewise: it takes a non-existent object as its condition, possesses conceptualization, and involves verbal expression.
This verse clarifies that there is a distinction because the three types of objects of cognition are respectively real and unreal.
The Treatise says:
Just as seeking understanding when one has not yet recognized [the truth], just as reading the Dharma of right reception,
and just as understanding the meaning of the Dharma received— these three serve as analogies for the three types of knowledge in their respective order.
The commentary states:
For example, it is like a person who, not yet having mastered the treatises, seeks only to recognize the characters.

Non-conceptual wisdom of application (*prayoga-nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is likewise: not yet having recognized *tathatā*, one merely studies the means for perceiving *tathatā*. This indicates that [the practitioner] has not yet attained full understanding.

For example, it is like a person who already knows the characters but has not yet understood their meaning; while reading the characters, they can only receive the words but have not yet received the meaning.

Fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (*mūla-nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is likewise: the function of self-benefit has already been accomplished, but the function of benefiting others has not yet arisen; this indicates that [the former] has already been understood.

For example, suppose a person has already recognized the characters and has also understood their meaning while they are in the process of reflection; this person possesses two capacities—the capacity to recognize the characters and the capacity to understand the meaning—because their application has reached its consummation.

The subsequent non-conceptual wisdom is likewise: having already realized suchness and having emerged from meditative absorption, one explains without error exactly as previously perceived; this demonstrates that understanding has reached its ultimate consummation.
This verse reveals that there are distinctions because the merits of training differ; thus, there is differentiation.
The three successive stages have already been clarified: namely, not yet understanding, having understood, and the culmination of understanding.
The first one has no object, while the latter two have objects— namely, phenomena (*dharma*) and their meanings (*artha*).
Regarding the difference between these latter two that possess objects,
the treatise says:
Just as when a person has their eyes closed, so too is non-conceptual wisdom;
just as when a person has their eyes open, so too is subsequently attained wisdom.
The commentary states:
This verse merely reveals the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), which differ due to their distinct bases of reliance.
Fundamental wisdom relies upon that which is neither mind nor non-mind, whereas subsequently attained wisdom relies upon the mind; therefore, these two wisdoms differ with respect to their objects.
Fundamental wisdom does not grasp objects because there is no distinction between object and wisdom;
subsequently attained wisdom grasps objects because there is a distinction between object and wisdom.
Fundamental wisdom does not take objects as its cognitive support, just as one with eyes closed.
The object-conditioned wisdom attained subsequently (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is like opening one's eyes.
This verse clarifies that there is a distinction because there is a difference between not apprehending an object and apprehending an object.
What, then, is the distinction in the majestic power (*prabhāva*) of these two types of wisdom?
The treatise says:
Just as space is without discrimination, Without defilement, obstruction, or extremes,
And just as forms appear within space, So too is subsequently attained wisdom.
The commentary states: For example, space possesses four qualities: first, it is unstained; second, it is unimpeded; third, it is non-conceptual; and fourth, it is boundless.
Fundamental wisdom is likewise: it cannot be stained by any of the eight worldly dharmas or the seven floods and so forth. Because it serves as their antidote, it is said to be "unstained."
Regarding all objects, because they are unobstructed and unattached in accordance with reality and in accordance with the full extent of phenomena, it is called "unimpeded.
Regarding all dharmas, because the single-flavor true suchness (tathatā) pervades them as emptiness, it is called "non-conceptual."
Because it is free from all extremes and the Middle Way is immeasurable, it is said to be "boundless.
For example, just as form appears within space, while space cannot be differentiated, form can be differentiated.

The subsequently attained wisdom is also like this: its cause cannot be conceptually differentiated, whereas this wisdom can be conceptually differentiated, in that it is both the differentiator and the differentiated.
If the fruit of Buddhahood is manifested by non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), how can one who is free from conceptualization perform deeds for the benefit of sentient beings?
To show that such activity occurs spontaneously (*anābhoga*) in accordance with reality and without error, the verse is repeated.
The treatise says:
Just as the mani-jewel and the celestial drum accomplish their own tasks without thought,
so too, without conceptual discrimination, the various deeds of a Buddha are accomplished.
The commentary states:
For example, just as the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) is devoid of conceptual discrimination yet can accomplish whatever matters beings desire and seek;

or just as the celestial drum (*devadundubhi*), though struck by no one, can produce four kinds of sounds according to the inclinations of those beings—namely, the arrival of enemies, the departure of enemies, the enjoyment of desires, and the arising of world-weariness.
The Buddhas are likewise; though they have already transcended conceptual discrimination, they are able to perform various deeds that benefit sentient beings.
There are two kinds of such beneficial deeds:
first, benefiting through the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), which is like a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*).
Second is the benefit of teaching the Dharma, which is like a celestial drum.
What is the meaning of the profound nature of this non-conceptual wisdom?
Its profundity is established in relation to its object.
Does this wisdom arise by taking the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)—which is the object of conceptual construction—as its object, or does it arise by taking some other object?
If so, what is the problem?
If it were to take the dependent nature, which is the object of conceptual construction, as its object, then the meaning of this wisdom being non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) would not be established.

If it were to arise by taking another object as its condition, then apart from this [present] object, there would be no other distinct object; thus, the meaning of "taking another object" would also not be established.
Furthermore, if it were to arise by taking another object as its condition, the principle that object and cognition are non-different would not be established.
The Treatise says:
It is neither this nor not this; it is neither wisdom nor not wisdom.
Being indistinguishable from its object, wisdom is termed "non-conceptual."
The commentary states:
This wisdom does not take the dependent nature as its object. Why is this?
Because this wisdom does not take conceptual discrimination as its object, it is said to be "not this.
Nor does it take other objects as its condition. Why is this so?
Because this wisdom takes as its object only the suchness (tathatā) of phenomena that dependently arise, phenomena and their suchness cannot be said to be either identical or different;
for they are respectively the objects of the impure and the pure, and are characterized by being both universal and non-universal.
It is not that it does not take consciousness as its object; therefore, one says it is "not non-this.
Furthermore, is this wisdom to be considered wisdom, or is it to be considered non-wisdom?
If so, what harm is there?
If its nature is wisdom (*jñāna*), how can it be non-conceptual?
For wisdom is by nature conceptual.
If its nature is not wisdom, how can it be called "wisdom"?
Since non-conceptuality is not of the nature of cognition, how can it be called "non-conceptual wisdom"?
The treatise says:
It is neither cognition nor non-cognition.
The commentary states:
Why is it called "non-wisdom"?
Because it does not arise within the wisdom of application (*prayoga-jñāna*) or the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), it is termed "non-wisdom."
If that were so, why would it not constitute a non-cognitive delusion?
This argument also does not hold. Why is this?
It is not that non-wisdom arises from improper mental attention to produce the outflows of desire and so forth;

rather, this [wisdom] arises from non-conceptual preparatory wisdom (*prāyogika-jñāna*) and can produce non-conceptual subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). Therefore, it is said to be "not non-wisdom."
Furthermore, because this wisdom does not arise within conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it is said to be "not wisdom.
Because this wisdom does not arise elsewhere, but arises solely within the suchness (*tathatā*) of conceptualized phenomena, it is said to be "not non-wisdom."
The first line of this verse explains the second.
The Treatise says:
"Non-differentiation from the object is what is called non-conceptual wisdom."
The commentary states:
If wisdom arises through the two aspects of grasper and grasped, it possesses conceptual construction and, like preparatory wisdom (*prayoga-jñāna*), is not called non-conceptual.
If wisdom arises in a state of perfect equality, being no different from the grasped object, it is called non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
In other sūtras, the Buddha taught that all phenomena are by nature non-conceptual.
To clarify this principle, he spoke these verses again.
The treatise says:
The Buddha taught that all phenomena are by nature non-conceptual;
because there is nothing to be conceptualized, they are devoid of even non-conceptuality.
Commentary:
The self-nature of all phenomena is non-conceptual; how can this meaning be known?
To establish this meaning, the third phrase is set forth.

Because the categories of what is conceptually differentiated do not truly exist, while the reality of non-conceptual phenomena truly exists, it is said that the self-nature of all phenomena is non-conceptual.
If all phenomena were non-conceptual by virtue of the non-existence of that which is conceptually constructed, how is it that sentient beings are not liberated by their own nature?
The treatise says:
That [non-existence] is itself non-conceptual.
The commentary states:
Because the non-conceptual wisdom regarding the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is non-conceptual with respect to its object,
if that is so, why is it not liberated by its own nature?

It is indeed so that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is non-conceptual, and wisdom, like its object, is also non-conceptual by intrinsic nature; yet, one does not attain liberation through intrinsic nature.

One attains this dharma by cultivating wisdom, for wisdom cannot arise due to cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); since liberation is only attained once these obstructions are extinguished through the cultivation of wisdom, there is no sense of "liberation through intrinsic nature."
If one gives rise to conceptual discrimination within the non-conceptual nature, this is non-wisdom; it is precisely ignorance.
I shall now explain the distinctions regarding the non-conceptual wisdom that exists within phenomena that are by nature non-conceptual.
The treatise states:

Within this context, there are three kinds of non-conceptual [wisdom]: first, preparatory non-conceptual wisdom; second, non-conceptual wisdom; and third, subsequent wisdom following non-conceptual wisdom.
The commentary states:

Within the non-conceptualization of intrinsic nature, if these three types are spoken of collectively, they manifest the skillful means of the path, the actual practice of the path, and the culmination of the path;
that is to say, the skillful means of entry, the skillful means of abiding, and the skillful means of emergence.
If explained separately according to cause, person, and matter, there are eleven types.
The treatise says:

There are three kinds of non-conceptualization through application (*prayoga-nirvikalpa*), namely, because of the distinctions in their arising from the power of causal conditions, the power of leading and penetrating, and the power of repeated cultivation.
The commentary states:
These three differ according to their causes.

Non-conceptualization through preparatory application is accomplished by three powers: either by the power of causal conditions, or by the power of drawing forth supernormal powers, or by the power of repeated cultivation.
Because these three powers are established, there arises a distinction in their manifestation.
If it is established by the power of causes and conditions, it is established by the power of nature (*dhātu*).
If it is established by the power of projecting and drawing forth, it is established by the power of previous births.
If it is accomplished through the power of repeated cultivation, then it is accomplished in the present through the exertion of effort.
The treatise says:

Non-conceptual wisdom also has three types, namely, that which is contented, that which is non-erroneous, and that which is free from conceptual proliferation, due to the distinctions among these types of non-conceptuality.
The commentary states: These three are distinguished according to persons, namely: ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), and bodhisattvas.

Regarding "contentment and non-conceptuality" (*saṃtuṣṭi-nirvikalpa*): it should be understood that this arises from having attained the culmination of both the wisdoms of hearing (*śruta*) and reflection (*cintā*). Because one is contented, there is no conceptualization; therefore, it is called "contentment and non-conceptuality."

If an ordinary bodhisattva reaches the culmination of the wisdoms of hearing and reflection, they have fully attained all that is to be attained; because they give rise to a mind of contentment, they are without conceptual discrimination.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings in the world who possess contentment and non-conceptuality. By virtue of this contentment, those beings are reborn above in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), where they reckon it to be the ultimate liberation, beyond which there is no further realm to be traversed.
Having given rise to a mind of contentment, they no longer advance in their cultivation; therefore, they are without conceptual discrimination (*avikalpa*).

To be without inversion and without conceptual discrimination refers to the followers of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayānika*); because they have already thoroughly realized the true object—the fourfold non-inverted characteristics such as impermanence—they never again conceptually discriminate by means of the four inverted characteristics such as permanence; thus, they are without conceptual discrimination.
Free from conceptual proliferation and free from discrimination—this refers to the bodhisattvas.
Bodhisattvas do not discriminate any phenomena, even up to not discriminating unsurpassed enlightenment.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are beyond verbal expression.
To forcibly establish verbal expressions within that which is beyond verbal expression is therefore called conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
There are four kinds of verbal expression, which are the four types of false denial (paryādāya-pralāpa).
To say that something "exists" is the false denial of superimposition (samāropa);
to say that it "does not exist" is the false denial of repudiation (apavāda).
If one says it both exists and does not exist, this is the slander of contradiction;
if one says it neither exists nor does not exist, this is the slander of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

Because the Bodhisattva has attained non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which cannot be manifested through verbal expression, it is termed "without conceptual proliferation" and "non-conceptual."
Why is this? Because it transcends mundane wisdom, and furthermore, because it is not something known by mundane wisdom.
The treatise says:
Subsequent non-conceptual wisdom has five types, namely: the distinction of penetration, retention, establishment, intermingling, and manifestation according to one's will.
The commentary states:
These five differ according to their objective referents (*vastu*).
Subsequent attainment wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) has the capacity for manifestation as its nature; herein, "manifestation" (*saṃdarśana*) has the meaning of "clear comprehension" (*avabodha*).

Because this wisdom, at a time subsequent to the thorough penetration [of reality], manifests such matters by saying, "In my contemplation, I have known and seen such and such matters," it is called "manifesting thorough penetration."
Because this wisdom, after emerging from meditative equipoise, retains what has been realized without loss, it is called "the manifestation of retention.
Because this wisdom, in accordance with what it has itself realized, can establish the authentic teaching so that others may practice it, it is called "the manifestation of establishment."

By means of this wisdom, the bodhisattva takes all phenomena as objects of cognition just as before; that is to say, just as previously, through the wisdom that observes mixed objects, one observes these objects by means of this observation and thereby attains the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*). Therefore, it is called "manifestation through intermingling."

Through this wisdom, the bodhisattva has already attained the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*); whatever the bodhisattva intends or desires is accomplished exactly as wished. That is to say, the great elements such as earth and so forth are transformed into gold and other substances; therefore, it is called "manifestation according to wish" (*yatheṣṭa-prakhyāna*).

The Commentary explains:

Because the mind differs even when the object is one, that object is admitted to be established.
Commentary:

For example, a single river is differentiated by four types of beings and thus becomes four objects: hungry ghosts perceive it as pus and blood; fish and other animals perceive it as their dwelling place; humans perceive it as water; and devas perceive it as land. According to each respective differentiation, it becomes a distinct object for each.

If objects were real, they would necessarily obstruct one another; it should not be possible for four objects to be established simultaneously in a single location. One should know that all such [appearances] are merely the products of the mental consciousness's conceptual construction.

If you admit that the four consciousnesses arise simultaneously with their respective objects, and that consciousness does not exist apart from its object, then you must also admit that there are four objects existing simultaneously in one place.
If you admit that there are four objects existing simultaneously, then you must believe that all conceptual constructions are devoid of real existence.
If there were no real objects, consciousness would arise spontaneously, not arising in dependence upon objects.
If that were so, the four difficulties within the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra) would be reinstated, and the four meanings would fail to be established.
This objection is explained in that treatise as follows:
"If there is consciousness but no object, what fault is there?
To clarify this meaning, the verse is repeated.
The treatise says:
Regarding the past and the future, and within dreams and the two kinds of reflections, cognition takes as its object that which does not exist;
this non-existent [object] functions as the objective field.
The commentary states:

Past and future phenomena possess only names but lack substantial reality. If the mind takes these two time periods as its object, there is only consciousness without an external object; the same applies to objects perceived within a dream.
There are two kinds of reflections: first, reflections in a mirror; second, reflections within meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The appearances of blue, yellow, and so forth that arise from the concentrated mind have no existence apart from the mind itself; therefore, they are called "reflections."
If the mind takes these two images as its objects, there is likewise only consciousness and no external object.
If these four types of objects do not exist, what is it that consciousness perceives?
The treatise says:
"This has no transformation as its object.
The commentary explains:

External objects are originally non-existent; they are produced by the transformations of consciousness. Since consciousness takes these very [transformations] as its objects, it is said that there is no transformation as an object.
This principle having been established, one should no longer harbor doubts. Why is this?
If one were to deny this principle, there would be no possibility of attaining Buddhahood.
To clarify this meaning, the verse is repeated.
The treatise says:
If sensory objects were to become actual objects, there would be no non-conceptual wisdom.
The commentary states:
If objects possessed substantial existence as the referents of cognition were established, then non-conceptual wisdom would not exist. Why is this?
If the objects of conceptualization were real, then the conceptualizing subject would not be in error; it is only when there is no [real] object of conceptualization that error occurs.
If that were so, all ordinary beings would be free from inversion, and all noble ones would be in error.
What fault is there in this?
The treatise says:
If this [state] were without the fruit of Buddhahood, it would be impossible for it to be attained.
The commentary states:
Non-conceptual wisdom is the true path; if one claims that this wisdom does not exist yet asserts that the fruit of Buddhahood should be attained, such a position is impossible.

This attachment contradicts both the scriptures (*āgama*) and logical reasoning (*yukti*); therefore, one should know that all objects lack an intrinsic nature that can be conceptually differentiated.

Because the entity that is the object of conceptualization does not exist, conceptualization itself is also non-existent; therefore, non-conceptual wisdom is in accordance with reality and non-erroneous.
Furthermore, there is another principle that proves that all objects lack an entity that can be conceptually constructed.
The treatise says:
Bodhisattvas who have attained mastery, by the power of their vows and aspirations, accomplish the earth and other elements according to their will;
those who have attained meditative concentration are likewise so.
The commentary states:

A bodhisattva attains mastery over entering, abiding in, and emerging from meditative concentration; mastery over transformation, subjugation, and penetration through the superknowledges (abhijñā); and mastery over the ten [masteries] regarding the stages (bhūmi).

A bodhisattva first makes a vow to perform deeds for the benefit of sentient beings; after attaining non-conceptual wisdom and emerging from meditative equipoise, whatever they intend to do is accomplished according to their will, whether by means of a present aspiration or a fundamental vow.

Aspiration is the cause and joy is the fruit; first one generates the aspiration to perform deeds for the benefit of sentient beings, and subsequently, whatever joy one desires according to one's mind is accomplished without exception—this refers to such things as the transformation of the earth and other elements.

If a bodhisattva of shallow practice wishes to perform deeds for the benefit of sentient beings, they first make a vow in the present; having made the vow, they immediately enter true contemplation (*bhūta-darśana*), and upon emerging from contemplation, they achieve success according to their desired inclinations.

If a bodhisattva of deep practice wishes to perform deeds for the benefit of sentient beings, they need not currently form aspirations or enter and emerge from meditative absorption; rather, by the power of their original vows, everything they wish to accomplish is fulfilled accordingly.

If śrāvakas and others attain mastery over the nine meditative absorptions, they thereby attain mastery over the six supernormal powers; within a single object, according to the power of their aspirations and inclinations, each is able to transform it into immeasurable varieties.
If all objects possessed an intrinsic nature, this matter could not be established;
they would be like the two kinds of emptiness, which cannot be altered by any sovereign power.
Why is this? Because it is based on reality (*tattva*).
This verse clarifies that external objects lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*); how, then, is the meaning of their lack of intrinsic nature with respect to internal objects to be understood?
The treatise says:
For one who has achieved discernment, a wise person who has attained meditative concentration,
when contemplating all phenomena internally, they appear according to their true meaning.
The commentary states:
Discernment (*pravicaya*) is precisely *vipaśyanā*.
To obtain the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) is called "attainment" (*samanvāgama*).
From the stage of stream-enterer (srotāpanna) up to the fruit of arhatship, one is called a person who has achieved discernment (*viveka*).
A "person of wisdom" refers to a bodhisattva.

To clarify that such a person of wisdom is not defined by the stages of hearing and reflection (*śruta* and *cintā*), but rather by having entered the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), it is said that they have attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

When Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas internally contemplate all phenomena, just as these two individuals reflect upon the meanings revealed by the teachings of the twelve divisions of the scriptures, so too do those meanings manifest for these two individuals.
If one contemplates the meaning of the Buddha, the meaning of the Buddha manifests within various phenomena.
Just as the meaning of the Buddha manifests, so too do the five aggregates—form and the rest—and the ten perceptions such as impermanence manifest in this same way.
This verse clarifies that all objects lack intrinsic nature by means of the internal realm.
How is it known that both external and internal realms lack intrinsic nature?
The treatise says:
"When practicing non-conceptual cultivation, no objects appear;
one should know that there are no external entities, and because of this, there is no consciousness.
Commentary:

If, while a bodhisattva is in non-conceptual contemplation, all objects—whether internal, external, or both—no longer appear, one should therefore know that all sensory objects are in reality non-existent.
If there are no external objects, then there is no internal consciousness. Why is this?
Since that which is cognized does not exist, how can that which cognizes exist?
This principle is indeed so.
Because that which is known does not exist, that which knows also does not exist; this meaning should be understood as having been fully revealed within the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*.
Is this wisdom identical to or distinct from the *prajñāpāramitā*?
The Treatise says:
This non-conceptual wisdom is precisely the Prajñāpāramitā; the names differ, but the meaning is the same.
The Commentary says:
One does not consider them different because their names are distinct, but regards them as one because their meaning is the same. Because they are one, it is said that they are identical.
If the names were different, how could the meaning be the same?

The Tathāgata establishes the Dharma by subsuming all phenomena under the same category based on their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), not by subsuming them under the same category based on names. Why is this?
Because names differ across various regions, whereas meanings remain the same across all regions.
Names are provisional designations established to refer to these meanings; thus, they vary according to different regions.
Meanings possess a determinate nature, and therefore the meaning remains the same.
Practice is accomplished by relying on the meaning, not by relying on the name.
How is it known that their meaning is the same?
The treatise says:
As the Sūtra states:
If a bodhisattva abides in the *prajñāpāramitā*, by practicing through what is not a [proper] basis (*asthāna*), they are able to bring the cultivation of the remaining *pāramitās* to fulfillment.
The commentary states:
Because one wishes to establish that non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is not distinct from the *prajñāpāramitā*, the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* is cited as proof.
When a bodhisattva cultivates the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), it is called "abiding" because there is no falling back or loss.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva wishes to cultivate the other perfections, they first take the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom as their skillful means.
The remaining *pāramitās* are accomplished by abiding within the *prajñāpāramitā*; therefore, it is said that they "abide" [in it].

When a bodhisattva abides within the *prajñāpāramitā*, they practice the remaining *pāramitās* while remaining detached from five points; by practicing each individual *pāramitā* for a certain period of time, they bring them to fulfillment, which is why they are called "perfected."
The treatise says:
What constitutes practice in an improper sphere that enables the complete cultivation of the remaining perfections?
It refers to being free from five types of spheres.
"First, it is free from the locus of the non-Buddhists' grasping at a self.
The commentary explains:
Just as the non-Buddhists dwell within that *prajñā* and give rise to grasping at a self, saying, "I now dwell in *prajñā*; *prajñā* is mine."
Bodhisattvas dwelling in prajñā do not act in this way; therefore, it is said that they are free from the locus of attachment to the view of a self, because they do not conform to that locus.
The Treatise says:
Second, they are free from the locus of conceptualization of bodhisattvas who have not yet seen suchness.
The commentary states:

Just as a bodhisattva prior to the stages has not yet seen suchness (*tathatā*), he takes conceptualization and non-conceptualization to be the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), thinking, "This is the perfection of wisdom."

If a bodhisattva has already seen suchness, then within the perfection of wisdom there is no such conceptual discrimination; therefore, it is said to be "free from the sphere of discrimination," because that sphere does not apply there.
The Treatise says:
"Third, it is the state that is free from the two extremes of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
The Commentary explains:

Just as ordinary beings dwell on the extreme of saṃsāra and śrāvakas dwell on the extreme of nirvāṇa, the bodhisattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) apart from these two extremes; therefore, it is said that he dwells in the state free from the two extremes, because he does not abide in those [extremes].
The Treatise says:
The fourth is the sphere of practice characterized by detachment, which consists solely in the cessation of the obstacle of afflictions and the cultivation of contentment.
The Commentary explains:

Just as a śrāvaka gives rise to contentment regarding the cessation of the afflictive obscurations (kleśāvaraṇa) and no longer seeks anything further in other realms—namely, the cessation of the cognitive obscurations (jñeyāvaraṇa)—the bodhisattva is not like this.

Because they practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) for the sake of eliminating the cognitive obscurations, it is said that they depart from the sphere of contentment and do not abide in that state.
The Treatise says:
The fifth [type of person] is one who does not contemplate the work of benefiting sentient beings and dwells in the realm of nirvana without remainder.
The Commentary says:
Just as a pratyekabuddha does not attend to the welfare of sentient beings and dwells in nirvana without remainder, a bodhisattva is not like this;
dwelling in the perfection of wisdom, they do not abandon the work of benefiting sentient beings.
Parinirvāṇa is both with remainder and without remainder; it is without remainder in relation to the *dharmakāya*, and with remainder in relation to the *nirmāṇakāya* and *sambhogakāya*.
It is said that he does not abide in the place of nirvāṇa without remainder, because that place is not appropriate for him.
Non-conceptual wisdom has five types of distinctions, which differ from the five points previously identified as objects to be abandoned.
First is the distinction of non-perversion, because this [wisdom] is non-perverted while that [object] is perverted.
Second, the distinction of non-conceptuality: this is non-conceptual, whereas that is conceptual.
Third, the distinction of having no abode: this has no abode, whereas that has an abode.

Fifth, the distinction of correct practice: this correct practice is able to extinguish both the cognitive and afflictive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa* and *kleśāvaraṇa*), whereas that [other] correct practice can only extinguish the afflictive obscuration.
Sixth, the distinction of attainment: this attains the three eternally abiding bodies as its fruit, whereas that attains the nirvāṇa of eternal cessation as its fruit.
The Treatise says:
What is the distinction between the wisdom of the śrāvakas and the wisdom of the bodhisattvas?
The Explanation says:

It has already been stated that non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) are one and the same; now, we wish further to demonstrate the distinction between this non-conceptual wisdom—the perfection of wisdom—and the wisdom of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
The treatise says:
It should be understood through the distinctions of non-conceptuality.
The commentary says:
Śrāvakas possess conceptual discrimination, whereas Bodhisattvas are without conceptual discrimination; one should know that there is a distinction based on this meaning.
The treatise says:
because they do not conceptually discriminate the various dharma-gates such as the aggregates (skandhas) and so forth.
The commentary states:
Śrāvakas take the various dharma-gates, such as the aggregates (skandhas), as their objects through wisdom, and thus conceptual characteristics arise.
Bodhisattvas do not differentiate the various dharma-gates, such as the aggregates, and thus non-conceptual characteristics arise; hence, there is a distinction between them.
The treatise states:

Because one penetrates the two kinds of emptiness and suchness—not merely partially but in their full differentiation—and thereby enters into all aspects of the knowable, as well as because one relies upon the welfare and benefit of all sentient beings.
The commentary states:
There are two divisions: first, the division of the objects of knowledge; second, the division of benefiting sentient beings.
Within the division of the objects of knowledge, there are further two types, namely, the two kinds of emptiness: that of persons and that of phenomena.
Within the section on benefiting sentient beings, there are also two types: namely, one's own person and others' persons.

Regarding the section on the objects of knowledge, the Śrāvaka merely penetrates the emptiness of persons and halts at the Four Noble Truths, such as suffering, thereby giving rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
Within the portion concerning the benefit of sentient beings, one merely relies upon matters of one's own benefit to make aspirations and engage in practice.
Thus, within these two portions, there is only one portion for each.

Regarding the aspect of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), the bodhisattva fully masters the two emptinesses of persons and phenomena, as well as all wisdoms that accord with reality (*yathābhūta*) and accord with the measure of things (*yathāmātra*).
Regarding the aspect of benefiting sentient beings, based on all matters for the benefit of sentient beings, they cultivate practice through making vows concerning their own and others' bodies.
Within these two parts, each possesses its own two parts.
Because these two parts differ from the single part, it is said that they are not merely a differentiation of one part.
The treatise says:
This is due to the distinction of non-abiding, because they abide in the nirvana of non-abiding.
The commentary states:
Śrāvakas cling to nirvana, just as ordinary beings cling to saṃsāra.

The Bodhisattva is not so; seeing that both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are equally products of conceptual construction and share the same nature of signlessness (animitta), he does not abide in either state.
The Commentary states:
Because of constant differentiation, he does not fall into the extreme of total extinction within the nirvāṇa without remainder.
The commentary states:
Because there is a distinction between these two types of persons regarding *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, there is a distinction in their wisdom.

Regarding *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, the two vehicles lack the two bodies—the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) and the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body)—because they do not contemplate the welfare of others. Lacking the *nirmāṇakāya*, they fall into annihilation; lacking the *saṃbhogakāya*, they fall into exhaustion.
The Bodhisattva constantly manifests two bodies within *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* without limit; how much more so for the *dharmakāya*.

Because self-benefit and benefit for others are perfected, there is the *sambhogakāya*, and thus one does not fall into annihilation; because there is the *nirmāṇakāya*, one does not fall into exhaustion.
The Treatise says:
"By virtue of its unsurpassed distinction, there is truly no other vehicle superior to this.
The Commentary explains:
The vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are "surpassable" because they do not equal the Great Vehicle.
The vehicle of the bodhisattvas is "unsurpassable" because there is no other vehicle superior to the Great Vehicle.
It takes wisdom as its essence, for within the Mahāyāna, wisdom is the foremost.
Due to these five meanings, there is a distinction between the wisdom of the two vehicles and the wisdom of the bodhisattvas.
The treatise says:
Herein a verse is spoken.
The commentary says:
To summarize the five preceding meanings and to manifest the merits of these five meanings, the verse is repeated.
The treatise says:
"By means of the fivefold excellence of wisdom, One relies upon great compassion to cultivate merit."
The commentary states:
The wisdom of the bodhisattvas is superior to that of the two vehicles by virtue of five distinctions.
They are not only content with their superior wisdom, but further cultivate merit based upon that wisdom; this merit consists of the remaining five perfections.

This phrase reveals that his self-benefit surpasses that of the two vehicles; furthermore, there is another sense of superiority: namely, for the sake of benefiting others, he cultivates merit based on great compassion, wherein "merit" refers to the other five perfections.
If a person possesses these two capacities, what karmic fruit will they obtain?
The treatise says:
"Both worldly and supramundane wealth and happiness—these are said not to be far off."
The commentary states:

Becoming a Wheel-Turning King, one of the five kings of the heavens above the desire realm, or a Brahmā king of the form realm; furthermore, attaining the meditative absorptions of the formless realm as well as the mundane concentrations uniquely attained by Bodhisattvas—these are termed "worldly wealth and happiness."
The liberation of the two vehicles and unsurpassed enlightenment are termed supramundane wealth and happiness.
Since such fruits are easily obtained according to one's wishes, they are not considered remote.
These bodhisattvas have already attained the state of ultimate mastery and constantly practice compassion toward the impoverished and suffering beings of the world.
By virtue of this intention, the bodhisattva does not bestow material wealth. What is the function of this intention?
The treatise says:
If the bodhisattva perceives that which truly exists in the world, it can likewise be known.
The commentary states:
This reveals that the Bodhisattva possesses both substantiality and beneficence.
Because they possess substantiality, they are said to "truly exist"; because they possess beneficence, they are said to be "knowable."
The Treatise says:

If a bodhisattva thus accords with the accumulation of merit from training in ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom, they will attain the ten kinds of mastery and achieve incomparable, supreme capability in all matters of benefiting others.
The commentary states:
The three trainings encompass the ten perfections and all mundane virtues; therefore, they are called the "accumulation of merit.
If a bodhisattva has not yet attained what is to be attained, or has attained it and does not lose it, this is called "conformity," which constitutes the perfection of the cause.
Upon reaching the ten kinds of mastery, the fruition is perfected.
Regarding the activities for benefiting others, there are either two kinds or four kinds.
The two kinds refer to first reflecting and then acting.
Furthermore, there are two kinds, namely the latter two fearlessnesses.
Alternatively, there are four kinds, as previously explained.
Having attained such peerless and supreme capability, one’s qualities of grace and virtue are perfected.
Among these three virtues, the two virtues of cause and effect manifest self-benefit, while the virtue of grace manifests benefit for others.
Having completed the explanation of the three trainings, this meaning is clarified in order to demonstrate the perfection of the Bodhisattva’s three virtues.
The Treatise says:
Why is it that within the world one sees sentient beings encountering grave suffering and calamity?
The Commentary explains:
This objection is raised as follows:
If a bodhisattva possesses these three virtues solely for the purpose of rescuing all sentient beings, why do sentient beings still encounter the hardships and calamities of the world?
If one perceives suffering but does not rescue it, then there is no superior capacity; if there is no superior capacity, then there is no bodhisattva.
There are two kinds of suffering and difficulty: namely, internal and external.
These two types of suffering, internal and external, may be either light or heavy; that which can be remedied is light, while that which cannot be remedied is heavy.
The treatise states:
This is because the Bodhisattva perceives that those sentient beings possess karma capable of inducing the retribution of suffering, thereby obstructing the attainment of superior and joyful fruits.
The commentary states:

When a bodhisattva perceives that sentient beings possess karmic obstructions which hinder the bodhisattva’s superior capacity and cause them to experience bitter retribution, the bodhisattva possesses knowledge of this karma regarding them;
thus, although they harbor superior capacity, they relinquish it and do not employ it. This is precisely the power of the bodhisattva’s karma.

It is like a river possessing water of eight meritorious qualities; while sentient beings may drink from it as they please without anyone to obstruct or guard them, hungry ghosts, due to the obstruction of their karma, are unable to drink.

The Bodhisattva is like a river, and material wealth is like its water; sentient beings with karmic obstructions are like hungry ghosts, who, due to those karmic obstructions, are unable to enjoy the Bodhisattva’s wealth.
The treatise says:
Because the bodhisattva perceives it thus:
"If I bestow upon them the requisites for happiness, it will obstruct their production of wholesome roots."
The commentary states:

The Bodhisattva perceives that there are sentient beings who lack karmic obstructions; if they are poor, they are able to cultivate and grow wholesome dharmas, whereas if they are wealthy and at ease, they become negligent and commit transgressions.

The Bodhisattva wishes that they may experience the suffering of poverty in the present life so as to accord with and accomplish the arising of wholesome dharmas; for this reason, the Bodhisattva does not bestow upon them the requisites of pleasure.
This is the Bodhisattva’s power regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-bala*).
The treatise says:
Because the Bodhisattva perceives that those beings lack the means for happiness, he is able to manifest a revulsion toward *saṃsāra*.
The commentary states:

When a bodhisattva perceives sentient beings who, due to the suffering of poverty, maintain a constant presence of mind that loathes birth and death, he does not bestow upon them the requisites for pleasure.
This is because he wishes for them to achieve a mind of renunciation and to conform to wholesome conduct; therefore, he does not grant them those pleasurable things.
This is precisely the power of the bodhisattva’s faculties, inclinations, and nature.
The treatise states:
Because the bodhisattva perceives that if one were to bestow articles of pleasure upon them, it would become the causal condition for the growth and proliferation of all unwholesome dharmas.
The commentary states:
When a bodhisattva sees sentient beings who are even constantly receiving the retribution of poverty, during that time he does not cultivate unwholesome dharmas.

The bodhisattva wishes for them to continue receiving the retribution of poverty, rather than wishing for them to receive the retribution of wealth and pleasure for even a single moment and thereby create the causes and conditions for various unwholesome dharmas—namely, self-love and hatred toward others, these two being the causes and conditions that can give rise to and grow unwholesome dharmas.

If a bodhisattva were to bestow material wealth upon others, they would thereby foster attachment and aversion in those recipients; for this reason, the bodhisattva does not bestow such objects of pleasure.
This is the bodhisattva’s power of knowledge regarding the thorough practice of the path.
The treatise states:

Because the Bodhisattva perceives that if he were to bestow articles of pleasure upon those [beings], it would become a cause and condition for the oppression and harm of countless other sentient beings.
The commentary explains:

When a bodhisattva sees a sentient being who, upon attaining great wealth, not only harms themselves but is also able to harm and afflict immeasurable other sentient beings, the bodhisattva wishes that they instead undergo the suffering of poverty;

the bodhisattva does not wish for them to possess great wealth and pleasure, lest it harm the body and mind of sentient beings or their roots of goodness. Therefore, the bodhisattva does not bestow such instruments of pleasure upon them.
This is also the Bodhisattva’s power of knowledge regarding the path traversed everywhere.
The Commentary says:
Therefore, it is not that the Bodhisattva lacks such superior capability, nor is it that such sentient beings do not appear in the world.
The commentary states:
There are three superior capacities, which are the three virtues (*guṇa*). First is the capacity to attain the cause, namely the three bases of training (*śikṣāpada*);
second is the capacity to attain the fruit, namely the ten masteries (*vaśitā*).
Third, it is able to benefit others, meaning that one discerns the faculties, inclinations, and dispositions of sentient beings.
If one sees that giving will be beneficial, one gives; if one sees that not giving will be beneficial, one does not give.
A bodhisattva takes benefit as the definitive standard, not whether a gift is given or not.
It is because giving does not bring benefit that there are sentient beings in the world who undergo suffering.
The Treatise says:
A verse is spoken herein.
The Commentary explains:
To summarize the preceding five points, the verse is repeated.
The treatise says:
Seeing that karma obstructs the wholesome, one becomes weary of the present and perceives the increase of evil.
Those sentient beings who harm others do not elicit the giving of a Bodhisattva.
The commentary states:
There are sentient beings who possess karmic obstructions and thus do not elicit the giving of a Bodhisattva.

There are sentient beings for whom the possession of objects of pleasure obstructs the cultivation of virtue; there are sentient beings who, due to poverty, have a mind of revulsion toward birth and death that is constantly present; there are sentient beings who, possessing objects of pleasure, grow in unwholesome dharmas; and there are sentient beings who, by means of great wealth and pleasure, are able to oppress and harm others. When a Bodhisattva perceives such circumstances, wishing to prevent them from causing harm to themselves or others, he does not bestow those objects of pleasure upon them. Therefore, those sentient beings do not receive the Bodhisattva’s gift.
The Commentary on the Mahāyānasaṃgraha, Scroll 12;
The Commentary on the Mahāyānasaṃgraha, Scroll 13;
Explained by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha from Central India.
Chapter Nine: Explaining the Superior Characteristics of the Cessation that is the Fruit of Training. The Treatise says:
Thus far, the distinctions of training in wisdom have been explained; how should the distinctions of cessation be understood?
The commentary states:

Since there is a distinction between the path of a bodhisattva and the paths of the two vehicles, and since cessation is attained through the path, there must likewise be a distinction between the cessation of a bodhisattva and the cessation of the two vehicles. How is this to be known?
The Treatise says:
The extinction of the afflictions of all bodhisattvas is precisely non-abiding nirvāṇa.
The Commentary says:

The two vehicles and the bodhisattvas alike take the extinction of afflictions as the truth of cessation; however, while the extinction of afflictions for the two vehicles involves a one-sided turning away from saṃsāra toward nirvāṇa, the extinction of afflictions for a bodhisattva does not turn away from saṃsāra nor turn away from nirvāṇa. Thus, they differ from the two vehicles.

This cessation of the bodhisattva is the "non-abiding" among the four kinds of nirvāṇa: first, originally pure nirvāṇa; second, non-abiding nirvāṇa; third, nirvāṇa with remainder; and fourth, nirvāṇa without remainder.

The Bodhisattva does not perceive any difference between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; by means of prajñā, they do not abide in saṃsāra, and by means of compassion, they do not abide in nirvāṇa. If one discriminates saṃsāra, one abides in saṃsāra; if one discriminates nirvāṇa, one abides in nirvāṇa. The Bodhisattva attains non-discriminative wisdom and, being without discrimination, has no place of abiding.
The treatise asks:
What are these characteristics?
The commentary explains:
What are the characteristics of the nirvāṇa without abode?
The treatise states:
Its characteristic is the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), which is the relinquishing of afflictions while not relinquishing saṃsāra, and the cessation of the two bases of death.
The commentary states:

If a bodhisattva is in the state of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), they do not share the locus of origination with the various afflictions (*kleśa*); therefore, this is called "abandoning.
However, because afflictions necessarily give rise to conceptual discrimination when one is in the state of emerging from meditative absorption, this is called "not abandoning saṃsāra."
If one contemplates these two meanings separately, whether in terms of the preceding or the succeeding, one may still find that both meanings are present simultaneously;
if one contemplates both meanings together, they must necessarily exist at the same time. Both of these meanings take the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) as their basis.

Non-abiding nirvāṇa has the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) as its characteristic; that is, it transforms two attachments: the attachment of ordinary beings to saṃsāra and the attachment of the two vehicles to nirvāṇa.

When a bodhisattva attains non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), they do not perceive any distinction between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. Thus, although they extinguish delusions, they do not abide in nirvāṇa; and although they give rise to conceptualization, they do not abide in saṃsāra. Therefore, this nirvāṇa takes the transformation of the basis as its characteristic, and this transformation of the basis is precisely the reliance upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
The treatise says:
Herein, saṃsāra has as its essence one portion of the impure class of the dependent nature, while nirvāṇa has as its essence one portion of the pure class of the dependent nature.
The commentary states:
This explains the meaning of the two bases.

The fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) is called the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva). If the fundamental consciousness gives rise to conceptualization (vikalpa), it constitutes the impure category; this one portion is said to be the essence of saṃsāra.

Just as one discriminates the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), this nature does not exist in the way it is so discriminated; this non-existence of such discrimination is the pure category (*viśuddha-pakṣa*), and based on this aspect, it constitutes the essence of nirvāṇa.
The Treatise says:
"The fundamental basis" refers to the other-dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) which possesses the two parts of the pure and impure categories.
The Commentary explains:

The nature of conceptual differentiation is saṃsāra, and the nature of ultimate reality is nirvāṇa; from the very beginning, these two categories have relied upon the nature of dependence as their basis, and thus the nature of dependence is said to be the fundamental basis.
The Commentary states:

Regarding the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), when the antidote arises, this dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) permanently alters its nature through its impure aspect and permanently perfects its nature through its pure aspect.
The commentary states:
The transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) also belongs to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

The paths of the three vehicles are the remedies; when this path of the dependent nature has not yet arisen—such as during the stage of seeing the truths (*satyadarśana*) and so forth—it is capable of giving rise to various karmas that induce retribution in the evil realms, and is thus termed the "impure category" (*aśuddha-pakṣa*).
Once the Path has arisen, such impure factors are extinguished and do not arise again; therefore, it is said that its original nature is permanently transformed.

This dependent nature, along with the Path and the fruit of the Path, is termed the "pure category. The Path consists of morality, concentration, and wisdom. There are two kinds of fruits of the Path: namely, the conditioned and the unconditioned.
The conditioned consists of liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation; the unconditioned consists of the cessation of fundamental afflictions and the non-arising of future afflictions.
When the Path has not yet arisen, the pure factors such as ethical discipline have not yet been established, and there exists only natural purity.

Because it arises from the Path, it is associated with the fivefold Dharma-body and stainless purity; such association remains without change until the attainment of Buddhahood, and is therefore said to be the eternal perfection of the original nature.
The Treatise says:
If this transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) is explained briefly, there are six kinds of transformation.
The Commentary says:

If categorized according to the paths and fruits of the three vehicles, there would be many meanings of transformation (āśraya-parāvṛtti) when explained in detail; however, as it is explained here briefly, there are only six kinds.
The treatise says:

First is the transformation that augments power and diminishes capacity, because at the stage of following through faith and delight, one abides by the power of the permeation of hearing (śruta-vāsanā).
The commentary states:

Through the arising of the noble paths of the three vehicles within the ālayavijñāna, the functional capacity of the perfuming of hearing (*śrutavāsanā*) increases further; this is termed "augmenting power.

Conversely, regarding all the perfumings of the afflictions (*kleśa*) within the ālayavijñāna, because their antidotes have arisen, they no longer possess their original efficacy; this is termed "diminishing capacity."
By what stage and by what causes are these two matters accomplished?

If a person abides in the stage of aspiration and joy (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), hears the vast and profound correct teaching (*saddharma*) spoken by the Tathāgata, and therein gives rise to the three types of faith (*śraddhā*), aspiring to and joyfully practicing in accordance with it without opposition—this benefit and harm has as its cause the power of the perfuming of hearing (*śruta-vāsanā*). The wisdom of hearing and reflection (*śruta-mayī-prajñā* and *cintā-mayī-prajñā*) constitutes the essence of the perfuming of hearing.
From these two types of wisdom, cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) arises; cultivated wisdom is the power of the permeation of hearing (*śruta-vāsanā*).
If cultivated wisdom were absent, the fundamental basis would not be able to undergo transformation.
By virtue of this power, the principles of diminution and augmentation are established.
If a person has already attained such a transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), how do the afflictions behave within that person?
The treatise says:
Because the afflictions either manifest with a sense of shame, manifest with diminished strength, or no longer manifest at all.
The commentary states:
If a person has already attained this transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), whenever afflictions arise, they immediately feel shame;
furthermore, they do not persist for long, are weakened, or may never arise again.
Why is this? Because one is able to feel shame for oneself and perceives all faults deeply.
The treatise says:

Second is the transformation of thorough penetration (*prativedha-parāvṛtti*), which refers to those bodhisattvas who have already ascended the stages (*bhūmi*). This is because both the real and the unreal manifest as the capacity [of cognition].
The commentary states:
Because they attain non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and realize suchness (*tathatā*), it is called "thorough penetration."
Due to this penetration, there is a distinct transformation that differs from the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*).
Once one has ascended to the grounds, when one occasionally enters meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*), this penetration serves as the cause for the manifestation of reality.
Why is this? Just as at the beginning one penetrates and clearly realizes suchness, so it is when subsequently entering contemplation.
At times, upon emerging from contemplation, this penetration becomes the cause for the manifestation of what is false.

Why is this? Just as before entering meditative observation one cultivated conventional practices for the benefit of oneself and others with a distracted mind, it is the same now upon emerging from observation.
The treatise says:
This transformation extends from the first stage to the sixth stage.
The commentary states:
because there is a difference in the entry into and emergence from meditative absorption within this context, the sixth stage is established as its limit.
The Treatise says:
The third is the transformation through cultivation, because for those who have not yet abandoned the obstructions, it is the basis for the non-appearance of all signs and the appearance of reality.
The Commentary explains:
The cultivation of the preceding stage arises based on signs (*nimitta*); the cultivation of this stage arises based on signlessness (*animitta*).

Having already abandoned the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*), yet not having fully abandoned all cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it is the Mahāyāna practitioner in training (*śaikṣa*) who can attain this transformation.
All characteristics refer to the characteristic of characteristics, the characteristic of arising, and the characteristic of reality.
The substance of these three characteristics does not manifest; it is by relying on this transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) that they are established.
The manifestation of the three absence-of-characteristics is also established by relying on this transformation of the basis.
The Treatise says:
This transformation proceeds from the seventh stage to the tenth stage.
The Commentary explains:
In this context, because one practices the conduct of signlessness (*animitta-caryā*) together [with others], the fourth stage is established as its level.
The treatise states:

"The transformation of the four fruits is perfected by those who have already abandoned the hindrances; for all signs no longer appear, pure *tathatā* appears, and one attains the basis for mastery over all signs."
The commentary states:
The perfection of the three qualities is called the fulfillment of the fruit.
Those who have already abandoned all obscurations are the Buddhas; they are able to attain this transformation.
The non-manifestation of all marks is the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*),
because all marks have been extinguished.
The manifestation of pure *tathatā* is the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*).

Because the wisdoms of reality (*yathābhūta*) and extent (*yāvadbhāva*) are perfected—meaning he possesses all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) and has attained mastery over all characteristics—this constitutes his beneficent virtue.
Based on the mastery attained over all appearances, and by virtue of this mastery, one is able to perform deeds that benefit all sentient beings according to their wishes.
These three qualities likewise take this [mastery] as their basis for transformation.
The Treatise says:

There are five types of inferior transformation. Because the śrāvakas have thoroughly realized the selflessness of persons, they turn their backs exclusively on saṃsāra in order to permanently abandon it.
The commentary states:
The three meanings of person, object, and capacity are all inferior.
Because this is a śrāvaka, the person is inferior.
Because they contemplate only the selflessness of persons, their objects of focus are inferior.

Their minds seek only to escape birth and death for themselves and exit the triple world; having not yet attained the ultimate, they are further unable to bring universal salvation to sentient beings, and thus their functional capacity is inferior.
The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the bondage of the śrāvaka; to eliminate this view, one cultivates the contemplation of the selflessness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*).

Suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) are collectively termed birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); if one attains the selflessness of persons, one is then able to turn away from suffering and abandon its origin.
The Treatise says:
There are six types of vast transformation, because the bodhisattva penetrates the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
The Commentary explains:
The three meanings of person, object, and capacity are all vast.
Because this is a Bodhisattva as a person, the person is vast.
Because they contemplate the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), the object is vast.
Because they deliver themselves and others and can do so to ultimate completion, their functional capacity is vast and great.
Discursive discrimination is a bondage for bodhisattvas; in order to eliminate this bondage, they cultivate the contemplation of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).

The selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) is the root, while the selflessness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*) is the branch; if one attains the selflessness of phenomena, one must first have attained the selflessness of persons.
Although it is attained first, it is not yet pure because the root has not been eliminated; only after realizing the selflessness of phenomena does it become pure.
The objective realm of dharma-nairātmya (selflessness of phenomena) can manifest the four virtues; therefore, by contemplating this realm, one attains liberation from the eight inversions.
The treatise says:
"Because therein one contemplates the virtue of tranquility."
The commentary states:
This refers to observing the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) within the cycle of birth and death; therefore, it is called the merit of tranquility (*śāntaguṇa*).
The treatise says:
"Because of abandoning what is not abandoned.
The commentary states:

This reveals the function of the contemplation of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*). Within saṃsāra, by means of contemplating tranquility, one is able to distance oneself from conceptual construction; because one is not defiled by afflictions, one abandons the afflictions.
Because one perceives that saṃsāra and tranquility are no different from true suchness (tathatā), one does not abandon saṃsāra.
The treatise says:
If a bodhisattva is in the stage of inferior transformation, what fault is there?
The commentary states:
This question is posed in order to reveal that there are three faults.
The treatise says:
"Because they do not consider the welfare of sentient beings.
The commentary states:
This clarifies the loss of a bodhisattva’s benevolent virtue (*guṇa*).
The Treatise says:
"Transgressing and departing from the Bodhisattva-dharma.
The Commentary explains:

The wisdom of reality as it is (*yathābhūta*) and the wisdom of the full extent of phenomena (*yāvadbhāvikatā*), along with the merit arising from these two types of wisdom, constitute the qualities of a bodhisattva. To fail to practice the qualities of bodhisattva wisdom is a fault, and to abandon or distance oneself from the qualities of bodhisattva merit is a departure [from the path]; this clarifies the loss of wisdom and virtue.
The Treatise says:
To attain liberation in common with those of the Lesser Vehicle (hīnayāna) is a fault.
The Commentary explains:

It merely extinguishes the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) but does not extinguish the obscuration of knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); this clarifies the loss of the quality of abandonment (*prahāṇaguṇa*).
The treatise asks:
When Bodhisattvas abide in the stage of vast transformation, what qualities do they possess?
The commentary states:
This question is posed again in order to demonstrate that there are three qualities.
The treatise says:
Within the phenomena of birth and death, by taking one's own transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) as the support, one attains all forms of mastery.
The commentary states:
One attains non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and extinguishes the seeds of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); this extinction is itself the transformation of the basis.
Relying upon this transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), the bodhisattva attains ten kinds of mastery (*vaśitā*) over all phenomena.
The treatise states:
"Within all paths, one is able to manifest all bodies."
The commentary states:
Relying upon mastery, one manifests various bodies according to the forms and types within the six realms of existence.
The treatise says:

Regarding worldly wealth and happiness as well as the three vehicles, through the superior power of various skillful means of instruction, one is able to establish others in the true teaching; this is the merit of the vast turning [of the wheel].
The commentary states:
"Wealth and happiness" refers to the wholesome paths within the three realms.

First, one causes them to attain the worldly wholesome paths; subsequently, one causes them to attain the noble paths of the Three Vehicles. Through transformation and deliverance by means of the three wheels, one establishes them in the True Dharma.
What dharma constitutes the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) that is the intrinsic nature of Great Enlightenment?
The intrinsic nature of Great Enlightenment is distinct from that of the two vehicles.
This transformation of the basis should be understood as having four characteristics:

First, it has the characteristic of being the basis for arising; second, it has the characteristic of being the basis for the perpetual non-arising [of afflictions]; third, it has the characteristic of being the fruit of the maturation of the objects of knowledge through reflection; and fourth, it has the characteristic of the purification of the dharmadhātu.
That which has the characteristic of being the basis for arising is the supramundane path included within the continuum of a Buddha.
Otherwise, until this transformation of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti) is attained, the noble path of a Buddha would not be established, which is illogical.
If the Buddha-way were accomplished through a transformation of this basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), then the path prior to that transformation should have already been accomplished.

As for "having as its characteristic the basis of the permanent non-arising [of defilements]," it refers to the basis upon which all afflictions (*kleśa*) and their latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) never again arise.

If it were not so, then even though the causes and conditions have already assembled, until this transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) is attained, it would be unreasonable for the various afflictions and their latencies to never arise again.

That which has the characteristic of being the basis for the fruit of mature reflection upon the objects of knowledge consists in the fruit of mature investigation and the thorough penetration of the suchness (*tathatā*) and the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the objects of knowledge.
If it were not so, the intrinsic nature of the Buddhas would have to be further investigated and their obstructions further extinguished.
That which has the purification of the *dharmadhātu* as its characteristic is manifested by the most pure *dharmadhātu*, having suppressed and extinguished all marks (*nimitta*).
If it were not so, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the Buddhas would be impermanent and subject to conceptualization.
However, the intrinsic nature of the Buddha is eternally abiding; its characteristic is that it is inconceivable and cannot be expressed in words.
The Treatise says:
A verse is spoken herein.
The Commentary explains:
To reveal this transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti), the verse is repeated.
The treatise says:
"For ordinary beings, it conceals the real; for them, it manifests the false."
The commentary states:
Ignorance regarding the truths (satyāvidyā) obscures for ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) the true emptiness of the selflessness of persons (pudgalanairātmya) that pervades all phenomena.
"For them" refers to ordinary beings.

This ignorance inverts that mind, causing it to perceive the marks of a self, the marks of sentient beings, and the marks of the six sense objects—all of which are false dharmas; thus, through this manifestation, ignorance serves as its basis.
The Treatise says:
"Toward the bodhisattva who is single-minded, he abandons the false to reveal the true.
The Explanation says:

Because the non-conceptual wisdom of a bodhisattva extinguishes ignorance, it abandons all false dharmas—such as the notion of a self-characteristic—and manifests the true suchness of the two kinds of emptiness.
The arising of ignorance is the basis for ordinary beings; the extinction of ignorance is the basis for bodhisattvas.
This verse clarifies that cessation constitutes the characteristic of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
The Commentary states:
Non-manifestation and manifestation, The false and the real.
The commentary states:
Falsehood is the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); when conceptual construction does not arise, falsehood does not manifest.
Reality is the threefold absence of intrinsic nature (*tri-niḥsvabhāvatā*); because falsehood does not manifest, reality manifests.
The Treatise says:
This is the bodhisattva’s transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), because liberation is attained according to one's will.
The Commentary explains:

The manifestation of that which was previously unmanifest is the bodhisattva’s transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*); this transformation of the basis is itself the bodhisattva’s liberation. Having attained liberation, they are no longer subject to bondage.

For the sake of benefiting others, they traverse the six realms of existence at will according to their resolve; this differs from the liberation of the two vehicles, which is a permanent cessation devoid of the capacity to benefit others, like one whose head has been severed and whose life can never be restored.
This verse clarifies that liberation is the pure *dharmakāya* which is free from falsehood.
These two are accomplished through non-conceptual wisdom; thus, the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) is explained in terms of the three virtues.
The Treatise says:
Regarding saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, if wisdom arises as equal.
The Commentary explains:
Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are both products of conceptual discrimination; they are identical with true suchness (*tathatā*).
If one attains non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), it arises in relation to this equality.
The treatise states:
Birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa, because these two lack the distinction of "this" and "that.
The commentary states:
the impure category is called birth-and-death; the pure category is called nirvāṇa.
The delusory nature of birth and death, being devoid of both the self of persons and the self of phenomena, is itself nirvāṇa.

When one attains non-conceptual wisdom and perceives that birth and death do not exist, one simultaneously perceives that nirvāṇa does not exist; therefore, there is no distinction between this and that.
What is the functional capacity of one who has attained this wisdom?
The treatise says:
Therefore, regarding saṃsāra, it is neither abandoned nor not abandoned.
The commentary states:
Although one contemplates selflessness, not departing from birth and death, this does not mean there is abandonment.
Although one constantly contemplates selflessness while remaining within birth and death, this does not mean there is non-abandonment.
If that is so, what is the case regarding nirvāṇa?
The treatise says:
