Regarding the basis and that which depends upon it, one should speak of both words and knowledge;
to the one who possesses unimpeded eloquence in speaking, I pay homage to that speaker.
The commentary says:
"Those who can resolve the difficulties of all sentient beings, I pay homage to them.
Commentary:
From this point on, one and a half verses clarify the four types of unhindered analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).
Because they possess four kinds of understanding, they are able to resolve the difficulties of sentient beings.
The treatise says:
Regarding the basis and that which depends upon it, one should speak of both words and wisdom.
The commentary states:
Regarding this meaning, that which depends [upon it] refers to the various dharma-gates; these should be described as "regional dialects," while wisdom constitutes "skillful eloquence.
The treatise says:
"One is able to speak without impediment.
The commentary states:
"In these four [factors], one's capacity is unimpeded, and in speaking to others, one is likewise unimpeded."
The Treatise says:
I prostrate to the Speaker.
The Commentary explains:
Having already abandoned delusion and craving, his speech is stainless and he possesses the virtue of being able to teach; therefore, he is called a "speaker.
The treatise says:
"Taking up and relinquishing the life-span, manifesting transformations and altering the nature."
I prostrate my head to the World-Honored One, who has attained mastery over meditative concentration and wisdom.
Commentary: This verse elucidates the supernormal knowledge of penetration (abhijñā).

If their lifespan is destined to end, they can further sustain it to extend it, even for as long as eighty thousand great kalpas; it does not stop at merely eighty thousand kalpas. If they wish to remain for many kalpas, they can remain as they intend; if they wish to relinquish it, they can relinquish it as they intend.

Furthermore, within the various meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), these three capacities also exist: the ability to emanate immeasurable bodies from a single body constitutes transformation (*nirmāṇa*), and the ability to transform gold, earth, and so forth constitutes modification (*pariṇāma*).

All supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) are accomplished through meditative concentration (*samādhi*); because they are as they wish and unimpeded, it is said that one attains mastery over concentration and wisdom.
The treatise says:
When sentient beings see the Honored One, they believe and revere him, calling him a "Superior Being" (*satpuruṣa*).
I prostrate with a pure mind to the one who can generate [realization] through the vision of others.
Commentary:
This single verse collectively elucidates the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*) and the eighty minor marks (*anuvyañjana*).
Sentient beings perceive the major and minor marks of the Buddha and give rise to faith and reverence, thinking in their hearts that the Tathāgata is the most supreme of beings.
Both the major and minor marks of the Tathāgata are capable of generating a pure mind in sentient beings.
The Treatise says:
Therefore, following the sounds of those various classes, you practice, come and go, and emerge;
you realize and know all sentient beings—homage to the Teacher of the True Path!
The commentary states:
This verse clarifies the four kinds of purity in all aspects, manifesting in accordance with the forms, types, voices, and languages of sentient beings.

Just as those sentient beings experience birth in the past as "going" and experience birth in the present as "returning," they move within these two time periods and attain the fruits of the paths of the three vehicles as their "departure."
The Buddha fully realizes and knows these matters and teaches the correct doctrine according to what is appropriate.
This capacity exists by virtue of the four purities.
The treatise says:
I prostrate with my head to the one who, through skillful means, provides refuge and purity, Who obstructs sentient beings therein,
yet brings them forth from the Great Vehicle, And who crushes the Māras. Commentary:
From the time of renouncing the household life and receiving the precepts up until the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*), all are termed "expedient means" (*upāya*).

From the Patience regarding the Dharma of Suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) up until the second fruit [of stream-entry] constitutes "taking refuge," because one has attained the four kinds of indestructible faith (*avetyaprasāda*). The third and fourth fruits constitute "purity," because one has become detached from the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) up through the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Within this, Māra is able to obstruct sentient beings, preventing them from attaining the fruits of this path.

Even within the Mahāyāna, when one cultivates the practices of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and seeks transcendence from the three obstacles (*trividha-āvaraṇa*), Māra likewise can create hindrances therein.
Because the Tathāgata is endowed with the ten powers, he is able to subdue all māras for the sake of sentient beings.
The Commentary says:
"He can clearly explain the cessation of ignorance, the transcendence [of suffering], and the obstacles to these matters."
"To those who, for the benefit of both self and others, Subdue the heterodox—I prostrate.

Commentary: This verse elucidates the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*): "wisdom" refers to the fearlessness of omniscience; "extinction" refers to the fearlessness of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-vaiśāradya*); "departure" refers to the fearlessness of teaching the path leading to the end of suffering; and "obstructing matters" refers to the fearlessness of teaching the obstacles to the path.

If there are non-Buddhists who challenge the Buddha, saying that he is not omniscient; or that his outflows (*āsrava*) are not yet exhausted; or that although the Tathāgata has taught the path for the exhaustion of suffering, practicing it cannot bring about liberation from suffering; or that he has taught obstructive dharmas which, when they arise as obstructions, do not prevent one from attaining the Way.
The Tathāgata is fearless therein and is able to subdue heterodox challenges.
The Treatise says:
Without restraint and without fault, without defilement and without dwelling.
Unwavering toward all phenomena, I prostrate to you who are free from conceptual proliferation.
Commentary:
This verse elucidates the four kinds of non-protection.
Without the need for a teacher’s restraint, his body, speech, mind, and livelihood are naturally free from the ten non-virtuous actions and other such faults.

Not only are the afflictions of greed, hatred, and wrong views absent, but all afflictions have been completely extinguished; because he does not cling to any phenomena, it is said that he is unstained and non-abiding.

One does not engage in mental attention regarding the knowledge of all phenomena; knowing that all phenomena are such that there is no further meaning to be learned, one is free from conceptual discrimination and wisdom is all-pervading; therefore, it is said to be "unmoving.
Since faults have already been eliminated, there is no conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
The treatise says:
To him who subdues others among the assembly, who is far removed from the two types of delusion,
who is without need for protection and free from forgetfulness, and who gathers the multitude— to him I prostrate my head.
The commentary states:
This verse clarifies the three applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
If there are sentient beings who, upon hearing the Tathāgata preach the Dharma within the great assembly, give rise to slander, the Tathāgata does not become angry.
If they can believe and accept [the teaching], the Tathāgata does not harbor attachment;
if they neither disparage nor believe, the Tathāgata does not abandon them.
Toward these three situations, he constantly gives rise to great compassion, employing the power of skillful means to skillfully preach the true Dharma so that they may enter into the principle.
Within the great assembly, he is able to subdue such sentient beings and preach the True Dharma for them without giving rise to the two delusions of anger and desire.
Since there is neither anger nor desire, one knows that ignorance is absent; because he does not need to guard his mind, he does not forget or lose it.
Because his great mindfulness and great compassion are always naturally firm, he is without forgetfulness; by means of this great compassion, he is able to gather the great assembly.
The treatise says:
Regarding the task of benefiting others, the Honored One does not bypass the proper time.
"His deeds are never in vain; I prostrate to the One Without Delusion.
Commentary:

Throughout the ten directions, immeasurable sentient beings ought to receive benefit within a single kṣaṇa. By the power of his great compassion, the Tathāgata causes all of them to obtain that benefit within a single kṣaṇa, so that none is left empty-handed. Furthermore, there is not a single sentient being for whom the time to attain the Path has not yet arrived, such that [the Buddha] would go to their location in advance and wait for the time to come before preaching the Dharma for them.
Whatever one does, all shall bring benefit in accordance with the occasion; therefore, what is performed is never in vain.
Delusion is ignorance (*avidyā*); ignorance is the essence of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Because these habitual tendencies are exhausted, the benefits are not in vain.
The Treatise says:
In all activities and dwellings, there is nothing that is not the work of perfect wisdom;
I prostrate my head before the one who universally knows all worlds in their true essence.
The commentary states:
This verse clarifies non-forgetfulness.
"Activity" refers to those who have already taken birth and those who have not yet taken birth; "abiding" refers to those currently undergoing birth.
Because all matters of the three periods of time for sentient beings are the domain of perfect wisdom, one is able to know the three periods of time universally.
Because its essence is *tathatā* (suchness), it is called the "substantial reality"; because the wisdom based on this substantial essence is perfect, there is no loss or forgetfulness.
Furthermore, when the Buddha was in the causal stage, he cultivated the ten stages as his practice; upon attaining Buddhahood, this became his abiding state.
Perfect wisdom can penetrate these matters of its own cause and fruit, universally knowing all worldly luminosity, and is able to penetrate the three periods of time regarding sentient beings.
This interpretation clearly demonstrates the ability to know both oneself and others.
The treatise says:
"Six times throughout the day and night, one contemplates the realm of all sentient beings."
Endowed with great compassion, I pay homage to the one whose intent is to bring benefit and happiness.
Commentary:
This verse elucidates great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

When the Buddha constantly observes sentient beings and speaks of the "six periods," he does so because he wishes to establish a model for all beings, demonstrating that the cultivation of the Path consists of practices for both self-benefit and the benefit of others; specifically, cultivating practices for the benefit of others during six periods and cultivating practices for one's own benefit during six periods.
The realm of sentient beings is identical to the nature of sentient beings.

This nature of sentient beings is not uniform; some produce goodness through evil, some produce goodness through virtuous deeds, some produce goodness through fearful circumstances, and some produce goodness through joyful events.
Because great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is able to transform and deliver beings by conforming to this nature, it is in all cases associated with great compassion.
The same applies to the faculties (*indriya*) and inclinations (*ruci*).
The treatise states:
By way of practice and by way of attainment, By way of wisdom and by way of activity,
To you who are peerless among all those of the two vehicles, I prostrate with my head.
Commentary:
This verse elucidates the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).

Practice is the cause, attainment is the fruit, wisdom is the knowledge that accords with reality and its full extent, and activity refers to the work of benefiting sentient beings. These eighteen unique qualities do not transcend these four meanings; they are called "unique" because they are not shared with those of the two vehicles.
The Commentary says:
I prostrate to the Honored One who, having arrived by means of the three bodies,
possesses the marks of unsurpassed enlightenment and is able to remove all doubts regarding the dharmas of others.
The commentary states:
This verse elucidates the supreme wisdom of all aspects (*sarvākāra-jñāna*).

The three bodies (*trikāya*) are themselves the three virtues: the *dharmakāya* is the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), the *saṃbhogakāya* is the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), and the *nirmāṇakāya* is the virtue of grace (*anugraha-guṇa*).
By virtue of the three bodies, one attains the fruit characterized by the possession of the three excellences.
Because of the attainment of unsurpassed enlightenment, it is supreme; regarding all phenomena, whatever doubts sentient beings may harbor, the Tathāgata is fully capable of severing them all.
The treatise says: Unbound and without fault, without coarseness or turbidity, without abiding,
unmoving amidst all phenomena, and free from conceptual proliferation— to you, I prostrate.
The commentary states:
This verse reveals the six kinds of purity of the Tathāgata.
First is the purity from the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), which is "non-bondage," because of the extinction of the three obstacles, namely afflictions and so forth.
Second is the purification of karmic obstacles (*karmāvaraṇa*), which means being free from faults due to the extinction of twenty-two types of karmic obstacles.
Third is the purification of retributive obstacles (*vipākāvaraṇa*), which means being free from coarseness and turbidity due to the elimination of seven kinds of birth and death.
Fourth is the purity of benefit, which refers to non-abiding, because there is no obstruction between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
Fifth is the purity of mastery, which refers to being unmoved regarding all phenomena, because one can manifest all phenomena at will through effortless power.
The sixth is purity free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), because it transcends the sphere of verbal expression, discursive thought (*vitarka*), and mental investigation (*vicāra*).
Since the first three clarify self-benefit and the latter three clarify benefit for others, the word "etc. refers to these six purities.
The Treatise says:
The Dharma-body of all Buddhas is not only constantly associated with such qualities as these, but is also associated with other qualities.
The Commentary says:
The virtues explained previously apply to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles.
It has already been taught that the dharmakāya is endowed with these virtues; furthermore, there are Mahāyāna-specific virtues that are also associated with the dharmakāya.
The treatise says:
This refers to the correspondence of intrinsic nature, cause, fruit, activity, association, and the performance of meritorious deeds.
The commentary explains:

In this context, the six kinds of qualities of the Mahāyāna that correspond to the dharmakāya are briefly explained: namely, the intrinsic nature of the dharmakāya, the cause of the dharmakāya, the fruit of the dharmakāya, the activity of the dharmakāya, the correspondence of the dharmakāya, and the manifestation of the dharmakāya.
The treatise says:
Therefore, one should know that the dharma-body of all Buddhas possesses unsurpassed qualities.
The commentary says:
Because it is not shared with others within either the Mahāyāna or the Hīnayāna, it is unsurpassed.
The treatise says:
Herein, a verse is spoken.
The commentary states:
These verses are spoken in order to manifest these six kinds of merit.
The treatise says:
The Honored One has realized suchness, Cultivated the stages of transcendence,
Reached the peerless state of others, And liberated all sentient beings.
The Commentary says:
"The Venerable One has realized suchness.
Explanation:
This phrase clarifies the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
The realization of suchness is stainless purity.
If, prior to the Path or during the Path, defilements have not yet been exhausted, it cannot be called "realization";
only when defilements have been completely exhausted after the Path is it termed "realization."
This suchness is the intrinsic nature of the dharmakāya.
The treatise states:
"One practices the transcendence of the various stages."
The commentary states:
This passage clarifies the cause of the *dharmakāya*.

While in the causal stage, one cultivates true suchness (*tathatā*), which is fully manifested at the culmination of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). One thereby transcends the three obstacles of skin, flesh, and heart; this is precisely the twofold transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) consisting of wisdom and abandonment. Through this transformation of the basis, one attains the *dharmakāya*.
The Treatise says:
"Reaching the stage of being unequaled by others.
The Commentary explains:
This sentence clarifies the fruit of the Dharmakāya.

If one realizes the fruit of the Dharmakāya, one attains the four virtues of purity, self, bliss, and permanence: purity not shared with icchantikas, self not shared with non-Buddhists, bliss not shared with śrāvakas, and permanence not shared with pratyekabuddhas.
The Treatise says:
"Liberating all sentient beings.
The Commentary explains:
This passage clarifies the activity of the Dharmakāya.
If this fruit is attained, sentient beings are liberated.

There are four kinds of liberation: namely, establishing [beings] in the wholesome paths and the activities of the three vehicles, thereby liberating both ordinary worldlings and those of the three vehicles.
The Treatise says:
These inexhaustible and other virtues manifest in the world in association [with the Buddha];
they are easily seen by those within the three spheres, but difficult for gods, humans, and others to perceive.
The Treatise says:
"Inexhaustible and other such qualities manifest in the world in conjunction [with it].
The Commentary explains:
These two lines clarify the correspondence with the Dharmakāya.

There are five kinds of inexhaustible qualities that correspond with the Dharmakāya: first, excellence through purity; second, excellence through universality; third, excellence through immeasurability; fourth, excellence through inconceivability; and fifth, excellence through inexhaustibility.

From the first stage through the seventh stage, the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) that are the objects of antidotes such as envy are forever extinguished and do not arise; because these serve as the basis, the purity of all virtues becomes supreme, and one is in union with the *dharmakāya*.
In the eighth stage, because one relies upon a path that is non-conceptual, uninterrupted, and spontaneously uncontaminated (*anāsrava*),
all the merits within the uncontaminated realm are supreme for the Buddhas, as they are in union with the *dharmakāya*.
In the ninth stage, because one is able to take as a basis an immeasurable ocean of samādhis and dhāraṇī-doors that encompass infinite knowledge of the Dharma,
each and every merit arising from this ocean is supreme in its immeasurability and is in accord with the Dharmakāya.
In the tenth stage, because one relies on the manifest realization of all the secret places of all Tathāgatas, it is preeminent as being inconceivable and is in correspondence with the Dharma-body.

Subsequently, when the stage of Buddhahood is realized, because it takes as its basis the wisdom that is liberated from all obscurations, it is preeminent in the inexhaustibility of all qualities and is in union with the Dharmakāya.
The inexhaustible is precisely the eternally abiding; it is said to "manifest in the world" in order to reveal this eternal abiding.

Although the first four merits clarify their distinctions according to the various stages (*bhūmi*), they all reach their ultimate fulfillment only upon attaining the fruit, and are therefore entirely associated with the *dharmakāya*.
The Treatise says:
"The three wheels are easy to see; humans, devas, and so forth are difficult to see.
The Commentary explains:
These two lines clarify the process of arising.
The three wheels are the three bodies (trikāya).
Among the three bodies, the two—the emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) and the enjoyment body (saṃbhogakāya)—are easy to perceive, whereas the dharma body (dharmakāya) is difficult to perceive.

Furthermore, the Dharma-body is easy to perceive for bodhisattvas of profound practice and for all Buddhas, but difficult to perceive for four types of sentient beings: first, ordinary worldlings; second, śrāvakas; third, pratyekabuddhas; and fourth, bodhisattvas who have only recently begun their practice.
As the Sūtra says:

"The Tathāgatagarbha is not the domain of sentient beings who have fallen into the view of a self; it is not the domain of sentient beings who sport in perversion; nor is it the domain of Bodhisattvas who are distracted regarding emptiness."

Why is this? Ordinary persons lack such a nature regarding form and all other phenomena; they cling to the notions of "self" and "what belongs to self," and are unable to have faith or take delight in the nectar-like realm that is the cessation and departure from the view of a self-existent body (satkāyadṛṣṭi), let alone being able to correctly awaken to the Tathāgatagarbha, the sphere of all Buddhas.

Regarding that which is eternally abiding, supreme, and worthy of cultivation, those of the two vehicles practice erroneously by perceiving the characteristic of eternal abiding as impermanence; their sporting with the characteristic of impermanence, and likewise their cultivation of [the notions of] pleasure, self, and purity, are also thus.
Thus, because these followers of the two vehicles practice erroneously, they cannot attain the path to the Buddha’s Dharma-body.
Since they do not sport within it, the Dharma-body endowed with the four virtues is not within their sphere of experience.

At the beginning of their practice, bodhisattvas are deluded regarding the principle of the emptiness of the *tathāgatagarbha*; they take pleasure in the liberation door of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*) by reckoning the extinction of existing things as emptiness, asserting that all phenomena existed previously and subsequently undergo total annihilation, which they identify as emptiness.

Furthermore, there are other bodhisattvas who, by attaining the mental discernment of the mark of emptiness, conceive of the meaning of emptiness as follows: they hold that there exists a distinct entity apart from phenomena such as form which constitutes emptiness, and they think, "I now practice this cultivation so that I shall certainly attain this emptiness in the future."
Because the Tathāgatagarbha is a principle that is neither existent nor non-existent, it is not an object for the biased grasping at existence or non-existence by those with distracted minds.
Humans, devas, and so forth—namely, the aforementioned four classes of beings—are not its sphere, because the Dharmakāya is profoundly deep.

Because these four types of deluded conduct of sentient beings arise, and because these four conditions exist within the *dharmakāya*, the *svabhāvakāya* cannot be seen by humans or devas among the three spheres.
The Treatise says:
Furthermore, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is profound, most profoundly profound.
The Commentary says:
Because it is difficult to practice, difficult to penetrate, and difficult to attain, it is profound and most profound.
Furthermore, it is called "profound" because its verbal expression is difficult to comprehend, and it is called "most profound" because its underlying principles are bottomless.
Furthermore, because its words and meanings are difficult to measure, it is called "profound"; because its categories are not of a single kind, it is called "most profound.
The Treatise asks:
How is this profundity to be perceived?
The commentary asks:
By what characteristic can this profundity be manifested so that it may become visible?
The treatise states:
Regarding this, a verse is spoken.
The commentary states:
As revealed in the Mahāyāna, there are twelve kinds of profound meanings concerning the Dharmakāya; these meanings are now set forth in verse.
The Treatise says:
The Buddha takes non-arising as arising, and takes non-abiding as abiding;
his activities are performed without effort, and he takes the fourth nutriment as food.
The Treatise says:
"The Buddha takes non-arising as arising.
The Commentary explains:
The following verse clarifies the first profoundity.
Within this profoundity, there are four further types of profundity: first, arising; second, non-abiding; third, karma; and fourth, abiding.
This passage clarifies the profundity of birth. The taking of birth by all Buddhas has "non-arising" as its characteristic;

this meaning is established through ten kinds of causes: (1) because it does not share the same characteristics as ignorance; (2) because it is of various different types; (3) because it possesses mastery over appropriation; (4) because it possesses mastery over abiding; (5) because it possesses mastery over relinquishing; (6) because it is characterized by non-duality; (7) because it is merely a semblance of manifestation; (8) because it is analogous to illusions and transformations; (9) because it takes that which has no dwelling place as its dwelling place; and (10) because it is able to accomplish great deeds.
The Treatise says:
"To abide by means of non-abiding.
The Commentary explains:
This passage clarifies the profundity of non-abiding. All Buddhas abide in neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa;

furthermore, there are ten reasons that substantiate this meaning: first, because they are not permanently separated [from saṃsāra]; second, because cessation is not exhaustive; third, because Buddhas do not possess [any] dharmas; fourth, because they know the nature of the non-conditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fifth, because there is nothing to be attained and no conceptual differentiation; sixth, because they themselves are free from the mind; seventh, because they have attained the mind; eighth, because the mind is equanimous; ninth, because the cause for abiding cannot be found; and tenth, because the cause for non-abiding cannot be found.
The Treatise says:
"The performance of tasks is effortless.
The Commentary explains:

This verse clarifies the profound depth of karma, which is further substantiated by ten reasons: first, because all obstructions have been extinguished; second, because there is no basis for reliance; third, because there is no volition regarding what ought to be done; fourth, because the agent has no mental engagement with the act; fifth, because karma is not a physical movement; sixth, because there is effortless spontaneity regarding that which does not exist; seventh, because of the swiftness and sharpness resulting from past vows; eighth, because what was to be accomplished has already been completed; ninth, because there remains that which ought to be accomplished; and tenth, because of mastery over all phenomena through the full maturation of cultivation.
The Treatise says:
The fourth nutriment serves as food.
The Commentary explains:

This passage clarifies the profundity of abiding, which is further substantiated by ten reasons: first, to demonstrate that while all Buddhas do not rely on the four types of sustenance (*āhāra*) to manifest their own bodies, they nonetheless abide by means of food; second, to cause the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of sentient beings to grow; third, to manifest equality with ordinary people; fourth, to cause disciples to learn and accept the four conditions for sustaining life in accordance with the Dharma; fifth, to cause others to train in the practice of contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*); sixth, to cause others to give rise to right diligence (*samyag-vīrya*) and skillful means (*upāya*); seventh, to bring the roots of goodness of others to maturity; eighth, to manifest that one’s own person is free from defiled attachment; ninth, to counteract the mind of reverence toward the True Dharma; and tenth, to fulfill the arising of one's original vows.
If the Tathāgata eats for this reason, among the four kinds of nutriment, which one is it?
It is the fourth nutriment. As for the four nutriments:

first is the nutriment that is the basis for non-pure subsistence, namely the four nutriments such as edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), which cause the bodies of sentient beings in the desire realm to continue and persist.

Because sentient beings in the desire realm possess both the fetters of views and those to be abandoned through cultivation, their basis is impure; since this basis subsists by means of the four nutriments, it is called "subsisting on food with an impure basis."

The second is the sustenance that abides in both the pure and the impure, namely the three sustenances of karmic consciousness and contact; these cause the bodies of sentient beings in the form and formless realms to continue and abide.

Because the sentient beings of these two realms have already abandoned the afflictions of the lower realms but have not yet abandoned the afflictions of their own level or those of higher levels, their basis is both pure and impure.
Because this support subsists by means of the three nutriments, it is called the "support for the subsistence of the pure and impure.
The three supports for the subsistence of the pure refer to the four nutriments, such as edible food, which cause the bodies of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas to continue and endure.

Because those of the two vehicles have exhausted the afflictions of the three realms, their basis is pure; since this basis subsists by means of the four kinds of nutriment, it is called "subsisting on the nutriment of the pure basis."
Fourth, it can clarify the sustenance upon which they rely for their abiding.
The four kinds of sustenance, such as edible food and so forth, are all the sustenance of the Buddhas. Why is this?

Because the Buddhas partake of this food, they manifest their own bodies as abiding in the world; for the sake of causing the pure faith of donors to grow, and because it serves as the cause for their meritorious roots of virtue, this food does not function as the sustenance of a Tathāgata.

When the Tathāgata eats, the devas receive it and bestow it upon all sentient beings; because this is permitted by the intention of the Tathāgata, sentient beings shall attain Buddhahood by means of this food.
In order to enable sentient beings to attain Buddhahood, the Tathāgata manifests the act of touching food with his hand.
Such meanings as these are all profoundly deep.
The treatise says:
Without distinction and without measure, The single reality beyond number and quantity;
The most firm and yet non-firm karma, The unsurpassed corresponds to the three bodies.
The Commentary says:
"Neither different nor immeasurable.
The commentary states:
The following verse clarifies the second profundity.
Within this profundity, there are further three kinds of profundity: first, establishment; second, number; and third, activity.
This passage clarifies the profundity of establishment.
Because the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas is without distinction, it is non-different; because numerous supports realize this *dharmakāya*, it is immeasurable.
The Treatise says:
"An immeasurable single entity.
The Commentary explains:
This sentence clarifies the profundity of number.
Sentient beings of the three vehicles are beyond measure;
therein, all Buddhas constitute a single entity.
The Treatise says:
"The most firm and non-firm karma corresponds to the three bodies of the Unsurpassed One.
The Commentary explains:
These two lines clarify the profundity of karma.
The Buddhas possess the three bodies in correspondence; because their essential substance is eternally abiding, it is called supreme.
Because the karma of the Nirmāṇakāya Tathāgata is firm and unalterable, it is due to its being true reality.

Because the karma of the Nirmāṇakāya Tathāgata is not fixed, he employs provisional skillful means to draw forth those of the Two Vehicles, and subsequently uses the Saṃbhogakāya to instruct them in the cultivation of the Bodhisattva path.
The Treatise says:
There is not a single dharma that can awaken; there is nothing whatsoever that does not awaken.
Each and every thought-moment is immeasurable, manifesting both existence and non-existence.
The Treatise says:
There is not a single dharma that can awaken.
The Commentary explains:
The following verse clarifies the third point: the profundity of perfect enlightenment.
Since both the person and phenomena do not exist, that which is realized is absent; therefore, that which realizes is likewise non-existent.
The Commentary states:
"All are without exception awakened.
The commentary states:
Because all Buddhas exist by way of conventional designation, there is none who is not a Buddha; therefore, there is not a single one who is not awakened.
What is the awakening to this dharma?
The treatise says:
Each and every moment is immeasurable.
The commentary states:
In each and every moment, there are immeasurable Buddhas whose perfect awakening is suchness (*tathatā*).
If this is so, are the Buddhas identical to or different from suchness?
If they were identical, there would be no awakening; if they were different, there would be no suchness.
The treatise says:
"The non-existent is manifested by means of the existent."
The commentary states:
All phenomena are termed "existent" and "non-existent," meaning that all phenomena are empty.
Since the Buddhas are manifested by the emptiness of all phenomena, it cannot be said that they awaken, nor can it be said that they do not awaken.
The Treatise says:
There is neither desire nor the departure from desire; it is by relying on desire that one attains liberation.
Having realized that desire is non-desire, one thus enters into the suchness of the phenomena of desire.
The Treatise says:
There is neither desire nor freedom from desire.
The Commentary explains:
The following verse clarifies the fourth profundity, that of being free from desire.
Because desire does not exist, the Tathāgata is without desire;
because he has been without desire from the very beginning, he is also without the state of being "free from desire."
If desire existed, there could be the transcendence of desire;
since desire is fundamentally non-existent, there is no transcendence of desire.
The treatise says:
"Attaining deliverance by relying on desire.
The commentary explains:
Because bodhisattvas have eternally eliminated manifest desire (*paryavasthāna-kāma*) while retaining only latent desire (*anuśaya-kāma*), bodhisattvas attain deliverance and achieve buddhahood.
Why is this? If suffering did not retain these latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), it would be identical to the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles;
if one does not eliminate the manifest desires, then one is no different from ordinary worldlings.
As stated in the *Anuttarāśrayasūtra*, a bodhisattva reflects thus:
"The various afflictions have never entered the naturally pure mind of sentient beings from the very beginning.
These afflictions are merely adventitious dust, arising solely from one's own conceptual discrimination."
"I now possess the capacity to expound the correct teaching in accordance with reality in order to eliminate the adventitious afflictions of all sentient beings.
With this reflection, the bodhisattva does not give rise to a base or inferior mind.
By means of this mindfulness, the bodhisattva gives rise to a sense of noble respect toward sentient beings.
Furthermore, the bodhisattvas reflect:
"All afflictions are powerless and incapable."
Why is this? Because all afflictions have no real basis; they are merely afflictions produced by false discrimination.

When one observes through correct reflection in accordance with reality, no further opposition arises. Therefore, we should cultivate such and such contemplations, so that through these contemplations, afflictions will no longer give rise to defiled attachment.
If all afflictions are no longer stained by attachment, that is most excellent; it is not stained attachment.
If I were stained by the attachment of self-love and delusion, how could I untie the bonds of affliction for sentient beings and preach the correct teaching according to reality?
This affliction can cause the continuity of birth and death, yet it is associated with roots of goodness and brings sentient beings to maturity.
Therefore, I should now retain and maintain this affliction.
The Treatise says:
Having already known desire and the absence of desire, one therefore enters into the suchness of the dharmas of desire.
The Commentary says:

Because the Bodhisattva perceives that desire is of the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), desire does not exist; the signless nature (*animitta-lakṣaṇa*) of desire is precisely the suchness (*tathatā*) of the dharma of desire.
Since the Bodhisattva knows that desire does not exist and thereby gains entry into this suchness, they achieve liberation from desire.
The Treatise says:
The Buddhas have transcended the five aggregates, yet they dwell within the five aggregates;
they are neither identical to nor different from the aggregates, and they do not abandon the aggregates in their parinirvāṇa.
The Treatise says:
All Buddhas transcend the five aggregates (skandhas) yet abide within the five aggregates.
The Commentary explains:
The following verse clarifies the fifth point: the profundity of the extinction of the aggregates (*skandha*).

The Buddhas have already transcended the five appropriated aggregates (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*); because they do not apprehend these five aggregates, they abide in the suchness (*tathatā*) of the phenomena of the aggregates.
The Treatise says:
It is neither identical to nor different from the aggregates (*skandha*).
The Commentary explains:
The Buddhas have already abandoned the discrimination of the aggregates (*skandha*); the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is neither identical to nor different from the aggregates.

Why is this? Because the *tathatā* (suchness) of the five aggregates in which the Buddhas abide is the dharma belonging to the category of the discriminated and dependent aggregates; therefore, it is not different.
According to this principle, although they are one, they are not without distinction.
Suchness is the realm of purity, whereas the aggregates (skandhas) are not the realm of purity; therefore, they are not one.
The treatise says:
"Parinirvāṇa without abandoning the aggregates.
The commentary states:
Because it is eternally conjoined with the *tathatā* (suchness) of the aggregates, there is no sense of relinquishing them; therefore, the *parinirvāṇa* of the Tathāgata is supreme.
The treatise says:
The activities of all Buddhas are intermingled, like the waters of the great ocean;
"What I have already done, what I am currently doing, and what I ought to do" is my concern—there is no such thought regarding the affairs of others.
The Treatise says:
The activities of all Buddhas are intermingled, just like the waters of the great ocean.
The Commentary explains:
The following verse clarifies the sixth profound maturation:
regarding the common benefit for sentient beings, the Buddhas act like the various rivers flowing into the great ocean, all equally available for the enjoyment of turtles, fish, and other creatures.
In this way, all Buddhas enter the Dharma-realm together; through the equality of *tathatā*, they perform deeds of benefit and bring sentient beings to maturity.
The Commentary says:
"I have already done what was to be done, and I have no thought for the affairs of others."
The commentary states:
I have performed, am performing, and shall perform deeds for the benefit of others; throughout the three periods of time, there is no volitional deliberation regarding them.
Although there is no such volition, the beneficial deeds are accomplished in accordance with the Dharma.
For example, the wish-fulfilling gem and the celestial drum accomplish their functions without any deliberate intention.
The Commentary says:
Because the Honored One does not appear due to [the disciples'] faults, he is like the moon reflected in a broken vessel.
Pervading all worlds, it is like the sun through the light of the Dharma.
The commentary says:
Because of their faults, the Honored Ones do not appear, just as the moon does not appear in a broken vessel.
The commentary states:
The following verse clarifies the seventh profundity, that of manifestation.
Although the Buddhas do not manifest in the world, the world says that the bodies of the Buddhas are eternally abiding.
If the body were permanent, why would it not be manifest?
For example, water cannot remain within a broken vessel.
Because the water does not remain, the moon that truly exists within the broken vessel cannot be manifested.
In this way, for those sentient beings who lack a supple continuity of *śamatha* and possess only a continuity of faults, even though the Buddhas truly exist, they do not appear before them.
Water is used as an analogy for *śamatha* because of its soft and smooth nature.
If the Buddha does not manifest, could it be that there is no Buddha?
The treatise says:
"Pervading all worlds, by means of the light of the Dharma like the sun.
The commentary states:

If the Buddhas are perceived even by sentient beings who possess faults and are not [fit vessels], they nonetheless constantly perform the true work of the Buddhas—expounding the twelve divisions of the Tripitaka—just like radiance. It is certain that these are the beneficial deeds the Buddhas ought to perform, such as planting the seeds of enlightenment, bringing beings to maturity, and granting liberation.
Just as in the world, although those born blind do not see the sun, the sunlight constantly illuminates all forms and images so that those with eyes may see them.
The Treatise says:
Sometimes they manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment, and sometimes their nirvāṇa is like a fire;
these two do not truly exist, for all Buddhas abide eternally.
The Treatise says:
"Either manifesting the attainment of perfect enlightenment, or entering nirvāṇa like a fire.
The Commentary explains:
The following verse clarifies the eighth [aspect]: the profundity of awakening and parinirvāṇa.
Buddhas manifest attaining perfect enlightenment in some places and manifest entering parinirvāṇa in others.

Just as the nature of fire burns in some places and extinguishes in others, so it is with the Buddhas: for those sentient beings who have already reached maturity, the Tathāgata manifests parinirvāṇa;
for those not yet matured, he manifests the attainment of perfect enlightenment, in order to bring them to maturity and liberation.
For example, the nature of fire is one by virtue of its genus; likewise, the *dharmakāya* is one by virtue of the nature of *tathatā*.
The treatise states:
"These two do not truly exist [as separate entities], because all Buddhas abide eternally."
The commentary states:

Awakening (bodhi) and parinirvāṇa are two; however, these are merely transformations of the minds of others that cause them to perceive duality. In reality, they do not exist, because the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and devoid of before or after.
The Treatise says:
Regarding evil deeds, the human realm and the evil destinies,
and regarding practices that are not the holy life— the Tathāgata abides in the supreme dwelling of the self.
The commentary states:
This verse clarifies the profundity of the ninth dwelling.
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, dwell in the most supreme dwelling; they dwell in the most supreme self.
If the Buddhas abide, they do not depart from these two places: either they abide in the most excellent abiding, or they abide in the most excellent self.

"Evil matters" refers to all unwholesome dharmas; the Tathāgata constantly abides in the most excellent abiding regarding unwholesome dharmas. This "most excellent abiding" refers to the meditative concentration of true emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), which is precisely the noble abiding (*āryavihāra*).
Whether sentient beings are in the human realm or in the evil realms, the Tathāgata abides by taking them as his object.
Alternatively, the fourth dhyāna is itself the divine abode (devasthāna), which is called the most excellent abode.
Alternatively, great compassion itself is the Brahma-abode, meaning the most excellent abode.

Regarding that which is not the practice of Brahma—namely, attachment to the six sense objects—the Buddha dwells herein as the most excellent self; this most excellent self is the purity of the dharmadhātu.
The Tathāgata constantly contemplates the six sense objects as having emptiness as their essence and as their objective sphere; this is the Buddha’s dwelling.
The treatise says:
"The Buddha acts in all places, yet he does not act in any single place."
Manifesting in all births, yet not within the domain of the six sense faculties.
The Commentary says:
The Buddha traverses all places.
The commentary states:
The following verse clarifies the tenth point, the profundity of the manifestation of the essential nature.
The subsequent wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of the Tathāgata pervades and functions constantly amidst wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena.
The Treatise says:
Nor does one practice in a single place.
The Commentary explains:
Because non-conceptual wisdom transcends the sphere of cognition and is beyond conceptual differentiation, it does not function in any single location.
Furthermore, because the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) has no place where it does not act, while the dharma body (dharmakāya) and the enjoyment body (saṃbhogakāya) have no locus of movement.
The Treatise states:
It manifests in all births, yet it is not within the domain of the six sense faculties.
The Commentary explains:
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, manifest through their nirmāṇakāyas (emanation bodies) as possessing all the marks among all sentient beings.
By means of these nirmāṇakāyas, the Buddhas are even seen by those in the realms of hell and so forth to be born there, for the purpose of transforming and liberating them.

Because the Buddhas do not manifest as having the nature of an apparitional transformation (*nirmāṇa*), those sentient beings, although they see them, cannot discern that they are Buddhas; rather, they perceive them as being of their own kind. Therefore, the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of a Buddha is not within the sensory range of the six faculties of beings in the hells and other realms.
The treatise says:
All afflictions have been extinguished and subdued, Like poison neutralized by a mantra;
From the cessation of one affliction to the end of all, The Buddha realizes all-encompassing wisdom.
The Treatise says:
"All afflictions already extinguished or suppressed are like poison neutralized by a mantra.
The Commentary explains:
The following verse clarifies the eleventh [aspect], the profundity of the extinction of delusions.
"Delusions" refers to the afflictions of both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation, which have already been completely extinguished within the bodhisattva stages.

Although other mental afflictions have not yet been extinguished, they are suppressed by wisdom and mindfulness, their functional power being rendered inert; they are like various poisons whose inherent capacities are neutralized by the power of mantras so that they no longer possess their original efficacy.
The delusion of the mind is likewise: when guarded by wisdom and mindfulness, it can no longer give rise to the defilement of dualistic delusions.
The treatise says:
"From the cessation of one delusion to the exhaustion of all delusions, the Buddha realizes all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*)."
The commentary states:

The Bodhisattvas retain their latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) as factors conducive to the path (*mārga-aṅga*), unlike the followers of the two vehicles who enter parinirvāṇa prematurely. By virtue of this fact, they bring the cultivation of the path to completion, thereby attaining the total extinction of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and realizing perfect wisdom (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*).
The Treatise says:
Truths and delusions become factors of enlightenment; birth and death become nirvāṇa.
Having attained such great skillful means, the Buddha is inconceivable.
The Treatise says:
"Truths and delusions constitute the factors of enlightenment.
The Commentary explains:
The following clarifies the twelfth [point], the inconceivable profundity:

if one attains the exhaustion of afflictions by retaining them, then the *satya-samudaya* (truth of origination) of the two vehicles becomes the *bodhipakṣa-dharma* (factors of enlightenment) for a bodhisattva.

Just as the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) of the two vehicles can extinguish that truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*), the Bodhisattva uses that very truth of origination to extinguish the delusions of the mind; thus, it becomes a factor of enlightenment.
The treatise says:
"Birth and death are *nirvāṇa*."
The commentary states:
If the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya) were a factor of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa), then the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya) would be nirvāṇa. Why is this?

All bodhisattvas, while remaining within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), are not defiled by it; they give rise to the benefit of both themselves and others, attaining perfection in both. This is like the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) in the *nirvāṇa with remainder*, which are not defiled by the two types of afflictions and are thus able to attain their own benefit.
The Treatise says: Because he has attained great skillful means (*mahopāya*), the Buddha is inconceivable.
The Commentary explains:
While in the causal stage, he attains great skillful means, namely *prajñā* (wisdom) and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
In the state of fruition, one attains great skillful means, namely the three bodies (*trikāya*).
The Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is the skillful means for self-benefit, while the other two bodies are the skillful means for the benefit of others; therefore, the Tathāgata is inconceivable.

The Commentary states: By virtue of this meaning, twelve kinds of profundity should be understood, namely: the profundity of birth, non-abiding, and the abiding of karma; the profundity of establishment, enumeration, and karma; the profundity of perfect awakening; the profundity of detachment from desire; the profundity of the cessation of the aggregates; the profundity of maturation; the profundity of manifestation; the profundity of the manifestation of awakening and parinirvāṇa; the profundity of abiding; the profundity of the manifestation of the essential nature; the profundity of the eradication of delusions; and the profundity of the inconceivable.
The commentary states:
The Buddha has three bodies. When bodhisattvas practice the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*), which body should they take as their object?
They should take the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) as their object.
The Treatise says:
When Bodhisattvas recollect the Buddha by taking the Dharma-body as their object, how many aspects does this recollection take as its object?
The Explanation says:
The Dharma-body possesses immeasurable and profound principles. If one takes the Dharma-body as an object of focus, how many aspects should one take as objects?
The treatise says:
Briefly stated, when bodhisattvas practice the recollection of the Buddha based on the Dharma-body, there are seven kinds of aspects.
The commentary states:
These seven aspects are the primary functions of the Dharmakāya; that is, they are the perfect virtues of the Dharmakāya.
Because it is necessary to take these perfect virtues as the object of recollection when practicing *buddhānusmṛti*, the seven aspects are explained in brief.
First, the perfect virtues of all Buddhas belong to their own minds, because they possess mastery over the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
Second, these virtues are eternally abiding, because they are truly wholesome (*kuśala*).
Third, they are most faultless, because the latencies (*vāsanā*) have been completely extinguished.
Fourth, there is no weariness and no difficulty, because it is free from effortful exertion.
Fifth, one experiences the great joy of the Dharma, due to the purity of all lands.
Sixth, there is neither suffering nor difficulty, because there are no afflictions or hindrances.
The seventh is the great purposeful activity, because it equally benefits others.
If a bodhisattva recollects these seven kinds of perfect virtues, they will be able to penetrate the dharmakāya.

Those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha in accordance with the Dharma-body do so to demonstrate that all gates of meditative cultivation are accomplished by taking True Suchness as their object; if one does not take True Suchness as the object, then the meditative cultivation will not be pure.
The treatise says:
What are the seven?
First, all Buddhas have attained peerless mastery over all phenomena.
The commentary states:

The Buddhas of the three periods of time have attained supreme mastery over the objects of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). Beings of similar class cannot obstruct them, and beings of inferior class cannot reach their level. This mastery is never abandoned, whether in states of consciousness or unconsciousness, because it has been brought to full maturity through cultivation; therefore, it is called "mastery" (*vaśitā*).
It is not attained by Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Bodhisattvas, and furthermore, it has no analogue in the world; therefore, it is called "unequaled.
The treatise says:
One cultivates mindfulness of the Buddha in this manner.
The commentary states:
It is called "cultivation" because it causes this mindfulness to become one with the Dharma-body.
The treatise says:
"Because they have attained unimpeded and boundless knowledge of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) throughout all worlds.
The commentary explains:

The Buddhas are endowed with the six supernormal powers; in the worlds of the ten directions, these cannot be obstructed or diminished, nor do they have any limit or end. This is unlike those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*), which are both impeded and limited; thus, the Tathāgata’s supernormal wisdom is sovereign and peerless.
The Treatise says:
Herein a verse is spoken.
The Commentary explains:
If the Buddhas possess mastery over all phenomena, such as their existence or non-existence, why do not all sentient beings attain parinirvāṇa?
To resolve this objection, this verse is spoken.
This verse is intended to clarify this cause; by virtue of this cause, they do not enter parinirvāṇa.
The Commentary says:
Because the causes for [attaining] liberation are obstructed and incomplete, [this applies to] the entire realm of sentient beings.
"While abiding within the two types of meditative concentration, the Buddhas possess no sovereign power.
The commentary states:
"This is because they are obstructed and the causes are incomplete."
The commentary states:

If all sentient beings possess obstacles such as karma and the like, the Buddhas cannot cause them to enter parinirvāṇa within this state; because their supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) is obstructed, they do not attain mastery.

If sentient beings lack the nature of parinirvāṇa, it is called the "incompleteness of causes"; in such a state, the Buddhas cannot cause them to attain parinirvāṇa, nor do they possess mastery over their supernormal wisdom.
Lacking the nature of *nirvāṇa* refers to those who are greedily attached to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and do not have faith or delight in the Mahāyāna.
The Commentary says:
"The entire realm of sentient beings abides within two kinds of fixed states; even the Buddhas have no mastery over them."
The commentary states:
Regarding the realm of sentient beings, the six elements—namely the four great elements, space, and consciousness—are real.
Based upon these six elements, the designation "sentient being" is conventionally established; thus, "sentient being" is a mere nominal construct.
Because there are distinctions among the six realms of existence, it is said that "all" [sentient beings] are meant.
Thus, if such sentient beings are within two kinds of determinism: first, the determinism of the karma they have performed; second, the determinism of the retribution they shall experience.
Certainty of action (*karmapatha-niyata*) refers to the ten unwholesome actions and so forth performed by ordinary persons, which are certain to result in retribution in the four evil realms.
Certainty of retribution (*vipāka-niyata*) refers to sentient beings of extremely dull faculties who are insane, as well as those currently undergoing retribution in the four evil realms.
The Tathāgata likewise has no mastery over these sentient beings.
Why is this? Because there are no external conditions.
The treatise states:
"The two bodies of the Tathāgata are eternally abiding.
The commentary explains:
By means of ten kinds of causes, the eternality of the *dharmakāya* and its manifold virtues are collectively established.
Three causes establish the *dharmakāya*, while seven causes establish the remaining bodies.
Regarding the three causes that establish the *dharmakāya*, it is as stated in the treatise.
The Treatise says:
Because True Suchness is immediately liberated from all defilements.
The Commentary says:
This is one of the three causes.
True Suchness (*tathatā*) refers to the True Suchness subsequent to the Path.

The stage of immediate succession (*ānantarya-avasthā*) is the Buddha’s Vajra-mind; it is able to extinguish the final subtle ignorance as well as the two truths of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-satya*) within saṃsāra. Therefore, it is said to be liberated from all defilements.
This stainless, pure suchness is an eternally abiding dharma; because all Buddhas take this as their body, the bodies of all Buddhas are eternally abiding.
Because this body is eternally abiding, and because various virtues exist in reliance upon this body, these various virtues are also eternally abiding.
This permanence has true reality (*tathatā*) as its characteristic.
The treatise states:
Because the three types of Tathāgatas are most free from error, having eternally separated themselves from all afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
The commentary states:
Among all sentient beings, whether possessed of faults or free from them, the Tathāgata is most faultless because the causes and conditions of faults have been completely extinguished.
Since they have already ceased in the present and will not arise in the future, he is said to be eternally and utterly free from them.
The Treatise states:
The fourfold activities of all Tathāgatas are accomplished without effort.
The Commentary explains:
Mental application (*manasikāra*) is defined as effort;
it arises with reference to the three periods of time, namely: "I have already done," "I am currently doing," and "I shall do.
To be free from such mental application is called effortless (*anābhoga*).
However, by the power of their original vows, whatever they wish to accomplish is spontaneously fulfilled.
The Commentary states:
This is because, without relying on deliberate effort, they constantly initiate correct activities and never abandon them.
The commentary states:
If there were a correct activity by means of effort, then there would be instances of its arising and non-arising.
Since it does not depend on effort, it therefore arises constantly.
Because their original vows are inexhaustible, they never abandon [sentient beings].
Since sentient beings are inexhaustible, the original vows are inexhaustible.
The Treatise says:
"The state of the five Tathāgatas' great wealth and bliss.
The commentary explains:
"Great wealth arises from external riches; great bliss arises from the True Dharma."
The Treatise says:
Because all Buddha-lands are supremely subtle, pure, and constitute wealth and bliss.
The Commentary explains:
Within the Pure Land, there are eight things that cannot be found and two that can be found; therefore, it is called the most subtle, wondrous, and pure.

The eight things that cannot be found are: first, non-Buddhists; second, sentient beings who suffer; third, distinctions such as birth, lineage, family, or wealth; fourth, those who practice evil deeds; fifth, those who violate the precepts; sixth, the evil realms; seventh, those of the inferior vehicles; and eighth, bodhisattvas with inferior intentions and inferior practices.
Regarding the two that can be attained: first, the bodhisattvas who practice the supreme mental activities; second, the Tathāgatas appearing in the world.
That which is dwelt upon is the most subtle purity, and that which is able to dwell therein is the most wondrous purity.
The Treatise says:
The six Tathāgatas are most free from defiled attachment.
The Commentary explains:
The delusions of the manifest mind (*paryavasthāna*) constitute defilement (*saṃkleśa*), while the latent delusions (*anuśaya*) constitute attachment (*abhiniveśa*).
Furthermore, with respect to the obstacles of delusion, those that obstruct wisdom constitute defilement, while those that obstruct knowledge constitute attachment.
Moreover, afflictions have two characteristics: first, the characteristic of joy; second, the characteristic of sorrow.
Desire, pride, views, and so forth have joy as their characteristic; hatred, doubt, ignorance, and so forth have sorrow as their characteristic.
Delusions characterized by joy constitute defilement (*saṃkleśa*); delusions characterized by sorrow constitute attachment (*abhiniveśa*).
Because both types of delusion are completely extinguished, it is called "untainted.
The treatise says:
Appearing in the world, one is not defiled by any worldly phenomena, just as dust cannot defile space.
The commentary states:
It is called "transcending the world" (*lokottara*) because it establishes the cause; it is called "manifesting in the world" (*loka-vyavasthita*) because it accomplishes the fruit.
Furthermore, it is called "transcending the world" because self-benefit is perfected; it is called "manifesting in the world" because benefiting others is perfected.
Alternatively, when a Buddha appears in the world but has not yet manifested in it— such as when he has already attained the Way but has not yet turned the wheel of Dharma—
if he were to turn the wheel of Dharma, the world would then be able to discern that this is a Buddha and that he is the All-Knowing One.
That which is cognized by the world is therefore called the "present.

Although the Tathāgata makes use of the four conditions, such as food and clothing, it is for the purpose of cultivating the roots of goodness in sentient beings, and not for his own personal benefit.
Within these conditions, one gives rise to neither sorrow nor joy; therefore, one is not defiled by worldly dharmas.
Emptiness takes non-existence as its essence, and because its essence is unimpeded, it is not defiled by existing things; the Tathāgata is likewise.
The Treatise says:
The seven Tathāgatas have a great purposeful activity in the world.
The Commentary says:
When a Tathāgata appears in the world, the events from his attainment of enlightenment through his parinirvāṇa by means of the nirmāṇakāya (emanation body) are called the "great matter.
The benefit for sentient beings accomplished by this body is called its "function."
The treatise says:
Because it brings about the actualization of unsurpassed enlightenment and great parinirvāṇa, it matures those sentient beings who are not yet matured and liberates those who are already matured.
The commentary states:
In order to cause sentient beings who have not yet planted the seeds or whose seeds have not yet matured to plant them and reach maturity, he manifests the attainment of enlightenment (*bodhi*).
In order to liberate those sentient beings who are already matured but not yet liberated, he manifests *parinirvāṇa*.
The Treatise says:
A verse is spoken herein.
The Commentary says:
In this context, two verses are spoken to further clarify the seven characteristics and reveal the seven kinds of perfect virtues of the Dharmakāya.
The treatise says:
"Subordinate to the mind of the Tathāgata, The perfect virtues are eternally without loss."
Effortlessly, they are able to bestow upon sentient beings the great Dharma-joy.
The Commentary says:
This belongs to the Tathāgata’s virtue of mental perfection.
The commentary states:
The perfect virtues of the Buddhas—namely, the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and so forth—belong solely to their own minds and are not dependent on external conditions.
The treatise says:
“Permanent.
The commentary states:
Because these perfect virtues have as their nature the true goodness of the eternally abiding *dharmakāya*, all the qualities are permanent.
The treatise says:
There is no fault.
The commentary says:
Because the Dharmakāya is free from all obscurations, its basis is without loss; therefore, that which depends upon it is also without loss.
The treatise says:
"Without effort."
The commentary states:
Because the causal practices and original vows have reached maturity, all Buddha-activities are accomplished spontaneously, without weariness or difficulty; therefore, it is said to be "effortless."
The treatise says:
"It is able to bestow upon sentient beings the great joy of the Dharma.
The commentary explains:

Because they have attained mastery over the pure land, these great beings are able to receive the Great Dharma; having attained the expansive practice of the Dharma according to principle, they cause others to practice according to principle as well—therefore, it is called the "Joy of the Dharma."
The Treatise says:
Pervasive and without obstruction, Equally benefiting many people— All Buddhas, in every respect;
The wise take these as their object of recollection.
The Treatise says:
"The universal [factors] are without obstruction.
The Commentary explains:

Regarding the eight worldly dharmas, the Tathāgata’s subsequent cognition (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna) constantly discriminates these matters; because he is free from the states of sorrow and joy therein, his universal activity is unimpeded.
Where there is obstruction, there is suffering; because there is no obstruction, there is peace and bliss.
Although the Buddhas engage with the six sense objects, they transcend verbal expression because they are free from the grasping of existence and non-existence.
The Treatise says:
"They equally benefit many people."
The commentary states:

Ordinary beings, those of the two vehicles, bodhisattvas who have newly entered the path, and bodhisattvas of deep practice are called "many people. The Tathāgata is able to benefit them equally by teaching the practice of great wealth, the practice of the good path, the practice of peace and happiness, the practice of self-benefit, and the practice of benefiting both self and others; this is precisely what constitutes his great purposeful activity.
The Treatise says:
"All Buddhas, in their entirety, are the objects of mindfulness for the wise.
The Commentary explains:
"All" refers here to those possessed of wisdom, namely the bodhisattvas.
These bodhisattvas take these seven aspects as their object and recollect the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas.
*Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, Fascicle 14.
Commentary on the Mahāyānasaṃgraha, Volume Fifteen.
Explained by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu;
translated by Paramārtha, the Tripiṭaka Master from Central India during the Chen Dynasty.
The Tenth Chapter on the Superior Characteristics of the Discrimination of Wisdom, Part Three. The Treatise says:
Furthermore, regarding the purity of the pure lands of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, how should their characteristics be understood?
The commentary states:
Previously, within the context of the seven recollections, it was clarified that the great wealth and bliss of the Tathāgata is itself the Pure Land.

However, while it was previously stated that eight types of persons cannot be found and two types can be found, it had not yet been clarified where these "unfindable" and "findable" individuals reside.
Now, in order to reveal this location, the characteristics of the Pure Land are questioned.
The Treatise says:
As it is stated in the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-utpatti* within the hundreds of thousands of sūtras.
The commentary states:
It is called "according to the words" because it cites various sūtras in general.
Within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, there is a specific Sūtra on the Pure Land consisting of one hundred thousand verses; therefore, it is called the "Hundred-Thousand Verse Sūtra."

Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* consists of hundreds of thousands of verses, and is thus called the *Śatasāhasrikā Sūtra*. Within its exposition on dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), it describes in detail the characteristics of the Pure Land.
What virtues do the words and phrases of such a Pure Land manifest?
The Treatise says:
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was in a place adorned with the seven treasures and pervaded by universal radiance.
The Commentary says:
First gold, second silver, third lapis lazuli, fourth musāragalva, fifth aśmagarbha, sixth indranīla, and seventh lohitamuktā; the radiance of each of these jewels pervades all places.
This place is adorned with the seven precious gems, and the Buddha dwells therein.
The treatise says:
He is able to emit great radiance, universally illuminating immeasurable worlds.
The commentary states:
This explains that the places illuminated by the radiance of the seven treasures signify the meaning of pervasiveness.
These two lines clarify the perfect purity of the physical marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
The Treatise says:
The immeasurable and wondrously adorned realms and bases are each established individually.
The Commentary explains:
This adornment is rare and peerless; therefore, it is called "wondrously embellished.
Because there are many such wondrous embellishments, it is called "immeasurable.
The ground upon which one traverses is the realm (*dhātu*); the ground where one dwells is the location (*sthāna*).
Each realm and each location is fully adorned; therefore, it is said to be "established.
This phrase clarifies that the form and appearance are perfect and pure.
The treatise states:
"The boundaries of the great region are immeasurable.
The commentary states:
"Diameter is 'measure' (du), and circumference is 'extent' (māna)."
The limits of each Buddha’s pure land cannot be measured by ordinary beings using units such as *yojana*.
This phrase clarifies the perfection of measure.
The Commentary states:
"Transcending the sphere of activity of the three realms.
The commentary states:
the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) within the three realms constitutes "activity," while the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) within the three realms constitutes the "sphere."
The Pure Land is not subsumed under the suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*) of the three realms; therefore, it is said to transcend the spheres of activity of the three realms.
This phrase clarifies the perfection of the place.
If it were not subsumed under the truths of suffering and origin, by what cause could one be born there?
What is its essential nature?
The treatise says:
It is produced from the functional capacity of supramundane wholesome dharmas.
The commentary states:

The virtues of the two vehicles are called "transcending the world" (*lokottara*). From the eighth stage upward, up to the stage of Buddhahood, they are called "transcending the transcendent" (*lokottarottara*).
Transcendent dharmas serve as the antidote to worldly dharmas; transcending-the-transcendent dharmas serve as the antidote to transcendent dharmas.

The functional capacity (kāritra) has the four conditions as its characteristic; because this Pure Land arises from the functional capacity of supramundane wholesome dharmas, it does not take the truth of origination (samudaya-satya) as its cause.
This sentence clarifies the purity of the cause.
What constitutes supramundane wholesome dharmas?
The roots of goodness produced by non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) are called supramundane wholesome dharmas.
The treatise says:
Its characteristic is the most pure and sovereign representation-only (*vijñapti-mātra*).
The commentary explains:
The consciousness-only wisdom of Bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas is called "pure" because it is signless and effortless;
it is called "sovereign" because it is free from all obstacles and never subject to decline.
Because this wisdom of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*) constitutes the essence of the Pure Land, it does not take the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) as its essence.
This phrase clarifies the perfect purity of the fruit.
The Treatise says:
"Wherein the Tathāgata resides.
The commentary explains:
In such a pure land characterized by these features, the Tathāgata constantly dwells.
It is called "stabilizing" (*zhen*) because it is the most preeminent.
This phrase clarifies the sovereign perfect purity.
The treatise states:
"The dwelling place of peace and happiness for a bodhisattva.
The commentary states:
"To personally practice the true teaching and to teach others to practice the true teaching is called 'peace and happiness'."
The Bodhisattva assists the Buddha and assists the Path within the Pure Land; because these two matters are complete therein, it is called the "Abode of Peace and Bliss.
This phrase clarifies the assistance toward perfect purity.
The Treatise says:
It is the sphere of activity for immeasurable devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth.
The commentary states:

In the Pure Land, there are in fact no such sentient beings; however, because the Buddha wishes to prevent it from being empty, he manifests these various types through his transformative power (*nirmāṇa*).
This sentence clarifies the perfect purity of the retinue.
If there are such sentient beings, what do the bodhisattvas and others consume?
The treatise says:
They are sustained by the joy and bliss of the flavor of the Great Dharma.
The commentary states:
The twelve divisions of the Mahāyāna sūtras are called the "Great Dharma," and suchness, liberation, and so forth constitute its flavor.
By taking this flavor of the Dharma as an object, all bodhisattvas give rise to joy and delight, which nourishes their fivefold dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*).
This phrase clarifies the maintenance of perfect purity.
What kind of activity is performed by partaking of this flavor of the Dharma?
The treatise says:
"It has the welfare of all sentient beings as its function.
Commentary:
"All sentient beings" refers to ordinary worldlings and those of the three vehicles.
According to their respective capacities, he expounds the true teaching to them, causing them to practice in accordance with what has been taught.
To be free from the four evil realms, free from birth and death, and free from the self-cherishing conduct of the two vehicles is called "all-encompassing benefit."
This verse clarifies the purity of action.
If a bodhisattva performs such actions toward sentient beings, what benefit is gained from both the performance of the action and its object?
The treatise says:
"Free from all afflictions and calamities.
The commentary states:
"All afflictions" refers to the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*) within the three realms; "all calamities" refers to the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) within the three realms.
Being entirely free from these two, one is able to practice within the sphere of practice.
This phrase clarifies the perfection and purity of benefit.
If one is free from such phenomena, is there any further fear?
The treatise says:
It is not a place frequented by all Māras.
The commentary explains:
Because the Pure Land is free from the demon of the aggregates, the demon of afflictions, the demon of death, and the celestial demon, it is devoid of all fear.
This phrase clarifies the perfect purity of being without fear.
If there is no fear whatsoever within the Pure Land, are all the objects experienced by the six sense faculties fully present there?
The treatise says:
It is the locus of the adornments of the Tathāgata Adorned with All Supreme Ornaments.
The commentary states:

It is not merely that all requisites for enjoyment are supreme and peerless; rather, this place is the basis for the Tathāgata’s preeminent retribution, which is induced by the causes of the Tathāgata’s perfected practices of merit and wisdom. For this reason, it is supreme.
This passage clarifies the perfect purity of the dwelling place.
By what means does one enter and exit within the Pure Land?
The treatise says:
"Great mindfulness, wisdom, practice, and renunciation.
The commentary states:

The True Dharma of the Mahāyāna is called the "Great Dharma. Within this Great Dharma, the wisdom arising from hearing is called "mindfulness," the wisdom arising from reflection is called "wisdom," and the wisdom arising from cultivation is called "practice."
These three constitute the path of coming and going within the Pure Land; therefore, they are called "renunciation.
This phrase clarifies the perfection and purity of the path.
If this path exists, by what dharma does one ride it?
The treatise says:
"The vehicle of great śamatha and vipaśyanā.
The commentary explains:
In the Mahāyāna, the five hundred meditative concentrations are called śamatha, and the wisdoms of suchness and suchness-in-extent are called vipaśyanā; these two constitute the vehicle.
This sentence clarifies the perfect purity of the vehicle.
If there is this vehicle, through which gate does one enter?
The treatise says:
One enters by way of the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
The commentary states:

Within the Mahāyāna, the three gates of liberation are of one essence; because they lack intrinsic nature, they are empty; because they are empty, they are signless; and because they are signless, they are wishless.
If one reaches this gate, one attains entry into the Pure Land.
This phrase clarifies that the gate is perfectly pure.
In the mundane world, the earth-disk rests upon the water-disk, and the water-disk rests upon the wind-disk; upon what dharma does the Pure Land rely?
The Treatise says:
It takes as its support the great king of lotuses, adorned by a mass of immeasurable merits.
The Commentary explains:
The great lotus king is used as a metaphor for the dharmadhātu-tathatā revealed by the Mahāyāna;
